# Once UI

> Once UI is an open-source design system and component library for Next.js and React Native: layout primitives, components, form controls, data display and effects, with tokens, themes and a machine-readable spec for coding agents.

The complete docs for @once-ui-system/core 3.0.0-rc.1 (3.0 beta), one page after another, after the rules generated code must follow. The index is at https://next.docs.once-ui.com/llms.txt.

---

# Once UI — code generation rules

Rules for writing Once UI code. Follow every rule; each shows the correct form first.

## Before you build

When the request doesn't specify design intent, ask these five questions first (one short message, all at once), then build:

1. **Content style** — bold / restrained / conservative?
2. **Layout** — wide or narrow, centered or left-aligned?
3. **Color** — single accent, bold colors, visually distinct sections?
4. **Decoration** — gradients, MatrixFx, animated blobs, none?
5. **Imagery** — placeholder images, or avatars/logos/icons only?

For a product's own landing page or homepage, find its world first (recipes.md #9, brand world): a direction card and three worlds before any code. For any other marketing page, or when the person asks for a plain one: if you can't ask (or the user says "you decide"), default to: restrained, centered with `maxWidth="m"` content, single brand accent, one subtle gradient (recipes.md #1), no placeholder images (use `Avatar`, `Logo`, `Icon`).

That default is for a landing page. For an app (signed-in, records, forms), the first build step is the theme, not a page: set it from the theme preset for the app's domain, in `once-ui.config` or in the props of `ThemeInit`, `ThemeProvider` and `DataThemeProvider` wherever the app mounts them, `themePreset("ops" | "care" | "creative" | "commerce")` (rule 30c), which sets page and surface in both themes, brand, accent, solids, corners, density and the faces to load with `next/font`. Change only what is the product's own, usually `brandSeed`. One brand accent, no ambient layers or effects. Shipping the starter's gray/blue/contrast unchanged reads as unbranded.

## Layout primitives

1. Use `Row` and `Column` for layout. `Flex` with `direction` is only for dynamic direction. A `Flex` with no direction at all is a `Row` (`Flex` defaults to row).

```tsx
// Good
<Column gap="16">...</Column>
// Bad
<Flex direction="column" gap="16">...</Flex>
```

2. Use shorthands — they replace multi-prop combinations:

| Write | Instead of |
|-------|------------|
| `fill` | `fillWidth fillHeight` |
| `fit` | `fitWidth fitHeight` |
| `center` | `horizontal="center" vertical="center"` |

```tsx
// Good
<Row fill center>...</Row>
// Bad
<Row fillWidth fillHeight horizontal="center" vertical="center">...</Row>
```

3. Never write a prop that equals its default, or one that another prop on the same element already implies. The spec marks defaults with `= value`. Common offenders:
   - `position="relative"` (default on all layout components)
   - `direction="row"` on `Row`, `direction="column"` on `Column`
   - `variant="primary"`, `size="m"` on `Button`
   - `fillWidth` beside `maxWidth` — `maxWidth` already fills the width up to the cap
   - `minWidth={0}` beside `fillWidth` — `fillWidth` already sets `min-width: 0`
   - a colour on `border` (or `borderTop`, `borderBottom`, `borderX`, …) that only restates the default — bare `border` draws the default border, `--default-border` (`neutral-alpha-weak` unless the app sets it in its custom CSS); name a colour only to deviate from it

```tsx
// Good
<Column maxWidth="l" border radius="l">
// Bad
<Column fillWidth maxWidth="l" minWidth={0} position="relative" border="neutral-alpha-weak" radius="l">
```

3b. `zIndex` belongs to a stacking group, not to a page. Use it only inside an isolated group that needs an order — a decorative absolute layer and the content sibling above it (rule 21), a sticky header over the pane it covers — and keep the values small within that group. A `zIndex` on a lone element, or a page-wide ladder of `zIndex={3}`, `{5}`, `{9}`, means the hierarchy is being managed by hand; restructure the tree instead.

## Spacing and sizing

4. Use spacing tokens, never raw CSS: `gap`, `padding`, `margin`, `paddingX/Y`, `marginX/Y` accept the full `SpacingToken` scale (`"0" "1" "2" "4" "8" "12" "16" "20" "24" "32" "40" "48" "56" "64" "80" "104" "128" "160"`, or `"xs" "s" "m" "l" "xl"`). The top of the scale is what rule 17 calls for between sections — it is not an extension, it is part of the same list.

```tsx
// Good
<Column gap="8" padding="24">
// Bad
<div style={{ gap: 8, padding: 24 }}>
```

5. `width`/`height`/`maxWidth`/`minHeight` (and every spacing and offset prop) accept a number on the **token scale** (`width={320}`: `n` renders as the token `"n"` would, n/16 rem scaled by `data-scaling`, so 320 px at the defaults), a spacing token string (`"16"`), or a CSS length string (`"40rem"`, `"50%"`, `"100dvh"`, `calc(…)`). Prefer tokens; write `"320px"` for a length that must not scale. `maxWidth={40}` is 2.5rem, not 40rem (2.x).

6. Only use `style={{}}` for things no token prop covers (e.g. `isolation`, custom filters). If a prop exists, the prop wins.

## Color and surfaces

7. Colors are semantic tokens, never hex/rgb: `{tone}-{weight}` or `{tone}-alpha-{weight}` where tone = `neutral | brand | accent | info | danger | warning | success` and weight = `weak | medium | strong`. A component's palette is its `tone` prop (Button, IconButton, Tag, Feedback, Toast, `addToast`, `StatusIndicator pulse`, gauges, Timeline items); `scheme` is a palette hue (`blue`, `green`…) on the plain StatusIndicator dot and Avatar's `statusIndicator`. Two exceptions: a seed, which only takes a colour (`brandSeed`, `accentSeed`, `pageBackground`, `surfaceBackground`, a Mascot's `color`), and artwork: the cast, props and textures of a hero scene, drawn in classes named for what they draw (`.emChair`) in one sheet scoped under the page class. Nowhere else.
   - `background` also accepts `surface | overlay | page | transparent`
   - `onBackground` colors text/icons on a background
   - Inline SVG paint too: `fill="currentColor"` (colour the wrapper with `onBackground`) or a token, `stroke="var(--brand-solid-strong)"` — never `fill="#15D9EF"`

8. Standard surface recipe: `background="surface"` (or `"overlay"` over imagery) + `border` + `radius="l"`. Bare `border` is the default border; name a colour (`border="neutral-alpha-medium"`, `border="brand-alpha-medium"`) only when the surface should differ from it.

```tsx
<Column background="surface" border radius="l" padding="24" gap="16">
```

8b. Same-shaped records (members, bookings, tickets) go on **one** surface with row dividers and aligned columns, or in a `Table`, which is already a surface. Never a bordered card per row, and never a surface inside a surface: no `Table` or filled tile inside a bordered panel. Put the section heading above the surface, not in it.

```tsx
<Column as="ul" background="surface" border radius="l">
  {rows.map((r, i) => (
    <Row as="li" key={r.id} borderTop={i > 0} paddingX="16" paddingY="12" gap="16" vertical="center">
      <Column flex={1} gap="4">{/* name, then metadata at body-default-s */}</Column>
      <Row width={128}>{/* status Tag: fixed width keeps the column aligned */}</Row>
      <IconButton icon="moreHorizontal" variant="tertiary" tooltip="Actions" />
    </Row>
  ))}
</Column>
```

8c. Critical is louder than status. A routine state (confirmed, active) is a plain `Tag` with a `tone`; a critical one (an allergy, a failed payment, an overdue check) adds weight: a `Tag` with `prefixIcon="warning"`, or a `Feedback tone="danger"` with `icon` and `title` at the top of the record. Urgency is always `danger` or `warning`, and the same state takes the same tone everywhere; `info` is never urgent.

8d. Surface hierarchy is deliberate. In an app the `page` background sits behind the frame (sidebar, header) and the content gets **one** raised `surface` panel; inside it, sections are separated by spacing and `borderTop`, with headings, not by more grey-filled cards. Grey on grey (surface cards on a surface page, `neutral-alpha-weak` tiles in a panel) reads as unfinished. Reserve fills for one thing: an input well, a selected row, a callout.

8e. Use the system's parts for brand, alerts and charts; hand-built versions read as off-brand:
- The product mark is a `Logo`: `<Logo text="Seatwise" monogram href="/" />` without a designed mark, or `icon`/`wordmark` sources when there are files. Never an `Icon` beside a `Text`.
- An inline alert or notice is a `Feedback` (`tone`, `icon`, `title`, children), never a `Column role="alert"` with a tinted background.
- A chart is `LineChart`, `BarChart`, `LineBarChart`, `PieChart`, `Sparkline`, `Treemap`, `Heatmap` or `DivergingBars` from `@once-ui-system/core/data`, never hand-drawn SVG. They take the theme's data palette, tooltips and axes.
- Give a single-series chart the brand: series `color: "brand"` (not `"brand-strong"`, a text colour: white in dark). Its `height` is a string (`height="16rem"`): `height={16}` is the 1rem token and collapses the chart to a line.

8f. Work apps are dense and quiet. An app people use all day (a front desk, a planner, an admin) sets `density: "compact"` and `border: "conservative"` in the config `style`; spacious and rounded oversize every control and corner. Key numbers are one bordered strip of divided cells (label, then value, a `StatusIndicator` for state), not a row of grey tiles. One screen has one primary action: the same "Book appointment" in the header and on the page is one too many.

## Text

9. Use `Text` and `Heading` with `textVariant="{type}-{weight}-{size}"` (the same prop as on Flex; `variant` was 2.x): type = `body | heading | display | label | code`, weight = `default | strong`, size = `xs | s | m | l | xl`. Examples: `body-default-m`, `heading-strong-s`, `label-default-s`, `display-strong-m`.

10. If a layout component only wraps text, put `textVariant` (and `onBackground`) directly on it instead of nesting a `Text`:

```tsx
// Good
<Row textVariant="label-default-s" onBackground="neutral-weak">Updated today</Row>
// Bad
<Row><Text textVariant="label-default-s" onBackground="neutral-weak">Updated today</Text></Row>
```

10b. App type floor: anything a user must read in an app (metadata, labels, table cells, timestamps) is `body-default-s` or larger, or `label-default-s`. `xs` text in `neutral-weak` is for what nobody needs to read.

## Responsive

11. Use breakpoint props (`xl l m s xs`) with override objects — never media queries or conditional rendering for layout:

```tsx
<Row gap="24" s={{ direction: "column" }}>
<Grid columns="3" s={{ columns: 1 }}>
```

Breakpoints, padding, background, border, radius, sizes and `hide` exist only on `Flex`, `Row`, `Column` and `Grid`. Leaf components (`Button`, the fields and controls, `Text`, `Heading`, `Icon`, `Avatar`, `Kbd`…) take `LeafProps` — margins, `flex`, `fillWidth`, `position` and offsets, `className`, `style` — so wrap one to change the rest: `<Row s={{ hide: true }}><Button …/></Row>`, `<Column padding="8"><Text …/></Column>`.

## Components over primitives

12. Reach for the purpose-built component before composing primitives:
    - `Card` is for **interactive** surfaces only (`href` or `onClick`). Static panels (pricing tiers, testimonials, stat boxes) = `Column`/`Row` with the surface recipe (#8), not `Card`
    - Image/video → `Media`, not `img`
    - Links → `SmartLink` / `Button href`, not `a`
    - Status dot → `StatusIndicator`; progress → `ProgressBar`; loading → `Spinner` / `Skeleton`
    - Labels/metadata → `Tag` (`variant="announce"` + `href` for the "New" pill above a hero; `selected` (+ `onClick`) or `onRemove` for a filter toggle), `Kbd`, `InlineCode`. Badge and Chip are Tag in 3.0
    - Tabs → `Tabs` > `TabList` > `Tab` with a `TabPanel` per value (`orientation="vertical"` for a settings nav). `SegmentedControl` picks a value; it is not a tab set
    - Mobile nav, filters, a side sheet → `Drawer` (`side`, `size`); it brings the focus trap, scroll lock and Escape a hand-made overlay misses
    - Where-am-I trail → `Breadcrumbs items={[{ label, href }, ...]}`; the last item is the current page
    - Keyboard shortcuts → `useHotkeys("mod+k", fn)` (it skips while the user types), shown with `Kbd keys="mod+k" label="Search"`. Put `aria-keyshortcuts` on the control the shortcut presses (`<Button aria-keyshortcuts="Control+K Meta+K">Search</Button>`), so screen readers announce it too
    - A `Table` row that opens something → a link or `Button` in one of its cells (`cell: row => <SmartLink href={row.href}>{row.name}</SmartLink>`). `onRowClick` alone is a pointer shortcut: a row is not a tab stop and Enter does nothing on it
    - Text for screen readers only, skip links → `VisuallyHidden` (`focusable` for a skip link)
    - Markdown/MDX content → `mdxComponents` or `createMdxComponents({...})` from `/mdx` (rule 30), never a hand-written element map

13. Use the distinctive features when the design calls for them — they exist and are cheap:
    - `Dialog` supports `stack` (stacked dialogs) and `base` props, and `variant="sheet"` (a full-height sheet from the bottom, with a `backdrop` slot)
    - Effects: `RevealFx`, `LetterFx`, `TypeFx`, `CountFx`, `GlitchFx`, `HoloFx`, `TiltFx`, `FlipFx`, `MatrixFx`, `BlobFx`, `ParticleFx`, `ShineFx`, `CelebrationFx`
    - `HoverCard` (`placement="cursor"` follows the pointer, `"cover"` draws over the trigger), `Dropdown openOn="contextmenu"` (a right-click menu), `Tooltip content` with no children (an info icon), `EmojiPicker trigger`, `Scroller` (track mode with `infinite`/`markers`/`proximity`, or `auto` for a marquee), `Carousel mode="snap"`, `CompareImage`, `OgCard`, `Timeline`, `Grid masonry`, `InfiniteScroll`, `SegmentedControl`, `Kbar` (command palette)
    - Forms: `Input` (`type="password"` has a show/hide toggle), `OTPInput`, `NumberInput`, `TagInput`, `Select`, `DatePicker` (`range` for a date range), `DateInput` (`range`), `ColorInput`, `Slider` (`range` for a `[min, max]` pair), `Switch`, `Checkbox`, `Tag selected`

14. Buttons: `variant` is the appearance, `primary | secondary | tertiary | ghost | link | subtle` (`primary` is the default), and `tone` the palette, `brand | accent | neutral | info | success | warning | danger`: a destructive button is `<Button tone="danger">`; pair with `prefixIcon`/`suffixIcon` (icon names, not elements). `IconButton` for icon-only actions with `tooltip`.

14a. Select or a Button with a Dropdown: `Select` is a form value. It has a `label`, sits in a `Form` or a settings row, and is submitted (timezone, country, a member's role). Sort, filter, view and action pickers on a toolbar or page header are a secondary `Button` with `suffixIcon="chevronDown"` as a `Dropdown` trigger, holding `Option`s, with the button's label naming the current choice ("Sort: Newest", "Role: Admin"). Select already draws its chevron; do not pass one. A toolbar filter over a long list someone searches is the exception: `Select size="xxs"` with a `label` and `searchable`. Two to four choices that should stay visible are a `SegmentedControl`.

14b. Icon names must come from `iconNames` in catalog.json (spec.json carries the same list). In 2.0 `IconName` is a real union, so an unregistered name is a type error rather than a blank space — do not guess a plausible one, and never reach for `as IconName` to silence the check. If no registered icon fits, omit the icon. The registry is 99 icons; brand marks (github, discord, google) are deliberately not among them, so an app registers its own.

14c. Components with a text prop render it — never pass the same text as both prop and children, it renders twice:

```tsx
// Good
<Tag size="s">{unread}</Tag>  or  <Tag size="s" label="Save 20%" />
// Bad: one of the two is dropped
<Tag label={`${unread} unread`}>{unread}</Tag>
<Tag label="Save 20%">Save 20%</Tag>
```

14d. `Fade` is an **edge overlay strip** (scroll-fade at the boundary of a scroll container), not a content wrapper. Wrapping a message list or section in `Fade` washes the whole content out:

```tsx
// Good: thin absolute strip over the scroll edge
<Column flex={1} overflowY="auto">...</Column>
<Fade position="absolute" top="0" left="0" fillWidth height="40" to="bottom" base="surface" pointerEvents="none" />
// Bad
<Fade to="top" fill><Column overflowY="auto">...</Column></Fade>
```

14e. Multi-part components: a list prop (`items`, `columns`, `options`) for same-shaped data, else plain named parts (`<SortableItem>`, `<StylePanelBrand>`). Never a dotted name (`Sortable.Item`, `StylePanel.Brand`): 3.0 has none, and one fails from a server component.

## Composition rhythm

15. Page skeleton: `Column as="main" fillWidth horizontal="center"` → content `Column maxWidth={...}` → sections. Gaps between siblings, padding inside surfaces; avoid margins for layout when a parent `gap` can do it.

    `maxWidth` conventions: primary page containers `"xl"`–`"m"` (marketing/landing toward `"xl"`/`"l"`, app and docs content `"m"`). `"s"` is only for narrow reading content (about, legal); `"xs"` for special surfaces (drawers, popovers).

16. One-off theme overrides on a subtree, not custom CSS. On `Flex`/`Row`/`Column`/`Grid`, and on every component built on them whose slice lists the typed props (`Background`, `Tag`, `RevealFx`, `BlobFx`, …), use the typed props: `theme="dark"`, `themeBorder="rounded"`, `themeSolid="contrast"`, `themeSurface="translucent"` (they write `data-theme`, `data-border`, `data-solid`, `data-surface`). Attributes without a prop stay raw: `data-brand="emerald"`, and `data-border="rounded"` on `Button` and `IconButton`, which have no typed prop. `theme="dark"` makes a subtree dark; the `dark` boolean only shows an element in a dark theme.

## Scale and hierarchy (marketing/landing pages)

17. Vertical rhythm is generous. Gap between page sections: `"80"`–`"160"` (typical `"104"`). Gap inside a section: `"24"`–`"40"`. Spacing tokens go up to `"160"` — use the top of the scale between sections, not `"48"`.

18. Heading scale: hero = `display-strong-l` (or `xl`), section headings = `display-strong-xs` or `display-strong-s` — never `heading-*` variants for section titles. Hero supporting text = `body-default-l`; section supporting text = `body-default-m`.

19. Type hierarchy must be monotonic: quotes, testimonials, and body content never render larger than the section heading above them. Testimonial quotes = `body-default-m` max, not `BlockQuote` default size.

20. Don't repeat the same centered heading + subtitle block for every section — it reads dated. Vary: left-aligned headers, heading-only sections, or an eyebrow label above the heading. Eyebrow = plain text, not a `Tag` with an icon:

```tsx
// Good eyebrow
<Text textVariant="label-default-s" onBackground="brand-medium">Pricing</Text>
// Bad eyebrow
<Tag tone="neutral" prefixIcon="sparkle">Pricing</Tag>
```

20b. **Proportion is a decision, not a leftover.** Two columns in a row finish at
roughly the same place, or one of them is wrong. A tall card beside a strip of
small controls leaves a column of dead space that reads as an unfinished page —
and the fix is almost never more whitespace tokens.

Give the thin side real content instead. Tiles grow to carry their own height,
with a placeholder, a preview, a swatch, a count — something true about the
thing they stand for. Then keep them quiet: low-contrast surfaces, small labels,
no competing headline. A grid of twenty loud tiles takes the section away from
the card it was meant to support.

```tsx
// Bad: a tall card and 20 chips, most of the row empty
<Row fillWidth gap="32">
  <Column flex={1} maxWidth="26rem"><FeatureCard /></Column>
  <Column flex={1}><Row wrap gap="4">{items.map(i => <Button key={i} size="s">{i}</Button>)}</Row></Column>
</Row>

// Good: both sides carry weight, the card still leads
<Row fillWidth gap="32">
  <Column flex={2}><FeatureCard /></Column>
  <Column flex={3}>
    <Grid columns={5} s={{ columns: 3 }} gap="8" fillWidth>
      {items.map(i => (
        <Column key={i} aspectRatio="1 / 1" padding="12" radius="l"
                background="page" border vertical="between">
          {/* a preview of the thing, not just its name */}
        </Column>
      ))}
    </Grid>
  </Column>
</Row>
```

Check it by squinting at the two columns' bottom edges. If one ends halfway up
the other, change the flex ratio, the tile size, or what the tiles contain —
in that order.

## Decorative layers

21. Every absolute decorative layer uses the full recipe — `top="0" left="0"` are required or the layer gets offset by parent padding:

```tsx
<Background position="absolute" top="0" left="0" fill pointerEvents="none" ... />
```

Siblings holding content get `zIndex={1}`. That layer and its content sibling are the whole stacking group — nothing else in the section needs a `zIndex` (rule 3b). `overflow="hidden"` goes on the parent **only when it has a radius** (cards, panels) — clipping a full-bleed section turns the glow into a hard-edged band.

21b. Ambient section layers (hero glows) live on the **full-width section wrapper**, outside the `maxWidth` content column, with generous room (`paddingY="80"`+). Inside a narrow container the gradient gets clipped at the container edge and reads as a misplaced card:

```tsx
// Good: full-bleed section, narrow content inside
<Column fillWidth horizontal="center" paddingY="80">
  <Background position="absolute" top="0" left="0" fill pointerEvents="none" gradient={{...}} />
  <Column zIndex={1} maxWidth="48rem">...</Column>
</Column>
```

22. `Background` gradient units: `x`/`y` place the centre as a percentage string of the container (`"50%"`/`"50%"` = center) or a number on the token scale. `width`/`height` are the ellipse's radii, as a percentage string of the container (`"100%"`, the default) or a number. A soft corner glow is `width: "100%"`–`"200%"`; `"500%"` overshoots the container. `Mask` is the same: `x`/`y` percentage strings, `radius` a CSS length (`"50vh"`, the default) or a number.

23. Color visibility: `*-background-weak` is nearly the page color — it is invisible as an accent. For tints and glows use alpha tokens (`brand-alpha-medium`, `brand-alpha-strong`) or solid tokens (`brand-solid-strong`) and do not stack a low `opacity` on top of an already-weak color.

## Effect units

24. Time is **milliseconds** everywhere: every `duration`, `delay`, `hold` and interval. Stagger with `delay={index * 100}`, never `index * 0.1` (that was 1.8.x, and 2.0 reads it as a tenth of a millisecond, i.e. no stagger at all). That covers `RevealFx` `duration` and `delay`, `ShineFx` and `CountFx` `duration`, `TypeFx` `charDuration`, `delay` and `hold`, `CelebrationFx` and `WeatherFx` `duration` (`5000`, not `5`), `MatrixFx` `bulge.duration`, `FlipFx` `autoFlipInterval`, `Animation`/`HoverCard` `delay` and `duration`, `HoverCard placement="cover"` `hideDelay`, `Skeleton` `delay`. `speed` is only ever a **multiplier** — `1` is the default, `2` twice as fast, `0.5` half — or `"slow"`/`"medium"`/`"fast"` (0.5/1/2), on `MatrixFx`, `WeatherFx`, `ParticleFx`, `CelebrationFx`, `Effect`, `Scroller` `auto.speed`, `GlitchFx` and `LetterFx`. `translateY` as a number is on the token scale (`16` = `"16"` = 1rem) — use a token like `"16"` or `translateY={16}`.

25. `LogoCloud` extends `Grid` — always set `columns` (and responsive overrides), or logos stack in one column: `columns="4" m={{ columns: 3 }} s={{ columns: 2 }}`.
   A logo that changes with the theme is one `Logo` with a source per theme — `<Logo wordmark={{ light: "/logo-light.svg", dark: "/logo-dark.svg" }} />`, and `icon` takes the same pair — not a `<Logo showIn="dark">` beside a `<Logo showIn="light">`. Keep `showIn` for a logo that should only appear in one theme.

26. Use decoration recipes from `recipes.md` verbatim, then adjust. Application shells — a dashboard with a sidebar, a data-driven nav, a two-pane editor, a phone header, a plan or map canvas, a selection with a details panel — come from `layouts.md` the same way. Budget: at most one ambient background layer per section, ambient motion in at most the hero and final CTA, one accent color family per page. A hero scene that shows the product's work (recipes.md #9) is artwork, outside that budget; every other section keeps it.

## Motion

27. Animations are **eye-leading, not eye-grabbing**: they direct attention to the one thing that should be read next, they don't announce themselves. Small distances (`translateY="8"`–`"16"`, i.e. 0.5–1rem, or 8–16 as numbers), short staggers (`delay={index * 100}` max), and only on elements worth leading the eye to — the hero heading, stat numbers, the highlighted card in a set.

28. Do **not** wrap every section in `RevealFx` — uniform entrance animation on everything reads dated and makes scrolling feel slow. Entry-animation budget per page: the hero, plus at most one or two key moments (stats, a card set). Everything else just renders.

28b. Animate **coherent blocks, all-or-none**. Within a sibling set (cards, list items), either every sibling animates with a stagger or none do — never a single item out of the set (e.g. only the highlighted pricing card). For a hero, reveal it as 1–3 stacked chunks with increasing delay (`0 / 100 / 200`), not individual text fragments. One entrance moment per viewport: if the hero animates, the cards below it don't.

29. Trigger below-the-fold animations with `useInViewport`, latched so they play once. `RevealFx` takes `revealed`; `CountFx` has no trigger prop — drive its `value` instead:

```tsx
const ref = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
const inViewport = useInViewport(ref);
const [seen, setSeen] = useState(false);
useEffect(() => {
  if (inViewport) setSeen(true); // latch: useInViewport flips back to false on scroll-out
}, [inViewport]);

<Column ref={ref} gap="16">
  <RevealFx revealed={seen} translateY="8">...</RevealFx>
  <CountFx value={seen ? 2400 : 0} duration={1500} separator="," textVariant="display-strong-m" />
</Column>
```

Without this, mount-timed animations play while still off-screen and the user scrolls into an already-finished state.

## Imports

30. Most things come from the package root, but these modules do not, because
their dependencies are optional peers (or, for `EmojiPicker`, a large dataset)
and a root re-export would drag them into every consumer's module graph, or
because they are packages of their own (the effects and the blocks):

| Import | From | Peer the app installs |
|--------|------|-----------------------|
| charts, gauges, chart chrome | `@once-ui-system/core/data` | none |
| `CodeBlock` | `@once-ui-system/core/code` | `prismjs` |
| `MediaUpload` | `@once-ui-system/core/media` | `compressorjs` |
| `MediaAudioPlayer`, `MediaVideoPlayer`, `Scrubber`, `CompareImage` | `@once-ui-system/core/media` | none |
| `EmojiPicker` | `@once-ui-system/core/emoji` | none |
| `Map`, `MapMarker`, `MapMarkers`, `MapPin`, `MapPopup`, `MapCircle`, `useMap` | `@once-ui-system/core/map` | `maplibre-gl` |
| `mdxComponents`, `createMdxComponents`, the `Mdx*` elements | `@once-ui-system/core/mdx` | `prismjs` (for fenced code) |
| the effects: `RevealFx`, `CountFx`, `TypeFx`, `MatrixFx`, `Effect` and every other `*Fx` | `@once-ui-system/fx` | `@once-ui-system/fx` itself |
| `Banner`, `Book`, `LogoCloud`, `ScrollToTop`, `StylePanel`, `StyleOverlay` | `@once-ui-system/blocks` | `@once-ui-system/blocks` itself |

Naming one of these from the root does not resolve, and there are no deep
imports (`@once-ui-system/core/components/…` is not an entry point). The
effects and the blocks are packages of their own, built on core: add
`@once-ui-system/fx` or `@once-ui-system/blocks` to the app's dependencies
before importing from them (the manifest's `imports` row says `install`).
Each component slice in `ai/components/`, each catalog entry, and each hook or
function in `spec.json`'s `functions` carries the specifier to import it from
when it is not the root; `ai/manifest.json`'s `imports` lists every entry
point with its exports.

```tsx
// MDX through Once UI: headings with anchors, SmartLink, Media, CodeBlock, Table
import { MDXRemote } from "next-mdx-remote/rsc";
import { createMdxComponents, MdxHeading } from "@once-ui-system/core/mdx";

const components = createMdxComponents({
  h2: (props) => <MdxHeading as="h2" marginTop="64" {...props} />, // typed against MDX's props
  Pricing, // an app component, used as <Pricing /> in the content
});
<MDXRemote source={source} components={components} />
```

30b. In a **Next.js** app, `LayoutProvider` comes from
`@once-ui-system/core/next`:

```tsx
import { LayoutProvider } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";
```

The root export resolves and renders, which is what makes it easy to miss: it
installs the plain DOM adapters, so `SmartLink`, `Button`/`Card`/`ToggleButton`
with an `href`, `Media`, `Logo`, `MegaMenu` and `Kbar` render a plain `<a>` and
`<img>` — no client-side navigation, no `next/image`, and no error. The
validator flags it (`LayoutProvider.next`) and `--fix` moves the import. An app
that composes `NextAdapterProvider` itself is already covered.

The same entry has the route handlers `OgCard` and `useOgData` call. Each
returns `{ GET }`, checks every address and redirect is public, and answers at
the paths the client defaults to:

```ts
// app/api/og/fetch/route.ts
import { createOgFetchRoute } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";
export const { GET } = createOgFetchRoute();

// app/api/og/proxy/route.ts
import { createOgProxyRoute } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";
export const { GET } = createOgProxyRoute();
```

Do not hand-write these routes with `handleOGFetch` and a `fetch` of your own.

30c. Type `once-ui.config` with `defineConfig` from
`@once-ui-system/core/config` (the dependency-free entry; the root exports it
too). It rejects a misspelt key or value in `style`, `dataStyle` and `fonts`
and keeps the literal types, so the sections spread into the providers with no
casts:

```tsx
// once-ui.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "@once-ui-system/core/config";
export const { style, dataStyle } = defineConfig({ style: { brand: "cyan", theme: "system" }, dataStyle: { mode: "categorical" } });
```

Or, for an app, from a theme preset: a whole look for its domain.

```tsx
// once-ui.config.ts
import { defineConfig, themePreset } from "@once-ui-system/core/config";
const ops = themePreset("ops", { style: { brandSeed: "#0f766e" } }); // ops | care | creative | commerce
export const { style, dataStyle } = defineConfig({ style: ops.style, dataStyle: ops.dataStyle });
// ops.fonts.heading.nextFont is "Space_Grotesk": import it from next/font/google as --font-heading

// layout.tsx
<ThemeInit config={style} dataStyle={dataStyle} />
<ThemeProvider {...style}><DataThemeProvider {...dataStyle}>...</DataThemeProvider></ThemeProvider>
```

A denser or roomier app is `style.density` (`"compact"`, `"normal"`, `"spacious"`), not a
`size` on every control: Button, IconButton, ToggleButton, SegmentedControl, Tag, Switch,
Checkbox, RadioButton, RadioGroup and Slider with no `size` take s, m or l from it, and
it picks `scaling` 95/100/105 unless `scaling` is set. A `size` on a control still wins.

30d. The theme a visitor starts on is `defaultTheme` in `style`; `ThemeInit`
paints it and `ThemeProvider` lets the visitor change it. `theme: "light"` or
`"dark"` *forces* the theme on `ThemeProvider` — `setTheme` then does nothing —
so leave `theme` out (or `"system"`) for a switchable site. An exact brand
colour is `brand: "custom", brandSeed: "#0F766E"`: the hex is step 500, which
every brand solid uses in both themes, and the other steps are generated
around it (`accentSeed`, `neutralSeed` likewise). With a brand colour, mark
the page you are on in it: `<Nav tone="brand">` tints the current NavItem and
colours its label and icon (the default `neutral` is a grey fill). Only a brand book that fixes
every shade needs `brandScale`, `accentScale` or `neutralScale`, one colour per
step (`{ 100: "#…", …, 1200: "#…" }`), numbered dark to light in both themes:
100 is the darkest, 1200 the lightest (the reverse of Tailwind). A seed fills
the steps a scale leaves out; a ramp per theme is `{ light: { … }, dark: { … } }`. The page and filled-surface
colours are `pageBackground` and `surfaceBackground` (a token or CSS colour, or
`{ light, dark }`). All render on the server through `ThemeInit`. Do not
override the semantic variables (`--page-background`, `--brand-solid-strong`…)
in CSS instead.

31. `IconName` is a real union, not `string`. An unregistered name is a type
error now, where it used to render a blank space with a console warning — so
take icon names from `catalog.json`'s `iconNames` rather than guessing a plausible
one. An app registers its own by augmenting `IconLibraryOverrides`.

# About

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/about

> Once UI is an open-source design system built for indie creators, small teams, and startups to fuel the next generation of web applications.

## About

Once UI is an open-source design system built for indie creators, small teams, and startups to fuel the next generation of web applications. It pairs an opinionated set of accessible React components with a flexible token system, so you can move from idea to polished product without fighting your tooling.

Developed and maintained by [Lorant](https://lorant.one) and the [Design Engineers Club](https://designengineers.club), Once UI is free and licensed under the MIT license.

## Vision

We believe great software shouldn't require a large team or a big budget. Our vision is a web where a single creator can ship products that look and feel as refined as those from companies many times their size.

To get there, Once UI focuses on:

- **Compact, expressive syntax** — describe intent with minimal markup and let smart defaults handle the rest.
- **Design consistency by default** — tokens for color, spacing, typography, and motion keep every screen coherent.
- **An agent-first foundation** — a system that AI tools can read, reason about, and extend reliably.

## Mission

Our mission is to lower the barrier to building beautiful, responsive, and accessible web applications. Every decision — from API design to documentation — is measured against a simple question: does this make it easier for creators to ship?

That means sensible defaults, predictable behavior, thorough documentation, and components that compose cleanly instead of locking you into rigid patterns.

## Maintenance

Once UI is actively maintained as an open-source project. We ship regular releases with new components, fixes, and refinements, and we track upcoming work transparently:

- Review what shipped in each release in the [changelog](https://github.com/once-ui-system/core/releases), generated from the
  repository's `CHANGELOG.md`.
- Follow planned work in [ROADMAP.md](https://github.com/once-ui-system/core/blob/main/ROADMAP.md).
- Report bugs, request features, or open a pull request on [GitHub](https://github.com/once-ui-system/core).

We aim to keep the system stable and backwards-compatible, and to communicate breaking changes clearly when they're necessary.

## Community

Once UI is shaped by the people who build with it. Whether you're filing your first issue or shipping your hundredth project, you're part of the community.

- Join the conversation in the [Design Engineers Club](https://designengineers.club) on Discord.
- Share what you build and get feedback from other creators.
- Contribute components, docs, or ideas — every contribution helps the whole community.

## How it compares

If you're choosing between design systems, the [comparisons on once-ui.com](https://once-ui.com/compare) set Once UI side by side with shadcn/ui, Radix, Tailwind and others. For the agent side, see [Design system for AI coding agents](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/ai-coding).

## Get started

Ready to build? Head to the [Quick start](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/quick-start) to set up your first Once UI project in minutes.

---

# Design system for AI coding agents

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/ai-coding

> Once UI is an agentic design system: compact rules, a component catalog, task bundles and gold examples that Claude, Cursor and other coding agents follow.

## About

Once UI is an [agentic design system](https://once-ui.com/agentic-design-system): besides the components and tokens, it ships the rules and references a coding agent needs to use them correctly. Your agent reads a few kilobytes of rules, picks components from a catalog, follows a task bundle and checks its output with a validator, so the screens it writes stay on your brand.

## Agent harness (recommended for codegen)

For **writing UI code**, use the harness — not full doc pages. Bootstrap plus one task bundle is about 45–50KB, read in two or three steps.

| Artifact | URL | When to load |
|----------|-----|--------------|
| Manifest | [/ai/manifest.json](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/ai/manifest.json) | Entry point — lists all harness files, and in `imports` every entry point (`/data`, `/code`, `/media`, `/mdx`, `/next`, `/config`) with its exports |
| Compact rules | [/ai/rules.compact.md](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/ai/rules.compact.md) | Always, before any UI task (~7KB) |
| Component catalog | [/ai/catalog.json](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/ai/catalog.json) | Pick components by purpose; also lists the icon names |
| Task index | [/ai/tasks/index.json](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/ai/tasks/index.json) | Match user intent → a task id (`pricing`, `dashboard`…) |
| Task bundle | [/ai/bundles/pricing.json](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/ai/bundles/pricing.json) | One file per task: the task, every component slice it names, their types, mixins and gotchas |
| Component slice | [/ai/components/Grid.json](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/ai/components/Grid.json) | Only for a component the bundle doesn't have — one file per component, with its types and `importFrom` when it is not on the package root |
| Tokens | [/ai/tokens.json](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/ai/tokens.json) | Design tokens, mixins and layout shorthands |
| Functions | [/ai/functions.json](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/ai/functions.json) | The hooks and helpers (`useHotkeys`, `defineConfig`, `createMdxComponents`, the OG route handlers) with their signatures and types |
| Spec | [/ai/spec.json](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/ai/spec.json) | Everything above in one 131KB file, for tooling. Agents don't need it |
| Gold example | [/ai/examples/*.tsx](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/ai/examples/marketing-hero.tsx) | Mimic structure for the task type |
| Pro blocks | [/ai/examples/blocks/manifest.json](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/ai/examples/blocks/manifest.json) | Production-quality composition references |
| Gotchas | [/ai/gotchas.json](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/ai/gotchas.json) | When using Background, Card, RevealFx, Fade, and for the behaviour fixed in 2.1 (Toast, NumberInput, Select, ContextMenu) |

**npm imports** (version-pinned):

```bash
npm install @once-ui-system/core
npx once-ui-init-agent   # writes AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and a Cursor rule in your app (one-time)
```

```tsx
// Conceptual — read in your agent environment
// @once-ui-system/core/ai/manifest.json
// @once-ui-system/core/ai/rules.compact.md
// @once-ui-system/core/ai/bundles/pricing.json
```

Machine-readable discovery: `onceUi` field in `@once-ui-system/core` `package.json`.

**Workflow:**

1. Load `rules.compact.md` and `catalog.json`
2. Resolve intent → pick a task from `tasks/index.json` and read its bundle (e.g. `bundles/pricing.json`). Read everything you need in one step: an agent re-sends every file it has read on each later turn
3. Fetch a component slice only for a component the bundle doesn't have
4. Read the gold example for structure; for production fidelity, read matching **Pro blocks** from `examples/blocks/manifest.json`
5. Generate code
6. Validate: `npx once-ui-validate-ai-code path/to/file.tsx` (in a Next.js app it also checks that `LayoutProvider` comes from `@once-ui-system/core/next`)

## MCP server

Once UI ships its own MCP server in `@once-ui-system/core`. It runs on your machine over stdio and answers from the harness of the version you install: no account, no network, nothing hosted.

Add it to your agent's MCP config (`.mcp.json` for Claude Code, `.cursor/mcp.json` for Cursor, `mcp_config.json` for Windsurf):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "once-ui": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "-p", "@once-ui-system/core@next", "once-ui-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Drop `@next` once 3.0 is the `latest` release. In a project that already has the package installed, `"command": "npx", "args": ["once-ui-mcp"]` uses that copy.

| Tool | What it returns |
| --- | --- |
| `search_components` | Components for a need ("date range", "toast"), with the entry point to import each from |
| `get_component` | A component's import, props with types and defaults, what it pairs with, and its gotchas |
| `get_type` | What a type or inherited prop group allows: `TShirtSizes`, `IconName`, `SpacingProps` |
| `get_task` | The task bundles: components, recipes and a worked example for a whole page |
| `get_rules` | The codegen rules, compact or full |
| `validate_code` | The checks of `once-ui-validate-ai-code`, on code the agent just wrote |

For open questions about the docs, [Context7](https://context7.com/once-ui-system/core) also indexes them (`npx -y @upstash/context7-mcp@latest`, then `get-library-docs /once-ui-system/core`).

## Syntax advantage

Compared to Tailwind + shadcn, Once UI yields **more compact** output, with **cleaner, more natural syntax** — semantic `Row`/`Column`, token props, and purpose-built components.

That compactness only pays off when agents load the harness and follow the rules — especially layout shorthands (`fill`, `center`), surface recipes, and component appropriateness (`Card` is interactive-only).

# Configuration

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/config

> Configure Once UI with app-level design settings.

Once UI manages app-level design configuration with the help of Providers and a config file. Write the config once with `defineConfig`, then hand its sections to `ThemeInit` and the providers exactly as written — no casts, no renamed keys:

once-ui.config.js:

```tsx
import { defineConfig } from "@once-ui-system/core/config";
import { Geist, Geist_Mono } from "next/font/google";

const heading = Geist({ variable: "--font-heading", subsets: ["latin"], display: "swap" });
const body = Geist({ variable: "--font-body", subsets: ["latin"], display: "swap" });
const label = Geist({ variable: "--font-label", subsets: ["latin"], display: "swap" });
const code = Geist_Mono({ variable: "--font-code", subsets: ["latin"], display: "swap" });

export const { baseURL, fonts, style, dataStyle } = defineConfig({
  baseURL: "https://example.com",
  fonts: { heading, body, label, code },
  style: {
    theme: "system",
    neutral: "gray",
    brand: "blue",
    accent: "indigo",
    solid: "contrast",
    solidStyle: "flat",
    border: "playful",
    surface: "filled",
    transition: "all",
    scaling: "100",
    density: "normal", // compact | normal | spacious: the controls' default size
  },
  dataStyle: {
    variant: "gradient",
    mode: "categorical",
    height: "24rem",
    axis: { stroke: "var(--neutral-alpha-weak)" },
    tick: { fill: "var(--neutral-on-background-weak)", fontSize: 11, line: false },
  },
});
```

layout.tsx:

```tsx
import "@once-ui-system/core/css/styles.css";
import "@once-ui-system/core/css/tokens.css";

import classNames from "classnames";
import { Column, Flex, ThemeInit } from "@once-ui-system/core";
import { dataStyle, fonts, style } from "../resources/once-ui.config";
import { Providers } from "../components/Providers";

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <Flex
      as="html"
      lang="en"
      suppressHydrationWarning
      className={classNames(
        fonts.heading.variable,
        fonts.body.variable,
        fonts.label.variable,
        fonts.code.variable,
      )}
    >
      <head>
        <ThemeInit config={style} dataStyle={dataStyle} />
      </head>
      <Providers>
        <Column as="body" background="page" fillWidth margin="0" padding="0" minHeight="100vh">
          {children}
        </Column>
      </Providers>
    </Flex>
  );
}
```

Providers.tsx:

```tsx
"use client";

import { DataThemeProvider, IconProvider, ThemeProvider, ToastProvider } from "@once-ui-system/core";
import { LayoutProvider } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";
import { dataStyle, style } from "../resources/once-ui.config";

export function Providers({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <LayoutProvider>
      <ThemeProvider {...style}>
        <DataThemeProvider {...dataStyle}>
          <ToastProvider>
            <IconProvider>{children}</IconProvider>
          </ToastProvider>
        </DataThemeProvider>
      </ThemeProvider>
    </LayoutProvider>
  );
}
```

This setup provides everything you need to get started with Once UI. Read more about the customization and usage of each provider in the [Contexts](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/contexts/themeProvider) section.

## defineConfig

`defineConfig` returns its argument unchanged. What it adds is checking and inference:

- **Every value is checked** against the values Once UI accepts, so `brand: "yelow"` fails to compile instead of rendering without a brand colour.
- **A misspelt key fails** in the sections Once UI reads (`style`, `dataStyle`, `fonts`), so `solidstyle: "flat"` is caught rather than ignored.
- **The literal types survive**, so `style.brand` is `"blue"`, not `string`, and the sections go straight to `ThemeProvider`, `DataThemeProvider` and `ThemeInit`.

Anything else in the object — `schema`, `social`, your own `layout` settings — belongs to your app and passes through untouched.

The file can stay JavaScript: TypeScript reads the types through the call. To see the errors inside the config file itself, name it `once-ui.config.ts`, or add `// @ts-check` at the top of the `.js` file.

Import it from `@once-ui-system/core/config`. That entry has no runtime dependencies, so the config file stays cheap to import from route handlers, middleware and scripts; the root `@once-ui-system/core` export works too, but pulls in the whole package.

### OnceUIConfig

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `baseURL` | `string` | `-` | The site's origin, as Meta and Schema take it. |
| `fonts` | `OnceUIFonts` | `-` | heading, body, label and code, each a next/font result (anything with a variable class). Extra keys are allowed. |
| `style` | `OnceUIStyleConfig` | `-` | ThemeProvider's props. See ThemeProvider. |
| `dataStyle` | `OnceUIDataStyleConfig` | `-` | DataThemeProvider's props. See DataThemeProvider. |

## Theme presets

A theme that only changes the brand colour still looks like the default. A preset sets every axis together: a tinted page and a lifted surface in both themes, the brand and accent, how solids fill, corners, density, motion, and the faces it was drawn with. Start from the one closest to the product and change only what is yours, usually `brandSeed`.

| Preset | For | Starts in | Heading face |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ops` | Operations, incidents, dispatch, maps, monitoring | dark, compact | Space Grotesk |
| `care` | Consumer, health, home, food, pets, plants | light | Bricolage Grotesque |
| `creative` | Editors, studios, media and design tools | dark | Sora |
| `commerce` | Stores, bookings, marketplaces, venues | light | Instrument Sans |

once-ui.config.ts:

```ts
import { Bricolage_Grotesque, Geist, Geist_Mono } from "next/font/google";
import { defineConfig, themePreset } from "@once-ui-system/core/config";

// The preset, with the product's own brand colour on top.
const care = themePreset("care", { style: { brandSeed: "#c2410c" } });

export const { style, dataStyle } = defineConfig({
  style: care.style,
  dataStyle: care.dataStyle,
});

// care.fonts names the faces: heading.nextFont is "Bricolage_Grotesque".
const heading = Bricolage_Grotesque({ variable: "--font-heading", subsets: ["latin"] });
const body = Geist({ variable: "--font-body", subsets: ["latin"] });
const label = Geist({ variable: "--font-label", subsets: ["latin"] });
const code = Geist_Mono({ variable: "--font-code", subsets: ["latin"] });
export const fonts = { heading, body, label, code };
```

`themePreset(name, overrides)` returns `style`, `dataStyle` and `fonts`. A `brandSeed` or `brandScale` in the overrides switches the brand to `"custom"`; a named `brand` drops the preset's seed. `themePresets` holds the presets themselves, for a picker or a `StyleScope` preview like the one above.

## Upgrading a 2.0 config

A 2.0 layout cast every value (`style.brand as Schemes`) and renamed keys for `ThemeInit` (`"solid-style": style.solidStyle`). Both still compile. To drop them, wrap the existing objects in `defineConfig`, then pass `config={style} dataStyle={dataStyle}` to `ThemeInit` and spread the sections into the providers.

One thing changes on the way: the 2.0 docs filled `ThemeInit`'s `"viz-style"` from `dataStyle.variant`. That attribute is the chart *mode* (`categorical`, `divergent` or `sequential`); passing `dataStyle` reads it from `dataStyle.mode`, which is what the charts style themselves by.

# Tailwind CSS

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/tailwind

> Add Once UI to a Tailwind CSS v4 app, or Tailwind to a Once UI app. One import turns Once UI's tokens into Tailwind classes, and neither system restyles the other.

## Setup

Once UI works next to Tailwind CSS v4 with one import. Put it in the stylesheet where you import Tailwind, **before** Tailwind:

globals.css:

```css
@import "@once-ui-system/core/tailwind.css";
@import "tailwindcss";
```

layout.tsx:

```tsx
import "@once-ui-system/core/css/styles.css";
import "@once-ui-system/core/css/tokens.css";
import "./globals.css";
```

Card.tsx:

```tsx
<div className="rounded-l border border-neutral-medium bg-surface p-6 shadow-m">
  <p className="font-heading text-heading-s text-neutral-strong">Plan</p>
  <p className="mt-2 text-body-s text-neutral-weak">Billed monthly</p>
  <span className="rounded-m bg-brand-solid-strong px-3 py-1 text-label-s text-brand-on-solid-strong">
    Pro
  </span>
</div>
```

# Structure

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/basics/structure

> How a page is composed: two layout primitives, spacing that comes from gaps, and props instead of CSS.

Layout in Once UI is composition, not stylesheets. You nest a handful of
primitives and set props on them; there is no CSS file, no class names, and no
media queries.

There are only two primitives. `Flex` lays children out along one axis, `Grid`
along two. Everything else — a `Card`, a `Button`, a `Dialog` — is built from
them and accepts the same props.

## Row and Column

You will almost always write `Row` or `Column` rather than `Flex`. They are the
same component with `direction` preset, and they say what they mean:

Row and Column:

```tsx
<Column gap="8">
    <Row gap="8">
        <Flex fillWidth/>
        <Flex fillWidth/>
    </Row>
    <Flex fillWidth/>
</Column>
```

Reach for `Flex` itself only when the direction changes at a breakpoint, which
is the one thing a preset cannot express: `<Flex s={{ direction: "column" }}>`.

## The page skeleton

Nearly every page is the same three layers — a full-width main element, a
centred column that caps the reading width, and the sections inside it:

Page skeleton:

```tsx
<Column as="main" fillWidth horizontal="center">
    <Column maxWidth="m" gap="104" padding="24">
        <Column gap="24">  // a section
            ...
        </Column>
        <Column gap="24">  // another
            ...
        </Column>
    </Column>
</Column>
```

`maxWidth` caps the line length, `horizontal="center"` centres that cap in the
viewport, and the gaps do the rest. Sections sit far apart (`"80"`–`"160"`),
content inside them sits close (`"24"`–`"40"`).

## The app shell

A dashboard scrolls a pane, not the page, so the header and sidebar stay put.
The pane is "the viewport below the header" tall, and that is a value of its
own: `height="below-header"`.

App shell:

```tsx
<Column fill>
    <Row as="header" height="56" fillWidth>...</Row>
    <Row fill>
        <Column position="sticky" top="56" fitHeight>...</Column>
        <Column fill height="below-header" overflowY="auto">
            ...
        </Column>
    </Row>
</Column>
```

`"below-header"` is `calc(100dvh - var(--header-height))`, and `height`,
`minHeight` and `maxHeight` all take it — `maxHeight="below-header"` caps a
mobile menu or a dropdown that hangs from the header. `--header-height` is a
token, 56px by default (the header above), so most shells never set it. One
with a different header sets it once, and every pane follows:

A taller header:

```css
:root {
    --header-height: 4rem;
}
```

It is read where it is used, so it can also be set on a subtree. A sticky
offset that should follow it is `top="calc(var(--header-height))"`.

## Space comes from gaps

Space **between** siblings is `gap` on the parent. Space **inside** an element is
`padding`. Between them they cover almost everything:

Gap and padding:

```tsx
<Column gap="16" padding="24">   // between children, and inside the box
<Column marginBottom="16">       // last resort
```

Prefer both over `margin`. A layout built from gaps stays correct when a child
is added, removed or reordered; one built from margins has to be re-tuned each
time, and margins collapse into each other in ways gaps do not.

## Everything is a token

Sizes, colours, radii and shadows are named values, not numbers you invent:

Tokens:

```tsx
<Column gap="16" padding="24" radius="l"
    background="surface" border="neutral-alpha-medium" onBackground="neutral-strong">
```

`gap="16"` is a step on the spacing scale, not 16 pixels — it moves with the
`data-scaling` setting. So does a number: `gap={16}` is the same step. `neutral-alpha-medium` is a scheme and a weight, so it
follows the theme instead of being re-picked for dark mode. If a value cannot be
expressed as a token, that is usually a sign the design has drifted from the
system rather than a reason to reach for `style`.

## Responsive without media queries

Every layout prop can be overridden per breakpoint. Pass an object to `xl`, `l`,
`m`, `s` or `xs`; they cascade downward, so `s` also covers `xs`.

Breakpoints:

```tsx
<Row gap="24" s={{ direction: "column", gap: "16" }}>
    <Column maxWidth="20rem" m={{ hide: true }}>Sidebar</Column>
    <Column fill>Content</Column>
</Row>
```

## Where to go next

That is the whole model. The full prop reference lives on the two primitives:

- [Flex](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/flex) — direction, alignment, size, spacing, surface,
  display and text, each with its table
- [Grid](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/grid) — columns and rows, plus everything Flex has
- [Spacing](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/basics/spacing) — the scale behind `gap` and `padding`
- [Color](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/basics/color) — schemes, weights and alpha
- [Responsive](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/basics/responsive) — the breakpoints themselves

# Color

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/basics/color

> Design harmonious and accessible interfaces with Once UI's flexible color system.

Once UI's color system is designed to be accessible and consistent, allowing you to create
harmonious, functional interfaces. It consists of two layers: the{" "}
`base layer` that contains all possible color tokens and the{" "}
`semantic layer` that aliases the base tokens to give them
meaningful names.

## Base tokens

In Once UI, we call the different color spaces `schemes`. Color tokens
are constructed from pairing a scheme with a weight, such as `sand-700`. Base tokens serve as the foundational layer of the
color system and they are not meant to be used directly.

### Schemes

Schemes provide a comprehensive and consistent initial color palette. Each scheme
has 12 weights `(100–1200)`, giving you fine-grained control over contrast and tone:

## Semantic tokens

Semantic tokens are contextual - they adapt based on your theme configuration. Each of the 7 semantic schemes provides tokens for backgrounds, text, solids, borders, and overlays across the `strong`, `medium`, and `weak` weight variants. 

## Additional token groups

Beyond the semantic and function token systems, Once UI provides several
specialized color token groups for specific UI concerns.

## Applying colour

Colour arrives in pairs. `background` sets a surface and `onBackground` sets the
text that sits on it; `solid` sets a filled control and `onSolid` the text on
that. Setting the text colour on the container means every label inside inherits
it, so it is written once rather than on each child.

The four pairings:

```tsx
<Row background="brand-medium" onBackground="brand-medium">
<Row solid="brand-strong" onSolid="brand-strong">
<Row background="brand-alpha-weak" onBackground="brand-strong">
<Row background="surface" border="neutral-alpha-medium">
```

Which to reach for:

- **`background`** for a panel, a section, a page area.
- **`solid`** for something interactive that has to read as pressable — a
  button, a checkbox, a filled badge.
- **an alpha weight** when the colour should tint whatever is behind it rather
  than replace it. This is what keeps a layer working over both an image and a
  plain surface.
- **`surface`** for the neutral raised panel, which follows the theme without
  naming a scheme at all.

## The brand colour

`solid="contrast"`, the default solid style, draws filled controls in neutral:
near-white in dark mode, near-black in light. So under it
`--brand-solid-strong` is not the brand colour, by design, and anything that
reads it for "the brand colour" loses its hue.

When something needs the brand hue whatever the solid style, such as an
effect, an illustration, a gradient or a highlight, use `--brand-color-strong`,
`--brand-color-medium` or `--brand-color-weak`. They are the brand solids as
`data-solid="color"` draws them, in both themes, and no solid style changes
them.

Under data-solid=\:

```tsx
// Follows the solid style: neutral under data-solid="contrast"
<Background gradient={{ display: true, colorStart: "brand-solid-strong" }} />

// Always the brand hue
<Background gradient={{ display: true, colorStart: "brand-color-strong" }} />
```

Keep `--brand-solid-*` for what it is for: filled, pressable things that
should follow the solid style. `--brand-on-background-*` keeps the hue too,
but is tuned for text on a background, so it runs light in dark mode.

## Colour format

Scheme tokens are `oklch()`. The values are the same colours the palette has
always used — every one round-trips to the hex it replaced — but expressed in
a space where the numbers mean something: `oklch(0.6743 0.1670 261.54)` reads
as "two thirds as light as white, moderately saturated, blue", where
`#5A93FC` reads as nothing.

That needs Chrome 111, Safari 15.4 or Firefox 113, all from 2022–23. There is
no fallback: a browser that does not understand `oklch()` drops the
declaration rather than approximating it.

## Custom schemes

`data-brand="custom"` reads `--scheme-brand-*` (and `data-accent` and
`data-neutral` the same way), which your app supplies. Rather than
hand-picking twelve steps that sit evenly against each other, generate them
from one colour. In the config, that is a seed:

```tsx
export const { style } = defineConfig({
  style: { brandSeed: "#5A93FC" },
});
```

`ThemeInit` generates the scheme on the server and renders it in a `<style>`,
so it is there before the first paint; `ThemeProvider` applies the same values
on the client when the seed changes. See
[ThemeProvider](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/contexts/themeProvider#custom-color).

To apply a scheme yourself at runtime, `customSchemeProperties` returns the
properties to write, from the same pure function both of those use:

```tsx
import { customSchemeProperties } from "@once-ui-system/core";

for (const [property, value] of Object.entries(customSchemeProperties({ brand: "#5A93FC" }))) {
  document.documentElement.style.setProperty(property, value);
}
document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-brand", "custom");
```

`generateColorScheme` and `schemeAlphaVariants` underneath it return the raw
twelve steps and the three alphas, if you need the values for something other
than the page's scheme.

The seed can be hex, `rgb()`/`rgba()` or `oklch()` — which covers what
[ColorInput](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/colorInput) produces with and without
`supportAlpha`. An unparseable seed returns `null` rather than something
wrong, so you can leave the current scheme in place.

Steps are anchored to a contrast ratio against black, not to fixed lightness
values, so a generated ramp holds the same contrast relationships as the
built-in schemes whichever hue it starts from. Hue and chroma come from the
seed and stay put; only lightness moves.

One thing it does not do is copy the built-in schemes' hand-tuning. Those were
drawn by eye, and at the saturated dark end — step 400 especially — several
carry more chroma than their own step 600. A ramp built from a single seed
cannot know that. Regenerating each built-in scheme from its own step 600
lands within 0.11 OKLab ΔE at the worst step, and inside 0.05 for most.

# Spacing

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/basics/spacing

> Once UI's spacing system is based on a custom 8px grid.

Once UI utilizes a spacing system based on a custom 8px grid to provide options for setting white spaces effortlessly and consistently.

## Spacing system

Once UI relies on the type called `SpacingToken` to define static and responsive spaces. It's used for margins, paddings, gaps, and position distances. Static spaces are set in REMs and can be referenced with their pixel value calculated with a 16px root font size. For a more illustrative example, visit the [Structure](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/basics/structure) page. These spacings will slightly adjust based on your `--font-scaling` variables.

Responsive spaces are also set in REMs, but they are rescaled at the `m` and `s` breakpoints. They can be accessed through the T-shirt size model.

## Breakpoints

Once UI uses a custom PostCSS config with custom-media to define and use breakpoints globally. Breakpoints are defined in the `styles/breakpoints.scss` file.

| Breakpoint | Variable | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--s` | `@custom-media --s (max-width: 768px)` | `max-width: 768px` |
| `--m` | `@custom-media --m (max-width: 1024px)` | `max-width: 1024px` |

> We recommend setting paddings and margins with the `Flex` and `Grid` components. Flex props are exposed on most Once UI components to prevent unnecessary nesting.

### Auto margin

Every margin prop also takes `"auto"`, at the base and in a breakpoint object: `marginLeft="auto"` pushes an item to the end of its row, and `marginX="auto"` centres a block with a width. The classes are `.m-auto`, `.mx-auto`, `.my-auto`, `.mt-auto`, `.mr-auto`, `.mb-auto` and `.ml-auto`, with an `.s-ml-auto`-style variant at each breakpoint. Padding and gap have no `auto`.

Auto margin:

```tsx
<Row fillWidth vertical="center" gap="8">
  <Text>Invoices</Text>
  <Text marginLeft="auto" s={{ hide: true }}>3 due</Text>
</Row>
```

# Typography

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/basics/typography

> Once UI's typography system is built using CSS variables and utility classes.

Once UI manages typography properties with the [`Text`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/text) and 
[`Heading`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/heading) components. They apply utility classes and CSS variables under the hood. See the [Config](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/config) page for our recommended font setup.

## Font family

Add `font-family` classes to elements.

| Class | Variable | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| .font-display | `var(--font-heading)` | `var(--font-primary)` |
| .font-heading | `var(--font-heading)` | `var(--font-primary)` |
| .font-body | `var(--font-body)` | `var(--font-primary)` |
| .font-label | `var(--font-label)` | `var(--font-primary)` |
| .font-code | `var(--font-code)` | `var(--font-code)` |

## Font size

Add `font-size` classes to elements. The value adjusts to the adjacent or closest parent `font-family` class.

| Class | Variable |
| --- | --- |
| .font-size-inherit | — |
| .font-xl | dynamic |
| .font-l | dynamic |
| .font-m | dynamic |
| .font-s | dynamic |
| .font-xs | dynamic |

## Font weight

Add `font-weight` classes to elements. The value adjusts to the adjacent or closest parent `font-family` class.

| Class | Variable |
| --- | --- |
| .font-weight-inherit | — |
| .font-default | --font-weight-display-default |
| .font-normal | --font-weight-display-normal |
| .font-medium | --font-weight-display-medium |
| .font-strong | --font-weight-display-strong |

Every family reads the display weights unless you give it its own: `--font-<family>-weight-<weight>`, for `heading`, `body`, `label` and `code`. Setting one changes only that family, so bolder body text leaves headlines and labels alone.

```css
:root {
  --font-body-weight-strong: 700;  /* body-strong-* */
  --font-label-weight-strong: 500; /* label-strong-* */
}
```

# Border

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/basics/border

> Adjusting shape language with border radius and border style.

Shape language in design profoundly influences the style of an interface. For instance, a website employing a large border radius often appears more playful, whereas one with small borders and sharp corners tends to convey a more conservative feel.

## Shape style

Override the default shape style with the `data-border` attribute on a native HTML element.

Radius style:

```tsx
<Flex data-border="conservative | playful | rounded" radius="m"/>
```

## Border radius

In Once UI, we adopt the T-shirt size model for managing border radius, with values ranging from `xs` to `xl`.

Border radius:

```tsx
<Flex radius="xs" />
<Flex radius="s" />
<Flex radius="m" />
<Flex radius="l" />
<Flex radius="xl" />
```

## Nested radius

A common challenge in border-radius systems is nesting. For nested elements to maintain an aesthetic and natural appearance, they require varying border radius sizes. Once UI addresses this issue by providing additional border radius values specifically for containers with `static-size-4` and `static-size-8` paddings, which are the most frequently used nesting sizes.

Nested radius:

```tsx
// Any size from xs to xl: the outer box adds -8, the next one -4.
<Flex padding="8" radius="m-8">
  <Flex padding="4" radius="m-4">
    <Flex radius="m" />
  </Flex>
</Flex>
```

## Border width

Sets the `border-width` property.

| Class | Preview |
| --- | --- |
| .border-1 | <Flex width="64" height="20" border="neutral-strong" radius="xs"/> |
| .border-2 | <Flex width="64" height="20" border="neutral-strong" borderWidth="2" radius="xs"/> |

## Border style

Sets the `border-style` property.

| Class | Preview |
| --- | --- |
| .border-solid | <Flex width="64" height="20" border="neutral-strong" radius="xs"/> |
| .border-dashed | <Flex width="64" height="20" border="neutral-strong" borderStyle="dashed" radius="xs"/> |

## Border color

Sets the `border-color` property.

# Breakpoints

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/basics/responsive

> Per-component responsive breakpoint system with type-safe prop selection.

# Responsive Breakpoints

Once UI provides a type-safe responsive breakpoint system where each component only exposes the props it actually supports at each breakpoint.

## Breakpoint values

The breakpoints are fixed, and each one applies at its width and below. `xl` is the base state above all of them, not a media query. `LayoutProvider` reports the current one through `useLayout`; it no longer takes a `breakpoints` prop (removed in 2.0, see the [migration guide](https://github.com/once-ui-system/core/blob/main/MIGRATING.md)).

| Breakpoint | Applies at | Typical Device |
| --- | --- | --- |
| xs | `≤ 480px` | Mobile portrait |
| s | `≤ 768px` | Mobile landscape / Tablet portrait |
| m | `≤ 1024px` | Tablet landscape / Small laptop |
| l | `≤ 1440px` | Desktop |
| xl | `above 1440px` | Large desktop (the base) |

Breakpoints cascade downward: `xl` → `l` → `m` → `s` → `xs`. A value set at `xl` applies to all smaller breakpoints unless overridden.

## Per-component props

Each component defines its own breakpoint type using `BreakpointProps<Source, Keys>`, a generic that picks specific keys from the component's prop interfaces and makes them optional.

### Flex / Row / Column

Supports layout, spacing, sizing, colors, typography, and effects.

Responsive Flex:

```tsx
<Flex
  direction="row"
  padding="16"
  background="surface"
  xl={{ direction: "row", padding: "32" }}
  m={{ direction: "column", padding: "16" }}
  s={{ direction: "column", padding: "8" }}
>
  <Flex flex={1}>Item 1</Flex>
  <Flex flex={1}>Item 2</Flex>
</Flex>
```

**Supported breakpoint props:**

| Category | Props |
| --- | --- |
| Layout | <InlineCode>direction | horizontal | vertical | center | wrap | flex</InlineCode> |
| Spacing | <InlineCode>padding | paddingLeft | paddingRight | paddingTop | paddingBottom | paddingX | paddingY | margin | marginLeft | marginRight | marginTop | marginBottom | marginX | marginY | gap</InlineCode> |
| Position | <InlineCode>top | right | bottom | left | position | hide</InlineCode> |
| Sizing | <InlineCode>width | height | maxWidth | minWidth | minHeight | maxHeight | fit | fitWidth | fitHeight | fill | fillWidth | fillHeight | aspectRatio</InlineCode> |
| Colors | <InlineCode>background | solid | border | borderTop | borderRight | borderBottom | borderLeft | borderX | borderY | borderStyle | borderWidth | radius | shadow | onBackground | onSolid</InlineCode> |
| Typography | <InlineCode>align | textVariant | textSize | textWeight | textType</InlineCode> |
| Effects | <InlineCode>opacity | zIndex | pointerEvents | transition | scrollbar | dark | light</InlineCode> |
| Display | <InlineCode>overflow | overflowX | overflowY</InlineCode> |
| Escape hatch | `style` |

### Grid

Supports grid-specific, spacing, sizing, colors, typography, and effects. Does **not** support `direction`, `horizontal`, `vertical`, `center`, `wrap`, `flex`.

Responsive Grid:

```tsx
<Grid
  columns="3"
  gap="16"
  m={{ columns: 2 }}
  s={{ columns: 1 }}
>
  <Flex padding="16">Cell 1</Flex>
  <Flex padding="16">Cell 2</Flex>
  <Flex padding="16">Cell 3</Flex>
</Grid>
```

**Supported breakpoint props:**

| Category | Props |
| --- | --- |
| Grid-specific | <InlineCode>columns | rows</InlineCode> |
| Spacing | <InlineCode>padding | paddingLeft | paddingRight | paddingTop | paddingBottom | paddingX | paddingY | margin | marginLeft | marginRight | marginTop | marginBottom | marginX | marginY | gap</InlineCode> |
| Position | <InlineCode>top | right | bottom | left | position | hide</InlineCode> |
| Sizing | <InlineCode>width | height | maxWidth | minWidth | minHeight | maxHeight | fit | fitWidth | fitHeight | fill | fillWidth | fillHeight | aspectRatio</InlineCode> |
| Colors | <InlineCode>background | solid | border | borderTop | borderRight | borderBottom | borderLeft | borderX | borderY | borderStyle | borderWidth | radius | shadow | onBackground | onSolid</InlineCode> |
| Typography | <InlineCode>align | textVariant | textSize | textWeight | textType</InlineCode> |
| Effects | <InlineCode>opacity | zIndex | pointerEvents | transition | scrollbar | dark | light</InlineCode> |
| Display | <InlineCode>overflow | overflowX | overflowY</InlineCode> |
| Escape hatch | `style` |

### Card / Dialog / Mask

These extend `Flex` and inherit all Flex breakpoint props.

Responsive Card:

```tsx
<Card
  background="surface"
  radius="l"
  padding="24"
  xl={{ padding: "32" }}
  m={{ padding: "16" }}
>
  Content
</Card>
```

### Leaf components

Button, IconButton, ToggleButton, the form fields, Switch, Checkbox, Text,
Heading, Icon, Avatar, Spinner, Kbd and the other leaf components take no
breakpoint objects. They take the small `LeafProps` set (margins, `flex`,
`fillWidth`, `position` and the offsets); to change one at a breakpoint, wrap
it in a `Row` or `Column` and put the breakpoint object there.

A leaf at a breakpoint:

```tsx
<Row s={{ hide: true }}>
  <Button>Desktop only</Button>
</Row>
```

## How it works

### Type system

The generic `BreakpointProps<Source, Keys>` type picks specific keys from a source interface and makes them optional:

```ts
type BreakpointProps<Source, Keys extends keyof Source> = {
  [K in Keys]?: Source[K];
};
```

Each component defines its allowed props:

```ts
// Flex supports everything
type FlexBreakpointProps = BreakpointProps<AllFlexProps,
  | 'direction' | 'horizontal' | 'vertical' | 'center' | 'wrap' | 'flex'
  | 'padding' | 'gap' | 'width' | 'height' | 'background' | 'opacity'
  // ... etc
>;

// Grid excludes layout props
type GridBreakpointProps = BreakpointProps<AllGridProps,
  | 'columns' | 'rows'
  | 'padding' | 'gap' | 'width' | 'height' | 'background' | 'opacity'
  // ... etc (no direction, horizontal, vertical, center, wrap, flex)
>;
```

### Runtime behavior

1. **Values with a class (server-rendered):** a breakpoint value that maps to a utility class — a spacing token, a direction, an alignment — renders as that class on the server (e.g. `m-padding-l`, `s-flex-column`), so the layout is right in the first paint.

2. **Values without a class (client-rendered):** `width`, `height` and their min/max siblings, `aspectRatio`, `style`, and spacing given as a number (px) or a CSS length have no class behind them. An element that sets one of these at a breakpoint renders through `ClientFlex`/`ClientGrid`, which applies it as an inline style after hydration, for the breakpoint `LayoutProvider` reports. Prefer tokens where you can.

3. **Cascade order:** `xl` → `l` → `m` → `s` → `xs`. Larger breakpoints flow down to smaller ones. Setting `xl={{ padding: "32" }}` applies `padding: 32` at all sizes unless a smaller breakpoint overrides it.

## Examples

### Hide on mobile

Hide on desktop:

```tsx
<Flex
  hide
  s={{ hide: false }}
>
  Visible on mobile only
</Flex>
```

### Direction change

Direction change:

```tsx
<Flex
  direction="row"
  horizontal="between"
  m={{ direction: "column" }}
>
  <Flex>Left content</Flex>
  <Flex>Right content</Flex>
</Flex>
```

## Custom breakpoints

Breakpoints are not configurable since 2.0: the utility classes carry the widths inside their `@media` queries, and a prebuilt stylesheet cannot follow a width an app picks at runtime. If you need a different width for one layout, write a media query in a CSS module for it.

## TypeScript API

Exported types for extending the breakpoint system:

```ts
import {
  BreakpointProps,
  FlexBreakpointProps,
  GridBreakpointProps,
} from "@once-ui-system/core";

// Create custom breakpoint type for your component
type MyComponentBreakpointProps = BreakpointProps<
  MyComponentProps,
  'padding' | 'background' | 'opacity'
>;
```

### Available breakpoint types

| Type | Use Case |
| --- | --- |
| <InlineCode>BreakpointProps&lt;Source | Keys&gt;</InlineCode> | Generic: pick any keys from any source |
| `FlexBreakpointProps` | Flex, Row, Column, Card, Dialog, Mask, etc. |
| `GridBreakpointProps` | Grid |

# Components

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/basics/components

> The anatomy and architecture of Once UI components: props, states, and more.

Once UI components are prop-based, customizable, and built for real-world usage in modern apps. They aim to balance expressiveness with clarity—avoiding over-abstraction while supporting flexibility and scalability.

## Boilerplate

Use the following boilerplate to build Once UI components:

Boilerplate:

```tsx
"use client";

import React, { useState, useEffect, forwardRef } from "react";
import classNames from "clsx";
import styles from "./Component.module.scss";
import { Flex } from "@once-ui-system/core";

interface ComponentProps extends React.ComponentProps<typeof Flex> {
    children: React.ReactNode;
    className?: string;
    style?: React.CSSProperties;
}

const Component = forwardRef<HTMLDivElement, ComponentProps>(
    ({ children, className, style, ...rest }, ref) => {
      const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false);

      useEffect(() => {
        // Optional interactivity
      }, []);

      return (
        <Flex
          ref={ref}
          style={style}
          className={classNames(styles.component, className)}
          {...rest}
        >
          {children}
        </Flex>
      );
    }
);

Component.displayName = "Component";
export { Component };
```

## Principles

- No over-abstraction — components favor simplicity over excessive composition
- Named exports only — components are always exported as `export { Component }`
- Consistent naming
  - `displayName` matches the filename
  - Filenames are `PascalCase` (e.g. `CursorCard.tsx`)
- State conventions
  - Use `loading` instead of `isLoading`, `open` instead of `isOpen`
  - The exception is a name the DOM already declares on the element the
    component renders. `checked`, `prefix` and `size` are all inherited from
    React's HTML attribute types, so a component that wants them must
    `Omit` the inherited one and redeclare — as `Checkbox`, `Input` and
    `Textarea` do. Never reach for an `is`/`has` prefix to dodge the
    collision; that is what produced `isChecked`, `hasPrefix` and the
    `height`-that-meant-`size` before 2.0
  - Boolean props that toggle *visibility* read `showX` (`showLabel`,
    `showIcon`), so the unprefixed name stays free for the thing itself
- Layout primitives
  - Structure built with `Flex` and `Grid`
  - Interactive styles live in `*.module.scss`
- Client behavior
  - Use `"use client"` in any component using hooks or state
- Class names
  - Use `classNames()` to merge static and dynamic classes
- Children-first
  - Props like `children` are encouraged for flexibility

## Interactivity

- Use `ElementType` to dynamically render:
  - `<a>`, `<button>`, `NextLink`, or layout primitives like `Flex`
- External links automatically include `rel="noopener noreferrer"`

## Composition

- Use `forwardRef` for exposing `ref`
- Spread `Flex`/`Grid` props onto the outer wrapper
- Combine `className` and `style` props cleanly
- Prefer `ReactNode` over strings for flexibility and slot-style APIs
