# ThemeProvider

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/contexts/themeProvider

> The ThemeProvider enables dynamic light, dark, and system themes by syncing user preferences with the `data-theme` attribute and exposing a global theme context.

The `ThemeProvider` is a context that persists user theme preferences and syncs with the system’s light/dark setting. It provides a `useTheme` hook to manage theme state at runtime and sets data attributes on the `<html>` element.

## Simple setup

Wrap your app with `ThemeProvider` and pass the style configuration as props.

layout.tsx:

```tsx
<ThemeProvider
    theme="system" // system | dark | light
    brand="blue" // blue | indigo | violet | magenta | pink | red | orange | yellow | moss | green | emerald | aqua | cyan
    accent="indigo" // blue | indigo | violet | magenta | pink | red | orange | yellow | moss | green | emerald | aqua | cyan
    neutral="gray" // sand | gray | slate | rose | mint | dusk
    solid="contrast" // color | contrast
    solidStyle="flat" // flat | plastic | glow
    border="playful" // rounded | playful | conservative | sharp
    surface="translucent" // filled | translucent
    transition="all" // all | micro | macro
    scaling="100" // 90 | 95 | 100 | 105 | 110
    density="normal" // compact | normal | spacious
>
    {children}
</ThemeProvider>
```

## Advanced setup

Keep every style choice in one file, typed with [defineConfig](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/config#defineconfig), and spread it into the provider. The keys are the provider's prop names, so nothing is cast or renamed. We also recommend a `Providers` component to wrap your app.

Providers.tsx:

```tsx
"use client";

import { DataThemeProvider, IconProvider, ThemeProvider, ToastProvider } from "@once-ui-system/core";
import { dataStyle, style } from "@/resources/once-ui.config";

export function Providers({ children }: {
    children: React.ReactNode
}) {
    return (
      <ThemeProvider {...style}>
        <DataThemeProvider {...dataStyle}>
          <ToastProvider>
            <IconProvider>
              {children}
            </IconProvider>
          </ToastProvider>
        </DataThemeProvider>
      </ThemeProvider>
    );
}
```

once-ui.config.js:

```tsx
import { defineConfig } from "@once-ui-system/core/config";

export const { style, dataStyle } = defineConfig({
  style: {
    theme: "system", // system | dark | light
    neutral: "gray", // sand | gray | slate | rose | mint | dusk
    brand: "blue", // blue | indigo | violet | magenta | pink | red | orange | yellow | moss | green | emerald | aqua | cyan
    accent: "indigo", // blue | indigo | violet | magenta | pink | red | orange | yellow | moss | green | emerald | aqua | cyan
    solid: "contrast", // color | contrast | inverse
    solidStyle: "flat", // flat | plastic | glow
    border: "playful", // rounded | playful | conservative | sharp
    surface: "translucent", // filled | translucent
    transition: "all", // all | micro | macro | none
    scaling: "100", // 90 | 95 | 100 | 105 | 110
    density: "normal", // compact | normal | spacious
  },
  dataStyle: {
    variant: "gradient", // flat | gradient | outline
    mode: "categorical", // categorical | divergent | sequential
  },
});
```

A 2.0 `Providers` that casts each value (`brand={style.brand as Schemes}`) still compiles; `defineConfig` is what makes the casts unnecessary.

If you don't pass any props to the `ThemeProvider`, it will fall back to defaults. If the visitor has theme preferences (saved in localStorage), the `ThemeProvider` will use those. To force a theme, set `theme` on the `ThemeProvider` as `light` or `dark`. A forced theme ignores `setTheme`, so a theme switch stops working. To start visitors on light or dark and still let them switch, leave `theme` as `system` and set `defaultTheme` instead; `ThemeInit` reads it too, so the first paint is right.

## Custom color

The quickest way to a custom palette is one colour. Give `brandSeed`, `accentSeed` or `neutralSeed` a hex, `rgb()` or `oklch()` value and the whole 12-step scheme is [generated from it](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/basics/color#custom-schemes). A seed implies `"custom"` when you have not named the scheme yourself. For exact colours from a brand book, give `brandScale`, `accentScale` or `neutralScale` the steps themselves, `{ 100: "#…", …, 1200: "#…" }`; a seed fills any step the scale leaves out.

once-ui.config.js:

```tsx
export const { style } = defineConfig({
  style: {
    brandSeed: "#5A93FC",
    accentSeed: "oklch(0.72 0.17 40)",
    neutral: "gray",
  },
});

// layout.tsx: the scheme is generated on the server
<ThemeInit config={style} />

// Providers.tsx
<ThemeProvider {...style}>
```

`ThemeInit` generates the scheme on the server and renders it into a `<style>` next to its script, so the page paints with the custom brand colour from the first frame. `ThemeProvider` applies the same values on the client, which is what lets a seed change at runtime, for example in an editor previewing a colour. A seed that cannot be parsed is ignored, and the scheme keeps its default rather than pointing at nothing.

A ramp tuned for a light page often reads wrong on a dark one. Give a scale per theme as `{ light: { … }, dark: { … } }`; a theme you leave out uses the other's, and a seed still fills missing steps. `ThemeInit` renders both, keyed off `data-theme`, so the first paint is right in either theme and a `theme="dark"` section on a light page gets the dark ramp.

The page background and the filled surface (cards, menus, dialogs) take a token or any CSS colour through `pageBackground` and `surfaceBackground`, once for both themes or `{ light, dark }`. A theme you leave out keeps the default: in light mode an off-white page under white surfaces.

once-ui.config.ts:

```tsx
export const { style } = defineConfig({
  style: {
    accentScale: {
      light: { 100: "#0B1A00", 600: "#4E7A00", 1200: "#F6FBEA" },
      dark: { 100: "#101A04", 600: "#B8F23A", 1200: "#F4FFE0" },
    },
    pageBackground: { light: "#F7F5EF" },
    surfaceBackground: { light: "#FFFDF8", dark: "neutral-background-strong" },
  },
});
```

To hand-pick every step instead, set the scheme to `custom` and supply the `--scheme-*` variables yourself. You can generate palettes using the [Once UI customize page](https://once-ui.com/customize).

custom.css:

```css

--scheme-brand-200: #04025c;

    --scheme-accent-100:  #030b10;
    --scheme-accent-200:  #0d181d;

    --scheme-accent-400:  #505d64;

```

once-ui.config.js:

```tsx
export const style = {
theme: "system",
neutral: "custom",
brand: "custom",
accent: "custom",
solid: "contrast",
solidStyle: "flat",
border: "playful",
surface: "translucent",
transition: "all",
scaling: "100"
};
```

## Reading and changing the theme

Access and modify theme state with `useTheme`:

useTheme:

```tsx
const { theme, setTheme } = useTheme();

useEffect(() => {
console.log("Current theme:", theme);
}, [theme]);
```

## SSR hydration

Add the `<ThemeInit>` component to the `<head>` to set the initial theme before hydration in `layout.tsx`. It will prevent flash of unstyled content (FOUC). It takes the same `style` object as the provider, plus `dataStyle` for the chart mode:

```tsx
<head>
    <ThemeInit config={style} dataStyle={dataStyle} />
</head>
```

Each key is written to `<html>` as `data-<kebab-key>` (`solidStyle` becomes `data-solid-style`), and `dataStyle.mode` as `data-viz-style`. A choice the visitor saved, through a `StylePanel` for example, is applied on top before the first paint.

The 2.0 form, with attribute names as keys (`"solid-style": style.solidStyle`), is still accepted. Its `"viz-style"` key is the chart *mode*: the 2.0 docs filled it from `dataStyle.variant`, which matches no style, so charts fell back to categorical. Passing `dataStyle` reads `dataStyle.mode` instead.

### ThemeInit

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `config (required)` | `ThemeInitConfig` |  | The style section of once-ui.config, as written. |
| `dataStyle` | `{ mode?: ChartMode }` |  | The dataStyle section; its mode becomes data-viz-style. |

## Style your app

Visit the [ThemeSwitcher](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/themeSwitcher) or [StylePanel](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/stylePanel) page for native, out-of-the-box `ThemeProvider` implementation with localStorage persistence. Use these components to provide user-facing style controls or to quickly test different styles during development.

## Style overrides

The `ThemeProvider` relies on data attributes to set theme and style preferences. Data modes are inherited from the parent and can be applied to any
semantic HTML element, providing simple, seamless style overrides.

Just add the `data-theme`, `data-neutral`, `data-brand`, `data-accent`, `data-border`, `data-surface`, `data-solid`, `data-solid-style`, `data-transition` or `data-scaling` attributes to any semantic HTML element to override its default style.

On `Flex`, `Row`, `Column` and `Grid`, the four you reach for most are typed props, checked against the same values as this provider: `theme` writes `data-theme`, `themeBorder` writes `data-border`, `themeSolid` writes `data-solid` and `themeSurface` writes `data-surface`. `border` and `solid` already mean colours on those components, hence the prefix.

```tsx
<Column theme="dark" themeSolid="contrast" background="page" padding="40">
  ...
</Column>
```

## Density and scaling

`scaling` multiplies everything sized on the spacing scale: the tokens (`"16"` is
`calc(1rem * 1.1)` at `"110"`), a number on a size, spacing or offset prop (`16` is
the same step), and the controls built on them. It is written as `data-scaling`,
and as the `--scaling` factor (1 by default) that numbers read.

`density` sets how roomy the controls are, as `data-density` on `<html>`. Every
Button, IconButton, ToggleButton, SegmentedControl, Tag, Switch, Checkbox,
RadioButton, RadioGroup and Slider that is given no `size` takes the density's:

| density | control size | scaling, unless `scaling` is set |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"compact"` | `s` | `"95"` |
| `"normal"` (default) | `m` | `"100"` |
| `"spacious"` | `l` | `"105"` |

```tsx
<ThemeProvider density="compact">
```

It works in CSS: a control with no `size` renders its m look plus a class that
`[data-density]` restyles, so server components and pages before any JS follow it
too. A `size` on the control, or on its `Form`, always wins. A `scaling` you set
wins over the density's; a density chosen in the StylePanel brings its scaling
along until a scaling is chosen there. The attribute is read on `<html>` only,
so unlike the overrides below it is one setting for the whole page. Input and
the fields built on it follow it once their `s` size lands.

## Root font size and cursor

`desktopSize`, `tabletSize` and `mobileSize` set the root font size, in px, for each width range, which is what every `rem` in the system resolves to. `cursorInteractive` sets the cursor over buttons, links and other interactive elements. They have no defaults of their own: left unset, nothing is written to `<html>` and the stylesheet's values apply (16px, 16px, 15px and `pointer`).

```tsx
<ThemeProvider desktopSize="17" mobileSize="14" cursorInteractive="default">
```

They belong in the `style` section of the config like any other key, so `ThemeInit` applies them before the first paint.

`cursor` sets a cursor preset for the whole app: `"soft"`, `"rounded"` or `"dot"`, each with its own pointer, text and disabled states over the controls. Unset or `"system"`, the browser's own cursors. A `Flex` or `Grid` can set another one for its subtree: see [Flex](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/flex#cursor).

```tsx
<ThemeProvider cursor="soft">
```

## Persistence

Style choices are mirrored into `localStorage` under `data-<kebab-key>`. Set
`persistence` to change that:

- `"local"` — the default described above.
- `"none"` — choices apply to the document but are not stored. Use this when
  a host owns the state, such as an editor holding an unsaved draft.
- an adapter — route persistence somewhere else, such as a database.

```tsx
<ThemeProvider
  brand={site.brand}
  persistence={{
    set: (key, value) => saveSiteStyle(site.id, key, value),
  }}
>
```

`get` runs during hydration, so it must be synchronous — an await there would
show a flash of the wrong theme. When the values live somewhere async, omit
`get` and seed the provider through its props from the server instead. `set`
and `remove` may return a promise; nothing waits on them.

# LayoutProvider

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/contexts/layoutProvider

> The LayoutProvider component creates a listener for the Flex and Grid components to track window size.

The `LayoutProvider` component is a context provider that creates a listener for the Flex and Grid components to track window size, and installs the framework adapters that links and images render through.

## Simple setup

Wrap your app with `LayoutProvider`.

layout.tsx:

```tsx
<LayoutProvider>
    {children}
</LayoutProvider>
```

## Next.js

In a Next.js app, import `LayoutProvider` from `@once-ui-system/core/next`. It is the same provider with the Next adapters installed, so `SmartLink`, `Button`/`Card`/`ToggleButton` with an `href`, `Media`, `Logo`, `MegaMenu` and `Kbar` route through `next/link` and `next/image`. The export from the package root installs the plain DOM adapters instead: everything still renders, as a plain `<a>` and `<img>`, which is why it is easy to miss. `npx once-ui-validate-ai-code` flags it.

Providers.tsx:

```tsx
import { IconProvider, ToastProvider, ThemeProvider, DataThemeProvider } from "@once-ui-system/core";
import { LayoutProvider } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";

export function Providers({ children }: {
    children: React.ReactNode
}) {
    return (
      <LayoutProvider>
        <ThemeProvider>
          <DataThemeProvider>
            <ToastProvider>
              <IconProvider>
                {children}
              </IconProvider>
            </ToastProvider>
          </DataThemeProvider>
        </ThemeProvider>
      </LayoutProvider>
    );
}
```

The breakpoints are fixed since 2.0, so `LayoutProvider` no longer takes a `breakpoints` prop. See [Breakpoints](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/basics/responsive).

## API reference

### LayoutProvider

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `children (required)` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
## useLayout

`useLayout()` reads the resolved breakpoint state. Use it when a decision cannot
be expressed with the responsive props — mounting a different component per
breakpoint, say, rather than styling one. It throws outside a `LayoutProvider`.

useLayout:

```tsx
const { currentBreakpoint, maxWidth } = useLayout();

// At or below the s breakpoint, render the sheet instead of the popover.
return maxWidth("s") ? <Sheet {...props} /> : <Popover {...props} />;
```

`width` is `0` on the server and on the first client render, so branch on it
only inside an effect — or branch on `currentBreakpoint`, which is resolved
before paint.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `currentBreakpoint` | `xs` | `s` | m |
| `width` | `number` | `0` | Viewport width in pixels. 0 until measured. |
| `breakpoints` | `Record<BreakpointKey, number>` | `DEFAULT_BREAKPOINTS` | The breakpoint map. |
| `isBreakpoint` | `(key: BreakpointKey) => boolean` | `-` | True when the viewport is exactly at that breakpoint. |
| `maxWidth` | `(key: BreakpointKey) => boolean` | `-` | True at or below that breakpoint. |
| `minWidth` | `(key: BreakpointKey) => boolean` | `-` | True above that breakpoint. |

### DEFAULT_BREAKPOINTS

The widths every breakpoint class and `useLayout` use. Exported for reading; they are not configurable.

DEFAULT_BREAKPOINTS:

```ts
{ xs: 480, s: 768, m: 1024, l: 1440, xl: Infinity }
```

# AdapterProvider

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/contexts/adapterProvider

> The framework seam: how Once UI renders links and images without importing your framework.

Core no longer imports `next/*` at runtime. Four things a framework owns —
rendering a link, rendering an image, reading the current path, and navigating —
are read through **adapters** instead, and the defaults are plain DOM. That is
what lets Once UI install and run in a Vite app, a Remix app, or a plain React
app with no Next.js present.

Everything that routes or loads an image goes through this seam:
[`SmartLink`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/smartLink),
the internal link element behind them — and so any
[`Button`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/button),
[`Card`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/card) or
[`ToggleButton`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/toggleButton) with an `href` —
[`Media`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/media), [`Logo`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/logo),
[`MegaMenu`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/megaMenu) and [`Kbar`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/kbar).

## In a Next.js app

Import `LayoutProvider` from `@once-ui-system/core/next` instead of the root.
That is the entire migration: same props, same tree, and the Next adapters
(`next/link`, `next/image`, `next/navigation`) are installed for you.

The migration:

```diff
- import { LayoutProvider } from "@once-ui-system/core";
+ import { LayoutProvider } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";
```

Miss this and nothing crashes — which is the trap. The DOM defaults take over,
so internal links become full page loads and images stop being optimized. The
app still works, just worse. If routing suddenly feels heavy after upgrading,
this import is the first thing to check.

Apps that compose their own provider tree can keep using `NextAdapterProvider`
directly; `LayoutProvider` from `/next` only removes the boilerplate.

## In any other React app

Do nothing. The defaults render `<a>` and `<img>`, read
`window.location.pathname` (popstate-aware, `""` on the server) and navigate
with `window.location.assign`.

## Supplying your own

Pass `adapters` to `AdapterProvider`. It is a **partial** override merged onto
whatever the nearest provider already supplies, so you can replace only the
piece your framework does differently.

React Router:

```tsx
import { AdapterProvider } from "@once-ui-system/core";
import { Link, useLocation, useNavigate } from "react-router";

<AdapterProvider
  adapters={{
    Link: ({ href, ...props }) => <Link to={href} {...props} />,
    usePathname: () => useLocation().pathname,
    useNavigate,
  }}
>
  {children}
</AdapterProvider>
```

Because providers merge rather than replace, nesting one inside another is a
legitimate way to override a single adapter for one subtree.

## Why detection is not attempted

The obvious wish is for core to notice Next.js and wire itself up. It cannot,
and the reason is worth knowing before you try it in your own app.

Two of the four adapters are hooks, and the two implementations call **different
numbers of hooks**: the DOM `useNavigate` returns a closure and calls none, the
Next one calls `useRouter` and `useCallback`. Swapping them after mount raises
*"Rendered more hooks than during the previous render."* So resolution has to
settle before the first render — and a browser bundle has no synchronous way to
conditionally resolve an optional module. An explicit import is the
bundler-independent version of the same thing.

## Reading the adapters

`useAdapters()` returns the resolved set. Use it when you are building a
component of your own that should route the same way core's do.

useAdapters:

```tsx
const { Link, usePathname } = useAdapters();
const pathname = usePathname();

<Link href="/pricing" aria-current={pathname === "/pricing" ? "page" : undefined}>
  Pricing
</Link>
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `adapters (required)` | `Partial<OnceUIAdapters>` |  | Overrides. Anything omitted keeps the value from the nearest provider, or the DOM default. |
| `children (required)` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |

### OnceUIAdapters

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Link` | `ComponentType<AdapterLinkProps>` | `<a>` | Renders internal links. |
| `Image` | `ComponentType<AdapterImageProps>` | `<img>` | Renders images. Lazy unless priority is set. |
| `usePathname` | `() => string` | `window.location.pathname` | Current pathname. Popstate-aware; "" on the server. |
| `useNavigate` | `() => (href: string) => void` | `window.location.assign` | Imperative navigation. |

### AdapterImageProps

The image adapter's contract follows `next/image` semantics so the Next
implementation is a pass-through rather than a translation layer.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `src` | `string` | `-` | Image source. Required. |
| `alt` | `string` | `-` | Alternative text. Required. |
| `fill` | `boolean` | `false` | Absolutely fill the nearest positioned ancestor. |
| `priority` | `boolean` | `false` | Eager-load and raise fetch priority. |
| `unoptimized` | `boolean` | `false` | Skip framework image optimization. No-op for the DOM default. |
| `width` | `number` |  |  |
| `height` | `number` |  |  |

# DataThemeProvider

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/contexts/dataThemeProvider

> The DataThemeProvider enables global style default configuration for Once UI's data-viz components.

The `DataThemeProvider` is a context provider that allows you to override the default app-level data-viz styles configuration.

## Simple setup

Wrap your app with `DataThemeProvider` and pass the style configuration as props.

layout.tsx:

```tsx
<DataThemeProvider
variant="gradient" // flat | gradient | outline
mode="categorical" // categorical | divergent | sequential
height="24rem" // default chart height
axis={{
      stroke: "var(--neutral-alpha-weak)",
    }}
tick={{
      fill: "var(--neutral-on-background-weak)",
      fontSize: 11,
      line: false
    }}

>

    {children}

</DataThemeProvider>
```

## Advanced setup

Keep the chart defaults in one file, typed with [defineConfig](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/config#defineconfig), and spread them into the provider. The keys are the provider's prop names, so nothing is cast or renamed. We also recommend a `Providers` component to wrap your app.

Providers.tsx:

```tsx
"use client";

import { DataThemeProvider, ThemeProvider, IconProvider, ToastProvider } from "@once-ui-system/core";
import { dataStyle, style } from "@/resources/once-ui.config";

export function Providers({ children }: {
    children: React.ReactNode
}) {
    return (
      <ThemeProvider {...style}>
        <DataThemeProvider {...dataStyle}>
          <ToastProvider>
            <IconProvider>
              {children}
            </IconProvider>
          </ToastProvider>
        </DataThemeProvider>
      </ThemeProvider>
    );
}
```

once-ui.config.js:

```tsx
import { defineConfig } from "@once-ui-system/core/config";

export const { style, dataStyle } = defineConfig({
  style: { brand: "blue", accent: "indigo" },
  dataStyle: {
    variant: "gradient", // flat | gradient | outline
    mode: "categorical", // categorical | divergent | sequential
    height: "24rem", // default chart height
    axis: {
      stroke: "var(--neutral-alpha-weak)",
    },
    tick: {
      fill: "var(--neutral-on-background-weak)",
      fontSize: 11,
      line: false,
    },
  },
});
```

Pass the same `dataStyle` to [ThemeInit](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/contexts/themeProvider#ssr-hydration) as well, so `data-viz-style` is on `<html>` before the first paint: `<ThemeInit config={style} dataStyle={dataStyle} />`.

## API reference

### DataThemeProvider

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `children (required)` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
| `variant` | `ChartVariant` |  |  |
| `mode` | `ChartMode` |  |  |
| `height` | `number \| CSSUnit` |  |  |
| `axis` | `{ stroke: string; }` |  |  |
| `tick` | `{ fill: string; fontSize: number; line: boolean; }` |  |  |
| `variant` | `flat` | `gradient` | outline |
| `mode` | `categorical` | `divergent` | sequential |
| `height` | `number` | `24` |  |

## useDataTheme

`useDataTheme()` returns the current chart options plus a setter, so a control
can change how every chart on the page draws without each chart being rewired.
It throws outside a `DataThemeProvider`.

useDataTheme:

```tsx
const { mode, setChartOptions } = useDataTheme();

<SegmentedControl
  value={mode}
  buttons={[
    { value: "categorical", label: "Categorical" },
    { value: "divergent", label: "Divergent" },
  ]}
  onValueChange={(value) => setChartOptions({ mode: value as ChartOptions["mode"] })}
/>
```

`setChartOptions` takes a partial: anything you leave out keeps its current
value.

# IconProvider

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/contexts/iconProvider

> Once UI's icon provider component allows you to pass an object of icon instances to your application.

The `IconProvider` component is a context provider that allows you to pass an
object of icon instances to your application, merged with the 76 icons Once UI
ships built in.

An icon is anything that renders an SVG and needs no props — Once UI never
passes any. So icons from [react-icons](https://react-icons.github.io/react-icons/),
lucide, heroicons, or a component you wrote yourself all satisfy it. The
registry is typed structurally, so no icon library appears in your app's types
because of Once UI.

## Simple setup

Wrap your app with `IconProvider` and pass it the icons as props.

layout.tsx:

```tsx
import { HiHome } from "react-icons/hi2";

<IconProvider icons={{home: HiHome}}>
    {children}
</IconProvider>
```

## Advanced setup

You can create a separate file for all icons, for example `icons.ts`. We also recommend using a `Providers` component to wrap your app.

Providers.tsx:

```tsx
import { iconLibrary } from "../resources/icons.ts";
import { IconProvider, ToastProvider, ThemeProvider, DataThemeProvider } from "@once-ui-system/core";

export function Providers({ children }: {
    children: React.ReactNode
}) {
    return (
      <ThemeProvider>
        <DataThemeProvider>
          <ToastProvider>
            <IconProvider icons={iconLibrary}>
              {children}
            </IconProvider>
          </ToastProvider>
        </DataThemeProvider>
      </ThemeProvider>
    );
}
```

icons.ts:

```tsx
// Your own icons, merged with the ones Once UI ships
import {
    HiChevronUp,
    HiChevronDown,
    HiChevronRight,
    HiChevronLeft,
    HiOutlineArrowPath,
    HiOutlineSun,
    HiOutlineMoon,
    HiOutlineEye,
    HiOutlineEyeSlash,
    HiOutlineClipboard,
    HiOutlineMagnifyingGlass,
    HiOutlineLink,
    HiArrowUpRight,
    HiOutlineShieldCheck,
    HiOutlineSparkles,
    HiOutlineComputerDesktop,
    HiOutlineQuestionMarkCircle,
    HiOutlineInformationCircle,
    HiOutlineExclamationTriangle,
    HiOutlineExclamationCircle,
    HiOutlineCheckCircle,
    HiOutlineXMark,
    HiOutlineUser,
    HiOutlineEyeDropper,
    HiOutlineMinus,
    HiOutlinePlus,
    HiOutlineCalendar,
    HiOutlineDocumentDuplicate,
    HiOutlineCheck,
    HiOutlineArrowsPointingIn,
    HiOutlineArrowsPointingOut,
} from "react-icons/hi2";

export const iconLibrary = {
    chevronUp: HiChevronUp,
    chevronDown: HiChevronDown,
    chevronRight: HiChevronRight,
    chevronLeft: HiChevronLeft,
    refresh: HiOutlineArrowPath,
    light: HiOutlineSun,
    dark: HiOutlineMoon,
    help: HiOutlineQuestionMarkCircle,
    info: HiOutlineInformationCircle,
    warning: HiOutlineExclamationTriangle,
    danger: HiOutlineExclamationCircle,
    checkbox: HiOutlineCheck,
    check: HiOutlineCheckCircle,
    copy: HiOutlineDocumentDuplicate,
    eyeDropper: HiOutlineEyeDropper,
    clipboard: HiOutlineClipboard,
    person: HiOutlineUser,
    close: HiOutlineXMark,
    openLink: HiOutlineLink,
    arrowUpRight: HiArrowUpRight,
    minus: HiOutlineMinus,
    plus: HiOutlinePlus,
    calendar: HiOutlineCalendar,
    eye: HiOutlineEye,
    eyeOff: HiOutlineEyeSlash,
    search: HiOutlineMagnifyingGlass,
    security: HiOutlineShieldCheck,
    sparkle: HiOutlineSparkles,
    computer: HiOutlineComputerDesktop,
    minimize: HiOutlineArrowsPointingIn,
    maximize: HiOutlineArrowsPointingOut,
};

// Teach Once UI these names, so <Icon name="chevronUp" /> type-checks.
// Derived from the object above, so the two cannot drift apart.
declare module "@once-ui-system/core" {
  interface IconLibraryOverrides extends Record<keyof typeof iconLibrary, true> {}
}
```

## Type-checking your own names

`IconName` is a union of the built-in names, and `Icon` accepts nothing else.
Registering icons at runtime does not by itself teach TypeScript about them, so
extend the union by merging into `IconLibraryOverrides`:

icons.ts:

```tsx
export const iconLibrary = {
  rocket: HiOutlineRocketLaunch,
  github: FaGithub,
};

declare module "@once-ui-system/core" {
  interface IconLibraryOverrides extends Record<keyof typeof iconLibrary, true> {}
}
```

Deriving the interface from the object means the two cannot drift: add an icon
to the registry and its name type-checks immediately, remove one and every use
of it becomes a build error.

Two things to avoid. Do not annotate the registry as
`Record<string, IconType>` — that widens the keys to `string`, which collapses
`IconName` and lets every typo through. And do not list the names by hand; the
list will fall out of date.

## Default icons

Overwrite the default icons used in Once UI components (for example the chevron in the `Select` component) by providing new icons with the same keys to the `IconProvider`.

## Icon component

The [`Icon`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/icon) component is a wrapper around icon instances to control their size and color. We recommend
inserting icons through this component.

Example:

```tsx
<Icon
    name="help"
    onBackground="neutral-medium"
    size="m"/>
```
## useIcons

`useIcons()` returns the merged icon library — the defaults plus whatever the
nearest `IconProvider` added. Use it when you need to resolve a name to a
component yourself; for rendering, prefer
[`Icon`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/icon), which does this for you.

useIcons:

```tsx
const { icons } = useIcons();
const known = Object.keys(icons);

// Fall back rather than rendering nothing for an unregistered name.
<Icon name={known.includes(name) ? name : "info"} />
```

Unlike the other context hooks, `useIcons()` does not throw outside a provider —
it returns the default library, so a component that only needs built-in icons
works with no provider in the tree.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `icons` | `Partial<IconLibrary> \| Record<string, IconComponent>` |  | Icons to add or replace, keyed by name. Merged over the built-in library. |
| `children (required)` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |

# ToastProvider

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/contexts/toastProvider

> ToastProvider enables global toast notifications via context and renders them in a toast stack.

The `ToastProvider` wraps your app to provide access to `useToast`, allowing any component to trigger lightweight, dismissible toast messages globally.

## Simple setup

Wrap your app with `ToastProvider` to activate toast functionality.

layout.tsx:

```tsx
<ToastProvider>
    {children}
</ToastProvider>
```

## Advanced setup

We recommend using a `Providers` component to wrap your app. You can choose to display toasts at the top or bottom based on breakpoints.

ToastProvider:

```tsx
import { ToastProvider, ThemeProvider, DataThemeProvider, IconProvider } from "@once-ui-system/core";

export function Providers({ children }: {
    children: React.ReactNode
}) {
    return (
      <ThemeProvider>
        <DataThemeProvider>
          <ToastProvider
            s="top"
          >
            <IconProvider>
              {children}
            </IconProvider>
          </ToastProvider>
        </DataThemeProvider>
      </ThemeProvider>
    );
}
```

Use the `useToast()` hook to display notifications from anywhere in your app:

useToast:

```tsx
"use client";

import React, { useState } from "react";
import { Button, Row, useToast } from "@once-ui-system/core";

export function ToastExample() {
    const { addToast } = useToast();
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    const handleAddToast = (tone: 'success' | 'danger' | 'warning' | 'info') => {
      setCount(prev => prev + 1);
      const labels: Record<string, string> = {
        success: 'Success!',
        danger: 'Error!',
        warning: 'Warning!',
        info: 'Info',
      };
      addToast({
        tone,
        message: "Toast #" + (count + 1) + " - " + labels[tone],
        action: (tone === 'danger' || tone === 'warning') ? (
          <Button size="s" onClick={() => addToast({ tone: 'success', message: 'Retry successful!' })}>
            Retry
          </Button>
        ) : undefined,
      });
    };

    return (
      <Row gap="8" wrap>
        <Button size="s" onClick={() => handleAddToast('success')}>
          Show Success
        </Button>
        <Button size="s" variant="secondary" onClick={() => handleAddToast('danger')}>
          Show Error
        </Button>
        <Button size="s" variant="tertiary" onClick={() => handleAddToast('warning')}>
          Show Warning
        </Button>
        <Button size="s" variant="tertiary" onClick={() => handleAddToast('info')}>
          Show Info
        </Button>
      </Row>
    );

}
```

## Duration and removing a toast

`addToast` returns the new toast's id. Pass it to `removeToast` to take the toast down before it times out, such as a "Saving…" toast once the save is done. Each toast stays up for its `duration` in milliseconds: 6000 by default, and `Infinity` keeps it up until it is closed. The countdown pauses while the toast is hovered or has focus, and resumes with the time that was left.

Save with progress:

```tsx
const { addToast, removeToast } = useToast();

async function save() {
  const saving = addToast({ tone: "info", message: "Saving…", duration: Infinity });
  await saveDocument();
  removeToast(saving);
  addToast({ tone: "success", message: "Saved" });
}
```

`addToast` and `removeToast` keep the same identity for the provider's lifetime, so an effect can list them as dependencies without running again each time a toast appears. There is no need to hold them in a ref.

## The toast stack

The `ToastProvider` renders the toast stack itself, from the current list of toasts. The stack is internal in 3.0 (2.x exported it as `Toaster`), so there is nothing else to mount.

## API reference

### useToast

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `toasts` |  |  |  |
| `addToast` | `(toast: { message: ReactNode; tone: 'success' \| 'danger' \| 'warning' \| 'info'; action?: ReactNode; duration?: number }) => string` |  |  |
| `removeToast` | `(id: string) => void` |  |  |

### Toast

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `string` |  |  |
| `tone` | `brand` | `accent` | neutral |
| `message` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
| `action` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
| `duration` | `number` | `6000` | Milliseconds before it closes. Infinity keeps it up until it is closed. |

### ToastProvider

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `children (required)` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
| `xl` | `ToastPosition` |  |  |
| `l` | `ToastPosition` |  |  |
| `m` | `ToastPosition` |  |  |
| `s` | `ToastPosition` |  |  |
| `xs` | `ToastPosition` |  |  |

# Kbar

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/kbar

> The Kbar component provides a command palette for quick navigation and actions throughout your application using keyboard shortcuts.

The `Kbar` component provides a powerful command palette for your application, allowing users to quickly navigate and perform actions using keyboard shortcuts. It enhances productivity by providing a searchable interface for commands and navigation.

Kbar:

```tsx
const kbarItems: KbarItem[] = [
    {
      id: 'home',
      name: 'Home',
      section: 'Navigation',
      shortcut: ['H'],
      keywords: 'home main start',
      href: '/',
      icon: 'home'
    },
    {
      id: 'docs',
      name: 'Documentation',
      section: 'Navigation',
      shortcut: ['D'],
      keywords: 'docs guide help',
      href: '/docs',
      icon: 'document'
    }
];

function MyLayout({ children }) {
    return (
      <>
        <header>
          <Kbar items={kbarItems}>
            <Button prefixIcon="search">Search</Button>
          </Kbar>
        </header>
        <main>
          {children}
        </main>
      </>
    );
}
```

## Open from your own control

To open the palette from a header button, a menu item or a sidebar link, control it with `open` and `onOpenChange` and leave out `children`. ⌘K still toggles it, and Escape hands focus back to your button.

Controlled:

```tsx
"use client";

function Header() {
    const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
    return (
      <Row as="header" horizontal="between" vertical="center">
        <Logo />
        <Button prefixIcon="search" variant="secondary" onClick={() => setOpen(true)}>
          Search
        </Button>
        <Kbar items={kbarItems} open={open} onOpenChange={setOpen} />
      </Row>
    );
}
```

## Your own matching

By default a query matches item names, keywords and sections, case-insensitively, in the order you passed the items. To rank results yourself (typo tolerance, recent items first), pass `filter`: it gets the items and the query and returns the items to show, in order. Sections follow the order of their first item. Kbar only calls it for a non-empty query.

Ranking:

```tsx
const startsFirst: KbarFilter = (items, query) => {
    const q = query.toLowerCase();
    const hits = items.filter((item) => item.name.toLowerCase().includes(q));
    return [
      ...hits.filter((item) => item.name.toLowerCase().startsWith(q)),
      ...hits.filter((item) => !item.name.toLowerCase().startsWith(q)),
    ];
};

<Kbar items={kbarItems} filter={startsFirst} />
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `items (required)` | `KbarItem[]` |  | The commands, each with a label, an action and optional keywords. |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` |  | The trigger that opens it. Leave it out when your own control opens the palette. |
| `size` | `TShirtSizes` |  | Size of the search field. |
| `placeholder` | `string` |  |  |
| `filter` | `KbarFilter` |  | Your own matching and ranking: return the items to show for the query, in order. Without it, a case-insensitive match on name, keywords and section. |
| `labels` | `KbarLabels` |  | The palette's own words (dialog, results, noResults, navigate, goTo), for a translated interface. |
| `open` | `boolean` |  | Open or not, controlled, for opening the palette from a Button, a menu item or anywhere else. Leave it out and Kbar keeps its own state. |
| `defaultOpen` | `boolean` | `false` | The starting state when `open` is left out. |
| `onOpenChange` | `(open: boolean) => void` |  | Called with the state Kbar moves to: on ⌘K, the trigger, Escape, an option and a route change. |
| `children` |  |  |  |

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `string` |  |  |
| `name` | `string` |  |  |
| `section` | `string` |  |  |
| `shortcut` |  |  |  |
| `keywords` | `string` |  |  |
| `href` | `string` |  |  |
| `perform` | `() => void` |  |  |
| `icon` | `string` |  |  |
| `description` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
| `placeholder` | `string` |  |  |

size:

```tsx
const items = [
    { id: 'home', name: 'Home', section: 'Navigation', keywords: 'home', href: '/' },
];

<Kbar size="m" items={items}>
    <Button>Open</Button>
</Kbar>

<Kbar size="s" items={items}>
    <Button>Open (small)</Button>
</Kbar>

<Kbar size="l" items={items}>
    <Button>Open (large)</Button>
</Kbar>
```

## KbarItem

Each item in the command palette is defined by the `KbarItem` interface:

KbarItem:

```tsx
interface KbarItem {
    id: string;          // Unique identifier for the item
    name: string;        // Display name in the command palette
    section: string;     // Group name for organizing items
    shortcut: string[];  // Keyboard shortcut keys
    keywords: string;    // Search keywords
    href?: string;       // Navigation URL (optional)
    perform?: () => void; // Action to perform when selected (optional)
    icon?: string;       // Icon name from Once UI icon set (optional)
    description?: ReactNode; // Additional description (optional)
}
```

You must provide either `href` or `perform` for each item to define what happens when the item is selected.

## Accessibility

The Kbar component supports full keyboard navigation:

- `↑` / `↓`: Navigate between items
- `Enter`: Select the highlighted item
- `Esc`: Close the command palette

Users can also type to search and filter the available commands.

## Best practices

- Keep item names short and descriptive
- Use icons to make items more recognizable
- Group related items into logical sections
- Include relevant keywords to improve search results
- Provide keyboard shortcuts for frequently used actions
- Consider adding a visible button to open Kbar for discoverability

## Collapsing

`collapseBelow` folds the bar into an accordion, a list of groups that each expand in place, for narrow screens (2.x's `MobileMegaMenu`). Name a breakpoint and both are rendered, the bar shown above it and the accordion at and below it, switched by CSS, so nothing shifts on hydration. `"always"` renders only the accordion, for a mobile drawer of your own. `onClose` is called when a link in the accordion is chosen, to close the drawer around it.

Collapsing:

```tsx
// The bar above m, the accordion at m and below
<MegaMenu collapseBelow="m" menuGroups={menuGroups} />

// Only the accordion, inside a drawer of your own
<MegaMenu collapseBelow="always" menuGroups={menuGroups} onClose={() => setOpen(false)} />
```

## Usage

The bar is designed for desktop screens. Use `collapseBelow` (above) for the small ones, or hide it at a breakpoint yourself with `m={{hide: true}}`.

## Accessibility

The menu follows the disclosure navigation pattern, so every panel is reachable without a pointer.

- A group with a dropdown and no `href` renders its trigger as a button with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`. Enter or Space toggles its panel.
- A group with both an `href` and a dropdown stays a link, so Enter still navigates. Its panel opens when the link receives keyboard focus.
- ArrowDown on a trigger opens its panel and focuses the first item. ArrowDown and ArrowUp move between items inside a panel.
- Tab from an open trigger moves into its panel. Shift+Tab from the first item returns to the trigger, and Tab from the last item moves on to the next trigger.
- Escape closes the panel and returns focus to its trigger. Moving focus anywhere outside the menu closes it too.

Custom `content` takes part as well: any link, button or form field inside it is part of the panel's keyboard order.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `menuGroups (required)` | `MenuGroup[]` |  | The top-level items, each with the sections and links underneath it. |
| `className` | `string` |  |  |
| `collapseBelow` | `Breakpoint \| "always"` |  | Show the accordion instead of the bar at this breakpoint and below; "always" shows only the accordion. |
| `onClose` | `() => void` |  | Called when a link in the accordion is chosen, to dismiss the drawer around it. |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

### Types

```tsx
interface MenuGroup {
  id: string;
  label: ReactNode;
  suffixIcon?: string;
  href?: string;
  selected?: boolean;
  sections?: MenuSection[];
  content?: ReactNode; // Custom content slot for dropdown
}

interface MenuSection {
  title?: ReactNode;
  links: MenuLink[];
}

interface MenuLink {
  label: ReactNode;
  href: string;
  icon?: string;
  description?: ReactNode;
  selected?: boolean;
}
```

# Chat

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/chat

> Building blocks for chat interfaces: message bubbles, a message list that follows the conversation, a composer with send and attach, a typing indicator and inbox rows.

Five components cover the parts every chat has: `ChatMessage`, `ChatMessageList`, `ChatComposer`, `TypingIndicator` and `ConversationItem`. They work for conversations between people and for an assistant that streams its replies.

Conversation:

```tsx
import {
  ChatComposer,
  ChatMessage,
  ChatMessageList,
  Column,
  TypingIndicator,
} from "@once-ui-system/core";

<Column fillWidth height="448px">
  <ChatMessageList aria-label="Chat with Lorant" stack>
    {messages.map((message) => (
      <ChatMessage
        key={message.id}
        from={message.from}
        name={message.from === "other" ? "Lorant" : undefined}
        avatarProps={message.from === "other" ? { src: "/images/avatar.jpg" } : undefined}
        time={message.time}
        status={message.from === "self" ? "read" : undefined}
      >
        {message.text}
      </ChatMessage>
    ))}
    {typing && <TypingIndicator aria-label="Lorant is typing" marginLeft="48" />}
  </ChatMessageList>
  <ChatComposer onSend={({ text, files }) => send(text, files)} attach />
</Column>
```

## ChatMessage

One message: the bubble, its author, the time and the delivery state. `from="self"` puts it on the right with the brand tint. Set `grouped` on a follow-up from the same author: the name is dropped and the avatar keeps its space, so the bubbles line up. A `Date` in `time` is formatted for the reader and rendered as a `<time>` element: the time of day by default, or with `timeFormat="relative"` a short distance from now ("now", "2m", "1h", then the date) in the reader's language that keeps itself current, with the full time on hover.

ChatMessage:

```tsx
<ChatMessage name="Lorant" avatarProps={{ src: "/images/avatar.jpg" }} time="9:05">
  Did the new build go out?
</ChatMessage>
<ChatMessage grouped avatarProps={{ src: "/images/avatar.jpg" }} time="9:05">
  The release notes look good.
</ChatMessage>
<ChatMessage from="self" time="9:07" status="read">
  It did, about an hour ago.
</ChatMessage>
<ChatMessage from="self" time="9:08" status="failed" onRetry={retry}>
  Here is the link
</ChatMessage>
```

Relative time:

```tsx
<ChatMessage from="self" time={sentAt} timeFormat="relative" status="delivered">
  On my way.
</ChatMessage>
```

The same wording is exported as `formatRelativeTime(date, { style, locale })` for anything else that labels a time: `"narrow"` (the default) gives "now", "2m", "1h", "3d", "2w" and then the date; `"short"` and `"long"` give "5 min. ago" and "5 minutes ago". It uses the platform's `Intl`, so every locale reads in its own words with nothing to translate.

`variant="plain"` drops the bubble for a flat, team-chat layout where every message reads left to right. `attachments` takes media or link previews under the text, `footer` takes reactions, and `actions` takes controls that show while the message is hovered or focused (they are always shown on touch screens).

Plain:

```tsx
<ChatMessage
  variant="plain"
  name="Lorant"
  avatarProps={{ src: "/images/avatar.jpg" }}
  time="9:05"
  footer={
    <Row gap="4">
      <Tag size="s">👍 3</Tag>
      <Tag size="s">🎉 1</Tag>
    </Row>
  }
  actions={<IconButton icon="chat" variant="tertiary" size="s" tooltip="Reply" />}
>
  Shipping the chat blocks today.
</ChatMessage>
```

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `children` | `ReactNode` |  | The message body: text, or any content. |
| `from` | `"self" \| "other"` | `other` | Whose message it is. `self` sits on the right. |
| `name` | `ReactNode` |  | The author's name, shown above the first message of a group. |
| `avatarProps` | `AvatarProps` |  | The author's avatar. Leave it out for no avatar column. |
| `time` | `ChatTime` |  | When it was sent. A `Date` is formatted; anything else renders as given. |
| `timeFormat` | `ChatTimeFormat` | `clock` | How a `Date` reads: the time of day, or relative ("2m", "1h"), kept current. |
| `status` | `ChatMessageStatus` |  | Delivery state, shown next to the time. |
| `statusLabels` | `Partial<Record<ChatMessageStatus, string>>` |  | Replaces the status words, for another language. |
| `onRetry` | `() => void` |  | Adds a retry button to a failed message. |
| `retryLabel` | `string` | `Retry` | The retry button's label. |
| `grouped` | `boolean` | `false` | A follow-up from the same author. |
| `stack` | `"start" \| "middle" \| "end"` |  | Its place in a stack of quick messages from one author. `ChatMessageList` sets it with `stack`. |
| `variant` | `"bubble" \| "plain"` | `bubble` | A tinted bubble, or a flat row. |
| `attachments` | `ReactNode` |  | Content under the bubble. |
| `footer` | `ReactNode` |  | A row under the attachments, such as reactions. |
| `actions` | `ReactNode` |  | Controls shown on hover or focus. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

## ChatMessageList

The scrolling column a conversation lives in. It starts at the newest message and follows new ones, including content that grows on its own like a streamed reply, while the reader is at the bottom. Once they scroll up to read history it stays where they are. `onReachStart` fires when they reach the top, to load older messages. The list is a `log` live region, so screen readers announce new messages.

Give it a parent with a fixed or flexible height; it fills the space and scrolls inside it.

`stack` draws a quick run of messages from one author as one block: the bubbles close up and round less where they meet, the name and avatar show once, and the time and delivery state show under the last message. Messages stack when they sit next to each other with the same `from`, `name` and `variant`, sent within `stackWithin` minutes (5 by default) of each other. There is nothing to compute per message; the conversation at the top of this page uses it.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `stickToBottom` | `boolean` | `true` | Start at the newest message and follow new ones while the reader is at the bottom. |
| `onReachStart` | `() => void` |  | Called when the reader scrolls to the top. |
| `aria-label` | `string` |  |  |
| `stack` | `boolean` | `false` | Draw a quick run of messages from one author as one block. |
| `stackWithin` | `number` | `5` | The longest gap, in minutes, between two messages that still stack. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

## ChatComposer

The input bar. The field grows with the draft up to about eight lines, Enter sends and Shift+Enter starts a new line (an Enter that confirms an IME composition never sends). `onSend` gets the trimmed text and the attached files. If it returns a promise the send button shows loading; the field clears when the promise resolves and keeps the draft when it rejects, so showing the error is up to you.

`attach` adds a button that opens the file picker. Pasted images are attached too. Picked images show as thumbnails, other files as chips with their name; each has a remove button. Pass `{ accept, multiple }` to limit what can be picked.

ChatComposer:

```tsx
<ChatComposer
  attach={{ accept: "image/*,.pdf" }}
  onSend={async ({ text, files }) => {
    await api.send(text, files);
  }}
/>
```

### Toolbar

`toolbar` adds a row under the field for chips, a model picker or other controls, and `hint` puts quiet text such as "Enter to send" before the send button. With either one, the attach button moves to the start of that row, and `actions` and send to its end. `sendIcon` swaps the send button's icon. Without them the composer stays one row.

Toolbar:

```tsx
<ChatComposer
  attach
  sendIcon="arrowUp"
  hint={<><Kbd>Enter</Kbd> to send</>}
  toolbar={
    <>
      <Tag selected label="Your library" prefixIcon="document" />
      <Tag label="Q4 pricing" suffixIcon="chevronDown" selected={false} />
    </>
  }
  onSend={({ text }) => ask(text)}
/>
```

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `onSend (required)` | `(message: ChatComposerMessage) => void \| Promise<void>` |  | Called with `{ text, files }`. Return a promise to show loading. |
| `value` | `string` |  | The draft, when the parent owns it. |
| `defaultValue` | `string` | `""` | The first draft, when the composer owns it. |
| `onValueChange` | `(value: string) => void` |  | Called on every edit. |
| `placeholder` | `string` | `Write a message` | Text shown in the empty field. |
| `attach` | `boolean \| { accept?: string; multiple?: boolean }` | `false` | Show the attach button; an object sets `accept` and `multiple`. |
| `sendOnEnter` | `boolean` | `true` | Enter sends. Off, Enter starts a new line. |
| `loading` | `boolean` | `false` | Show the send button loading and block another send. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | `false` | Disable the field and buttons. |
| `aria-label` | `string` |  |  |
| `sendLabel` | `string` | `Send` | The send button's label. |
| `attachLabel` | `string` | `Attach files` | The attach button's label. |
| `removeLabel` | `(fileName: string) => string = (fileName) => `Remove ${fileName}`` |  | The label of an attachment's remove button, from its file name. |
| `prefix` | `ReactNode` |  | Content before the field, such as an emoji picker. |
| `actions` | `ReactNode` |  | More controls before the send button. |
| `toolbar` | `ReactNode` |  | Controls in a row under the field, after the attach button. |
| `hint` | `ReactNode` |  | Quiet text before the send button, such as "Enter to send". Turns on the row under the field. |
| `sendIcon` | `IconName` | `send` | The send button's icon. |
| `maxLength` | `number` |  | The longest draft allowed. |
| `id` | `string` |  | The field's id. One is generated when it is left out. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

## TypingIndicator

Three pulsing dots for someone typing or a reply being generated. It is a `status` region, so its label is announced once. With reduced motion the dots fade instead of bouncing.

TypingIndicator:

```tsx
<TypingIndicator aria-label="Lorant is typing" />
<TypingIndicator bubble={false} label="Lorant is typing" />
```

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `ReactNode` |  | Visible text next to the dots. |
| `aria-label` | `string` |  |  |
| `bubble` | `boolean` | `true` | Draw the dots in a bubble, to stand in for a reply. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

## ConversationItem

One row of an inbox: the avatar, the name, the last message and its time, and an unread count. It is a button with `onClick` and a link with `href`, and `selected` marks the open conversation with `aria-current`. A `Date` in `time` shows the time today, the weekday this week and the date before that.

ConversationItem:

```tsx
<Column maxWidth="384px" gap="2">
  {conversations.map((conversation) => (
    <ConversationItem
      key={conversation.id}
      name={conversation.name}
      preview={conversation.lastMessage}
      time={conversation.updatedAt}
      unread={conversation.unread}
      avatarProps={{ src: conversation.avatar }}
      selected={conversation.id === openId}
      href={"/chat/" + conversation.id}
    />
  ))}
</Column>
```

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name (required)` | `ReactNode` |  | Who the conversation is with, or its title. |
| `preview` | `ReactNode` |  | The last message, cut to one line. |
| `time` | `ChatTime` |  | When the last message was sent. |
| `avatarProps` | `AvatarProps` |  | The avatar on the left. |
| `unread` | `number \| boolean` |  | Unread messages: a number shows a count, `true` a dot. |
| `unreadLabel` | `(count: number \| true) => string` | `defaultUnreadLabel` | What a screen reader hears for the unread count. |
| `selected` | `boolean` | `false` | The open conversation. |
| `typing` | `boolean` | `false` | Show the typing label in place of the preview. |
| `typingLabel` | `ReactNode` | `typing…` | The typing label. |
| `href` | `string` |  | Open the conversation as a link. |
| `onClick` | `(event: React.MouseEvent<HTMLElement>) => void` |  | Open the conversation as a button. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# AI

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/ai

> Pieces for AI products: a loader drawn from the Once UI mark, a working line that cycles through playful verbs, voice chat animations that follow the audio, and a customizable mascot.

Use these where an assistant is doing something the person is waiting on. Every piece takes the
brand color, so inside a themed chat it follows the chat's theme, and every piece keeps saying
"working" under reduced motion without moving.

## WorkingIndicator

A moving mark and a verb that changes every few seconds, like "Imagining…" or "Noodling…". The
first render always shows the first verb, so server and client agree; the order shuffles after
mount.

Default:

```tsx
<WorkingIndicator />
```

### Your own words

Pass `verbs` to give a product its own voice, or spread `workingVerbs` to add to the default list.
`label` shows one fixed line instead, for a step you can name.

Verbs:

```tsx
<WorkingIndicator verbs={["Brewing", "Steeping", "Pouring"]} />
<WorkingIndicator verbs={[...workingVerbs, "Defragmenting"]} />
<WorkingIndicator label="Searching the docs…" />
```

### Elapsed time and a hint

`showElapsed` counts seconds since `startedAt` (or since the indicator appeared), and `detail` adds
a quiet hint after it.

Elapsed:

```tsx
<WorkingIndicator showElapsed startedAt={run.startedAt} detail="esc to stop" />
```

### Sizes

Sizes:

```tsx
<WorkingIndicator size="s" />
<WorkingIndicator size="m" />
<WorkingIndicator size="l" />
```

## VoiceVisualizer

The animation for a voice conversation. Each state moves differently: idle breathes, listening
ripples, thinking swirls and speaking pulses like syllables. Give it the microphone stream while
listening and the reply's `<audio>` element while speaking, and it follows the real sound. Use
`orb` for a full-screen voice mode and `bars` for a composer or a call bar.

Audio:

```tsx
const [stream, setStream] = useState<MediaStream | null>(null);

<VoiceVisualizer state="listening" source={stream} />
<VoiceVisualizer variant="bars" state="speaking" source={replyAudioElement} />
```

Level:

```tsx
<VoiceVisualizer state={state} level={levelFromYourSdk} />
```

Levels are written straight to CSS variables every frame, so a live microphone never re-renders
React. When your voice SDK already gives you a loudness number, pass it as `level` instead. To drive
something of your own, `useAudioLevel(source)` returns the same loudness from 0 to 1.

Sizes and colors:

```tsx
<VoiceVisualizer size="s" state="speaking" />
<VoiceVisualizer size="m" state="speaking" tone="accent" />
<VoiceVisualizer size="m" variant="bars" bars={9} state="speaking" tone="neutral" />
```

## Mascot

A companion for an assistant: one soft, single-color shape with a pair of eyes. It idles, listens,
thinks, speaks and sleeps, with a mood on top (happy, surprised, sad, skeptical, wink, focused,
determined). By default the eyes are tiles of the Once UI mark, and while it thinks they turn like
the `LogoSpinner`. When it looks around, the eyes slide over the body and the one nearer the edge
narrows, as if the body were round; while speaking, the body pulses with the reply's audio.

States:

```tsx
<Mascot state="thinking" />
<Mascot state="listening" mood="happy" />
<Mascot state="speaking" source={replyAudioElement} />
```

### Make it yours

Every part of the look is a prop, so two products never have to share a character. `color` takes a
scheme or any CSS color and every shade comes from it; `roundness`, `aspect` or your own `bodyPath`
set the outline; `surface` is `glossy`, `matte`, `flat` or `glass`. `eyes` is `tile`, `pill`,
`round`, `wide`, `dot` or your own path, placed with `eyeSize`, `eyeSpacing` and `eyeHeight`.
`mouth`, `brows` and `cheeks` add features that follow the mood, `accessory` dresses it (below), and `personality` makes it `calm` or `bouncy`. Or pass a `seed` (a product name, a user
id) and `mascotLook(seed)` picks a whole look; props you pass still win.

Customize:

```tsx
<Mascot eyes="pill" brows mouth="smile" color="#3fb6ff" />
<Mascot surface="matte" roundness={0.3} cheeks mouth="dot" color="#5ee68a" />
<Mascot surface="glass" eyes="wide" aspect={1.3} color="accent" />
<Mascot surface="flat" eyes="dot" mouth="smile" color="#ffc53d" personality="bouncy" />
<Mascot seed="acme" />
<Mascot seed="zest" />
```

### Seeds that read words

A seed is split into words at dashes, underscores, spaces, digits and camelCase, and the words it
knows describe the mascot: colours set the hue (`red`, `mint`, `ink` or a hex like `#3fe3f2`), animals
set the body and, where they have them, the ears (`fox`, `panda`, `frog`, `robot`), moods set the eyes,
mouth and how it moves (`happy`, `sleepy`, `grumpy`), and objects add accessories (`royal` a crown, `dj`
headphones, `astro` a helmet). An animal brings its own colour unless the seed names one. Anything the
words leave open comes from the seed's hash, so a username with no known words still gets a stable
mascot of its own. `readSeedWords(seed)` says which words it understood, and `MASCOT_SEED_WORDS` lists
them all.

Seeds:

```tsx
<Mascot seed="happy-red-fox" />
<Mascot seed="sleepyPandaDJ" />
<Mascot seed={user.username} />

readSeedWords("royal-ink-cat");
// { matched: ["royal", "ink", "cat"], accessory: ["crown", "catEars"], look: { ... }, unmatched: [] }
```

### Canonical mascots

Some names stand for a real identity and draw a hand-made character instead of a generated one:
`once-ui` is the Once UI mark come alive, `quasar` is Quasar, and every Dopler product (`stack`,
`aveiro`, `chirio`, `tavilio`, `sigilio` and the rest) has its own. Spelling, case and dashes don't
matter ("Once UI", "onceui"), but the whole seed has to be the name, so `once-ui-fan` is generated as
usual. Props you pass still win, so the owner of an identity can recolour or dress it.

Core can't know who typed a seed. Where people choose the text (a username, an agent's name), show the
canonical mascot only to its owner and pass `canonical={false}` to everyone else; reserve
`MASCOT_IDENTITY_KEYS` in sign-ups so nobody else can hold the name.

Canonical:

```tsx
<Mascot seed="once-ui" />
<Mascot seed="quasar" mood="happy" />

// A name someone typed: canonical only for the identity's owner.
const owned = mascotIdentity(agent.name)?.owner === workspace.owner;
<Mascot seed={agent.name} canonical={owned} />

mascotSvg({ seed: "sigilio" }); // the same character in an OG image
```

### Accessories

Nine built-in accessories, flat and chunky so they read at avatar size: `antenna`, `bow`, `beanie`,
`headphones`, `sprout`, `helmet`, `crown`, `catEars` and `partyHat`. Each one is placed from the body's
own outline, a drawn `bodyPath` included, so it fits a block, an egg or a circle (ears grow out of the
head instead of floating over it), and moves and squashes with it. Pass a list to wear
several, and `accessoryColor` to tint them all one color. Your own SVG still works: draw it in the
body's 200 × 200 box.

Accessories:

```tsx
<Mascot surface="flat" accessory="helmet" />
<Mascot surface="flat" accessory={["crown", "bow"]} accessoryColor="#ffd24d" />
```

`accessory` moves with the body and leans a little toward where the mascot looks, like a head
tilting. Something that belongs to the face, such as a beak, a nose, glasses or whiskers, goes in
`faceAccessory` instead: it rides on the face layer, so it turns with the gaze, glances up while
thinking, drops when it sleeps or is sad, and jumps with a poke, as the eyes and cheeks do. Draw it in
the same 200 × 200 box; with the default look the eyes sit at 71,96 and 129,96.

Face accessories:

```tsx
<Mascot
  eyes="round"
  mouth="none"
  faceAccessory={<path d="M88 112 Q100 106 112 112 L100 130 Z" fill="#ffb648" />}
/>
```

### Cube

`working="cube"` gives the mascot something to do while it works. At rest it is the same soft
blob with its face. When it starts thinking, the face fades, the blob firms up into a 2 × 2 cube
and it turns its layers like a puzzle. When the work is done it solves the cube, turns it 45° into
the Once UI mark for a beat, and softens back into the blob with its face, a little happier.

`sides` colors the cube: `classic` keeps the puzzle colors with the front in the mascot's color,
`tints` uses shades of it, `mono` paints every side the same, or pass a color per side.
`face="flat"` draws the eyes, brows and mouth flat on the body; `surface="flat"` turns the light
off, so the shape is one solid color. Everything else from the flat mascot carries over.

Cube:

```tsx
<Mascot working="cube" state={busy ? "thinking" : "idle"} />
<Mascot working="cube" sides="tints" face="flat" eyes="tile" />
<Mascot working="cube" sides="mono" surface="flat" eyes="pill" color="accent" />
<Mascot working="cube" sides={{ top: "#ffc53d", right: "#3fb6ff" }} />
```

The cube draws with WebGL and no extra dependency. It only animates while it is on screen, and
where WebGL is missing it renders the flat mascot instead.

### D20

`working="d20"` works the same way with a twenty-sided die. While it thinks, the blob firms into
the die and tumbles, now slow, now in a quick spin. When the work is done it lands with a face
toward you, point up, holds it for a beat and softens back into the blob with its face. The die
takes the mascot's color, and every look prop carries over; `sides` only applies to the cube.

D20:

```tsx
<Mascot working="d20" state={busy ? "thinking" : "idle"} />
<Mascot working="d20" color="accent" eyes="pill" />
<Mascot working="d20" surface="matte" face="flat" />
```

## LogoSpinner

The four tiles of the Once UI mark, moving. `twist` parts the tiles, turns a quarter and clicks
them back; `wave` lifts one tile at a time. Keep `Spinner` for buttons and fields, and use this one
where the product's own loader belongs.

Variants:

```tsx
<LogoSpinner size="xl" />
<LogoSpinner size="xl" variant="wave" />
<LogoSpinner size="xl" tone="accent" />
<LogoSpinner size="xl" tone="neutral" speed={2.4} />
```

## Accessibility

`WorkingIndicator` is one `status` region with a fixed name, "Working" unless you pass `aria-label`,
so a screen reader announces it once instead of reading every new verb. With reduced motion the
tiles stop moving and fade in turn, the verbs swap without sliding and the shimmer is off.

`VoiceVisualizer` is a `status` region that announces its state ("Listening", "Speaking"). With
reduced motion its stand-in animations stop; real audio still shows, as glow on the orb and as bar
height, because that is feedback the person needs while they talk.

`Mascot` is one image named for what it is doing ("Assistant, thinking"). With reduced motion it
holds still and keeps its poses and expressions; it does not blink, bob or pulse on its own, and
the cube shows while it thinks but does not turn.

## API reference

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

# Social

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/social

> Animated reactions for posts, comments and chat: each reaction has its own gesture, a pick bursts and updates the count, and an app can bring its own images.

Reactions are the smallest way to answer a post, so they should feel good to leave. Every reaction
moves in its own way: a heart beats, a thumbs-up nods, a laugh shakes, fire flickers. Picking one
plays its gesture, sends a few copies flying out of the chip and updates the count. To roll the
number, pass `renderCount` and draw it with CountFx from `@once-ui-system/fx`.

## Reactions

A chip for each reaction in use, with how many people left it, and an add button that opens every
option. Tap a chip to add your reaction or take it back. One reaction per person by default.

Feed post:

```tsx
const options = [
  { value: "❤️", label: "Love" },
  { value: "👍", label: "Like" },
  { value: "😂", label: "Haha" },
  { value: "😮", label: "Wow" },
  { value: "😢", label: "Sad" },
  { value: "🔥", label: "Fire" },
];

<Reactions
  options={options}
  counts={post.reactionCounts}
  value={post.myReaction}
  onValueChange={(value, { option, selected }) => react(post.id, option.value, selected)}
/>
```

### Counts that keep up

`counts` includes the viewer's own reaction, as `value` has it. When the viewer picks another one,
the numbers move at once, before your server answers; when new `counts` arrive, they take over, and
the viewer is never counted twice. So you can send the change and refetch, without keeping an
optimistic copy of the counts yourself.

### Several per person

`multiple` lets a person leave several reactions, as in chat. `value` is then a list.

Chat:

```tsx
<Reactions size="s" multiple effect="float" options={options} counts={counts} value={mine} onValueChange={setMine} />
```

### Effects

`effect="burst"` (the default) sends six small copies out of the chip, `float` lifts one larger copy
up and away, and `none` keeps only the gesture.

## Your own reactions

A reaction can be an image instead of an emoji: give it `src`, such as an uploaded animated WebP or
GIF. It plays as it is, so set `motion="none"` when the image already moves, or pick a gesture for a
still one. An emoji can take a different gesture too.

Custom:

```tsx
<Reactions
  options={[
    { value: "party", label: "Party", src: "/reactions/party.webp", motion: "none" },
    { value: "ship", label: "Ship it", src: "/reactions/ship.webp", motion: "none" },
    { value: "orbit", label: "Orbit", emoji: "🪐", motion: "spin" },
  ]}
  counts={counts}
/>
```

Store the `value` with each reaction, not the image, so an app can change a reaction's picture later.
A counted value that `options` no longer lists still shows, as plain text, so no one's reaction
disappears when the set changes. For an animated set that matches the emoji, Google's
[Noto Animated Emoji](https://googlefonts.github.io/noto-emoji-animation/) (CC BY 4.0) works as
`src`, as above. To draw a reaction any other way, such as with Lottie, pass `renderGlyph`.

## Reaction

One reaction on its own, with its gesture. It plays once each time the pointer arrives
(`trigger="hover"`), every few seconds (`loop`), or when `playKey` changes (`manual`).

Gestures:

```tsx
<Reaction value="❤️" size="xl" trigger="loop" />
<Reaction value="party" label="Party" src="/reactions/party.webp" />
```

The gestures are `beat`, `nod`, `shake`, `pop`, `droop`, `flicker`, `spin`, `wave` and `bounce`.
Known emoji get a fitting one (`reactionMotion` tells you which); anything else bounces.

## Accessibility

The row is a group named "Reactions". Each chip is a toggle button named for its reaction and count
("Love, 12") with `aria-pressed` for the viewer's own. The add button opens a group of toggle
buttons that the arrow keys move through; Escape closes it and gives focus back. With reduced motion
nothing moves: the gestures and the burst are off, and the reactions still
change at once.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `options (required)` | `ReactionOption[]` |  | The reactions people can pick: value, label, emoji or src, motion. |
| `counts` | `Record<string, number>` |  | People per reaction, by value, including the viewer's own. |
| `value` | `ReactionValue` |  | The viewer's reaction: a value or null, or a list with multiple. |
| `defaultValue` | `ReactionValue` |  | The starting value when uncontrolled. |
| `onValueChange` | `(value: ReactionValue, change: ReactionChange) => void` |  | Called with the next value and { option, selected }. |
| `multiple` | `boolean` | `false` | Several reactions per person. |
| `showAll` | `boolean` | `false` | A chip for every option, even at zero. |
| `picker` | `boolean` | `true` | The add button that opens every option. |
| `open` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `defaultOpen` | `boolean` | `false` |  |
| `onOpenChange` | `(open: boolean) => void` |  |  |
| `effect` | `"burst" \| "float" \| "none"` | `burst` | burst, float or none. |
| `size` | `"s" \| "m" \| "l"` | `m` | s, m or l. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | `false` |  |
| `renderGlyph` | `(option: ReactionOption) => ReactNode` |  | Draw a reaction yourself, such as with Lottie. |
| `addLabel` | `string` | `Add reaction` | The add button's name. |
| `aria-label` | `string` |  |  |
| `renderCount` | `(count: number, value: string) => ReactNode` |  | Draw a count yourself, such as with CountFx from @once-ui-system/fx. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value (required)` | `string` |  | What the reaction is stored as; the emoji drawn when there is no emoji or src. |
| `label` | `string` |  | What screen readers hear. |
| `emoji` | `string` |  | The emoji to draw. |
| `src` | `string` |  | An image instead, such as an animated WebP. |
| `motion` | `ReactionMotion` |  | beat, nod, shake, pop, droop, flicker, spin, wave, bounce or none. |
| `size` | `"s" \| "m" \| "l" \| "xl"` | `m` | s, m, l or xl. |
| `trigger` | `"hover" \| "loop" \| "manual"` | `hover` | hover, loop or manual. |
| `playKey` | `number \| string` |  | Change it to play the gesture again. |
| `decorative` | `boolean` | `false` | Hidden from screen readers when a control already names it. |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
