# Map

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/map

> An interactive map on free OpenStreetMap tiles that follows the theme, with React markers, clustering, popups and a controlled viewport.

`Map` draws an interactive map with [MapLibre GL](https://maplibre.org/) on [OpenFreeMap](https://openfreemap.org/) tiles: OpenStreetMap data, no API key, no account and no view limit. The basemap switches between light and dark with the theme, and its background takes the page background token, so a map sits on the page instead of on top of it. Markers are React content, so prices, avatars and buttons on the map are ordinary Once UI components.

## Installation

`maplibre-gl` is an optional peer dependency, like `prismjs` for `CodeBlock`. Install it next to Once UI and import the map from its own entry point, so an app without a map never loads it:

```bash
npm install maplibre-gl
```

```tsx
import { Map, MapMarker } from "@once-ui-system/core/map";

<Map height={384} defaultViewport={{ center: [19.0402, 47.4979], zoom: 12 }}>
  <MapMarker position={[19.0402, 47.4979]} />
</Map>
```

Positions are `[longitude, latitude]`, the order MapLibre and GeoJSON use. The map renders on the client only; on the server and until MapLibre loads it draws an empty frame of the same size, so the page does not shift.

## Units and status

For things that move or change state (vehicles, crews, sensors), give each pin an `icon` for what it is and a `tone` for its state. Both show at rest, so a dispatcher reads the board without opening a pin; the name can wait until the pin is active.

```tsx
<MapPin
  icon="heart"
  tone="danger"
  active={unit.id === active}
  onClick={() => setActive(unit.id)}
  aria-label="M12, Responding"
>
  {unit.id === active ? "M12 · Responding" : undefined}
</MapPin>
```

## Listings, clustering and popups

`MapMarkers` takes your items (each with an `id` and a `position`) and renders one marker per item. `cluster` merges markers that overlap into a count that zooms in when pressed. `activeId` lifts one marker above the rest, for the item hovered in a result list. `bounds` frames a list of positions and frames it again whenever the list changes, so a new search is always in view.

```tsx
const [hovered, setHovered] = useState<string>();
const [open, setOpen] = useState<Listing>();

<Map height={512} bounds={listings.map((listing) => listing.position)}>
  <MapMarkers
    items={listings}
    cluster
    activeId={hovered ?? open?.id}
    renderItem={(listing) => (
      <MapPin
        active={listing.id === (hovered ?? open?.id)}
        onClick={() => setOpen(listing)}
        onMouseEnter={() => setHovered(listing.id)}
        onMouseLeave={() => setHovered(undefined)}
      >
        {formatPrice(listing.price)}
      </MapPin>
    )}
  />
  {open && (
    <MapPopup position={open.position} onClose={() => setOpen(undefined)}>
      <Text textVariant="label-strong-m">{open.title}</Text>
      <Button size="s" variant="secondary" href={`/listings/${open.id}`}>View listing</Button>
    </MapPopup>
  )}
</Map>
```

`MapPin` is the marker Once UI draws: a pill with a label, or a dot without one. With `href` it is a link and with `onClick` a button, so it is reachable by Tab; tabbing onto a pin outside the view pans it in. `MapPopup` is a surface card above a point; render it while it is open, and Escape or its close button call `onClose`.

## Any content as a marker

`MapMarker` pins whatever you give it. `anchor` says which part of the content touches the point: `bottom` (the default) for a pin, `center` for an avatar.

```tsx
<Map height={384} bounds={venues.map((venue) => venue.position)} controls={false}>
  {venues.map((venue) => (
    <MapMarker key={venue.id} position={venue.position} anchor="center">
      <Avatar size="m" value={venue.name[0]} />
    </MapMarker>
  ))}
</Map>
```

## Areas

`MapCircle` marks an area on the ground, sized in metres, in a `tone`. It scales with the map, which makes it the honest way to show an approximate address.

```tsx
<Map height={384} defaultViewport={{ center: [19.0545, 47.5065], zoom: 14 }}>
  <MapCircle position={[19.0545, 47.5065]} radius={400} />
</Map>
```

## Routes

`MapRoute` draws a path in a `tone`: a delivery, a run, a flight. Give it `progress` (0 to 1) and the part travelled is solid while the rest is dashed, so a moving courier reads at a glance. `dashed` draws a planned route. The line sits on a casing in the page colour, so it reads on either basemap.

```tsx
<Map height={384} defaultViewport={{ center: [19.0506, 47.5034], zoom: 14 }}>
  <MapRoute path={route} progress={0.4} />
</Map>
```

## Globe and 3D buildings

`projection="globe"` curves the world into a globe when zoomed out and flattens it as you zoom in, so a camera travelling between cities reads as a journey. `buildings="3d"` raises buildings to their real height from zoom 13. They run from the neutral surface up to the brand colour for the tallest, and follow the theme like the rest of the map. Tilt the camera with `pitch` to see them.

```tsx
<Map
  height={512}
  projection="globe"
  buildings="3d"
  defaultViewport={{ center: [19.0457, 47.507], zoom: 15.5, pitch: 60, bearing: -20 }}
/>
```

## Controlled viewport

`viewport`, `defaultViewport` and `onViewportChange` follow the same contract as every other controlled prop in Once UI. `onViewportChange` fires when a pan or zoom ends, which is also the moment to search the visible area.

```tsx
const [viewport, setViewport] = useState<MapViewport>({ center: [19.0402, 47.4979], zoom: 11 });

<Button onClick={() => setViewport({ center: [19.0457, 47.507], zoom: 15 })}>Parliament</Button>
<Map viewport={viewport} onViewportChange={setViewport} />
```

## Tiles from another provider

The default style is free, but you can point `mapStyle` at any MapLibre style: a URL or a style object, or a `{ light, dark }` pair that follows the theme. A provider that needs a key usually takes it in the style URL; one that wants a header gets it through `transformRequest`.

```tsx
import { DEFAULT_MAP_STYLE, Map } from "@once-ui-system/core/map";

// MapTiler, Stadia, Protomaps or your own tile server: any MapLibre style.
<Map
  mapStyle={{
    light: `https://api.maptiler.com/maps/streets-v2/style.json?key=${process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_MAPTILER_KEY}`,
    dark: `https://api.maptiler.com/maps/streets-v2-dark/style.json?key=${process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_MAPTILER_KEY}`,
  }}
/>

// A header instead of a query parameter.
<Map
  mapStyle="https://tiles.example.com/style.json"
  transformRequest={(url) => ({ url, headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } })}
/>
```

Keep the attribution the provider asks for: the map shows the attribution each style declares in its bottom corner. Pass `tint={false}` to keep a style's own background colour.

## Keyboard and motion

The map is a focusable region: arrow keys pan, `+` and `-` zoom, and the frame shows a focus ring. Pins with `href` or `onClick` are links and buttons in the tab order. With reduced motion on, fitting, zooming and following a controlled viewport jump instead of animating, and pins do not scale on hover. When WebGL is off, the frame says the map could not load instead of staying blank; set the text with `labels`.

## Escape hatch

`useMap()` inside a `Map` returns the MapLibre instance and the loaded module, and `onMapLoad` hands you the instance once the first style has loaded, for layers the components do not cover (routes, heatmaps, GeoJSON).

# Canvas

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/canvas

> An infinite canvas for editors: a camera that pans and zooms, items placed in world units, a selection box, resize and rotate handles, and snap guides.

`Canvas` is the surface under a design tool, a whiteboard or a flow builder: a camera over a plane that pans and zooms, with a grid and zoom controls. It doesn't keep a document. Your app owns the shapes, places them with `CanvasItem`, and draws the selection with `TransformHandles` and `SnapGuides`, which hand every change back to you.

## Import

`Canvas` has its own entry point, so apps that don't use it don't pay for it. It has no dependencies.

```tsx
import {
  Canvas,
  CanvasItem,
  TransformHandles,
  useCanvasDrag,
  rectsBounds,
} from "@once-ui-system/core/canvas";

<Canvas fit={rectsBounds(shapes)} onBackgroundClick={() => setSelected(null)}>
  {shapes.map((s) => (
    <CanvasItem key={s.id} x={s.x} y={s.y} width={s.width} height={s.height} rotation={s.rotation} />
  ))}
  {selected && <TransformHandles rect={selected} onTransform={(next) => update(selected.id, next)} />}
</Canvas>;
```

## The camera

`view` is `{ x, y, zoom }`: a world point `p` is drawn at `p × zoom + (x, y)`. It's controlled like any other 3.0 state (`view` / `defaultView` / `onViewChange`), and `minZoom` and `maxZoom` bound it.

- **Wheel.** With `wheel="pan"` (the default), scrolling and two fingers on a trackpad move the view, and ⌘/Ctrl + wheel or a pinch zooms towards the pointer, as design tools do. `wheel="zoom"` makes the wheel zoom, as maps do.
- **Dragging.** Holding Space, or dragging with the middle button, always pans. `panOnDrag` is the hand tool: every drag pans. Without it, a drag on empty canvas draws a selection box when `onSelectionBox` is set, and pans when it isn't.
- **Touch.** One finger works like the mouse, and two fingers pinch to zoom and pan.
- **Fit.** `fit` is the box the opening view and the fit button frame, usually `rectsBounds` of everything on the canvas. Until someone moves the view, the canvas keeps it framed as it resizes. Change `fitKey` to frame it again, for example when another document opens.
- **Shortcuts.** While the pointer is over the canvas or focus is in it: ⌘/Ctrl + and − zoom, Shift+0 goes to 100%, and Shift+1 fits. `shortcuts={false}` turns them off.

A `ref` gives the camera to the app: `zoomBy`, `zoomTo`, `fitTo(rect)`, `screenToWorld`, `worldToScreen` and `clientToWorld`. Inside the canvas, `useCanvasApi()` gives the same functions without re-rendering when the view moves, and `useCanvas()` adds the current `view`.

## Items, dragging and drawing

`CanvasItem` places its children in world units, and they scale with the view. The view moving never re-renders items, so a canvas with hundreds of them still pans smoothly. A press on an item never pans or starts a selection box. Hand that press to `useCanvasDrag()`, which reports the drag in world units (`delta`, `point`) at any zoom.

`onBackgroundPointerDown(event, point)` hears a press on empty canvas. Return `true` to take the gesture, as a rectangle or frame tool does, and track the drag yourself with `useCanvasDrag`. `onBackgroundClick` hears a press that didn't move, usually to clear the selection.

## Selection

`onSelectionBox(rect, { phase, additive })` hears the box in world units as it's drawn, then `null` when it's done. `additive` is true when Shift or ⌘/Ctrl was held. Test your shapes against it with `rectsIntersect` or `rectContains`.

## Resize and rotate

`TransformHandles` draws eight resize handles and a rotate handle around `rect`, in screen space, so they keep their size at any zoom. `onTransform(next, { phase, handle, start })` hears each step.

- Shift keeps the proportions (`keepRatio` always does), and Alt resizes from the centre.
- Shift snaps a rotation to `rotationStep` (15° by default).
- A turned box resizes along its own edges, and the side opposite the handle stays where it is.
- For several things, pass their bounds (`rectsBounds`) and apply the change to each one with `mapRect(child, start, next)`.
- `snap` adjusts a resized box before it's reported, for example `snapToGrid`.

## Snapping

`snapRect(rect, others, { threshold })` moves a box onto the nearest edge or centre of its neighbours and returns the `guides` to draw with `SnapGuides`, which labels the gap between them. Divide a threshold in screen px by `view.zoom` so snapping feels the same at every zoom.

## Screen-space layers

`CanvasAnchor` pins its children to a world point but keeps their size, for comments, labels or other people's cursors. `CanvasOverlay` puts anything in the screen layer over the world. `overlay` places toolbars over the canvas, and `controlsStart` adds your own buttons to the zoom bar.

## Accessibility

- The canvas is a named application region that takes focus, so keyboard users reach its shortcuts. Give it a `labels.canvas` naming the document.
- Every handle is a button with a name such as "Resize from the top-left corner". The arrow keys move that side by one unit (ten with Shift) and turn the rotate handle by one degree.
- The zoom controls are buttons with names, and the zoom readout goes back to 100%.
- The canvas can't describe your shapes for you. Give each `CanvasItem` a role and a name, or offer a layers list beside the canvas.

## Geometry

The maths is exported for your own tools and for tests: `resizeRect`, `rotateRect`, `snapRect`, `snapToGrid`, `rectsBounds`, `rectAABB`, `rectCorners`, `rectContainsPoint`, `rectFromPoints`, `mapRect`, `fitView`, `zoomAt`, `screenToWorld` and `worldToScreen`.

---

# Scene

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/scene

> A 3D viewport on three.js that wears the theme: token colours, studio lights, a floor shadow, pinned HTML labels, and a loop that pauses when nobody is looking.

`Scene` draws a 3D view with [three.js](https://threejs.org/) inside a Once UI frame. Shapes take token colours like any component, so `color="brand-strong"` follows the brand you pick. The lights, the floor shadow and the grid follow light and dark. You don't write a render loop: the scene draws when something changes, animates only while something asks it to, and stops when it scrolls out of view or the tab is hidden.

## Installation

`three` is an optional peer dependency, like `maplibre-gl` for `Map`. Install it next to Once UI and import the scene from its own entry point, so an app without a 3D view never loads it:

```bash
npm install three
```

```tsx
import { Scene, SceneMesh } from "@once-ui-system/core/scene";

<Scene height={384} controls="turntable" floor>
  <SceneMesh geometry="torus" args={[0.6, 0.18]} position={[0, 0.9, 0]} color="brand-strong" />
</Scene>
```

The scene renders on the client only. On the server and until three.js loads it draws an empty frame of the same size, so the page does not shift. Without WebGL it says so in the frame instead of failing.

## Build, animate and label

Group shapes with `SceneGroup` to move them together, and animate them with `useSceneFrame`, which runs before every frame. `SceneLabel` pins ordinary HTML to a point, so a status tag follows the robot's head as it turns. Click handlers work on meshes and groups.

```tsx
function Robot({ battery, onSelect }) {
  const head = useRef<Group>(null);
  useSceneFrame(({ elapsed }) => {
    if (head.current) head.current.rotation.y = Math.sin(elapsed * 1.2) * 0.35;
  });
  return (
    <SceneGroup onClick={onSelect}>
      <SceneMesh args={[1.1, 1, 0.9]} position={[0, 1.2, 0]} color="neutral-medium" />
      <SceneGroup ref={head} position={[0, 1.95, 0]}>
        <SceneMesh args={[0.8, 0.5, 0.6]} color="neutral-medium" />
        <SceneMesh args={[0.6, 0.16, 0.02]} position={[0, 0.02, 0.31]} color="brand-strong" emissive="brand-strong" />
        <SceneLabel position={[0, 0.85, 0]}>
          <Tag tone={battery < 30 ? "warning" : "neutral"} label={`${battery}%`} />
        </SceneLabel>
      </SceneGroup>
    </SceneGroup>
  );
}

<Scene height={448} floor="grid" camera={{ position: [4.5, 3.2, 5.5], target: [0, 1.1, 0] }}>
  <Robot battery={82} onSelect={() => setSelected(true)} />
</Scene>
```

## Models

`SceneModel` loads a `.glb` or `.gltf` file. The loader comes with `three` and loads the first time a model is placed. Each file is fetched once per scene, however many copies you place. `color` repaints a plain model in a theme colour; leave it out to keep the model's own materials.

```tsx
<Scene height={384} controls="turntable" floor>
  <SceneModel src="/models/rover.glb" scale={0.5} color="neutral-medium">
    <SceneLabel position={[0, 1.4, 0]}>
      <Tag label="Rover" />
    </SceneLabel>
  </SceneModel>
</Scene>
```

## Colours

A colour is a token pair, a custom property or any CSS colour.

| Value | Reads |
| --- | --- |
| `"brand-strong"`, `"accent-medium"`, `"neutral-weak"` | The tone's own hue: full strength for `strong`, lighter for `medium` and `weak`. It follows the brand, accent and neutral set around the scene, and ignores `data-solid`, so a brand part stays brand-coloured on a contrast theme. |
| `"--page-background"` | Any custom property, read where the scene sits. |
| `"#ff8800"` | A fixed colour. |

`emissive` makes a part glow regardless of the lights: visors, status lights, screens.

## Camera and lights

| Prop | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `controls` | `"orbit"` (drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, arrows to pan), `"turntable"` (turns on its own, drag to rotate) or `"none"`. |
| `camera` | `{ position, target, fov }`. Changing it moves the camera. |
| `zoom` | Scroll and pinch zoom. On for `"orbit"`, off otherwise, so the page scrolls past a turntable. |
| `lighting` | `"studio"` (fill, key light and a brand rim light), `"neutral"` (no rim) or `"none"`. |
| `floor` | `true` or `"shadow"` for a soft shadow on an invisible floor, `"grid"` to add a grid. |

## Behaviour you get without asking

- **Theme:** token colours are read again when the theme, brand, accent or neutral changes anywhere above the scene, including a `data-theme` section.
- **Performance:** the canvas draws on demand. It runs continuously only while a `useSceneFrame` callback is mounted, the turntable turns, or a drag is settling, and stops off screen and in hidden tabs. The pixel ratio is capped at 2 (`maxPixelRatio`).
- **Reduced motion:** the turntable stands still and frame callbacks get a zero `delta`, so animation pauses but the scene still draws.
- **Cleanup:** geometry, materials and the WebGL context are released when the scene unmounts.
- **Accessibility:** the canvas is an image named by `labels.scene`. Describe what it shows, and put anything a person must read or act on in the page or in a `SceneLabel`, not only in the 3D view.

## Going further

`useScene()` returns the three.js `scene`, `camera` and `renderer`, the loaded `three` module, `invalidate()` to draw after changing something yourself, and `color()` to read a token as a `THREE.Color`. `onSceneLoad` hands over the same object once the scene starts. Post-processing, shaders and particle effects belong in `@once-ui-system/fx`.

---

# Calendar

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/calendar

> A scheduling calendar: a month of days, or a week or day of hours, with overlapping events side by side, picking empty time and dragging events.

`Calendar` shows events the way calendar apps do. Overlapping events sit side by side in the week and day views, events that last a day or more run as bars, and a crowded month day folds into "n more". The calendar does not store events: picking empty time, dragging an event and opening one all call back to your app, which keeps the list.

## Import

`Calendar` has its own entry point, so it costs nothing in apps that don't use it. It has no dependencies.

```tsx
import { Calendar, type CalendarEvent } from "@once-ui-system/core/calendar";

const events: CalendarEvent[] = [
  { id: "1", title: "Design review", start: new Date(2026, 10, 12, 14), end: new Date(2026, 10, 12, 15) },
];

<Calendar events={events} defaultView="week" onEventSelect={(event) => open(event)} />;
```

An event's `end` is exclusive: an event from 9:00 to 10:00 ends at 10:00, and an all-day event on 12 November ends at midnight on 13 November. `tone` gives an event its palette (the default is `brand`), and `description` adds a second line in the week and day views, such as a room or a client.

## Booking and rescheduling

- `onSlotSelect` makes empty time pickable. In the week and day views, people drag down the hours to pick a stretch, or click to pick `defaultDuration` minutes. In the month view, they press a day. Both snap to `snapMinutes`.
- `onEventChange` lets people drag an event to another time or day, or drag its bottom edge to change when it ends. The calendar shows the new place while they drag, then hands you the new `start` and `end`. The event moves once you pass the changed list back, so you can save it first or refuse the change.
- `editable: false` on an event keeps it in place.

## Views and dates

`view` and `date` are controlled like any other 3.0 state (`view` / `defaultView` / `onViewChange`, `date` / `defaultDate` / `onDateChange`). `views` sets which views are on the switch, and with one view the switch is hidden. `dayStartHour` and `dayEndHour` limit the hours drawn, and `scrollToHour` sets where the week and day views open. `toolbar={false}` hides the header, and `toolbarEnd` adds your own controls to it, such as a "New event" button.

## Language

`locale` names the months, the weekdays and the times, and sets the first day of the week unless you give `weekStartsOn`. `labels` translates the calendar's own words: Today, the view names, All day and "n more".

```tsx
<Calendar
  events={events}
  locale="hu-HU"
  labels={{ today: "Ma", month: "Hónap", week: "Hét", day: "Nap", allDay: "Egész nap", more: (n) => `még ${n}` }}
/>
```

## Accessibility

- The month view is an ARIA grid. The arrow keys move between days, Home and End go to the ends of the week, and Page Up and Page Down change the month. Enter picks the day, or opens it in the day view when `onSlotSelect` isn't set.
- Every event is a button whose name gives its title, date and time.
- Each day in the week and day views is a named group.
- The title above the grid announces the period whenever it changes.

## Layout helpers

The layouts are exported too, for a list beside the grid or for counting on the server. `layoutDay(events, day)` gives a day's timed blocks with their lanes, `layoutSpans(events, days)` gives bars across a row of days, and `viewDays(view, date, weekStartsOn)` gives the days a view shows.

# CodeBlock

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/codeBlock

> A versatile component for displaying and formatting code snippets with syntax highlighting, copy functionality, and interactive previews.

The `CodeBlock` component provides a way to display code snippets with syntax highlighting, interactive tabs for multiple code examples, and optional live previews. It supports various customization options including copy buttons, fullscreen mode, and line numbers.

```tsx
<CodeBlock
    copyButton
    preview={
      <Button size="s" weight="default" prefixIcon="sparkle">
        Click me
      </Button>
    }
    codes={[
      {
        language: "javascript",
        label: "Example",
        code: "const greeting = 'Hello, world!';"
      }
    ]}
/>
```

## Preview

```tsx
<CodeBlock
		copyButton
		previewPadding="0"
		preview={
			<Row fillWidth center padding="16">
				<Background
					background="neutral-alpha-weak"
					lines={{display: true, color: "neutral-alpha-weak"}}
					shadow="m"
					fillWidth
					radius="m"
					height="12rem"
					border="neutral-alpha-medium"
				/>
			</Row>
		}
		codes={[
			{
				language: "tsx",
				label: "Preview",
				code: "..."
			}
		]}
/>
```

## Multiple code

The `CodeBlock` can display multiple code examples with tabs for easy navigation.

HTML:

```html
// JavaScript
const button = document.createElement('button');
button.textContent = 'Example Button';
button.classList.add('secondary');
document.body.appendChild(button);
```

CSS:

```css
<!-- HTML -->
<button class="secondary">
    Example Button
</button>
```

```tsx
/* CSS */
button.secondary {
    background-color: #f0f0f0;
    border: 1px solid #ccc;
    border-radius: 4px;
    padding: 8px 16px;
}
```

Multiple code:

```tsx
<CodeBlock
    copyButton={false}
    codes={[
      {
        language: "javascript",
        label: "JavaScript",
        code:
"// JavaScript
const button = document.createElement('button');
button.textContent = 'Example Button';
button.classList.add('secondary');
document.body.appendChild(button);",
      },
      {
        language: "html",
        label: "HTML",
        code:
"<!-- HTML -->
<button class="secondary">
    Example Button
</button>"
    },
    {
        language: "css",
        label: "CSS",
        code:
"/* CSS */
button.secondary {
    background-color: #f0f0f0;
    border: 1px solid #ccc;
    border-radius: 4px;
    padding: 8px 16px;
}"
      }
    ]}
/>
```

## Compact mode

Use the `compact` prop for a more condensed display.

```tsx
<CodeBlock
		compact
		copyButton={false}
		codes={[
			{
				code: "console.log('Compact mode example');",
				language: "javascript",
				label: "Compact"
			}
		]}
/>
```

## Line numbers

Line numbers:

```tsx
<CodeBlock
```

## Highlight

Use the `highlight` prop to highlight specific lines of code. The value should be a string with line numbers or ranges (e.g., "1,3-5").

```tsx
let total = 0;

			}
```

## Code Diff

Display Git-style diffs by setting the language to "diff". Numbering can be used from coordinates, also specified manually by setting the `startLineNumber` parameter. Numbering prioritizes as follows: `coordinates` > `startLineNumber` > `0` (fallback)

```tsx
diff --git a/src/utils/math.ts b/src/utils/math.ts
index 1a2b3c4..5d6e7f8 100644
--- a/src/utils/math.ts
+++ b/src/utils/math.ts
@@ -10,7 +10,10 @@
export function add(a: number, b: number): number {
   return a + b;
}

- export function multiply(a: number, b: number): number {
-  return a * b;
- }
+ export function multiply(a: number, b: number): number {
+  if (a === 0 || b === 0) {
+    return 0;
+  }
+  return a * b;
+ }

  export function subtract(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a - b;
  }
```

Code Diff:

```tsx
<CodeBlock
  codes={[
    {
      language: "diff",
      label: "Diff",
      startLineNumber: 1,
      code:
"diff --git a/src/utils/math.ts b/src/utils/math.ts\nindex 1a2b3c4..5d6e7f8 100644\n--- a/src/utils/math.ts\n+++ b/src/utils/math.ts\n@@ -10,7 +10,10 @@\n export function add(a: number, b: number): number {\n  return a + b;\n}\n\n-export function multiply(a: number, b: number): number {\n-  return a * b;\n-}\n+export function multiply(a: number, b: number): number {\n+  if (a === 0 || b === 0) {\n+    return 0;\n+  }\n+  return a * b;\n+}\n\n export function subtract(a: number, b: number): number {\n  return a - b;\n}",
    }
  ]}
/>
```

You can enable syntax highlighting by specifying a similar array as the language parameter: `[ “diff”, “typescript” ]`

```tsx
diff --git a/src/utils/math.ts b/src/utils/math.ts
index 1a2b3c4..5d6e7f8 100644
--- a/src/utils/math.ts
+++ b/src/utils/math.ts
@@ -10,7 +10,10 @@
export function add(a: number, b: number): number {
   return a + b;
}

- export function multiply(a: number, b: number): number {
-  return a * b;
- }
+ export function multiply(a: number, b: number): number {
+  if (a === 0 || b === 0) {
+    return 0;
+  }
+  return a * b;
+ }

export function subtract(a: number, b: number): number {
  return a - b;
}
```

Code Diff:

```tsx
<CodeBlock
  codes={[
    {
      language:  [ "diff", "typescript" ],
      label: "Diff",
      startLineNumber: 1,
      code:
"diff --git a/src/utils/math.ts b/src/utils/math.ts\nindex 1a2b3c4..5d6e7f8 100644\n--- a/src/utils/math.ts\n+++ b/src/utils/math.ts\n@@ -10,7 +10,10 @@\n export function add(a: number, b: number): number {\n  return a + b;\n}\n\n-export function multiply(a: number, b: number): number {\n-  return a * b;\n-}\n+export function multiply(a: number, b: number): number {\n+  if (a === 0 || b === 0) {\n+    return 0;\n+  }\n+  return a * b;\n+}\n\n export function subtract(a: number, b: number): number {\n  return a - b;\n}",
    }
  ]}
/>
```

# HeadingLink

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/headingLink

> The HeadingLink component creates linkable section headings that work with the HeadingNav component for automatic table of contents navigation.

The `HeadingLink` component creates linkable section headings that automatically integrate with the HeadingNav component to provide a smooth navigation experience throughout your content.

HeadingLink:

```tsx
<HeadingLink as="h2" id="example-section">
    Example Section
</HeadingLink>
<Text onBackground="neutral-weak">
    This is a section with a linkable heading
</Text>
```

## Usage

Use the `HeadingLink` component to create section headings throughout your content. When used with the `HeadingNav` component, these headings will automatically appear in the navigation.

Multiple headings:

```tsx

    First Section
</HeadingLink>

    Content for the first section
</Text>

    Subsection
</HeadingLink>

    Content for the subsection
</Text>
```

The `HeadingLink` component can be customized with the standard `Heading` styling props.

```tsx

    as="h2" 
    id="styled-heading" 
    onBackground="accent-weak"
    marginBottom="16"
>
    Styled Heading
</HeadingLink>
```

## HeadingNav

The `HeadingLink` component works seamlessly with the `HeadingNav` component to create an automatic table of contents.

## Features

- Creates linkable section headings with anchor IDs
- Automatically integrates with HeadingNav for table of contents
- Supports all heading levels (h1-h6)
- Provides hover link indicators for easy navigation
- Fully accessible with proper heading semantics

# MDX

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/mdx

> One component map that renders MDX content with Once UI: headings with anchor links, body text, links, images, code, quotes, lists and tables, plus the common components as tags.

`@once-ui-system/core/mdx` exports a component map for MDX content. Hand it to `next-mdx-remote` or `@next/mdx` and Markdown renders through Once UI: headings get an id and a link to themselves, links go through `SmartLink`, images through `Media`, fenced code through `CodeBlock`, and GFM tables through `Table`. Common components such as `Feedback`, `Accordion`, `Card` and `OgCard` are available in the content by name.

The map is typed against the props MDX passes for each element, so an override is checked when you write it, without casts.

> **Its own entry point** The map renders fenced code through `CodeBlock`, so it lives on its own subpath, like `/code`, and never adds `prismjs` to an app that does not import it. Install `prismjs` if your content has code blocks. No other dependency is needed.

## next-mdx-remote

Pass `mdxComponents` as the `components` prop. The map works in server components, so it can be used with `next-mdx-remote/rsc`.

```tsx
import { MDXRemote } from "next-mdx-remote/rsc";
import { mdxComponents } from "@once-ui-system/core/mdx";

export default async function Post({ params }: { params: Promise<{ slug: string }> }) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  const source = await getPostSource(slug);

  return <MDXRemote source={source} components={mdxComponents} />;
}
```

next-mdx-remote 6 blocks JavaScript expressions in MDX by default. If your content passes props such as `codes={[...]}`, set `options={{ blockJS: false }}`.

## @next/mdx

`@next/mdx` reads the map from `mdx-components.tsx` at the project root (or in `src/`). Spread the Once UI map first, so the components passed in can override it.

```tsx
import type { MDXComponents } from "mdx/types";
import { mdxComponents } from "@once-ui-system/core/mdx";

export function useMDXComponents(components: MDXComponents): MDXComponents {
  return { ...mdxComponents, ...components };
}
```

## Override or extend tags

`createMdxComponents` returns the default map with your entries applied. An HTML tag key (`h2`, `a`, `hr` and so on) replaces what Markdown renders for that element. Any other key registers a component the content can use by name.

```tsx
import { BlockQuote, Logo, Row } from "@once-ui-system/core";
import { createMdxComponents, MdxHeading } from "@once-ui-system/core/mdx";
import { MDXRemote, type MDXRemoteProps } from "next-mdx-remote/rsc";
import { Pricing } from "./Pricing";

const components = createMdxComponents({
  // Replace an element. `props` is typed as what MDX passes for an <hr>.
  hr: () => (
    <Row fillWidth horizontal="center" paddingY="64">
      <Logo icon="/trademark.svg" />
    </Row>
  ),
  blockquote: ({ children }) => (
    <BlockQuote separator="none" marginY="64">
      {children}
    </BlockQuote>
  ),
  // Keep the element, change its margins.
  h2: (props) => <MdxHeading as="h2" marginTop="64" {...props} />,
  // Register your own component as a tag: <Pricing /> in the content.
  Pricing,
});

export function CustomMDX(props: MDXRemoteProps) {
  return (
    <MDXRemote
      {...props}
      options={{ blockJS: false, ...props.options }}
      components={{ ...components, ...props.components }}
    />
  );
}
```

- To keep the plain HTML element, map the tag to its own name: `createMdxComponents({ hr: "hr" })`.
- An entry set to `undefined` is skipped, so a conditional override cannot remove an element by accident.
- The element components (`MdxHeading`, `MdxParagraph`, `MdxLink`, `MdxImage`, `MdxInlineCode`, `MdxCodeBlock`, `MdxBlockQuote`, `MdxList`, `MdxListItem`, `MdxTable`, `MdxHr`) are exported for wrapping. Each takes its element's MDX props plus margins. Setting any margin replaces the element's default margins.
- An override that needs a prop Markdown can never supply does not compile. For example, `h3: ({ level }: { level: number }) => ...` is rejected.

## What each element renders

| Markdown | Renders | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `# Heading` to `###### Heading` | `Heading` with a link to itself | The id is a slug of the heading's text, or the id MDX passes, for example from `rehype-slug`. |
| Paragraph | `Text` as a `<p>` | A paragraph that is only an image renders the image on its own. Text around an inline image renders as a `<div>`. |
| `[text](href)` | `SmartLink` | Internal paths use your router's link; external URLs open in a new tab. |
| `![alt](src)` | `Media` | Goes through the image adapter and enlarges on click. |
| `` `code` `` | `InlineCode` | |
| Fenced code | `CodeBlock` | The language comes from the fence (`ts`, `tsx`, `bash` and so on). Without one, the code renders as plain text. Needs `prismjs`. |
| `> quote` | `BlockQuote` | |
| `-` and `1.` lists | `List`, `ListItem` | An ordered list keeps its start number. |
| GFM table | `Table` | Needs `remark-gfm`. Column alignment carries over. |
| `---` | `Line` | Has the `separator` role. |

Tags available by name: `Accordion`, `AccordionGroup`, `BlockQuote`, `Button`, `Card`, `CodeBlock`, `Column`, `Feedback`, `FileTree`, `Grid`, `Heading`, `Icon`, `InlineCode`, `Line`, `List`, `ListItem`, `Media`, `OgCard`, `Row`, `SmartLink`, `Table` and `Text`.

## Headings and anchors

Each heading renders with an anchor link next to it. The link shows on hover, on focus, and always on touch screens. It is a real link to the section, so it works without JavaScript and can be reached with the keyboard. Activating it also copies the section's URL and confirms with a toast, so the content must render inside a `ToastProvider`, as it does in the standard Once UI provider setup. `HeadingNav` picks up the ids.

For links and images to use `next/link` and `next/image`, import `LayoutProvider` from `@once-ui-system/core/next`. Without it, they render as a plain `<a>` and `<img>`.

Ids are slugged from the text the same way Studio and this site do it: "Get started & deploy" becomes `get-started-and-deploy`. Two headings with the same text get the same id. To make them unique, add `rehype-slug`, whose ids take precedence.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mdxComponents` | `MdxComponents` | `-` | The default map. |
| `createMdxComponents` | `(overrides?: Partial<MdxComponents>) => MdxComponents` | `-` | The default map with overrides applied. |
| `MdxComponents` | `type` | `-` | Tag keys typed against MDX's props; other keys are components used by name. |
| `MdxElementProps` | `type` | `-` | The props MDX passes for an element: MdxElementProps<"h2">. |
| `MdxHeading` | `MdxHeadingProps` | `-` | A heading with an id and an anchor link. Takes as: "h1" to "h6". |

# Meta

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/meta

> Generate SEO-friendly metadata for your Next.js pages including OpenGraph and Twitter/X cards.

Generate SEO-friendly metadata for your Next.js pages including OpenGraph and Twitter/X cards.

Add metadata directly to your pages using the `Meta.generate`{" "}
function:

```tsx
import { Meta } from "@once-ui-system/core";

export async function generateMetadata() {
    return Meta.generate({
      title: "My Page Title",
      description: "A comprehensive description of the page content",
      baseURL: "https://example.com",
      path: "/docs/getting-started",
      type: "website"
    });
}
```

## Canonical URL

Each page names its own URL, `baseURL` plus `path`, as canonical, so search
engines index one address for it. Pass `canonical` to name another, or
`canonical: false` to leave the tag out.

Call `Meta.generate` in pages, not in a layout. Next
passes a layout's metadata down to every page that has none of its own, so a
layout's canonical would make each of those pages name the layout's URL. If a
layout sets site-wide metadata with it, pass `canonical: false` there.
`once-ui-validate-ai-code` flags a layout that doesn't.

## Advanced setup

For larger sites, store your metadata in a central configuration file to maintain
consistency across pages:

### 1. Config file

Store your site-wide metadata in a configuration file:

```tsx
// default metadata
const meta = {
    title: "Once UI: Build the future",
    description: "An open-source design system for indie creators to ship like teams of 10+ alone.",
    baseURL: "https://once-ui.com",
    type: "website",
    image: "/images/cover.jpg",
    author: {
      name: "Once UI Team",
      url: "https://once-ui.com"
    }
};

export { meta };
```

### 2. Reference

Reference the configuration in your pages:

```tsx
import { Meta } from '@once-ui-system/core';
import { meta } from '@/app/resources/seo';

export async function generateMetadata() {
    return Meta.generate({
      ...meta,
      path: "/",
    });
}
```

This approach makes it easier to maintain consistent metadata across your site and
update it from a single location.

## Social image route

Without an `image`, `Meta.generate` points the Open Graph and X images at `/api/og/generate?title=…`, a route you render with `next/og`. If yours lives elsewhere, pass `ogRoutes`; the same object can be given to `OgRoutesProvider` for `OgCard`.

```tsx
export async function generateMetadata() {
    return Meta.generate({
      title: "My Page Title",
      description: "A comprehensive description of the page content",
      baseURL: "https://example.com",
      ogRoutes: { generate: "/og/image" },
    });
}
// og:image → /og/image?title=My%20Page%20Title
```

## Output

The `Meta.generate` function will generate all necessary meta tags for SEO and social sharing:

```tsx
<title>Once UI: Build the future</title>
<meta name="description" content="An open-source design system for indie creators to ship like teams of 10+ alone.">

<meta property="og:title" content="Once UI: Build the future">
<meta property="og:description" content="An open-source design system for indie creators to ship like teams of 10+ alone.">
<meta property="og:type" content="website">
<link rel="canonical" href="https://once-ui.com">

<meta property="og:url" content="https://once-ui.com">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://once-ui.com/images/cover.jpg">

<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
<meta name="twitter:title" content="Once UI: Build the future">
<meta name="twitter:description" content="An open-source design system for indie creators to ship like teams of 10+ alone.">
<meta name="twitter:image" content="https://once-ui.com/images/cover.jpg">
```

## API reference

`Meta.generate` takes one object:

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `title (required)` | `string` |  |  |
| `description (required)` | `string` |  |  |
| `baseURL (required)` | `string` |  |  |
| `path` | `string` | `""` |  |
| `type` | `"website" \| "article"` | `website` |  |
| `image` | `string` |  |  |
| `publishedTime` | `string` |  |  |
| `author` | `{ name: string; url?: string; }` |  |  |
| `canonical` | `string \| false` |  |  |
| `robots` | `string` |  |  |
| `noindex` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `nofollow` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `alternates` | `Alternate[]` |  |  |
| `ogRoutes` | `Partial<OgRoutes>` |  |  |

# Schema

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/schema

> Add Schema.org structured data to your pages for SEO and rich search results.

Add Schema.org structured data to your pages for SEO and rich search results.

```tsx
<Schema
    as="webPage"
    title="My Page Title"
    description="A comprehensive description of the page content"
    baseURL="https://example.com"
    path="/docs/getting-started"
    author={{
      name: "John Doe",
    }}
/>
```

## Advanced setup
            
For larger sites, store your schema data in a central configuration file to maintain
consistency across pages:

### 1. Config file

Store your site-wide metadata in a configuration file:

```tsx
// default metadata
const meta = {
    title: "Once UI: Build the future",
    description: "An open-source design system for indie creators to ship like teams of 10+ alone.",
};

// default schema data
const schema = {
    title: "Once UI",
    description: meta.description,
    baseURL: "https://once-ui.com",
    path: "/",
    image: "/images/cover.jpg",
    author: {
      name: "Once UI Team",
      url: "https://once-ui.com"
    }
};

export { schema };
```

### 2. Reference

Reference the configuration in your pages:
          
```tsx
import { Schema } from '@once-ui-system/core';
import { schema } from '@/app/resources/seo';

export default function HomePage() {
    return (
      <>
        <Schema
          as="organization"
          title={schema.title}
          description={schema.description}
          baseURL={schema.baseURL}
          path={schema.path}
          image={schema.image}
          author={schema.author}
        />
        {/* Rest of your page component */}
      </>
    );
}
```

This approach makes it easier to maintain consistent schema data across your site and
update it from a single location.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `as (required)` | `"website" \| "aboutPage" \| "article" \| "blogPosting" \| "creativeWork" \| "techArticle" \| "webPage" \| "organization"` |  | The schema.org type to emit. |
| `title (required)` | `string` |  |  |
| `description (required)` | `string` |  |  |
| `baseURL (required)` | `string` |  |  |
| `path (required)` | `string` |  | The page's path, joined to baseURL for its URL. |
| `datePublished` | `string` |  |  |
| `dateModified` | `string` |  |  |
| `image` | `string` |  |  |
| `sameAs` | `string[]` | `[]` |  |
| `author` | `{ name: string; url?: string; image?: string; }` |  |  |

# Checkbox

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/checkbox

> Checkbox provides a selectable control for binary or indeterminate states with customizable labels and styling.

The `Checkbox` component provides a selectable control that can be toggled between checked, unchecked, and indeterminate states. Its `label` and `description` are drawn the same way as on `RadioButton` and `Switch`.

Checkbox:

```tsx
<Checkbox
    label="Accept terms and conditions"
    description="By checking this box, you agree to our terms of service."
/>
```

## State

Use the `checked` prop with React state to create controlled checkboxes. `onCheckedChange` receives the state the checkbox moves to, so the setter can be passed straight in.

State:

```tsx
const [checked, setChecked] = useState(false);

<Checkbox
    label="Controlled checkbox"
    checked={checked}
    onCheckedChange={setChecked}
/>

// You can also update the state programmatically
const handleReset = () => setChecked(false);
```

## Indeterminate

The checkbox can display an indeterminate state, useful for parent checkboxes that control a group of child checkboxes.

Indeterminate:

```tsx
const [items, setItems] = useState([
    { id: 1, label: 'Item 1', checked: true },
    { id: 2, label: 'Item 2', checked: false },
    { id: 3, label: 'Item 3', checked: true }
]);

const allChecked = items.every(item => item.checked);
const someChecked = items.some(item => item.checked);
const isIndeterminate = someChecked && !allChecked;

const toggleAll = () => {
    const newCheckedState = !allChecked;
    setItems(items.map(item => ({
      ...item,
      checked: newCheckedState
    })));
};

<Checkbox
    label="Select all items"
    checked={allChecked || isIndeterminate}
    indeterminate={isIndeterminate}
    onCheckedChange={toggleAll}
/>

{items.map(item => (
    <Checkbox
      key={item.id}
      label={item.label}
      checked={item.checked}
      onCheckedChange={() => {
        setItems(items.map(i => 
          i.id === item.id ? { ...i, checked: !i.checked } : i
        ));
      }}
    />
))}
```

## Disabled

Disable the checkbox to prevent user interaction.

Disabled:

```tsx
<Checkbox
    label="Disabled checkbox"
    disabled
/>
```

## Hover

Disable the hover pulse animation by setting `hoverable` to `false`.

Hover:

```tsx
<Checkbox
    label="No hover effect"
    hoverable={false}
/>
```

## Validation and size

`error` marks the Checkbox invalid (a danger border and `aria-invalid`);
`errorMessage` shows under it, linked with `aria-describedby`, and marks it
invalid too. `size` (`s`, `m`, `l`) scales the control and its text; left out,
it takes the enclosing `Form`'s `size`, as `Input` does.

Validation:

```tsx
<Checkbox
    label="I accept the terms"
    errorMessage="Accept the terms to continue"
/>
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `size` | `TShirtSizes` |  | s, m or l. Left out, the enclosing Form's size, else m. |
| `error` | `boolean` |  | Mark it invalid: a danger border and aria-invalid. |
| `errorMessage` | `ReactNode` |  | Shown under it, linked with aria-describedby; marks it invalid too. |
| `label` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
| `id` | `string` |  |  |
| `disabled` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `description` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
| `iconButtonProps` | `IconButtonProps` |  |  |
| `auto` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `checked` | `boolean` |  | Whether it is ticked, controlled. Leave it out and the checkbox keeps its own state. |
| `defaultChecked` | `boolean` | `false` | The starting state when `checked` is left out. |
| `indeterminate` | `boolean` | `false` | The third state, for a parent whose children are partly ticked. |
| `onCheckedChange` | `(checked: boolean) => void` |  | Called with the new state when it is flipped: true when it becomes ticked. |
| `hoverable` | `boolean` | `true` | Highlight the row on hover. |
| `label` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
| `description` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | `false` |  |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `iconButtonProps` | `IconButtonProps` | `-` | Props forwarded to the icon button beside the label. |
| `...InputHTMLAttributes` |  |  | Also takes these props |
| `onChange` | `ChangeEventHandler` | `-` | The native change event of the hidden input, with the rest of the input attributes (name, required, onBlur), so a form library's register() works. |
| `...LeafProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# Chip

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/chip

> Chip is Tag in Once UI 3.0: a Tag with selected, onClick or onRemove is a toggle.

`Chip` folded into [Tag](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/tag) in Once UI 3.0 and is no longer exported. A Tag given `selected`, `onClick` or `onRemove` is the same toggle, with `aria-pressed` and an optional remove button:

Chip → Tag:

```tsx
// 2.x
<Tag label="Design" selected={on} onClick={toggle} removeButtonProps={{ tooltip: "Remove" }} onRemove={remove} />

// 3.0
<Tag label="Design" selected={on} onClick={toggle} removeButtonProps={{ tooltip: "Remove" }} onRemove={remove} />
```

`selected` now defaults to **false**: a 2.x `<Tag selected label="x" />` was drawn and announced as selected. The 3.0 codemod writes `selected` where it was left out, so migrated chips keep their look, and renames `iconButtonProps` to `removeButtonProps`. See [Tag: Toggle](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/tag#toggle).

# ColorInput

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/colorInput

> ColorInput provides a user-friendly color picker with hex value display and visual color preview.

The `ColorInput` component provides an enhanced color picker that displays the selected color as a visual preview alongside its hex value. It extends the standard HTML color input with a more user-friendly interface.

ColorInput:

```tsx
const [colorValue, setColorValue] = useState("#4287f5");
  
const handleColorChange = (value: string) => {
    setColorValue(value);
};

<ColorInput
    id="color-input-example"
    label="Brand Color"
    value={colorValue}
    onValueChange={handleColorChange}
/>
```

## Features

- **Color Preview**: Shows a visual preview of the selected color
- **Hex Value Display**: Displays the hex code of the selected color
- **Native Color Picker**: Uses the browser's native color picker for selection
- **Reset Option**: Includes a button to clear the selected color
- **Alpha Support**: Optional opacity/transparency control via dropdown slider

## Alpha support

Enable alpha channel (transparency) control by setting `supportAlpha` to true. This adds an opacity button that opens a dropdown with a slider to adjust transparency from 0-100%.

With alpha:

```tsx
const [colorValue, setColorValue] = useState("rgba(66, 135, 245, 0.8)");
  
const handleColorChange = (value: string) => {
    setColorValue(value);
};

<ColorInput
    id="color-input-alpha-example"
    label="Brand Color"
    value={colorValue}
    onValueChange={handleColorChange}
    supportAlpha
/>
```

When `supportAlpha` is enabled:
- The value is automatically converted to `rgba(r, g, b, a)` format
- An opacity icon appears in the input suffix
- Clicking the icon opens a dropdown with a slider (0-100% opacity)
- The color preview shows transparency
- The display text shows RGBA values

## Localisation

`label` and `description` are yours to translate. The field's own controls
take `labels`: `remove` for the clear button ("Remove"), `adjustOpacity` for
the opacity button ("Adjust opacity") and `opacity` for its slider
("Opacity"). Whatever you leave out stays English.

```tsx
<ColorInput
  id="brand-colour"
  label={t("brandColour")}
  value={colour}
  onValueChange={setColour}
  labels={{ remove: t("remove") }}
/>
```

## Toolbar size

`size="xxs"` draws a 32px field, the height of a `size="s"` Button. The label shows as the placeholder until a colour is picked.

Toolbar size:

```tsx
const [color, setColor] = useState("#4287f5");

<ColorInput
    id="brand-color"
    label="Brand Color"
    size="xxs"
    value={color}
    onValueChange={setColor}
/>
```

## Props

The `ColorInput` component extends the standard `Input` component props with the following modifications:

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value` | `string` |  | The current colour, as hex or rgba, controlled. Leave it out and the field keeps its own. |
| `defaultValue` | `string` |  | The starting colour when `value` is left out. |
| `onValueChange` | `(value: string) => void` |  | Receives the colour string after a pick, an opacity change or a clear (""). Was onChange in 2.x. |
| `supportAlpha` | `boolean` | `false` | Adds an opacity slider and switches the value to rgba(). |
| `labels` | `ColorInputLabels` |  | The clear and opacity controls' text, to translate them. |
| `onChange` | `ChangeEventHandler` | `-` | The native change event of the colour input, as on Input. |
| `...LeafProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# DateInput

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/dateInput

> DateInput provides a user-friendly date and time picker with calendar interface.

The `DateInput` component provides an enhanced date picker that combines an input field with a dropdown calendar interface. It allows users to easily select dates with optional time selection.

DateInput:

```tsx
const [date, setDate] = useState<Date | undefined>(new Date());
  
const handleDateChange = (newDate: Date) => {
    setDate(newDate);
};

<DateInput
    id="date-input-example"
    label="Select Date"
    value={date}
    onValueChange={handleDateChange}
/>
```

## Time picker

Enable time selection by setting the `timePicker` prop to `true`.

TimePicker:

```tsx
const [dateTime, setDateTime] = useState<Date | undefined>(new Date());
  
const handleDateTimeChange = (newDateTime: Date) => {
  setDateTime(newDateTime);
};

<DateInput
  id="date-time-input-example"
  label="Select Date & Time"
  value={dateTime}
  onValueChange={handleDateTimeChange}
  timePicker
/>
```

## Range

With `range`, the field becomes two, a start and an end, over one calendar that picks both (2.x's `DateRangeInput`). `value`, `defaultValue` and `onValueChange` then take a `DateRange`, `{ startDate, endDate }`; `startLabel` and `endLabel` name the fields, and `id` is the base of their ids, `{id}-start` and `{id}-end`.

Range:

```tsx
<DateInput range
    id="trip"
    startLabel="Start date"
    endLabel="End date"
    value={dateRange}
    onValueChange={setDateRange}
/>
```

## Features

- **Calendar Interface**: Visual calendar for easy date selection
- **Time Selection**: Optional time picker for selecting hours and minutes
- **Formatted Display**: Displays selected date in a readable format
- **Dropdown Integration**: Uses `DropdownWrapper` for a clean UI experience

## Toolbar size

`size="xxs"` draws a 32px field, the height of a `size="s"` Button, for a date filter in a toolbar.

Toolbar size:

```tsx
const [date, setDate] = useState<Date>(new Date());

<DateInput
    id="date"
    placeholder="Select date"
    size="xxs"
    value={date}
    onValueChange={setDate}
/>
```

With `range`, `size="xxs"` draws both halves at 32px, rounded at `radius-m` on their outer corners.

Toolbar range:

```tsx
const [dateRange, setDateRange] = useState<DateRange>({ startDate: undefined, endDate: undefined });

<DateInput range
    id="range"
    startLabel="Start"
    endLabel="End"
    size="xxs"
    value={dateRange}
    onValueChange={setDateRange}
/>
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id (required)` | `string` |  |  |
| `range` | `boolean` |  | Two fields, start and end, over one calendar. value, defaultValue and onValueChange then take a DateRange. |
| `label` | `string` |  |  |
| `placeholder` | `string` |  |  |
| `value` | `Date \| DateRange` |  | The date, controlled. Leave it out and the field keeps its own. |
| `defaultValue` | `Date \| DateRange` |  | The starting date when `value` is left out. |
| `onValueChange` | `((date: Date) => void) \| ((range: DateRange) => void)` |  | Called with the date picked, and each time edit with timePicker. Was onChange in 2.x. |
| `open` | `boolean` |  | Whether the picker is open, controlled. |
| `defaultOpen` | `boolean` |  | Whether the picker starts open, when `open` is left out. |
| `onOpenChange` | `(open: boolean) => void` |  | Called with every open and close. |
| `minHeight` | `number` |  | Minimum height of the calendar popover. |
| `fillWidth` | `boolean` |  | Stretch the field (or both range fields) to the container's width, like the inputs around it. The calendar panel keeps at least its own width. Default false. |
| `timePicker` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `minDate` | `Date` |  | Earliest date the calendar allows. |
| `maxDate` | `Date` |  | Latest date the calendar allows. |
| `locale` | `string` |  | Locale for the field's date and the calendar's names, such as "de". US English when left out. |
| `labels` | `DatePickerLabels` |  | The calendar's own words, for a translated interface: the same { previousMonth, nextMonth, month, year, ... } as DatePicker's labels. Omitted fields stay English. |
| `startLabel` | `string` |  | With range, the label on the start field. |
| `endLabel` | `string` |  | With range, the label on the end field. |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `onChange` | `ChangeEventHandler` | `-` | The native change event of the field, as on Input. |
| `...LeafProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# DatePicker

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/datePicker

> A flexible calendar component for date and time selection with support for range selection and time picking.

The DatePicker component provides an interactive calendar interface for selecting dates and times. It supports various features like time selection, month navigation, and date range selection.

DatePicker:

```tsx
<DatePicker 
    value={selectedDate}
    onValueChange={handleDateChange}
/>
```

## TimePicker

TimePicker:

```tsx
<DatePicker 
    value={dateTime}
    onValueChange={handleDateTimeChange}
    timePicker
/>
```

With `timePicker`, picking a day opens the time panel. Every change reaches `onValueChange` as it happens; the panel's **Apply** button confirms the date and time, calls `onApply`, and closes the dropdown the picker is in (a `DateInput`, or your own `Dropdown`).

## Localization

Pass `locale`, a BCP 47 tag such as `"de"` or `"pt-BR"`, to show month and weekday names, and the time picker's time and AM/PM, in that language. The week starts on the locale's first day, Monday in `"de"`. The names and the week start come from the browser's `Intl` API, so no locale data is bundled. Without `locale` they are in English and the week starts on Sunday.

The picker's own words come from `labels`: `previousMonth`, `nextMonth`, `backToCalendar`, `apply`, `hours`, `minutes`, `am` and `pm` are strings, and `month` and `year` are functions that name the month and year buttons from the value they show (`"Month: March, change month"` by default; keep the value in the name, as it is the button's text). Any label left out stays English, and `am` and `pm` default to the locale's words. `DateInput`, `DateRangePicker` and `DateRangeInput` take the same `labels` and pass them to their calendars.

Localization:

```tsx
<DatePicker
    value={selectedDate}
    onValueChange={setSelectedDate}
    timePicker
    locale="de"
    labels={{
        previousMonth: "Vorheriger Monat",
        nextMonth: "Nächster Monat",
        month: (month) => `Monat: ${month}, Monat ändern`,
        year: (year) => `Jahr: ${year}, Jahr ändern`,
        backToCalendar: "Zurück zum Kalender",
        apply: "Übernehmen",
        hours: "Stunden",
        minutes: "Minuten",
    }}
/>
```

## Range

With `range`, the picker selects a start and an end date, highlighting the days between (2.x's `DateRangePicker`). `value`, `defaultValue` and `onValueChange` then take a `DateRange`, `{ startDate, endDate }`: the first pick sets the start alone, the second the end. `months={2}` shows two months side by side (2.x's `dual`), and `minDate` and `maxDate` bound the days that can be picked.

Range:

```tsx
const [range, setRange] = useState<DateRange>({
    startDate: new Date(),
    endDate: undefined,
});

<DatePicker range value={range} onValueChange={setRange} />
<DatePicker range months={2} value={range} onValueChange={setRange} />
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `range` | `boolean` |  | Select a start and end date. value, defaultValue and onValueChange then take a DateRange. |
| `style` | `React.CSSProperties` |  |  |
| `defaultValue` | `Date \| DateRange` |  | The starting date when `value` is left out. Replaces defaultDate, which 2.x never read. |
| `autoFocus` | `boolean` |  | Move focus onto the selected day as the picker appears, for a picker that has just been opened. |
| `className` | `string` |  |  |
| `value` | `Date \| DateRange` |  | The date, controlled. Leave it out and the picker keeps its own. |
| `size` | `CondensedTShirtSizes` |  |  |
| `onValueChange` | `((date: Date) => void) \| ((range: DateRange) => void)` |  | Called with the date picked, and each time edit with timePicker. Was onChange in 2.x. With range, called with the range after each pick: the start alone, then both ends. |
| `minDate` | `Date` |  |  |
| `maxDate` | `Date` |  |  |
| `previousMonth` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `nextMonth` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `timePicker` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `onApply` | `(date: Date) => void` |  | Called with the picked date and time when the time panel's Apply button is pressed. Inside a Dropdown or DateInput, Apply also closes the panel; on its own the picker returns to the calendar. |
| `defaultTime` | `{ hours: number; minutes: number; }` |  |  |
| `nested` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `onHover` | `(date: Date \| null) => void` |  |  |
| `open` | `boolean` |  | With autoFocus, focus moves in again each time this turns true. It does not show or hide the picker. |
| `locale` | `string` |  | Locale for month and weekday names and the time picker's time, such as "de". English when left out. |
| `labels` | `DatePickerLabels` |  | The picker's own words, for a translated interface: { previousMonth, nextMonth, month, year, backToCalendar, apply, hours, minutes, am, pm }. month and year are functions of the value shown. Omitted fields stay English. |
| `months` | `1 \| 2` |  | With range, how many months show side by side: 1 or 2. 2.x's dual was months={2}. |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

## Accessibility

- Keyboard navigation support for date selection
- Clear visual indicators for selected dates
- Proper ARIA attributes for screen readers
- The month and year buttons say what they do as well as what they show ("Month: March, change month"); `labels` translates them
