# Scroller

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/scroller

> A component for creating scrollable content areas with navigation buttons.

The `Scroller` component creates a scrollable container with automatic navigation buttons that appear when content overflows. It's perfect for horizontal or vertical scrolling of content like cards, images, or any elements that might not fit in the available space.

> **Two components scroll a row** Pick by the job. [Carousel](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/carousel) shows one image or slide at a time, with line or thumbnail indicators and autoplay, or as a touch-first track on native scroll snapping with `mode="snap"` (2.x Swiper). [Scroller](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/scroller) scrolls overflowing chips, tabs or cards behind arrow buttons and edge fades; in track mode it moves a run of tiles with drag, wrap-around, markers and proximity scaling (2.x ScrollContainer), and with `auto` it is a marquee that moves on its own (2.x AutoScroll).

Scroller:

```tsx
<Scroller fadeColor="transparent">
    <Row gap="16">
      {Array(10).fill(0).map((_, i) => (
        <Flex key={i}/>
      ))}
    </Row>
</Scroller>
```

## Vertical

The `Scroller` can be configured to scroll vertically by setting the `direction` prop to `column`.

Vertical:

```tsx
<Scroller direction="column" height="24rem" fadeColor="transparent">
    <Column gap="16" horizontal="center" fillWidth>
      {Array(6).fill(0).map((_, i) => (
        <Flex key={i} />
      ))}
    </Column>
</Scroller>
```

## Fade

You can customize the color of the fade effect that appears behind the scroll buttons.

Fade:

```tsx
<Scroller fadeColor="brand-medium">
    <Row gap="16">
      {Array(10).fill(0).map((_, i) => (
        <Flex key={i} />
      ))}
    </Row>
</Scroller>
```

## Track mode

Set any of `infinite`, `markers`, `draggable`, `step`, `clip`, `proximity`, `active`, `onActiveChange`, `controlPlacement` or `tile` and the children become a run of tiles moved by a transform: controls, drag, optional wrap-around, markers and proximity scaling. `tile` styles the box each item sits in (its size, aspect ratio); the other props style the Scroller. It was `ScrollContainer` in 2.x, which took the items as `items` and the tile props as its own.

ScrollContainer:

```tsx
<Scroller draggable><YourContent /><YourContent /><YourContent /></Scroller>
```

### Infinite

Past the last item the track continues into the first, in the same direction, with no rewind. Both controls stay enabled.

Infinite:

```tsx
<Scroller
  infinite>{items}</Scroller>
```

### Markers

Markers show how many items there are and which one is in front, and jump to one when pressed. `markers` takes `true` to put them opposite the controls, or `"top"` / `"bottom"` to name the side.

Markers:

```tsx
<Scroller
  markers="bottom"
  controlPlacement="top-end">{items}</Scroller>
```

### Drag

The track follows a pointer — mouse, pen or finger. A gesture is claimed for one axis on its first movement and never reassigned, so a vertical swipe still scrolls the page. Let go past a fifth of a tile, or flick, and the track advances; anything shorter settles back. Without `infinite` the track resists being pulled past either end and springs back.

A drag that ends on a tile does not also open it — the click is swallowed before it reaches the item.

Disable drag:

```tsx
<Scroller
  draggable={false}>{items}</Scroller>
```

### Proximity

`proximity` scales each tile by how far it is from the one in front, so the run has a focus that moves with it. It is continuous rather than stepped: halfway through a drag the outgoing and incoming tiles are the same size, so the emphasis crosses between them as the pointer moves instead of snapping when the track settles.

Pass `true` for a gentle default, or a number for how much smaller each whole step away is, as a fraction — `0.08` makes the immediate neighbour 92%. Tiles stop shrinking at 72%, so a long run does not trail off into nothing.

Proximity:

```tsx
<Scroller
  proximity
  infinite>{items}</Scroller>

<Scroller
  proximity={0.12}>{items}</Scroller>
```

### Driving it from your own UI

`active` brings an item to the front by its index, and `onActiveChange` reports the item that arrived there, however it got there — a control, a marker or a drag. Together they let something outside the component stand in for the markers: a row of names, a set of thumbnails, a table of contents.

`active` is a command, not a lock. The run still moves on its own, and it is `onActiveChange` that keeps the caller's own state level with it. An `active` that never changes does not pin the run in place.

Driving it from your own UI:

```tsx
const [active, setActive] = useState(0);

<Row gap="8">
  {names.map((name, i) => (
    <Button
      key={name}
      variant={i === active ? "primary" : "tertiary"}
      onClick={() => setActive(i)}
    >
      {name}
    </Button>
  ))}
</Row>

<Scroller
  active={active}
  onActiveChange={setActive}
  infinite>{items}</Scroller>
```

### Control Placement

Position navigation controls at the top or bottom with different horizontal alignments.

Control Placement:

```tsx
<Scroller
  controlPlacement="top-start">{items}</Scroller>

<Scroller
  controlPlacement="bottom-center">{items}</Scroller>
```

### Custom Styling

Every prop other than the ones listed below is applied to each tile, so a tile is styled from out here.

Tiles carry no appearance of their own: no border, no radius, no aspect ratio. The only sizing they arrive with is a `minWidth` floor, so a carousel of anything that fills its parent has something to fill. Give them whatever shape the content needs.

Custom Styling:

```tsx
<Scroller tile={{ border: "brand-alpha-medium", background: "brand-alpha-weak", onClick: (e) => {
    console.log('Item clicked');
  }, cursor: "interactive" }}>{items}</Scroller>
```

## Auto

`auto` loops the children across on their own, a marquee with no controls. `auto={{ speed, hover, reverse, gap }}` sets the speed (a multiplier, or `"slow"`/`"medium"`/`"fast"`), what hovering does (`"slow"`, `"pause"` or `"none"`), the direction and the space after each copy. It was `AutoScroll` in 2.x.

AutoScroll:

```tsx
<Scroller auto>
    <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="dark"/>
    <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="light"/>
    <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="dark"/>
    <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="light"/>
    <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="dark"/>
    <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="light"/>
</Scroller>
```

### Speed

The `speed` prop controls the speed of the scrolling: a multiplier on the 20-second loop (`2` is twice as fast), or `"slow"`, `"medium"` and `"fast"` (0.5, 1 and 2).

Speed:

```tsx
<Scroller auto={{ speed: "fast" }}>
    <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="dark"/>
    <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="light"/>
    <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="dark"/>
    <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="light"/>
    <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="dark"/>
    <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="light"/>
</Scroller>
```

### Fade

Combine with the `<Fade>` component to create a fade-in and fade-out effect.

Fade:

```tsx
<>
    <Fade zIndex="1" to="right" fillHeight width="64" position="absolute" left="0" top="0"/>
    <Scroller auto paddingY="40">
      <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="dark"/>
      <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="light"/>
      <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="dark"/>
      <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="light"/>
      <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="dark"/>
      <Logo wordmark="/logo.svg" size="s" href="#" showIn="light"/>
    </Scroller>
    <Fade zIndex="1" to="left" fillHeight width="64" position="absolute" right="0" top="0"/>
</>
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` |  | The items in the strip. |
| `direction` | `"row" \| "column"` |  | Which way it scrolls. |
| `fadeColor` | `BaseColor` |  | Colour of the fade at each end. Match the surface behind it. |
| `onItemClick` | `(index: number) => void` |  | Called with the index of the item clicked. |

| `children` |  |  |  |

## Accessibility

The Scroller component includes the following accessibility features:

- Scroll buttons are named "Scroll Previous" and "Scroll Next"; `labels` translates them
- Keyboard navigation support for the scroll buttons
- Preserves keyboard navigation and click events of child elements

# ScrollLock

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/scrollLock

> Freezes the page behind an overlay without moving it, while one region stays scrollable.

`ScrollLock` stops the page scrolling while an overlay is open. It renders
nothing — drop it in the tree and toggle `enabled`.

ScrollLock:

```tsx
const panel = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);

<>
  <ScrollLock enabled={open} allowScrollInElement={panel} />
  <Column ref={panel} overflowY="auto" maxHeight="24rem">
    {items.map(...)}
  </Column>
</>
```

## Why not `overflow: hidden`

The usual fix — setting `overflow: hidden` on the body — reflows the page when
the scrollbar disappears and drops the scroll position on some browsers, so
closing the overlay puts the reader somewhere other than where they left. This
component instead cancels the scroll *events* in the capture phase and records
the position on lock, so the page stays exactly where it was and comes back
untouched.

It covers all three ways a page scrolls: `wheel`, touch drag, and the keyboard
(arrows, Page Up/Down, Home, End, Space).

## Keeping one region scrollable

`allowScrollInElement` takes a ref to a region that should still scroll — the
overlay's own body. Scrolling inside it works normally; scrolling anywhere else
does nothing.

Two details make this reliable in practice:

- The **ref** is registered rather than the element, because the target is
  usually mounted a commit later than the lock (portals, `open &&` subtrees).
  A container that attaches late is still scrollable.
- The registry is **shared across instances**, so a dropdown opened inside a
  modal does not fight the modal's lock. Each allowed region stays scrollable
  while every other lock is in force.

Within the allowed region the nearest scrollable ancestor is resolved per
event, and only if it can actually move in that direction — so a list scrolled
to its end hands the gesture back rather than swallowing it.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled (required)` | `boolean` |  | Whether the lock is on. Required. |
| `allowScrollInElement` | `RefObject<HTMLElement \| null>` |  | A region that stays scrollable while locked. |

# Scrubber

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/scrubber

> A playhead over time: a seek bar on its own, an editor timeline once you give it tracks.

`Scrubber` positions things by **time** rather than by layout. With no tracks it
is a seek bar. Give it tracks and it is an editor timeline: stacked layers of
blocks sharing one playhead, each block selectable, movable and trimmable.
Import it from the media entry point: `import { Scrubber } from "@once-ui-system/core/media";`

It is not [`Timeline`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/timeline), which lays out a sequence
of steps or events down the page.

Seek bar:

```tsx
<Scrubber duration={125000} value={time} onValueChange={setTime} />
```

Times are in whatever unit you and the component agree on — milliseconds by
convention, which is what the default `m:ss` formatter assumes. Pass
`formatTime` for anything else, including frames or bars.

## Tracks

Each track is a row of blocks. `movable` lets the body be dragged along the
track, `resizable` puts trim handles on the edges, and `onAdd` turns a click on
empty track space into a new block. Blocks colour themselves from a `tone`,
so layers stay distinguishable.

Editor timeline:

```tsx
<Scrubber
  duration={40000}
  value={time}
  onValueChange={setTime}
  selected={selected}
  onSelectedChange={setSelected}
  onBlockChange={(trackId, blockId, next) => moveBlock(blockId, next)}
  tracks={[
    { id: "zooms", height: "32", movable: true, resizable: true, blocks: zooms },
    { id: "scenes", height: "48", blocks: scenes },
  ]}
/>
```

## Editor grade

The same component carries a full editor timeline. Turn on `ruler` for round
time ticks with a grabbable playhead, give tracks a `label` for a header column,
and the rest is per block or per timeline:

Editor timeline:

```tsx
<Scrubber
  duration={24000}
  value={time}
  onValueChange={setTime}
  ruler
  snap
  range={range}
  onRangeChange={setRange}
  markers={[{ id: "c1", time: 2600, label: "Click: Checkout" }]}
  renderPreview={(at) => <img src={frameAt(at)} alt="" width={128} />}
  tracks={[
    {
      id: "take",
      label: "Take",
      resizable: true,
      blocks: [
        { id: "cart", start: 0, end: 5000, label: "Cart" },
        { id: "idle", start: 5000, end: 8000, label: "idle 3 s", variant: "gap",
          description: "Cut: nothing moved on screen for 3 s" },
        { id: "load", start: 14000, end: 17000, label: "Loading", badge: "4×" },
      ],
    },
    {
      id: "audio",
      label: "Audio",
      tone: "info",
      blocks: [{ id: "music", start: 0, end: 24000,
        content: <ScrubberWaveform peaks={peaks} tone="info" /> }],
    },
  ]}
/>
```

- **`variant: "gap"`** draws a range that is not in the output: hatched,
  dashed and neutral. Put the reason in `label` and `description`; the
  description is the block's tooltip and what a screen reader announces.
- **`badge`** pins a small pill to the block's corner, such as a speed.
- **`content`** fills the block behind its label. `ScrubberFilmstrip` draws
  thumbnails from frame URLs; `ScrubberWaveform` draws loudness peaks (0 to 1).
- **`highlight`** sweeps a shimmer across the block once. Set it on the blocks
  that just changed under the user, after an AI rewrite or an undo, so the eye
  finds them. Blocks also glide to their new place when their times change.
- **`markers`** put dots on the ruler (clicks, keyframes, chapters).
- **`snap`** makes dragged edges stick to other edges, markers and the
  playhead within 8 px (or the number you pass), with a guide line.
- **`zoom`**, `defaultZoom` and `onZoomChange` magnify the timeline. `Ctrl`
  or `Cmd` with the wheel, or a pinch, zooms around the pointer;
  `+` and `-` work on the focused timeline. The view follows
  the playhead while it plays.
- **`range`** and `onRangeChange`: `Shift`-drag on the ruler or an
  empty track selects a span, and a plain click clears it.
- **`renderPreview`** shows what you return above the pointer while it hovers,
  with the time under it. A frame of the video is the usual answer.

## Editing is yours to accept

`onBlockChange` hands back **absolute** times, already clamped to
`[0, duration]` and measured from where the gesture started — not accumulated
per pointer move, so a block cannot drift away from the pointer over a long
drag. Everything past that is your rule: a minimum length, no overlap with the
next block, snapping to a grid. The block renders wherever you put it, so
refusing a change is simply not applying it.

```tsx
onBlockChange={(trackId, blockId, next) => {
  if (next.end - next.start < MIN_MS) return;  // refuse: nothing moves
  setBlocks((current) =>
    current.map((b) => (b.id === blockId ? { ...b, ...next } : b)),
  );
}}
```

`onGestureStart` fires once when a drag begins, which is the moment to snapshot
for undo — one entry per gesture rather than one per pointer move.

## Keyboard and pointer

The track is a `role="slider"`: `←` and `→` step the playhead
by `step` (a hundredth of the duration by default), `Home` and

### ScrubberTrack

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `string` |  |  |
| `blocks` |  |  |  |
| `height` | `SpacingToken` | `40` |  |
| `tone` | `neutral` | `brand` | accent |
| `movable` | `boolean` | `false` |  |

# SegmentedControl

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/segmentedControl

> The SegmentedControl component allows users to select a single option from a set of horizontally arranged buttons. It supports keyboard navigation and customizable options.

Use this component for toggle-style selection between discrete options. It supports keyboard interaction, styling, and controlled or uncontrolled usage.

Basic usage:

```tsx
<SegmentedControl
    fillWidth={false}
    buttons={[
      { value: "day", label: "Day" },
      { value: "week", label: "Week" },
      { value: "month", label: "Month" },
    ]}
    onValueChange={(value) => console.log(value)}
/>
```

## Sliding background

The selected background slides from one option to the next, even when the options have different widths. Visitors who ask for reduced motion see it move without the slide. Pass `sliding={false}` for the old jump; `compact` controls never slide.

Sliding:

```tsx
<SegmentedControl
    fillWidth={false}
    buttons={[
      { value: "all", label: "All" },
      { value: "unread", label: "Unread" },
      { value: "mentions", label: "Mentions and replies" },
      { value: "archive", label: "Archive" },
    ]}
/>
```

Without the slide:

```tsx
<SegmentedControl
    sliding={false}
    buttons={[
      { value: "all", label: "All" },
      { value: "unread", label: "Unread" },
    ]}
/>
```

## External state

Use `selected` to manage the selected state from the parent.

External state:

```tsx
<SegmentedControl
    fillWidth={false}
    value="month"
    buttons={[
      { value: "day", label: "Day" },
      { value: "week", label: "Week" },
      { value: "month", label: "Month" },
    ]}
    onValueChange={(value) => console.log(value)}
/>
```

## Internal state

Use `defaultValue` to define an initial active button in uncontrolled mode. Don't use it along with the `value` prop.

Internal state:

```tsx
<SegmentedControl
    fillWidth={false}
    defaultValue="week"
    buttons={[
      { value: "day", label: "Day" },
      { value: "week", label: "Week" },
      { value: "month", label: "Month" },
    ]}
    onValueChange={(value) => console.log(value)}
/>
```

## Radio group

A tab strip is the default, for switching views. For one choice among settings, `semantics="radio"` makes the segments a `radiogroup` of `radio`s: the arrow keys move and choose, as native radios do. Name it with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.

Radio group:

```tsx
<SegmentedControl
    fillWidth={false}
    semantics="radio"
    aria-label="Density"
    defaultValue="comfortable"
    buttons={[
      { value: "compact", label: "Compact" },
      { value: "comfortable", label: "Comfortable" },
    ]}
/>
```

## Compact

Use `compact` to create a compact variant.

Compact:

```tsx
<SegmentedControl
    compact
    defaultValue="week"
    buttons={[
      { value: "day", label: "Day" },
      { value: "week", label: "Week" },
      { value: "month", label: "Month" },
    ]}
    onValueChange={(value) => console.log(value)}
/>
```

## Controlled state

Control the selected value externally with the `value` prop.

Controlled:

```tsx
<SegmentedControl
  fillWidth={false}
  value="month"
  buttons={[
    { value: "day", label: "Day" },
    { value: "week", label: "Week" },
    { value: "month", label: "Month" },
  ]}
  onValueChange={(value) => console.log(value)}
/>
```

## Fill width

Distribute the button widths evenly across the container.

Fill width:

```tsx
<SegmentedControl
  buttons={[
    { value: "a", label: "A" },
    { value: "b", label: "B" },
    { value: "c", label: "C" },
  ]}
  onValueChange={(value) => console.log(value)}
/>
```

## Narrow spaces

Options that do not fit scroll behind a Next button. In a narrow sidebar that clips the last one; `scroll={false}` keeps them in a plain row that shares the width equally and truncates a label that does not fit. An option's `description` adds a second, dimmer line under its label. Without `onChange` the control keeps its own selection, starting from `defaultValue`.

Narrow spaces:

```tsx
<SegmentedControl
  scroll={false}
  aria-label="Answer mode"
  defaultValue="deep"
  buttons={[
    { value: "fast", label: "Fast", description: "Quick answers" },
    { value: "deep", label: "Deep", description: "Reads sources" },
  ]}
/>
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `buttons (required)` | `ButtonOption[]` |  |  |
| `value` | `string` |  | The selected button's value, controlled. Leave it out and the control keeps its own state. |
| `defaultValue` | `string` |  | The button selected first when uncontrolled. Defaults to the first one. |
| `onValueChange` | `(value: string, event?: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => void` |  | Called with the picked value (and the click, when it was one) on every pick. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | `false` | Disables every button. |
| `fillWidth` | `boolean` | `true` |  |
| `compact` | `boolean` | `false` | Tighter padding, for dense toolbars. |
| `semantics` | `"tabs" \| "radio"` | `tabs` | `tabs` (a tab strip) or `radio` (one choice from a set of settings, a radio group). |
| `sliding` | `boolean` | `true` |  |
| `scroll` | `boolean` | `true` | `false` shares the width between the options and truncates labels, instead of scrolling them. |
| `className` | `string` |  |  |
| `style` | `React.CSSProperties` |  |  |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# Setting

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/setting

> The settings row: a label on the left, one control on the right, in a panel that stacks.

Every editor UI grows the same row: a label, sometimes a description, sometimes
an explainer, and one control on the right. `Setting` is that row.

The control is passed as **children** rather than as a typed prop, so the
component never has to know what can sit in it — including controls that do not
exist yet.

Setting:

```tsx
<Setting label="Autoplay" description="Start playing on load">
    <Switch checked={autoplay} onCheckedChange={toggleAutoplay} />
</Setting>
<Setting label="Loop" info="Restarts from the beginning when it reaches the end.">
    <Switch checked={loop} onCheckedChange={toggleLoop} />
</Setting>
```

## Info

`info` puts a sentence of context behind a small icon beside the label, so a
setting can explain itself without spending a line of the panel on a description
that is only read once. It renders an `InfoTip`, which is also exported on its
own for use anywhere else.

InfoTip:

```tsx
<Tooltip content="Higher bitrates keep more detail in fast motion, at a larger file size." />
```

## Groups

With `control` or `open`, a Setting becomes a group (2.x's `SettingGroup`): it nests sub-settings **inside** its own box rather than beside it,
so the relationship survives a panel with ten groups in it. The header control
is what usually gates the body; `open` shows or hides it.

The group is a single surface — the header and the body it reveals share one
background, separated by a hairline — so opening one grows the panel instead of
stacking a second panel inside it. Its border is an alpha, which reads against
whatever the group is nested in.

Group:

```tsx
<Setting
  label="Watermark"
  control={<Switch checked={enabled} onCheckedChange={toggleEnabled} />}
  open={enabled}
>
    <Setting label="Opacity">
      <Slider value={opacity} onValueChange={setOpacity} />
    </Setting>
    <Setting label="Position">
      <SegmentedControl value={position} onValueChange={setPosition} buttons={positions} />
    </Setting>
</Setting>
```

## Axes

A property with more than one axis belongs in one row. `axes` (2.x's `SettingAxes`) puts them
side by side, and wraps when the panel is too narrow, instead of splitting into
two rows that read as unrelated settings.

Axes:

```tsx
<Setting
  label="Tilt"
  info="Rotates the frame in 3D. Both axes are degrees."
  axes={[
    { label: "X", control: <Slider value={x} min={-45} max={45} onValueChange={setX} /> },
    { label: "Y", control: <Slider value={y} min={-45} max={45} onValueChange={setY} /> },
  ]}
/>
```

## API reference

### Setting

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `React.ReactNode` |  | Name of the setting. |
| `description` | `React.ReactNode` |  | What it does, under the label. |
| `info` | `React.ReactNode` |  | Extra detail behind an InfoTip. |
| `controlWidth` | `number \| CSSUnit` |  | Width reserved for the control, so a column of settings lines up: a number is on the token scale (16 = 1rem), a string a CSS length. Default "14rem". |
| `children` | `ReactNode` |  | The control itself; in a group, the sub-settings it reveals. |
| `axes` | `{ label: React.ReactNode; control: React.ReactNode }[]` |  | Puts one control per axis side by side in one row: { label, control }[]. Takes no children. |
| `control` | `ReactNode` |  | Makes a group: the control in its header, usually a Switch gating the body. |
| `open` | `boolean` |  | Makes a group: its body shows only while open is true. |
| `axisWidth` | `number \| CSSUnit` |  | With axes, the least width of each axis before the row wraps: a number is on the token scale (16 = 1rem), a string a CSS length. Default "13rem". |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

### InfoTip

InfoTip folded into [Tooltip](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/tooltip) in 3.0. A setting's `info` shows its detail behind an info icon with a Tooltip.

# Settings blocks

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/settingsBlocks

> Profile, sign-in and security, and organization settings in one flow, for any auth provider.

Every app grows the same settings: a photo, a name, an email, a password,
two-step verification, signed-in devices, and the organization's name and
danger zone. The settings blocks are that flow, built once from `Setting`
rows with small controls of one height.

They come from `@once-ui-system/blocks` and know nothing about auth. Each one
reads and writes through an **adapter** the app supplies, so the same blocks
work on Supabase, Better Auth or anything else.

Settings:

```tsx
import {
  AccountSettings,
  OrganizationSettings,
  SecuritySettings,
  SettingsLayout,
} from "@once-ui-system/blocks";

<SettingsLayout
  sections={[
    { value: "profile", label: "Profile", icon: "person",
      content: <AccountSettings adapter={account} fields={{ username: true }} /> },
    { value: "security", label: "Sign-in & security", icon: "security",
      content: <SecuritySettings adapter={account} /> },
    { value: "organization", label: "Organization", icon: "organization",
      content: <OrganizationSettings adapter={organization} /> },
  ]}
/>
```

The preview runs on `createDemoAccountAdapter()` and
`createDemoOrganizationAdapter()`, which keep everything in memory. The
two-step code there is `123456`. An app's demo mode can use them too.

## How it behaves

- **Values at rest.** Each row shows its value with an Edit button. Edit turns
  that row alone into a field with Save and Cancel; Enter saves and Escape puts
  it back. Every row saves on its own, so switching sections loses nothing.
- **Sensitive changes in a dialog.** Changing the email or password, setting
  up two-step verification and deleting the account ask for the current
  password first. An account with no password passes `{ recentSignIn: true }`
  and the adapter checks the session's age.
- **Email changes wait for the link.** The row shows the new address as
  pending until it is confirmed, with a way to cancel.
- **Two-step verification in three steps.** Scan the code or copy the key,
  enter a code, save the backup codes.
- **Only what works.** A row appears only when the adapter implements it. A
  provider that cannot list sessions shows just "Sign out everywhere else". The
  last way to sign in cannot be disconnected.
- **Roles.** Owners and admins edit the organization; members see it read only
  and can leave. Deleting it asks for its address to be typed.

## Where buttons go

One rule for every row and dialog, so a button is always where the eye looks
for it:

- **Rows.** The value or status comes first, then a quiet action (`tertiary`,
  such as Remove or Cancel change), then the row's one action (`secondary`,
  such as Edit, Change or Set up) at the trailing edge. Rows never use a
  primary button: a page of rows has no single main action.
- **Committing.** The button that commits (Save, Send link, Verify, Delete) is
  `primary`, with `tone="danger"` when it destroys something, and always last.
  Cancel is `tertiary`, just before it. Inline edits and dialog footers follow
  the same order; a dialog's step count sits at the footer's start.
- **Narrow rows.** When a row is too narrow for both, the controls wrap under
  the label and stay at the trailing edge, as core's `Setting` places them.
- **One height.** Every control in the blocks is `size="s"`.

## The adapter

Only `getAccount` is required. Leave a method out and its row is not shown.

Adapter:

```tsx
import type { AccountAdapter } from "@once-ui-system/blocks";

export const account: AccountAdapter = {
  getAccount: () => fetch("/api/account").then((r) => r.json()),
  updateProfile: (changes) => patch("/api/account", changes),
  avatar: { upload: (file) => upload("/api/account/avatar", file) },
  changeEmail: (email, proof) => post("/api/account/email", { email, ...proof }),
  changePassword: (next, proof, { signOutOthers }) =>
    post("/api/account/password", { next, signOutOthers, ...proof }),
  twoFactor: {
    enabled: () => get("/api/account/2fa"),
    enroll: (proof) => post("/api/account/2fa", proof), // { secret, uri, qrCode? }
    verify: (code) => post("/api/account/2fa/verify", { code }), // { backupCodes? }
    disable: (code) => post("/api/account/2fa/disable", { code }),
  },
  sessions: { revokeOthers: () => post("/api/account/sessions/revoke-others") },
};
```

Uploads arrive cropped to a centred square of at most 512 px, so the app
stores what it shows.

## Languages

Every string goes through `labels`. Pass a partial object to change a few, or
`settingsLabelsHu` for the Hungarian set. `SettingsLayout` passes its labels to
every block inside it.

Hungarian:

```tsx
import { settingsLabelsHu, SettingsLayout } from "@once-ui-system/blocks";

<SettingsLayout labels={settingsLabelsHu} sections={sections} />
```

## App rows

`extraRows` adds rows only one app has: a public bio on the profile, API keys
under security, or business details on the organization.

```tsx
<OrganizationSettings adapter={organization} extraRows={<BusinessDetails />} />
```

# Sidebar

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/sidebar

> An app sidebar you compose from a header, a scrolling Nav and a footer. Drag it wider or narrower, fold it into an icon rail, and it remembers both.

A Sidebar is the frame around a [Nav](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/once-ui/components/nav): it owns the
width, the collapse, the resize handle and the phone drawer, so the Nav inside
only has to say what the rows are. Drag its edge to resize it. Drag past the
minimum and it folds into an icon rail; drag the rail out and it opens again.
Double-click the edge to reset it. ⌘B (Ctrl+B elsewhere) folds it from
anywhere outside a text field.

```tsx
<SidebarProvider persist="app">
  <Row as="header">
    <SidebarTrigger />
    <Breadcrumbs items={crumbs} />
  </Row>
  <Row fill>
    <Sidebar aria-label="Workspace">
      <SidebarHeader>
        <User name="Fjell" subline="Pro workspace" />
      </SidebarHeader>
      <SidebarContent>
        <Nav density="compact" aria-label="Product">
          <NavItem icon="home" label="Dashboard" href="/" selected />
          <NavSection label="Workspace">
            <NavGroup icon="people" label="Manage">
              <NavItem label="Users" href="/users" />
            </NavGroup>
          </NavSection>
        </Nav>
      </SidebarContent>
      <SidebarFooter>
        <UserMenu />
      </SidebarFooter>
    </Sidebar>
    <Column as="main" flex={1}>{children}</Column>
  </Row>
</SidebarProvider>
```

## Composition

- **Sidebar** is the frame: an `aside` that holds the width and draws the
  handle on its edge.
- **SidebarHeader** and **SidebarFooter** stay put. Put the workspace switcher
  on top and the account at the bottom. In the rail they clip to their
  leading mark rather than wrap.
- **SidebarContent** takes the space left and scrolls on its own. It holds the
  Nav.
- **SidebarTrigger** folds and unfolds it, or opens the drawer on a phone. Its
  tooltip names the shortcut. Put it in the top bar or in the SidebarHeader.
- **SidebarProvider** holds the state for the Sidebar and for anything outside
  it that reads or changes it: the trigger in the top bar, ⌘B, `useSidebar()`.
  A Sidebar with no provider around it makes its own.

## Remembering it

Give the provider a `persist` key and it keeps the width and the collapse in a
cookie. Read the cookie on the server and pass it back as the defaults, and the
first paint is already right: no default width that jumps once the browser has
looked.

```tsx
// app/(app)/layout.tsx
import { cookies } from "next/headers";
import { parseSidebarCookie, sidebarCookieName } from "@once-ui-system/core";

export default async function AppLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const store = await cookies();
  const saved = parseSidebarCookie(store.get(sidebarCookieName("app"))?.value);
  return (
    <SidebarProvider persist="app" defaultWidth={saved.width} defaultCollapsed={saved.collapsed}>
      {/* … */}
    </SidebarProvider>
  );
}
```

Both helpers are plain functions, safe to call in a server component and
outside Next.js: read the cookie however your framework does and pass its value
to `parseSidebarCookie`.

## Peeking from the rail

With `expandOnHover`, a mouse resting on the rail opens it over the page,
labels and all, and the page beside it does not move. Keyboard focus opens it
too; Escape or leaving closes it. Touch never opens it.

```tsx
<Sidebar aria-label="Workspace" expandOnHover>…</Sidebar>
```

In the rail, a NavGroup is its icon, and a click opens its rows in a menu
beside it.

## Off canvas

`collapsible="offcanvas"` slides it out entirely instead of leaving a rail, for
a chat list or a file tree that has no icons to keep. While it is out, nothing
in it can be reached by Tab. `collapsible={false}` keeps it open.

```tsx
<Sidebar aria-label="Chats" collapsible="offcanvas">…</Sidebar>
```

## Phones

Below `mobileBelow` (default `s`) the sidebar is a drawer from the left, with
the same children at full labels. The SidebarTrigger opens it, and following a
link inside closes it. `mobileBelow={false}` keeps the desktop sidebar at
every width.

## Keyboard

The edge is a focusable separator with its width as its value.

| Key | Does |
|---|---|
| ← / → | Narrower or wider by 8px; 32px with Shift. Past the minimum, ← folds it. |
| Home / End | The minimum or the maximum width. |
| Enter | Folds or unfolds it. |
| ⌘B / Ctrl+B | Folds or unfolds it from anywhere outside a text field (`shortcut`). |

## Motion

The width eases between open, rail and hidden on the macro transition, and the
Nav's labels fade on the micro one. Nothing animates while you drag, and with
`prefers-reduced-motion` nothing animates at all.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `collapsible` | `SidebarCollapsible` |  | "rail" folds it to its icons, "offcanvas" slides it out, false keeps it open. |
| `resizable` | `boolean` |  | Draw the handle on its edge. |
| `expandOnHover` | `boolean` |  | As a rail, open over the page on a resting mouse or keyboard focus. |
| `railWidth` | `number` |  | The rail's width in pixels. Left out, 52 for a compact Nav and 80 for a normal one. |
| `labels` | `{ resize?: string; menu?: string }` |  | The handle's and the drawer's words, for another language. |
| `defaultWidth` | `number` |  |  |
| `width` | `number` |  |  |
| `onWidthChange` | `(width: number) => void` |  |  |
| `defaultCollapsed` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `collapsed` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `onCollapsedChange` | `(collapsed: boolean) => void` |  |  |
| `minWidth` | `number` |  |  |
| `maxWidth` | `number` |  |  |
| `persist` | `string` |  |  |
| `shortcut` | `string \| false` |  |  |
| `mobileBelow` | `"xs" \| "s" \| "m" \| "l" \| false` |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `children` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
| `defaultWidth` | `number` | `256` | The open width to start from, in pixels, such as a saved one. |
| `width` | `number` |  | The open width, when the host owns it. |
| `onWidthChange` | `(width: number) => void` |  | Called once a resize ends. |
| `defaultCollapsed` | `boolean` | `false` | Start folded. |
| `collapsed` | `boolean` |  | Folded, when the host owns it. |
| `onCollapsedChange` | `(collapsed: boolean) => void` |  | Called with the state it moves to. |
| `minWidth` | `number` | `200` | The narrowest a drag can make it. |
| `maxWidth` | `number` | `400` | The widest a drag can make it. |
| `persist` | `string` |  | Keep width and collapse in a cookie under this key. |
| `shortcut` | `string \| false` | `mod+b` | The key that folds it. false for none. |
| `mobileBelow` | `"xs" \| "s" \| "m" \| "l" \| false` | `s` | Below this breakpoint it is a drawer. false never. |

# Skeleton

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/skeleton

> The Skeleton component is used to display loading placeholders for content that hasn't yet loaded. It supports different shapes, sizes, and delay animations.

Use `Skeleton` to maintain layout consistency and improve perceived performance during data loading states.

Skeleton:

```tsx
<Skeleton shape="circle" size="l" />
<Skeleton shape="line" delay={100} width="50%" size="xs" />
<Skeleton shape="line" delay={200} width="75%" size="s" />
<Skeleton shape="block" delay={300} minHeight="80" />
```

## Shape

Skeletons can be shaped as lines, circles, or blocks.

Shapes:

```tsx
<Skeleton shape="line" size="xs" />
<Skeleton shape="circle" />
<Skeleton shape="block" minHeight="48" />
```

## Size

Control the visual dimensions using predefined size tokens.

Size:

```tsx
<Skeleton shape="line" size="xl" width="100%" />
<Skeleton shape="line" size="l" width="75%" />
<Skeleton shape="line" size="m" width="50%" />
<Skeleton shape="line" size="s" width="33%" />
<Skeleton shape="line" size="xs" width="25%" />
```

## Animation delay

Apply delay classes to stagger loading effects for multiple items.

Delay:

```tsx
<Skeleton shape="line" width="75%" delay={100} />
<Skeleton shape="line" width="50%" delay={200} />
<Skeleton shape="line" width="33%" delay={300} />
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `width` | `number \| StaticSpacingToken \| CSSUnit` |  |  |

| `minWidth` | `number \| SpacingToken \| CSSUnit` |  |  |
| `maxWidth` | `number \| SpacingToken \| CSSUnit` |  |  |
| `minHeight` | `number \| StaticSpacingToken \| CSSUnit` |  |  |
| `maxHeight` | `number \| StaticSpacingToken \| CSSUnit` |  |  |
| `shape` | `"line" \| "circle" \| "block"` | `line` | A line of text, a circle, or a filled block. |
| `size` | `"xl" \| "l" \| "m" \| "s" \| "xs"` | `m` | Height of a line, or diameter of a circle. Width comes from Flex. |
| `delay` | `number` |  | Milliseconds before the shimmer starts, to stagger a set. |
| `style` | `React.CSSProperties` |  |  |
| `className` | `string` |  |  |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# Slider

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/slider

> The Slider component provides an interactive range input for selecting numeric values with visual feedback and customizable styling.

The Slider component provides an intuitive way to select a value from a range using a draggable thumb along a track.

Slider:

```tsx
const [value, setValue] = useState(50);

return (
    <Slider
      value={value}
      onValueChange={setValue}
      min={0}
      max={100}
    />
);
```

## Uncontrolled

Without `value`, Slider keeps its own state and starts at `defaultValue`, or at
`min` when there is none. `onValueChange` is optional then: give the slider a `name` and
a form submits its value, or read it from a ref.

Uncontrolled:

```tsx
<Slider label="Volume" name="volume" defaultValue={40} showValue />
```

For two thumbs that select a range, add [`range`](#range).

## Label

Add a descriptive label to the slider using the `label` prop.

Label:

```tsx
<Slider
  value={value}
  onValueChange={setValue}
  min={0}
  max={100}
  label="Volume"
/>
```

## Show value

Display the current value alongside the label using `showValue`.

Show value:

```tsx
<Slider
  value={value}
  onValueChange={setValue}
  min={0}
  max={100}
  label="Brightness"
  showValue
/>
```

## Step

Control the granularity of value changes with the `step` prop.

With step:

```tsx
<Slider
  value={value}
  onValueChange={setValue}
  min={0}
  max={100}
  step={10}
  label="Volume"
  showValue
/>
```

## Min and max

Define custom minimum and maximum values for your use case.

Custom range:

```tsx
<Slider
  value={value}
  onValueChange={setValue}
  min={10}
  max={30}
  step={1}
  label="Temperature (°C)"
  showValue
/>
```

## Disabled

Disable the slider to prevent user interaction.

Disabled:

```tsx
<Slider
  value={50}
  onValueChange={() => {}}
  min={0}
  max={100}
  label="Locked Setting"
  showValue
  disabled
/>
```

## Error

`error` paints the fill and thumb in the danger palette and marks the input invalid; `errorMessage` shows under the track and is tied to the thumb with `aria-describedby`, so a screen reader reads it on focus. Both work with `range` too.

Error:

```tsx
<Slider
  label="Volume"
  defaultValue={95}
  showValue
  error
  errorMessage="Above 90 can damage hearing."
/>
```

## Size

`size` sets the thumb and track, from `"xs"` to `"xl"` (default `"m"`). Inside a [Form](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/form) the slider takes the form's `size` when it sets none.

Size:

```tsx
<Slider label="Small" size="s" defaultValue={30} />
<Slider label="Medium" defaultValue={50} />
<Slider label="Large" size="l" defaultValue={70} />
```

## Range

With `range`, the slider selects a `[start, end]` pair with two thumbs on one track (2.x's `RangeSlider`). `min`, `max`, `step`, `label`, `showValue`, `disabled`, `error` and `size` work as above; the value is a pair, start first.

Range:

```tsx
<Slider range label="Duration (minutes)" defaultValue={[20, 70]} showValue />
```

Without `value` or `defaultValue`, the range starts as the whole track, `[min, max]`.

### Controlled

Pass `value` and `onValueChange` when something else owns the range, such as the filters
of a product list. `onValueChange` gets the new pair, start never above end. `formatValue`
sets how a value reads, in the readout and to a screen reader, and `minDistance`
keeps the thumbs apart.

Controlled:

```tsx
const [range, setRange] = useState<[number, number]>([120, 480]);

<Slider range
  label="Price"
  min={0}
  max={600}
  step={10}
  minDistance={50}
  value={range}
  onValueChange={setRange}
  formatValue={(value) => `$${value}`}
  showValue
/>
```

### Disabled

Disabled:

```tsx
<Slider range label="Locked range" defaultValue={[30, 60]} showValue disabled />
```

### Forms

Give the slider a `name` and a form submits both values under it, start first. Pass
two names to submit each under its own, as a search form's query string wants:

Forms:

```tsx
<form action="/search">
  <Slider range label="Price" name={["minPrice", "maxPrice"]} defaultValue={[0, 500]} max={1000} />
</form>
// → /search?minPrice=0&maxPrice=500
```

### Accessibility

The two thumbs sit in a group named by `label` (or `aria-label`). Each thumb is a
`slider` of its own, named "Minimum" and "Maximum": pass `thumbLabels` to name them
otherwise, or in another language. A thumb's bounds are the other thumb, so a
screen reader announces how far each one can go and the thumbs can never cross.

| Key | Does |
| --- | --- |
| Right / Up | One `step` higher. Left and Right swap in a right-to-left layout. |
| Left / Down | One `step` lower. |
| Page Up / Page Down | A tenth of the range higher or lower. |
| Home / End | The lowest or highest value the thumb can reach. |

A press on the track moves the nearer thumb there, and either thumb can be dragged.
When the two thumbs sit on the same value, the first move decides which one comes
along, since only one of them can go each way.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `range` | `boolean` |  | Two thumbs selecting a [start, end] pair. value, defaultValue and onValueChange then take the pair. |
| `value` | `number \| [number, number]` |  | The value, when the host owns the state. Pair with onValueChange. |
| `defaultValue` | `number \| [number, number]` |  | Where the slider starts when it keeps its own state. Defaults to min. |
| `onValueChange` | `((value: number) => void) \| ((value: [number, number]) => void)` |  | Called with the new value, as a number, on every step of a drag. |
| `onValueCommit` | `(value: number) => void` |  | Called with the value once a change is done: on pointer release, and after each key that moves the thumb. |
| `min` | `number` | `0` |  |
| `max` | `number` | `100` |  |
| `step` | `number` | `1` |  |
| `label` | `string` |  | Visible label that names the slider. |
| `showValue` | `boolean` | `false` |  |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | `false` |  |
| `error` | `boolean` | `false` | Paint the slider in its error state and mark it invalid. |
| `errorMessage` | `ReactNode` |  | Shown under the track and read with the thumb, when error is set. |
| `size` | `TShirtSizes` |  | Thumb and track size, xs to xl. Takes a Form's size when unset. |
| `minDistance` | `number` |  | With range, the smallest gap the thumbs keep between them. |
| `formatValue` | `(value: number) => string` |  | With range, how a value reads, in the readout and to a screen reader. |
| `thumbLabels` | `[string, string]` |  | With range, the thumbs' accessible names, start first. |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `...InputHTMLAttributes` |  |  | Also takes these props |
| `name` | `string` | `-` | The form field name. With range, one name for both values or one for each. |
| `onChange` | `ChangeEventHandler` | `-` | The native change event of the range input. |
| `...LeafProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# SmartLink

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/smartLink

> SmartLink is a styled anchor component that supports prefix/suffix icons, fill layout, and intelligent styling. It adapts behavior based on props like selection and unstyled mode.

`SmartLink` provides flexible and consistent inline navigation with built-in icon support and style overrides.

Basic usage:

```tsx
<SmartLink href="#" prefixIcon="link" suffixIcon="arrowRight">
  Learn more
</SmartLink>
```

## Fill width

Use `fillWidth` to stretch the link across the container. It's useful when you're using fluid children elements.

Fill width:

```tsx
<SmartLink href="#" fillWidth unstyled>
    <Row fillWidth background="surface" border="surface" radius="l" padding="16" horizontal="between" vertical="center">
      <Text>Full width link</Text>
      <Icon name="chevronRight" />
    </Row>
</SmartLink>
```

## Unstyled

Disable default padding and visual treatments using `unstyled`.

Unstyled:

```tsx
<SmartLink href="#" unstyled>
    Raw link
</SmartLink>
```

## Selected

Apply underline when `selected` is true.

Selected:

```tsx
<SmartLink href="#" selected>
    Active link
</SmartLink>
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `prefixIcon` | `IconName` |  | Icon before the text. |
| `suffixIcon` | `IconName` |  | Icon after the text — an arrow for an outbound link, say. |
| `iconSize` | `TShirtSizes` | `xs` | Size of either icon. |
| `selected` | `boolean` |  | Mark as the current page, for navigation. |
| `unstyled` | `boolean` | `false` | Drop the link styling, when the child carries its own. |
| `children (required)` | `ReactNode` |  | The link text. |
| `href` | `string` |  | Where it goes. Internal paths route through the framework adapter; external ones do not. |
| `children` |  |  |  |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `...AnchorHTMLAttributes` |  |  | Also takes these props |
| `fillWidth` | `boolean` | `-` | Fill the parent's width rather than hugging the text. |
| `...LeafProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# Sortable

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/sortable

> Lists people can reorder by mouse, touch or keyboard, and move rows between, with every step read out to screen readers.

`Sortable` makes a list reorderable. Wrap the list, wrap each row in
`SortableItem`, and apply the new order in `onReorder`. The rows themselves
stay whatever they were: NavItems, Cards, task rows.

- **Mouse and pen:** the drag starts after a 4px move, so a click still clicks.
- **Touch:** press and hold a row for 200ms, so a tap still taps and a swipe
  still scrolls. A `SortableHandle` drags at once.
- **Keyboard:** Space picks a row up, the arrow keys move it, Space drops it
  and Escape puts it back. Screen readers hear "Picked up Launch plan, 1 of 5"
  and every step after.
- **Reduced motion:** the rows jump into place instead of sliding.

Sortable keeps no order of its own. It reports the move and shows whatever
order `items` holds, so the order lives in your state, next to the data.

List:

```tsx
const [rows, setRows] = useState(["Inbox", "Drafts", "Sent", "Archive", "Spam"]);

<Sortable items={rows} onReorder={setRows}>
  {rows.map((row) => (
    <SortableItem key={row} id={row}>
      <NavItem href={`/${row.toLowerCase()}`} label={row} />
    </SortableItem>
  ))}
</Sortable>
```

`onReorder` gets the new order of ids and the move that made it. When your
rows are objects rather than ids, apply the move with `arrayMove`:

```tsx
onReorder={(_, { from, to }) => setTasks((tasks) => arrayMove(tasks, from, to))}
```

## A sidebar

Lists with the same `group` trade rows. Give each one a `name`, and
`onMove(id, to, from)` says where a row went, as `{ list, index }` on both
sides. Inside a [Nav](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/nav) the rows keep the nav's spacing, and a
closed NavGroup opens when a row is held over it.

Sidebar:

```tsx
<Nav density="compact">
  <NavSection label="Pinned">
    <Sortable group="chats" name="pinned" label="Pinned"
      items={pinned} onReorder={setPinned} onMove={move}>
      {pinned.map((chat) => (
        <SortableItem key={chat.id} id={chat.id}>
          <NavItem href={chat.href} icon="star" label={chat.title} />
        </SortableItem>
      ))}
    </Sortable>
  </NavSection>
  <NavSection label="Projects">
    <Sortable group="chats" name="projects" label="Projects"
      items={projects} onReorder={setProjects} onMove={move}>
      {/* … */}
    </Sortable>
  </NavSection>
  <NavGroup label="Archive" icon="document">
    <Sortable group="chats" name="archive" label="Archive"
      items={archive} onReorder={setArchive} onMove={move}>
      {/* … */}
    </Sortable>
  </NavGroup>
</Nav>
```

onMove:

```tsx
const move = (id: string, to: SortablePosition, from: SortablePosition) =>
  setChats((chats) => {
    const next = { ...chats, [from.list]: chats[from.list].filter((c) => c !== id) };
    next[to.list] = next[to.list].toSpliced(to.index, 0, id);
    return next;
  });
```

With the keyboard, an arrow key past the end of a list carries the row on into
the next list of its group. `label` names the list for screen readers: "Launch
plan, 1 of 4 in Projects".

Keep a "Move to" item in each row's menu as well. Dragging is the quick way,
not the only one.

## Handles

With `handle`, a row drags only from its `SortableHandle`. Use it when the
rows hold their own controls, such as a checkbox, or text people select. The
handle is a button named "Reorder" plus the row's `label`, and on a touch
screen it drags straight away with no press and hold.

Handles:

```tsx
<Sortable
  handle
  items={tasks.map((task) => task.id)}
  onReorder={(_, { from, to }) => setTasks((tasks) => arrayMove(tasks, from, to))}
>
  {tasks.map((task) => (
    <SortableItem key={task.id} id={task.id} label={task.label} vertical="center" gap="8">
      <SortableHandle />
      <Checkbox label={task.label} checked={task.done} onCheckedChange={() => toggle(task.id)} />
    </SortableItem>
  ))}
</Sortable>
```

## A board

The same `group` works for columns side by side. A `SortableItem` takes the
Flex props, so a row can be the card itself. Use `direction="row"` for a
horizontal list, such as a strip of media.

Board:

```tsx
<Row fillWidth gap="12">
  {columns.map(({ name, label }) => (
    <Column key={name} flex={1} gap="8" padding="8" radius="l" background="neutral-alpha-weak">
      <Text textVariant="label-default-s">{label}</Text>
      <Sortable group="board" name={name} label={label} gap="8"
        items={board[name]} onReorder={(items) => reorder(name, items)} onMove={move}>
        {board[name].map((card) => (
          <SortableItem key={card} id={card} padding="12" radius="m"
            background="surface" border="neutral-alpha-medium">
            <Text textVariant="body-default-s">{card}</Text>
          </SortableItem>
        ))}
      </Sortable>
    </Column>
  ))}
</Row>
```

An empty list keeps 40px of room so a row can still be dropped into it.

## Focus and screen readers

A row that holds a link or a button keeps that as its one tab stop, and Space
on it picks the row up. A row with nothing focusable becomes a tab stop itself.
Each tab stop is described with the keys to use, and one live region reads out
every pick up, move, drop and cancel. Pass `labels` to translate them:

```tsx
<Sortable
  items={rows}
  onReorder={setRows}
  labels={{
    instructions: "Leertaste zum Aufnehmen, Pfeiltasten zum Verschieben.",
    lifted: ({ item, position, total }) => `${item} aufgenommen, ${position} von ${total}.`,
  }}
>
```

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `items (required)` | `readonly string[]` |  | The rows' ids in their current order, the same ids the SortableItems carry. |
| `onReorder` | `(items: string[], move: SortableReorder) => void` |  | Called with the new order of ids and the move, `{ id, from, to }`, when a row is dropped somewhere new in this list. |
| `group` | `string` |  | Lists with the same group trade rows. |
| `name` | `string` |  | This list's name in onMove. Set it on every list of a group. |
| `onMove` | `(id: string, to: SortablePosition, from: SortablePosition) => void` |  | Called when a row lands in this list from another list of its group, with `(id, to, from)`, each `{ list, index }`. |
| `direction` | `SortableDirection` | `column` | `row` for a horizontal list. |
| `handle` | `boolean` | `false` | Drag only from a SortableHandle in each row. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | `false` | Turns dragging off for the whole list. |
| `label` | `string` |  | The list's name for screen readers when a row moves into it. |
| `labels` | `Partial<SortableLabels>` |  | The instructions and announcements, for a translated interface. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id (required)` | `string` |  | The row's id, as it appears in the list's items. |
| `label` | `string` |  | What screen readers call the row. Defaults to the row's text. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | `false` | Keeps this row where it is. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# SplitView

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/splitView

> A resizable split view component that allows users to adjust the size ratio between two panels.

The `SplitView` component creates a resizable divider between two panels, allowing users to adjust the size ratio. It supports both horizontal and vertical layouts with customizable resize handles.

```tsx
<SplitView 
    defaultSplit={0.4}
    leftPanel={
      <Column fillWidth padding="20" gap="12" border="surface" background="surface" radius="l">
        <Text textVariant="heading-strong-m">Left Panel</Text>
        <Text onBackground="neutral-weak">
          This is the left panel content. You can resize this panel by dragging the divider.
        </Text>
      </Column>
    }
    rightPanel={
      <Column fillWidth padding="20" gap="12" border="surface" background="surface" radius="l">
        <Text textVariant="heading-strong-m">Right Panel</Text>
        <Text onBackground="neutral-weak">
          This is the right panel content. The divider is draggable and provides visual feedback.
        </Text>
      </Column>
    }
/>
```

## Vertical Layout

SplitView also supports vertical orientation for top-bottom layouts.

```tsx
<SplitView
    defaultSplit={0.3}
    direction="column"
    leftPanel={
      <Column fill padding="20" gap="12" border="surface" background="surface" radius="l">
        <Text textVariant="heading-strong-m">Top Panel</Text>
      </Column>
    }
    rightPanel={
      <Column fill padding="20" gap="12" border="surface" background="surface" radius="l">
        <Text textVariant="heading-strong-m">Bottom Panel</Text>
      </Column>
    }
/>
```

## Customization

You can customize the resize handle size, appearance, and set minimum/maximum split ratios.

```tsx
<SplitView 
    defaultSplit={0.5}
    minSplit={0.2}
    maxSplit={0.8}
    leftPanel={
      <Column fillWidth padding="20" gap="12" border="surface" background="surface" radius="l">
        <Text textVariant="heading-strong-m">Custom Handle</Text>
      </Column>
    }
    rightPanel={
      <Column fillWidth padding="20" gap="12" border="surface" background="surface" radius="l">
        <Text textVariant="heading-strong-m">Constrained</Text>
      </Column>
    }
/>
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `leftPanel (required)` | `ReactNode` |  | Content on the left. |
| `rightPanel (required)` | `ReactNode` |  | Content on the right. |
| `labels` | `{ left: string; right: string }` |  | Tab labels used once the view has collapsed. |
| `collapseBelow` | `BreakpointKey \| false` | `s` | Breakpoint at which it becomes tabs. false keeps it split at every width. |
| `defaultSplit` | `number` | `0.3` | Starting position of the divider, as a fraction. |
| `minSplit` | `number` | `0.2` | How far left the divider can go. |
| `maxSplit` | `number` | `0.8` | How far right the divider can go. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

## Small screens

At or below `collapseBelow` (default `s`) the split becomes tabs showing one
panel at a time, and the drag handle is not rendered. A drag-resizable split is
a poor pattern on a phone whichever way it is oriented: neither pane is usable
at any ratio, and a drag handle competes with page scrolling. Pass `labels` so
the tabs are named, or `collapseBelow={false}` to keep the split at every size.

```tsx
<SplitView
  leftPanel={<Editor />}
  rightPanel={<Preview />}
  labels={{ left: "Editor", right: "Preview" }}
/>
```

## Usage Guidelines

- **Accessibility**: the divider is a focusable `role="separator"` — arrow keys
  move it in 5% steps within `minSplit`/`maxSplit`, and it reports its position
  through `aria-valuenow`
- **Input**: dragging uses pointer events, so it works with a mouse, a pen and
  touch alike
- **Responsive**: collapses to tabs on small screens rather than shrinking two
  panes past usefulness
- **Constraints**: Set min/max split ratios to prevent panels from becoming too small
- **Visual Feedback**: Handle changes color when being dragged for better UX

# StatusIndicator

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/statusIndicator

> StatusIndicator is a compact visual cue used to represent status or state with customizable size and palette hue.

Use `StatusIndicator` to show online/offline presence, availability, or categorical tags through color-coded dots.

StatusIndicator:

```tsx
<StatusIndicator scheme="green" />
<StatusIndicator scheme="red" />
<StatusIndicator scheme="yellow" />
```

## Sizes

Choose from small, medium, or large to fit the surrounding layout.

Sizes:

```tsx
<StatusIndicator size="s" scheme="blue" />
<StatusIndicator size="m" scheme="blue" />
<StatusIndicator size="l" scheme="blue" />
```

## Color variants

Supports full Once UI palette for flexibility.

Colors:

```tsx
<StatusIndicator scheme="blue" />
<StatusIndicator scheme="indigo" />
<StatusIndicator scheme="violet" />
...
<StatusIndicator scheme="gray" />
```

## Theme roles

`tone` takes a theme role (`brand`, `accent`, `neutral`, `info`, `danger`, `warning`, `success`) and follows the colour the theme assigns it, so `danger` stays the app's danger colour. `scheme` takes a fixed palette colour; `rose`, `mint`, `dusk`, `sand` and `slate` are there as well.

Roles:

```tsx
<StatusIndicator tone="success" aria-label="Online" />
<StatusIndicator tone="warning" aria-label="Degraded" />
<StatusIndicator tone="danger" aria-label="Down" />
<StatusIndicator tone="brand" aria-label="Syncing" />
<StatusIndicator scheme="sand" aria-label="Archived" />
```

## Pulse

With `pulse`, the dot sits in a ring that keeps pulsing outward, to draw the eye to something live (2.x's `Pulse`). A pulsing dot takes its palette from `tone` (default `"brand"`) rather than `scheme`, and `pulseSize` overrides the ring's size. It is decorative unless you give it an `aria-label`, which makes it an image like the plain dot.

Pulse:

```tsx
<StatusIndicator pulse size="s"/>
<StatusIndicator pulse size="m" tone="danger"/>
<StatusIndicator pulse size="l" tone="success"/>
```

### Tone

Set the palette of the pulse with `tone`; 2.x's Pulse called it `scheme`.

Color:

```tsx
<StatusIndicator pulse tone="brand"/>
<StatusIndicator pulse tone="accent"/>
<StatusIndicator pulse tone="neutral"/>
<StatusIndicator pulse tone="info"/>
<StatusIndicator pulse tone="warning"/>
<StatusIndicator pulse tone="danger"/>
<StatusIndicator pulse tone="success"/>
```

### Pulse dot size

Set the size of the pulse using the `size` prop.

Size:

```tsx
<StatusIndicator pulse size="s"/>
<StatusIndicator pulse size="m"/>
<StatusIndicator pulse size="l"/>
```

### Pulse size

Customize the pulse ring dimensions with the `pulseSize` prop, accepting a number or string value.

Pulse size:

```tsx
<StatusIndicator pulse size="m" pulseSize={80} />
<StatusIndicator pulse size="m" pulseSize="4rem" />
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `size` | `TShirtSizes` | `m` | Dot size. |
| `scheme` | `StatusIndicatorScheme` | `blue` | The dot's colour: a palette name, or a theme role such as danger or brand (2.x called it color). |
| `pulse` | `boolean` | `false` | Pulse a ring out from the dot. Decorative unless aria-label is set. |
| `tone` | `Tone` |  | The pulsing dot's palette. Only with pulse; the plain dot takes scheme. |
| `pulseSize` | `string \| number` |  | How far the ring travels, overriding the size's default. Only with pulse. |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `aria-label` | `string` | `-` | What assistive tech announces. Set it to the meaning, not the colour. |
| `...LeafProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# StyleOverlay

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/styleOverlay

> StyleOverlay displays a floating side panel triggered by an icon button. It is designed for visual design controls or configuration layers within the UI.

`StyleOverlay` renders a toggleable panel designed for accessing Once UI styling properties in a compact way during development. The panel slides out from the corner of the screen and overlays content.

StyleOverlay:

```tsx
<StyleOverlay>
    <Row paddingTop="8" paddingRight="12">
      <IconButton icon="sparkle" />
    </Row>
</StyleOverlay>
```

## Trigger

Set any element as trigger for the overlay in the `children` prop.

Trigger:

```tsx
<StyleOverlay>
    <Row paddingTop="8" paddingRight="12">
      <Button>Open</Button>
    </Row>
</StyleOverlay>
```

## Behavior

- The overlay appears in the top-right corner.
- Internally uses `StylePanel` as content which can be customized with `Flex` props.
- Automatically clamps height using safe spacing constraints.
- Contains close and trigger buttons with consistent z-index stacking and conditional rendering.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `iconButtonProps` | `Partial<React.ComponentProps<typeof IconButton>>` |  | Props forwarded to the trigger icon button. |
| `children (required)` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
| `zIndex` | `DisplayProps["zIndex"]` | `2` |  |
| `children` |  |  |  |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |
