# StylePanel

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/stylePanel

> StylePanel provides a live theming interface that allows users to customize global design tokens such as theme, shape, color, and visual density.

`StylePanel` is a component to set global styling options. It writes to the root HTML element’s `data-*` attributes to affect global styles in real time. It doesn't persist settings by default.

StylePanel:

```tsx
<StylePanel />
```

## Themes and shape

Choose between light/dark mode and various border radius presets.

Every row of options, swatches and segments alike, is a radio group named by the row's label: one Tab stop per row, on the current choice, and the arrow keys move and choose.

## Color systems

Change brand, accent, and neutral palettes. These affect buttons, links, surfaces, and other themed elements.

## Solid style and effects

Adjust the visual language of interactive elements (e.g., flat, plastic or glowing button styling).

## Advanced options

Modify surface behavior (translucent vs filled), scale intensity, and transition timing.

## Global output

Applies the following `data-*` attributes to the `<html>` element:
- `data-border`
- `data-brand`
- `data-accent`
- `data-neutral`
- `data-solid`
- `data-solid-style`
- `data-theme`
- `data-transition`
- `data-scaling`
- `data-density` (the Density row: compact, normal or spacious controls; a new density brings its scaling along until a scaling is chosen)
- `data-surface`
- `data-body-size`
- `data-body-line-height`

## Composing your own panel

`StylePanel` is a plain composition of its own parts. When you need a
different arrangement, or only some of the sections, drop it and compose the
pieces inside `StylePanelRoot`:

```tsx
<StylePanelRoot>
  <StylePanelGroup title="Brand">
    <StylePanelBrand />
    <StylePanelAccent />
  </StylePanelGroup>
</StylePanelRoot>
```

Each part is its own named export from `@once-ui-system/blocks`, named
`StylePanel` plus the part (`StylePanelRoot`, `StylePanelGroup`, `StylePanelRow`).
Rows: `Theme`, `Shape`, `Brand`, `Accent`, `Neutral`, `Solid`, `Effect`,
`Surface`, `Density`, `Scaling`, `Transition`, `DataStyle`, `BodySize`, `BodyLineHeight`.
Groups: `Page`, `Color`, `SolidStyle`, `BodyText`, `Advanced`.

Only `DataStyle` needs a `DataThemeProvider` in the tree, so a panel without
it has no such requirement.

Every row takes a `label`, and every group a `title` and `description`. Pass a
node to replace the default, or `false` to drop it:

```tsx
<StylePanelBrand label="Primary" />
<StylePanelColor title={false} description={false} />
```

To translate the panel, pass `labels` to the root instead — see
[Localisation](#localisation). A prop on a row or group still wins over it.

To keep the default arrangement and hide parts of it, use `visibility`.
Omitted keys stay visible; `section: false` hides a whole group.

```tsx
<StylePanel visibility={{ advanced: { section: false }, color: { neutral: false } }} />
```

`bodyText` is the exception: it is opt-in, so pass `{ bodyText: { section: true } }`
to show it.

## Narrow panels

Each row puts its label beside its control, which suits a page or a settings
screen. In a sidebar there is no room for both, so the colour strips scroll
after a few swatches. `stacked` puts every label above its control instead:

Stacked:

```tsx
<Column maxWidth="20rem" fillWidth>
  <StylePanel stacked />
</Column>
```

It is a prop rather than automatic because the panel cannot know it is narrow
before it has been laid out: a container query would need size containment,
which stops the panel taking its width from its content. Every row, including
one with a [custom colour](#custom-colour), still takes the layout props of a
`Flex` (`direction`, `horizontal`, `vertical`, `gap`), which win over
`stacked`. Stacked, the option rows take the whole row and drop a button
size, so that they fit a sidebar; whatever still overflows scrolls, and the chosen swatch or
option is scrolled into view.

## Size

`size="s"` tightens the panel: less padding in each row and less room between
groups, for an app where the default spacing is too much. `m` is the default.
MascotPanel takes the same prop.

```tsx
<StylePanel size="s" />
```

## Owning the state

By default the panel reads and writes `ThemeProvider`, which persists to
`localStorage`. Pass `value` and `onValueChange` to take that over — the panel then
writes nothing to the providers or to storage, and you decide what a change
means:

```tsx
<StylePanel
  value={draft}
  onValueChange={(next, changed) => {
    setDraft(next);
    saveToDatabase(changed);
  }}
/>
```

`changed` holds only the keys this interaction touched, which is what you want
to send to a server; `next` is the whole state.

That includes the Theme row: it shows `value.theme`, reading an unset theme as
`"system"`, and reports a choice as `{ theme }` without switching the page.

To keep the panel bound to `ThemeProvider` but change where choices are
stored, set `persistence` on the provider instead — see
[ThemeProvider](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/contexts/themeProvider).

## Localisation

`labels` translates every string the panel shows or announces: the group
headings, the row labels, the segmented options, the swatches' accessible
names and the theme switcher's. Pass it to `StylePanel` or `StylePanelRoot`,
and every group and row inside reads it, including the ones you compose
yourself. Every field at every depth is optional, and whatever you leave out
keeps its English default, so you can translate one section at a time.

```tsx
"use client";

import { StylePanel, type StylePanelLabels, type StylePanelValue } from "@once-ui-system/blocks";
import { useTranslations } from "next-intl";
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

export function SiteStylePanel({ saved, save }: {
  saved: StylePanelValue;
  save: (changed: Partial<StylePanelValue>) => void;
}) {
  const t = useTranslations("stylePanel");
  const [draft, setDraft] = useState(saved);

  const labels = useMemo<StylePanelLabels>(
    () => ({
      groups: {
        page: { title: t("page.title"), description: t("page.description") },
        color: { title: t("color.title"), description: t("color.description") },
      },
      rows: { theme: t("rows.theme"), brand: t("rows.brand"), accent: t("rows.accent") },
      options: {
        solid: { color: t("solid.color"), inverse: t("solid.inverse"), contrast: t("solid.contrast") },
        scaling: (value) => `${value} %`,
      },
      names: { schemes: { blue: t("schemes.blue"), red: t("schemes.red") } },
      swatches: {
        // A function, so the translation decides the word order.
        scheme: (name, row) => t("swatch.scheme", { name, row: t(`rows.${row}`) }),
      },
      themeSwitcher: { system: t("theme.system"), dark: t("theme.dark"), light: t("theme.light") },
    }),
    [t],
  );

  return (
    <StylePanel
      labels={labels}
      value={draft}
      onValueChange={(next, changed) => {
        setDraft(next);
        save(changed);
      }}
    />
  );
}
```

| Key | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| `groups` | Each group's `title` and `description`, keyed like `visibility`: `page`, `color`, `solidStyle`, `bodyText`, `advanced`. |
| `rows` | Each row's label, keyed by its part name: `theme`, `shape`, `brand`, `accent`, `neutral`, `solid`, `effect`, `surface`, `density`, `scaling`, `transition`, `dataStyle`, `bodySize`, `bodyLineHeight`. |
| `options` | The segmented options, by row and value (`solid.inverse`, `transition.micro`, `dataStyle.sequential`, `density.compact`), and a formatter for each numeric row: `scaling`, `bodySize`, `bodyLineHeight`. |
| `names` | Display names for `shapes`, `schemes` and `neutrals`. They default to the key (`"blue"`), and the swatches' names are built from them. |
| `swatches` | The swatches' accessible names, as functions of that display name: `shape`, `scheme` (which also gets the row, `"brand"` or `"accent"`) and `neutral`. The defaults read `Corner style: sharp`, `Brand colour: blue` and `Neutral colour: gray`. |
| `themeSwitcher` | "System theme", "Dark theme" and "Light theme". [ThemeSwitcher](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/themeSwitcher) takes the same object as its own `labels`. |
| `scroller` | The scroll buttons of the colour strips and option rows: "Scroll Previous" and "Scroll Next". [Scroller](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/scroller) takes the same object as its own `labels`. |
| `custom` | The custom colour's swatch, field and hint — see [Custom colour](#custom-colour). |

A row's `label` and a group's `title` and `description` still win over
`labels`, so one composed row can say something else:
`<StylePanelBrand label={t("rows.siteColour")} />`.

## Custom colour

`customColors` ends the Brand and Accent swatches with one more: a colour of
your own, such as a site's brand colour. It is painted with the current seed,
and shows a plus while there is none. Choosing it reports
`{ brand: "custom", brandSeed }` — the seed already in `value`, or `#5a93fc`
if there is none — and while it is chosen a colour field under the swatches
edits the seed. Every colour picked there comes through `onValueChange`, in both
`next` and `changed`.

```tsx
const [draft, setDraft] = useState<StylePanelValue>({
  brand: "custom",
  brandSeed: site.brandColor,
});

<StylePanel
  customColors
  value={draft}
  onValueChange={(next, changed) => {
    setDraft(next); // { ...draft, brand: "custom", brandSeed: "#c2410c" }
    saveSiteStyle(changed);
  }}
  labels={{
    custom: {
      // Shown under the field and read with it.
      description: () => t("custom.hint"), // "Buttons and links use this colour."
    },
  }}
/>
```

For one row only, compose the panel and set `custom` on that row:
`<StylePanelBrand custom />`.

It is for the controlled mode. Bound to `ThemeProvider`, whose `setStyle`
takes no seed, the panel would have nowhere to keep one, so the custom swatch
does not render there and the rows look as they always have.

Choosing a named scheme afterwards keeps the seed in the value, so the custom
swatch goes on showing it and one click brings it back; the seed only takes
effect while the row is `"custom"`. The field's clear button is not reported:
the panel keeps the last colour rather than leave the scheme with nothing to
point at. The field shows a hex seed; a seed in another format (`rgb()`,
`oklch()`) still paints the swatch but leaves the field empty until a colour is
picked.

| `labels.custom` | Default |
| --- | --- |
| `swatch(row)` | The swatch's accessible name: `Brand colour: custom` (`Accent colour: custom`). |
| `picker(row)` | The field's label: `Custom brand colour` (`Custom accent colour`). |
| `description(seed, row)` | None. Text under the field, wired to its `aria-describedby`. |
| `remove` | The field's clear button: `Remove`. |

### Rendering the colour

The panel never generates CSS. It reports the seed, and your app renders the
scheme from it with the same pure function Once UI uses everywhere. On the
published site, give the seed to `ThemeInit`: it generates the scheme on the
server and renders it into a `<style>` beside its script, so the page paints
in the site's colour from the first frame, with no flash. `ThemeProvider`
takes the same seed and applies it on the client.

```tsx
// app/[site]/layout.tsx: a server component
const { site } = await params;
const { brandSeed } = await getSiteStyle(site);

<html suppressHydrationWarning>
  <head>
    <ThemeInit config={{ brand: "custom", brandSeed }} />
  </head>
  <body>
    <ThemeProvider brand="custom" brandSeed={brandSeed}>
      {children}
    </ThemeProvider>
  </body>
</html>
```

In the editor, where the colour changes as it is picked, write the same
properties yourself with `customSchemeProperties`:

```tsx
import { customSchemeProperties } from "@once-ui-system/core";

useEffect(() => {
  const root = document.documentElement;
  const properties = customSchemeProperties({ brand: draft.brandSeed, accent: draft.accentSeed });
  for (const [property, value] of Object.entries(properties)) root.style.setProperty(property, value);
  if (draft.brand) root.setAttribute("data-brand", draft.brand);
  if (draft.accent) root.setAttribute("data-accent", draft.accent);
  return () => {
    for (const property of Object.keys(properties)) root.style.removeProperty(property);
  };
}, [draft.brand, draft.accent, draft.brandSeed, draft.accentSeed]);
```

See [Custom schemes](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/basics/color#custom-schemes) for how a scheme is
generated from one colour.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `size` | `StylePanelSize` |  | How much room rows and groups take: m (default), or s for a denser panel. |
| `visibility` | `StylePanelVisibility` |  | Which sections and rows to show. |
| `value` | `StylePanelRootProps["value"]` |  | Take ownership of the state. The panel then writes nothing to the providers or to storage. |
| `onValueChange` | `StylePanelRootProps["onValueChange"]` |  | Called with the whole state and just the keys that changed — the latter being what you send to a server. |
| `labels` | `StylePanelLabels` |  | Every string the panel shows or announces, over the English defaults. Groups and rows read it; their own props still win. |
| `customColors` | `boolean` |  | End the Brand and Accent swatches with a custom colour, reported as brandSeed and accentSeed. Controlled mode only. |
| `stacked` | `boolean` |  | Put each row's label above its control, for a narrow sidebar. |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# Swiper

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/swiper

> Merged into Carousel in 3.0.

`Swiper` folded into [`Carousel`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/carousel#snap-mode) in 3.0: use `<Carousel mode="snap">`. The 3.0 codemod rewrites it (see the migration guide, "Components that merged"), and everything it did is reachable from the new props.

# Table

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/table

> A table of typed rows from column definitions, with sorting, search and filters, row selection, pagination, column visibility, row actions, and empty and loading states.

`Table` renders an array of your own rows through a list of column definitions.
It keeps the rows as data, so it can sort by the values rather than by the text
on screen, select rows by id, search, and page through them. In 3.0 it is 2.x's
`DataTable` under the short name, and it absorbs 2.x `Table`'s search, row
actions and row clicks.

Table:

```tsx
type Invoice = { id: string; customer: string; status: Status; amount: number; issued: string };

const columns: TableColumn<Invoice>[] = [
  { key: "id", header: "Invoice", sortable: true },
  { key: "customer", header: "Customer", sortable: true },
  {
    key: "status",
    header: "Status",
    cell: (invoice) => <Tag size="s" tone={scheme[invoice.status]}>{invoice.status}</Tag>,
  },
  { key: "issued", header: "Issued", sortable: true },
  {
    key: "amount",
    header: "Amount",
    align: "right",
    sortable: true,
    cell: (invoice) => money(invoice.amount),
  },
];

<Table aria-label="Invoices" columns={columns} rows={invoices} />
```

`Table` is generic over the row type, so `cell` and `sort` receive your rows
typed. A column without `cell` shows `row[key]`. Name the table with `aria-label`,
or point `aria-labelledby` at a heading above it.

## Sorting

A `sortable` column's header is a button. Each press cycles ascending, descending
and back to the rows' own order, and the sorted header carries `aria-sort`. Without
a `sort` function the column compares `row[key]`: numbers as numbers, dates by
time, text in natural order ("Item 2" before "Item 10"), with empty values last
in both directions. Give the column a `sort` comparator, written ascending, when
the key is not a field of the row or its values need their own order:

Comparator:

```tsx
const priority = { high: 0, medium: 1, low: 2 };

{ key: "priority", header: "Priority", sortable: true,
  sort: (a, b) => priority[a.priority] - priority[b.priority] }
```

Table keeps the sort itself, starting from `defaultSort`, or follows `sort` and
`onSortChange` when the host owns it. `null` is unsorted. A new sort returns to the
first page.

## Selection and pagination

`selectable` adds a checkbox column. The header checkbox selects or clears the rows
on screen, and shows a mixed state when only some of them are selected; selection
is kept across pages. `getRowId` gives each row the id that selection reports;
without it a row's `id` field is used, or its index. `getRowLabel` names each
row's checkbox for screen readers.

`paginated` shows the rows a page at a time with [`Pagination`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/pagination)
below; `perPageOptions` adds a page-size select.

Selection:

```tsx
const [selected, setSelected] = useState<string[]>([]);

<Table
  aria-label="Invoices"
  columns={columns}
  rows={invoices}
  getRowId={(invoice) => invoice.id}
  getRowLabel={(invoice) => `Select ${invoice.id}`}
  selectable
  selected={selected}
  onSelectedChange={setSelected}
  paginated
  defaultPerPage={5}
  perPageOptions={[5, 10, 25]}
/>
```

## Server-side data

When the server sorts and pages, pass the current page's rows with `count`, the
number of rows on the server (or `total`, the number of pages). Table then
neither sorts nor slices the rows: it reports `onPageChange`, `onPerPageChange`
and `onSortChange`, and shows `loading` while you fetch. Give rows a `getRowId`
here, since an index repeats from page to page.

Server-side:

```tsx
const [page, setPage] = useState(1);
const [sort, setSort] = useState<TableSort | null>(null);
const { rows, count, loading } = useInvoices({ page, perPage: 5, sort });

<Table
  aria-label="Invoices"
  columns={columns}
  rows={rows}
  count={count}
  perPage={5}
  page={page}
  onPageChange={setPage}
  sort={sort}
  onSortChange={setSort}
  loading={loading}
/>
```

With `count` or `total` the search and filters are the server's to apply: Table
reports them and shows the rows you pass. Rather than one handler per piece,
`onQueryChange` hands you the page, page size, sort, search and filters together,
once per change, ready to fetch with. `keepRowsWhileLoading` keeps the last page on
screen, dimmed, while the next one loads, so the table does not flash skeletons on
every keystroke. Debounce the fetch if your API is slow to answer.

Server query:

```tsx
const [query, setQuery] = useState<TableQuery>({
  page: 1, perPage: 5, sort: null, search: "", filters: {},
});
const { rows, count, loading } = useInvoices(query);

<Table
  aria-label="Invoices"
  columns={columns}
  rows={rows}
  count={count}
  page={query.page}
  perPage={query.perPage}
  sort={query.sort}
  search={query.search}
  filters={query.filters}
  onQueryChange={setQuery}
  searchable
  loading={loading}
  keepRowsWhileLoading
/>
```

## Rows as arrays

A row can be an array of cells instead of an object: column n then shows the
cell at position n, with no `cell` needed, and sorts by it (an element by its
text). This is how 2.x `Table` took its data, `data={{ headers, rows }}`; in
3.0 each header is a column, its `content` the column's `header`.

Array rows:

```tsx
<Table
  aria-label="Team"
  columns={[
    { header: "Name", key: "name", sortable: true },
    { header: "Role", key: "role", sortable: true },
  ]}
  rows={[
    ["Alice", "Engineer"],
    ["Bob", "Designer"],
    ["Carol", "Product"],
  ]}
/>
```

## Search

`searchable` adds a field above the table that keeps the rows any of whose cells
reads as holding the query, ignoring case, with a count of what is left.
`searchPlaceholder` sets its placeholder. Table keeps the search itself (from
`defaultSearch`), or follows `search` with `onSearchChange`; pass `matchSearch`
to match rows otherwise. A new search returns to the first page.

Search:

```tsx
<Table searchable searchPlaceholder="Filter by name..." columns={columns} rows={rows} />
```

## Filters and columns

A column with a `filter` adds a select of its `options` beside the search. Both
are 32px controls, the height of a small `Button`, so your own controls fit
beside them in `toolbar`. Table keeps the filters itself (from `defaultFilters`),
or follows `filters` with `onFiltersChange`. `filters` is keyed by column:
`{ status: "paid" }`, or a list for a `multiple` filter. A filter passes rows
whose `row[key]` is the picked value (or holds it, for an array); give it a
`match` function for anything else. When the search and filters match nothing,
Table says so, with a button that clears them, instead of the no-data state;
pass your own as `noResultsState`.

`hide` drops a column, header and cells, at a breakpoint and below:
`hide: { s: true }`. It is CSS, so the server render is already right. Readers
choose columns themselves from `columnsMenu`; `columnVisibility` with
`onColumnVisibilityChange` puts that choice in your hands, to save it. Give a
column a `label` when its header is not plain text, to name its filter and menu
entry. Narrow this example to see Issued, then Customer, drop out.

Toolbar:

```tsx
const columns: TableColumn<Invoice>[] = [
  { key: "id", header: "Invoice", sortable: true },
  { key: "customer", header: "Customer", sortable: true, hide: { xs: true } },
  {
    key: "status",
    header: "Status",
    cell: (invoice) => <Tag size="s" tone={scheme[invoice.status]}>{invoice.status}</Tag>,
    filter: {
      options: [
        { value: "paid", label: "Paid" },
        { value: "pending", label: "Pending" },
        { value: "overdue", label: "Overdue" },
      ],
    },
  },
  { key: "issued", header: "Issued", sortable: true, hide: { s: true } },
  { key: "amount", header: "Amount", align: "right", sortable: true },
];

<Table
  aria-label="Invoices"
  columns={columns}
  rows={invoices}
  searchable
  columnsMenu
  toolbar={<Button size="s" variant="secondary" prefixIcon="download">Export</Button>}
  paginated
  defaultPerPage={5}
/>
```

## Row clicks and actions

`onRowClick` makes the rows clickable and receives the row and its index in
`rows`. `actions` adds a column of icon buttons; each action's `onClick` and
`disabled` receive the row and its index too (2.x passed the index alone).
`rowClassName` and `cellClassName` style a row or a cell from the same
arguments.

Row actions:

```tsx
<Table
  aria-label="Tasks"
  columns={columns}
  rows={tasks}
  onRowClick={(task: Task) => open(task.id)}
  actions={[
    { icon: "edit", label: "Edit", onClick: (task) => edit(task) },
    { icon: "trash", label: "Delete", variant: "primary", tone: "danger", onClick: (task) => remove(task) },
  ]}
/>
```

## Empty and loading

With no rows Table shows an empty state; pass your own as `emptyState`. While
`loading`, skeleton rows stand in for the page (as many as `perPage`), the table is
marked `aria-busy`, and sorting, selection and pagination are disabled.
`loadingState` shows your own placeholder instead of the skeleton rows.

Empty and loading:

```tsx
<Table columns={columns} rows={[]} emptyState={<Text>No members yet.</Text>} />
<Table columns={columns} rows={rows} loading paginated defaultPerPage={3} />
```

`stickyHeader` keeps the header row in view while the rows scroll; pair it with
`maxHeight`, which caps the scroll area. `striped`, `hoverable` and `compact` change
the look.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `columns (required)` | `TableColumn<T>[]` |  | The columns, in order. See TableColumn below. |
| `rows (required)` | `T[]` |  | Your rows: every row, or with count or total only the current page. An array row is read by position. |
| `onRowClick` | `(row: T, index: number) => void` |  | Called with the clicked row and its index. |
| `searchable` | `boolean` | `false` | Add a search field that filters the rows by their cells' text. |
| `searchPlaceholder` | `string` | `Search...` | The search field's placeholder. |
| `search` | `string` |  | The search text when the host owns it. |
| `defaultSearch` | `string` | `""` | The search text to start with. |
| `onSearchChange` | `(search: string) => void` |  | Called with the search text on each change. |
| `matchSearch` | `(row: T, query: string) => boolean` |  | Whether a row matches the trimmed, lowercased query. Defaults to any cell's text containing it. |
| `filters` | `TableFilters` |  | The active filters by column key when the host owns them. |
| `defaultFilters` | `TableFilters` |  | The filters to start with. |
| `onFiltersChange` | `(filters: TableFilters) => void` |  | Called with every active filter after each change. |
| `columnVisibility` | `Record<string, boolean>` |  | Which columns show, by key, when the host owns it; false hides a column. |
| `defaultColumnVisibility` | `Record<string, boolean>` |  | The column visibility to start with. |
| `onColumnVisibilityChange` | `(visibility: Record<string, boolean>) => void` |  | Called with the new column visibility. |
| `columnsMenu` | `boolean` | `false` | Add a menu that shows and hides columns. |
| `toolbar` | `ReactNode` |  | Your own controls at the end of the toolbar. |
| `onQueryChange` | `(query: TableQuery) => void` |  | Called once per change with page, perPage, sort, search and filters. |
| `actions` | `TableAction<T>[]` |  | Icon buttons in a last column, for each row. See TableAction below. |
| `rowClassName` | `(row: T, index: number) => string \| undefined` |  | A class for a row, from the row and its index. |
| `cellClassName` | `(row: T, index: number, columnIndex: number) => string \| undefined` |  | A class for a cell, from the row, its index and the column's index. |
| `loadingState` | `ReactNode` |  | What shows in place of the skeleton rows while loading. |
| `getRowId` | `(row: T, index: number) => string` |  | A stable id per row, which selection reports. Defaults to row.id, then the index. |
| `sort` | `TableSort \| null` |  | The sorted column and direction when the host owns it; null for unsorted. |
| `defaultSort` | `TableSort \| null` | `null` | The sort to start with. |
| `onSortChange` | `(sort: TableSort \| null) => void` |  | Called with the new sort, or null. |
| `selectable` | `boolean` | `false` | Add a checkbox column with select-all. |
| `selected` | `string[]` |  | The selected rows' ids when the host owns them. |
| `defaultSelected` | `string[]` |  | The ids selected to start with. |
| `onSelectedChange` | `(selected: string[]) => void` |  | Called with every selected id after each change. |
| `getRowLabel` | `(row: T) => string` |  | The accessible name of a row's checkbox. |
| `paginated` | `boolean` | `false` | Show the rows a page at a time. |
| `page` | `number` |  | The current page, from 1, when the host owns it. |
| `defaultPage` | `number` | `1` | The page to start on. |

| `count` | `number` |  | Rows on the server. The rows are then one page, sorted, filtered and sliced by the host. |
| `total` | `number` |  | Pages on the server, as count. |
| `loading` | `boolean` | `false` | Show skeleton rows and disable the controls. |

# Tabs

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/tabs

> A list of tabs and the panel each one shows, horizontal or vertical, with the keyboard behaviour screen readers expect.

`Tabs` shows one panel of content at a time and a list of tabs to switch between
them. It is four parts matched by `value`: `Tabs` holds the state, `TabList` holds
the `Tab` buttons, and each `TabPanel` holds the content for one tab. The parts are
separate so the list and the panels can sit in any layout.

Tabs:

```tsx
<Tabs defaultValue="overview">
  <TabList aria-label="Project">
    <Tab value="overview">Overview</Tab>
    <Tab value="activity">Activity</Tab>
    <Tab value="settings">Settings</Tab>
  </TabList>
  <TabPanel value="overview">…</TabPanel>
  <TabPanel value="activity">…</TabPanel>
  <TabPanel value="settings">…</TabPanel>
</Tabs>
```

Each `Tab` is a [`ToggleButton`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/toggleButton) with the `tab` role, so it
takes the same props: `prefixIcon`, `suffixIcon`, `size`, `variant`, `disabled`.
`Tabs`, `TabList` and `TabPanel` are Flex containers and take every Flex prop.

## Vertical

`orientation="vertical"` puts the list beside the panels and switches the arrow keys
to Up and Down. Tabs in a vertical list fill its width and align their label to the
start, which is the settings-sidebar layout. Change the direction at a breakpoint
with the usual responsive props: here the list moves above the panel on small
screens.

Vertical:

```tsx
<Tabs defaultValue="general" orientation="vertical" gap="24" s={{ direction: "column" }}>
  <TabList aria-label="Settings" minWidth="12rem" s={{ direction: "row" }}>
    <Tab value="general" size="l" prefixIcon="person">General</Tab>
    <Tab value="style" size="l" prefixIcon="sparkle">Style</Tab>
    <Tab value="security" size="l" prefixIcon="security">Security</Tab>
  </TabList>
  <TabPanel value="general"><General /></TabPanel>
  <TabPanel value="style"><StylePanel /></TabPanel>
  <TabPanel value="security"><Security /></TabPanel>
</Tabs>
```

## Controlled

Pass `value` and `onValueChange` when something else owns the selection: a URL search
param, say, so a reload opens the same tab. `onValueChange` is not called for the tab
that is already selected. Without `value`, Tabs keeps its own state and starts on
`defaultValue`, or on the first enabled tab if there is none.

Controlled:

```tsx
const [tab, setTab] = useState("general");

<Tabs value={tab} onValueChange={setTab}>
  …
</Tabs>
```

> In a page that renders on the server, pass defaultValue (or value). Without it the first tab is chosen when the list mounts in the browser, so the server HTML has no panel in it.

## Keyboard

Only the selected tab is in the page's Tab order, so Tab moves from the list to the
panel rather than through every tab.

| Key | Does |
| --- | --- |
| Left / Right | Previous and next tab, wrapping at the ends (Up / Down when vertical). Swapped in a right-to-left layout. |
| Home / End | First and last tab. |
| Enter / Space | Select the focused tab, when `activation="manual"`. |

By default a tab is selected as soon as the arrow keys reach it. Set
`activation="manual"` when showing a panel is slow, such as one that fetches: the
arrow keys then only move focus, and Enter or Space selects.

Disabled tabs stay visible and the arrow keys skip them.

## Panels

An unselected panel renders nothing inside it, so its effects stop and its state
resets. Pass `keepMounted` to keep a panel's content mounted and hidden instead:
a form with unsaved input, a video that should keep its position.

Every tab is wired to its panel with `aria-controls`, and every panel is labelled
by its tab, so a screen reader announces "Security, tab panel". A panel is
focusable, so a keyboard user can reach one that has no controls of its own. A tab
with no `TabPanel` (a list of tabs that changes the route, for instance) gets no
`aria-controls`.

Give the list a name with `aria-label` (or `aria-labelledby`) when no heading on the
page names it.

## API reference

### Tabs

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value` | `string` |  | The selected tab's value, when the host owns the state. Pair with onValueChange. |
| `defaultValue` | `string` |  | The tab selected first when Tabs keeps its own state. Without it, the first enabled tab. |
| `onValueChange` | `(value: string) => void` |  | Called with the newly selected tab's value. |
| `orientation` | `"horizontal" \| "vertical"` | `horizontal` | Which arrow keys move between tabs, and whether the list sits above or beside the panels. |
| `activation` | `"automatic" \| "manual"` | `automatic` | automatic selects a tab when the arrow keys reach it; manual waits for Enter or Space. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` |  | A TabList and its TabPanels, in any layout. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

### TabList

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `children` | `ReactNode` |  | The Tab buttons. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

### Tab

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value (required)` | `string` |  | Matches the TabPanel this tab shows, and is what onValueChange reports. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` |  | The tab's text. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | `false` | Visible, not selectable, skipped by the arrow keys. |
| `...LeafProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

### TabPanel

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value (required)` | `string` |  | The value of the Tab that shows this panel. |
| `keepMounted` | `boolean` | `false` | Keep the content mounted, hidden, while another tab is selected. |

| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# Tag

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/tag

> Tag is a compact label: a static status or category, an announcement pill that links somewhere, or a toggle that can be selected and removed.

`Tag` is a compact label with optional icons on either side. It comes in three kinds:

- a **static label** for a status, a category or a piece of metadata;
- an **announcement** (`variant="announce"`), the pill above a hero that links to what is new;
- a **toggle** (`selected` or `onRemove`), a choice in a filter row or a value in `TagInput`.

> **Badge and Chip are Tag in 3.0** 2.x had three components for this. `Badge` is `{''}` (`title` is `label`, `icon` is `prefixIcon`), and `Chip` is a Tag with `selected` or `onRemove`. `selected` now defaults to false. Tag's `scheme` is `tone`. The 3.0 codemod rewrites all of it.

Tag:

```tsx
<Tag tone="brand" label="New" />
<Tag tone="success" label="Passed" prefixIcon="check" />
<Tag variant="announce" label="Version 3.0 is out" href="/changelog" />
<Tag label="Selected" selected />
```

## Tone

A Tag is a neutral hairline, and its `tone` is a dot before the label: `brand`, `accent`, `neutral`, `info`, `success`, `warning` or `danger`. The colour stays in the dot, so a table full of statuses stays calm. Without a `tone` there is no dot; `dot` shows or hides it either way, and a `prefixIcon` takes the dot's place in the tone's colour. The gradient look is a `variant`.

Tone:

```tsx
<Tag tone="brand">Brand</Tag>
<Tag tone="accent">Accent</Tag>
<Tag tone="info">Info</Tag>
<Tag tone="warning">Warning</Tag>
<Tag tone="success">Success</Tag>
<Tag tone="danger">Danger</Tag>
<Tag tone="neutral">Neutral</Tag>
<Tag variant="gradient">Gradient</Tag>
```

## Sizes

Every kind of Tag takes the full size scale, `xs` to `xl`.

Sizes:

```tsx
<Tag size="xs" label="Extra small" />
<Tag size="s" label="Small" />
<Tag size="m" label="Medium" />
<Tag size="l" label="Large" />
<Tag size="xl" label="Extra large" />
```

## Announcement

`variant="announce"` is the pill that announces something: a rounded tag with a shine that sweeps across it now and then. It draws in `brand` unless given a `tone`. This was `Badge` in 2.x.

Announcement:

```tsx
<Tag variant="announce" label="New release" prefixIcon="rocket" />
<Tag variant="announce" label="Coming soon" prefixIcon="calendar" effect={false} />
<Tag variant="announce" tone="accent" label="Beta" />
```

### Link and arrow

`href` makes any Tag a link, and turns on an `arrow` that slides in on hover. Each tag's arrow follows hover on that tag alone, so a page can hold as many as it needs without giving them ids.

Link:

```tsx
<Tag variant="announce" href="/changelog" label="Read the changelog" />
<Tag variant="announce" href="/docs" label="Documentation" prefixIcon="pages" arrow={false} />
<Tag href="/docs" tone="brand" label="Docs" />
```

### Custom content

An announcement lays its children out in the pill itself, so they take its `gap` and padding.

Custom content:

```tsx
<Tag variant="announce" paddingY="4" paddingLeft="4" paddingRight="16" radius="m" gap="12" textVariant="label-default-s" border="neutral-medium" background="neutral-alpha-weak">
  <Tag tone="brand">New</Tag>
  Custom content
</Tag>
```

## Toggle

With `selected` or `onRemove` a Tag is a toggle: a `role="button"` with `aria-pressed`, pressed by a click, Enter or Space. An `onClick` alone keeps the static look, in its tone and size, as a plain button. Unselected, it is a hairline pill; selected, it is solid ink (solid in its `tone` when given one). `selected` defaults to false. This was `Chip` in 2.x, where it defaulted to true.

Toggle:

```tsx
const [selected, setSelected] = useState(true);

<Tag
  label="Clickable"
  selected={selected}
  onClick={() => setSelected(!selected)}
/>
```

With icons:

```tsx
<Tag selected label="Date" prefixIcon="calendar" />
<Tag selected label="Discord" prefixIcon="discord" />
<Tag selected label="Style" prefixIcon="style" />
<Tag selected label="Favorite" prefixIcon="like" />
```

### Removable

`onRemove` adds a remove button beside the tag. Removing never counts as a click on the tag, and `removeButtonProps` reaches the button, for its `aria-label` or icon. A tag with only `onRemove` is a plain label beside its button, not a toggle; `TagInput` renders its values this way, with `selected`.

Removable:

```tsx
const { addToast } = useToast();
const [tags, setTags] = useState([
  { id: "1", label: "React", icon: "code" },
  { id: "2", label: "TypeScript", icon: "code" },
  { id: "3", label: "Next.js" },
]);

<Row gap="8" wrap>
  {tags.map((tag) => (
    <Tag
      selected
      key={tag.id}
      label={tag.label}
      prefixIcon={tag.icon}
      onRemove={() => {
        setTags(tags.filter((t) => t.id !== tag.id));
        addToast({ tone: "danger", message: `Removed ${tag.label}` });
      }}
    />
  ))}
</Row>

<Tag
  selected
  label="Custom Remove"
  onRemove={remove}
  removeButtonProps={{ icon: "trash", tooltip: "Delete" }}
/>
```

## Inside text

A Tag is a div by default, which is not allowed inside a paragraph. With `as="span"` every
element in it is a span and it flows inline, so it can sit in a sentence. It looks the same.

Inside text:

```tsx
<Text as="p" textVariant="body-default-m">
  Exports are <Tag as="span" tone="brand" label="Beta" /> while we finish the API.
</Text>
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `tone` | `Tone` |  | The palette. Neutral on a static tag, brand on an announcement and on a selected toggle. 2.x called it scheme. |
| `variant` | `"default" \| "gradient" \| "announce" \| "solid"` | `default` | default, gradient, or announce (2.x's Badge). |
| `size` | `TShirtSizes` |  | xs to xl. |
| `label` | `string` | `""` | The text. |
| `prefixIcon` | `IconName` |  | Icon before the label. |
| `suffixIcon` | `IconName` |  | Icon after the label. |
| `dot` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `href` | `string` |  | Makes it a link. |
| `arrow` | `boolean` |  | An arrow that slides in on hover. On by default with href. |
| `effect` | `boolean = variant === "announce"` |  | A shine that sweeps across now and then. On by default with variant="announce". |
| `selected` | `boolean` |  | Makes it a toggle, pressed when true. Defaults to false. |
| `onClick` | `MouseEventHandler<HTMLDivElement>` |  | Called on a click, Enter or Space. With selected it is a toggle; alone, the tag keeps its static look as a button. |
| `onRemove` | `() => void` |  | Adds a remove button, called when it is used. |
| `interactive` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `removeButtonProps` | `Partial<IconButtonProps>` |  | Passed to the remove button. |
| `as` | `"div" \| "span"` |  |  |
| `children` | `ReactNode` |  | The text, when it needs markup. Shown when there is no label. |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# ThemeSwitcher

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/themeSwitcher

> ThemeSwitcher is a compact toggle group for switching between light, dark, and system themes using icon buttons. It can collapse to the active theme and reveal the rest on hover.

Use `ThemeSwitcher` to provide users with a quick way to toggle between themes. It integrates with `ThemeProvider` and uses `useTheme()` under the hood.

ThemeSwitcher:

```tsx
<ThemeSwitcher />
```

## Behavior

- Highlights the active theme using the `"primary"` variant, and exposes it to
  assistive technology with `aria-pressed`.
- Automatically updates the global theme via `useTheme().setTheme`.
- Renders a row of three icons: `system`, `dark`, `light`.
- In a settings form, `semantics="radio"` makes it a `radiogroup` instead: one
  tab stop on the active theme, and the arrow keys move and choose. Name it
  with `aria-label`, as StylePanel's Theme row does with its label.

Radio group:

```tsx
<ThemeSwitcher semantics="radio" aria-label="Theme" />
```

## Collapsed

`collapsed` shows only the active theme and reveals the rest on hover or focus.
Use it where the control has to be reachable from every page but should not
spend three slots of a header on itself.

It stays a real toggle group. Every option keeps its tab stop, so tabbing into
the group opens it; and a device that cannot hover gets all three from the
start, because otherwise the only way in would be to tap the visible button —
which would have already changed the theme. The width transition is the only
motion, and `prefers-reduced-motion` turns it off.

Collapsed:

```tsx
<ThemeSwitcher collapsed />
```

## Opening downwards

A collapsed group grows sideways by default, which is right when it has room beside it and wrong when it has neighbours: the group widening pushes them along, and the option the pointer was resting on slides out from under it. `direction="column"` lifts the options into a panel over the page instead. The control keeps a one-option footprint whatever it is doing, so nothing around it moves, and a sticky header does not change height when the panel opens.

It opens downwards rather than centring itself on the active option. An open panel is taller than a typical header, so anchoring it on the second or third option would put its top edge above the viewport.

The active option leads. Open in fixed order and the panel's first slot belongs to whichever theme is listed first, so the icon already under the pointer changes identity as the panel unrolls — hover the moon, and the computer arrives under your cursor. Leading with the active option keeps one invariant instead: the theme in force is the one in the anchor slot, before opening and again after choosing. The reorder is done in the markup, not with CSS `order`, so the tab order and the visual order stay the same thing.

On a device that cannot hover the panel is always open, and it takes its space in the layout rather than hanging over what is underneath.

Opening downwards:

```tsx
<ThemeSwitcher collapsed direction="column" />
```

## Custom layout

Pass any valid `Row` props to control spacing, padding, layout, etc.

Custom style:

```tsx
<ThemeSwitcher direction="column" padding="4" gap="8" background="surface" border="surface" radius="full" />
```

## Localisation

Each option is an icon button named "System theme", "Dark theme" and "Light
theme". `labels` translates those names; whatever you leave out stays English.
Inside a [StylePanel](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/stylePanel#localisation), its
`labels.themeSwitcher` reaches the Theme row's switcher.

```tsx
<ThemeSwitcher labels={{ system: t("theme.system"), dark: t("theme.dark"), light: t("theme.light") }} />
```

## Owning the state

By default the switcher sets the theme through `ThemeProvider`, which applies it
to the page and stores it. Pass `value` to own it instead: the switcher shows
your theme as active, reports a choice through `onValueChange`, and changes nothing
itself. That is what an editor previewing someone else's theme needs. Without
`value`, `onValueChange` is still called, after the theme has been set.

```tsx
<ThemeSwitcher value={draft.theme} onValueChange={(theme) => setDraft({ ...draft, theme })} />
```

A [StylePanel](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/stylePanel#owning-the-state) with `value` and
`onValueChange` does this for its Theme row.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value` | `Theme` |  | The active theme, when you own the state. The switcher then sets nothing. |
| `onValueChange` | `(theme: Theme) => void` |  | Called with the chosen theme. |
| `collapsed` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `direction` | `"row" \| "column"` | `row` |  |
| `labels` | `ThemeSwitcherLabels` |  | The options' accessible names, to translate them. |
| `semantics` | `"toggle" \| "radio"` | `toggle` | `toggle` (toggle buttons, the default) or `radio` (a radio group with one tab stop). |
| `ref` | `HTMLDivElement` |  |  |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `...flex` |  |  | Also takes these props |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# Timeline

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/timeline

> Display events or steps in chronological order. For a video editor's timeline, see Scrubber.

Timeline helps visualize sequences of events, process steps, or historical data. Configure items via an object array with simple props or custom React nodes.

It lays a sequence out **down the page**, one item after another. If you are
building a video or audio editor, the component you want is
[`Scrubber`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/scrubber): a playhead over time, with stacked tracks
of blocks that are selectable, movable and trimmable. The two share a name in
spirit and nothing in purpose.

## Basic usage

Use `label` and `description` props for quick setup.

Basic:

```tsx
<Timeline
    items={[
      {
        label: "January 2024",
        description: "Project kickoff",
        tone: "success"
      },
      {
        label: "October 2024",
        description: "Development in progress",
        tone: "brand"
      },
      {
        label: "December 2024",
        description: "Launch planned"
      }
    ]}
/>
```

## Alignment

Control timeline alignment with the `alignment` prop. Use `left` or `right` for different layouts.

Alignment:

```tsx
<Timeline
    size="s"
    items={[
      { label: "First milestone" },
      { label: "Current work", tone: "brand" },
      { label: "Future work" }
    ]}
/>
<Timeline
    alignment="right"
    size="s"
    items={[
      { label: "First milestone" },
      { label: "Current work", tone: "brand" },
      { label: "Future work" }
    ]}
/>
```

## Sizes

Control size with the `size` prop: `xs`, `s`, `m`, `l` or `xl`.

Sizes:

```tsx
<Timeline
    size="xs"
    items={[
      {
        label: "Step 1"
      },
      {
        label: "Step 2"
      },
      {
        label: "Step 3",
        tone: "brand"
      }
    ]}
/>
```

## Marker

Customize the marker with the `marker` prop.

Marker:

```tsx
<Timeline
    items={[
      {
        marker: 1,
        label: "Create account",
        description: "Sign up with email and password",
        tone: "success"
      },
      ...
    ]}
/>
<Timeline
    items={[
      {
        marker: <Icon name="check" size="s" />,
        label: "Payment received",
        tone: "success"
      },
      ...
    ]}
/>
```

## States

Each item takes a `tone`: its dot, the line into it and, for `danger`, its text. An item with no tone is a step not reached yet. (2.x called this `state`, and `active` was `tone: "brand"`.)

States:

```tsx
<Timeline
    items={[
      { label: "Default" },
      { label: "Active", tone: "brand" },
      { label: "Success", tone: "success" },
      { label: "Danger", tone: "danger" }
    ]}
/>
```

## Extra content

Extend the label and description with custom React nodes. Use the `children` prop with additional content to extend the layout.

Extra content:

```tsx
<Timeline
    items={[
      {
        tone: "success",
        label: <Row vertical="center" gap="8">Dispatched<Tag tone="success">Done</Tag></Row>,
        description: "Order #123456789",
        children: (
          <Row fitWidth radius="full" paddingY="4" paddingX="8" border="neutral-alpha-medium" textVariant="label-default-xs" onBackground="neutral-weak" marginTop="8">
            3 days ago
          </Row>
        )
      },
      ...
    ]}
/>
```

## Row

Set `direction="row"` to lay the steps out horizontally.

Custom markers:

```tsx
<Timeline
    fillWidth
    direction="row"
    size="xs"
    items={[
      {
        label: "Order",
        tone: "brand"
      },
      {
        label: "Confirmation",
        tone: "success"
      },
      {
        label: "Overview",
        tone: "danger"
      },
      {
        label: "Payment"
      }
    ]}
/>
```

## API reference

### Timeline
| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `items (required)` | `TimelineItem[]` |  | The events, in order. |
| `alignment` | `"left" \| "right"` | `left` | Which side of the line the content sits on. |
| `size` | `TShirtSizes` | `m` | Scale of the markers and text. |
| `direction` | `column` | `row` | column-reverse |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

### TimelineItem
| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
| `description` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
| `tone` | `brand` | `accent` | neutral |
| `marker` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
| `children` | `ReactNode` |  |  |

# Toast

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/toast

> A notification component that displays temporary messages with auto-dismiss and optional actions.

The `Toast` component displays temporary notification messages that automatically dismiss after 6 seconds, or after their `duration`. The countdown pauses while a toast is hovered or has focus. It's typically used through the [ToastProvider](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/contexts/toastProvider) context, but can also be used standalone.

> **Using Toasts** For most use cases, use the `useToast` hook from [ToastProvider](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/contexts/toastProvider) instead of rendering Toast components directly. The provider handles positioning, stacking, and lifecycle management automatically.

## Variants

Toast takes a `tone` (2.x called it `variant`): `success` for positive feedback, `danger` for errors, `warning` for cautionary messages, and `info` for informational notices.

Variants:

```tsx
<Toast tone="success">
    Your changes have been saved successfully!
</Toast>
<Toast tone="danger">
    Failed to save changes. Please try again.
</Toast>
<Toast tone="warning">
    Your session is about to expire.
</Toast>
<Toast tone="info">
    New update available. Refresh to see the latest.
</Toast>
```

## With actions

Add interactive elements like buttons to allow users to take action on the notification.

With action:

```tsx
<Toast 
    tone="danger"
    action={
      <Button size="s">
        Retry
      </Button>
    }
>
    Connection failed. Check your network.
</Toast>
```

## Without icon

Hide the tone's icon by setting `icon={false}`.

Without icon:

```tsx
<Toast tone="success" showIcon={false}>
    Task completed
</Toast>
```

## Where toasts appear

> **Automatic rendering** Toasts render on their own once your app is wrapped in `ToastProvider`; show one with `useToast()`. See the [ToastProvider documentation](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/contexts/toastProvider) for setup instructions.

`ToastProvider` renders the toast stack itself (an internal part; 2.x exported it as `Toaster`). The stack:
- Renders toasts in a fixed position at the bottom center of the screen
- Stacks multiple toasts with scale and opacity animations
- Uses React portals to render outside the normal DOM hierarchy
- Limits width to 32rem for optimal readability

## Accessibility

Toast components include proper ARIA attributes:
- `role="status"` with `aria-live="polite"` for `success`, `info` and `warning`, so the message is announced without interrupting
- `role="alert"` (assertive) for `danger` only
- The countdown pauses while the toast holds focus, so there is time to reach its action
- Keyboard-accessible close button with tooltip

## API reference

### Toast element

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `className` | `string` |  |  |
| `tone (required)` | `Tone` |  | Severity, which sets the colour and the icon. 2.x called it variant. |
| `showIcon` | `boolean` | `true` | Show the icon for the tone. |
| `onClose` | `() => void` |  | Called when it is dismissed. |
| `action` | `React.ReactNode` |  | A control in the toast — undo, retry, view. |
| `children (required)` | `React.ReactNode` |  | The message. |
| `duration` | `number` | `6000` | Milliseconds before it closes, paused while hovered or focused. Infinity keeps it up until it is closed. |
| `announce` | `boolean` | `true` |  |
| `children` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
| `className` | `string` |  |  |

# ToggleButton

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/toggleButton

> ToggleButton is an interactive button used for segmented controls or stateful actions. It supports icon placement, sizing, and selection styling.

`ToggleButton` provides a flexible button-like element that can act as a toggle, tab, or segmented control. It supports selected state, prefix/suffix icons, and optional link behavior.

Basic usage:

```tsx
<ToggleButton selected label="Selected" />
<ToggleButton label="Default" />
<ToggleButton label="Link" href="#" />
```

## Tone

`tone` sets the palette of the selected state, as on `Button`. The default `neutral` is a grey fill; `brand`, `accent` or a status tone tints the fill and colours the label and icons, the way a sidebar marks the page you are on. `Option` takes the same prop.

Tone:

```tsx
<ToggleButton selected tone="brand" prefixIcon="document" label="Welcome note" />
<ToggleButton tone="brand" prefixIcon="person" label="Team" />
```

## Icons

You can attach icons to the left or right using `prefixIcon` and `suffixIcon`.

With icons:

```tsx
<ToggleButton label="Back" prefixIcon="chevronLeft" />
<ToggleButton label="Forward" suffixIcon="chevronRight" />
```

## Sizes

Available in extra small, small, medium, large, and extra large.

Sizes:

```tsx
<ToggleButton label="XS" size="xs" />
<ToggleButton label="S" size="s" />
<ToggleButton label="M" size="m" />
<ToggleButton label="L" size="l" />
<ToggleButton label="XL" size="xl" />
```

Variants:

```tsx
<ToggleButton variant="ghost" label="Ghost" />
<ToggleButton variant="outline" label="Outline" />
<ToggleButton variant="subtle" label="Subtle" />
```

## Radius

Customize rounding for each side or corner.

Radius:

```tsx
<ToggleButton variant="outline" label="Left radius" corners="left" />
<ToggleButton variant="outline" label="No radius" radius="none" />
<ToggleButton variant="outline" label="Top right radius" corners="top-right" />
```

## Alignment

Customize content alignment.

Alignment:

```tsx
<ToggleButton variant="outline" label="Center" horizontal="center" fillWidth />
<ToggleButton variant="outline" label="End" horizontal="end" fillWidth suffixIcon="chevronRight" />
<ToggleButton variant="outline" label="Space between" horizontal="between" fillWidth prefixIcon="check" suffixIcon="chevronDown" />
```

## Custom content

You can pass custom content to the toggle button.

Custom content:

```tsx
<ToggleButton variant="outline">
    <Row vertical="center" gap="8">
      Dashboard
      <Tag label="New" size="s"/>
    </Row>
</ToggleButton>
<ToggleButton variant="outline">
    <Row vertical="center" gap="8">
      Notifications
      <StatusIndicator size="s"/>
    </Row>
</ToggleButton>
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
| `selected` | `boolean` | `false` |  |
| `variant` | `"ghost" \| "outline" \| "subtle"` | `ghost` |  |
| `tone` | `Tone` | `neutral` |  |
| `size` | `TShirtSizes` |  |  |
| `radius` | `RadiusSize` |  |  |
| `corners` | `"none" \| "top" \| "right" \| "bottom" \| "left" \| "top-left" \| "top-right" \| "bottom-right" \| "bottom-left"` |  |  |
| `rounded` | `boolean` | `false` | Fully rounded corners. |
| `horizontal` | `"start" \| "center" \| "end" \| "between"` | `center` |  |
| `weight` | `"default" \| "strong"` | `default` |  |
| `truncate` | `boolean` | `false` |  |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | `false` |  |
| `prefixIcon` | `IconName` |  |  |
| `suffixIcon` | `IconName` |  |  |

# Tooltip

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/tooltip

> Tooltip is a lightweight UI element used to display contextual information on hover or focus.

`Tooltip` is a non-interactive floating container used to communicate short hints or descriptions. It can be rendered manually or combined with a hover/focus trigger component. It is automatically hidden below the `m` breakpoint.

> **Tooltip or HoverCard** [Tooltip](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/tooltip) is a short text explanation on hover or focus: of its children, or of an info icon when it has none (2.x InfoTip), and the bubble a component's `tooltip` prop shows. [HoverCard](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/hoverCard) opens a card of rich content, such as a profile or a link preview, next to its trigger, following the pointer (2.x CursorCard) or over the trigger (2.x Hover).

Tooltip:

```tsx
<Tooltip label="Tooltip" />
```

## Icons

Add a leading or trailing icon to reinforce meaning.

Icons:

```tsx
<Tooltip prefixIcon="info" label="Helpful tip" />
```

## Custom styles

You can override styles using `Flex` props, `style` or `className`.

Custom styles:

```tsx
<Tooltip prefixIcon="info" label="Helpful tip" background="brand-medium" border="brand-medium" padding="8" />
```

## Info icon

A Tooltip with `content` and no children renders a focusable info icon as its trigger: the "what is this?" affordance that reveals a sentence on hover or focus, announced as the icon's description. `size` sizes the icon and `aria-label` names it ("More information" by default). With children, `content` opens from them instead. It was `InfoTip` in 2.x.

InfoTip:

```tsx
<Row gap="8" vertical="center">
  <Text textVariant="label-default-s">Bitrate</Text>
  <Tooltip content="Higher bitrates keep more detail in fast motion, at a larger file size." />
</Row>
```

### Sizing

`size` takes the same tokens as [`Icon`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/icon). Match it to
the text it sits beside — `xs` next to a label, `s` next to body copy — so the
icon reads as part of the line rather than an object dropped into it.

Sizes:

```tsx
<Tooltip size="xs" content="Extra small" />
<Tooltip size="s" content="Small" />
<Tooltip size="m" content="Medium" />
```

### When not to use it

Hover-only content is invisible on touch and to anyone scanning rather than
pointing, so an `Tooltip` must never carry information the reader needs in order
to make the choice in front of them. That belongs in a visible description —
[`Setting`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/setting) has a `description` prop for exactly
this. Reserve `Tooltip` for the second sentence: the caveat, the unit, the
reason a default is what it is.

Anything longer than a sentence or two wants a link to a page, not a tip.

### In a Setting

[`Setting`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/setting) renders an `Tooltip` for you when you
pass its `info` prop, which is the usual way you will meet this component.

Via Setting:

```tsx
<Setting
  label="Bitrate"
  info="Higher bitrates keep more detail in fast motion, at a larger file size."
>
  <Select id="bitrate" options={options} />
</Setting>
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `ReactNode` |  | The text. |
| `content` | `ReactNode` |  | The explanation, revealed on hover or focus of the children, or of an info icon when there are none (2.x InfoTip). |
| `children` | `ReactNode` |  | The trigger content describes. Omit it for the info icon. |
| `size` | `React.ComponentProps<typeof Icon>["size"]` |  | With content and no children: the info icon size. |
| `placement` | `Placement` |  | With content: where it opens. |
| `delay` | `number` |  | With content: milliseconds of hover before it opens. |
| `prefixIcon` | `IconName` |  | Icon before the text. |
| `suffixIcon` | `IconName` |  | Icon after the text. |
| `className` | `string` |  |  |
| `style` | `React.CSSProperties` |  |  |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# User

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/user

> The User component combines avatar, name, and metadata into a compact identity preview with optional loading states and tags.

`User` is a compact component used to represent a user or persona. It combines an avatar, primary name, optional subline, and a status or role tag.

User:

```tsx
<User
    name="Lorant One"
    subline="Design Engineer"
    tagProps={{ label: "Admin", tone: "accent" }}
    avatarProps={{ src: "/images/avatar.jpg" }}
/>
```

## Loading

Display skeletons with the `loading` prop to show a graceful placeholder before data is available.

Loading:

```tsx
<User loading name="Lorant One" subline="Design Engineer" />
```

## Custom content

You can override the default layout using `children`. This is useful for inline customization (e.g. badges, quick actions).

Custom content:

```tsx
<User avatarProps={{ value: "Q" }}>
    <Column paddingX="8">
      <Text textVariant="label-default-m">
        Quasar
      </Text>
      <Text textVariant="body-default-xs" onBackground="neutral-weak">
        Cyberforge
      </Text>
    </Column>
</User>
```

## Menu

With `dropdown`, the User is the trigger of an account menu; `selected`, `placement`, `minWidth`, `maxWidth` and `minHeight` set the trigger state and the menu. It was `UserMenu` in 2.x.

UserMenu:

```tsx
<User
    name="Lorant One"
    subline="Design Engineer"
    placement="right-end"
    avatarProps={{ src: "/images/avatar.jpg" }}
    dropdown={
      <Column gap="4" padding="4" minWidth="10rem">
        <Option fillWidth prefix={<Icon size="xs" onBackground="neutral-weak" name="settings" />} label="Settings" value="settings" />
        <Option fillWidth prefix={<Icon size="xs" onBackground="neutral-weak" name="logout" />} label="Log out" value="logout" />
      </Column>
    }
/>
```

### Loading state

You can show skeleton content while loading profile data by setting `loading={true}`.

Loading:

```tsx
<User loading dropdown={null} />
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `string` |  |  |

| `tag` | `string` |  | Short label shown next to the name. |
| `tagProps` | `TagProps` |  |  |

| `className` | `string` |  |  |

| `onSelect` | `(value: string) => void` |  |  |

# UserMenu

> Merged into User in 3.0.

`UserMenu` folded into [`User`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/user#menu) in 3.0: use `<User dropdown={…}>`. The 3.0 codemod rewrites it (see the migration guide, "Components that merged"), and everything it did is reachable from the new props.

# VisuallyHidden

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/visuallyHidden

> Content for screen readers only, and skip links that appear when a keyboard user tabs to them.

`VisuallyHidden` keeps its content in the accessibility tree and takes it off the
screen. Use it for the words a sighted user gets from context and a screen reader
user does not: the name of an icon-only control, the text of a status region, what
a symbol such as ⌘ stands for.

It uses the clip pattern rather than `display: none` or `visibility: hidden`, which
hide the content from screen readers as well. The content stays absolutely
positioned and clipped to nothing, which also holds inside a transformed or
`overflow: hidden` parent.

Label:

```tsx
<Button variant="secondary">
  <Icon name="search" size="s" />
  <VisuallyHidden>Search the docs</VisuallyHidden>
</Button>
```

## Status regions

A live region announces changes without moving focus. The visible interface often
already shows the result (a list that filters, a badge that updates), so the
announcement itself can be hidden. Render the region once and change its text; a
region that mounts with its message is often not announced.

Status:

```tsx
<VisuallyHidden as="div" role="status">
  {results.length} results
</VisuallyHidden>
```

## Skip links

With `focusable`, the content appears while it, or anything inside it, has keyboard
focus, and hides again when focus moves on. Put it first in the page, so the first
Tab offers a way past the header and navigation. It stays absolutely positioned when
revealed, so it draws over the page instead of pushing the layout down.

`as` types the element's own attributes, so the link can be the hidden element
itself: `<VisuallyHidden as="a" href="#main" focusable>Skip to content</VisuallyHidden>`.

Skip link:

```tsx
<VisuallyHidden focusable>
  <Button href="#main" size="s">Skip to content</Button>
</VisuallyHidden>
<Header />
<Column as="main" id="main" tabIndex={-1}>
  {children}
</Column>
```

> VisuallyHidden has no hooks and no client directive, so it renders in a server component.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `children` | `ReactNode` |  | What a screen reader announces and a sighted user does not see. |
| `focusable` | `boolean` | `false` | Show the content while it, or anything inside it, has keyboard focus. For skip links. |
| `className` | `string` |  |  |
| `style` | `React.CSSProperties` |  |  |
| `as` | `ElementType` | `span` | The element to render, typed by it (as="a" takes href). A span sits inside a line of text; use div for a block, such as a live region. |

---

# Setup

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/setup

> Get started with Once UI's charts: what is in the data-viz module, your first chart, the app-wide chart config and the props every chart shares.

Once UI's charts are drawn as SVG by Once UI itself: no chart library to install, no canvas, nothing to configure before the first one. They render on the server, so the first HTML already holds the chart, they size themselves to their container, and they follow the theme in light and dark.

## What's in the module

Everything imports from `@once-ui-system/core/data`.

- [`LineChart`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/lineChart): change over time, one or more series, stacked or not.
- [`BarChart`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/barChart): comparing categories, grouped, stacked or horizontal.
- [`LineBarChart`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/lineBarChart): a line and bars on one scale, such as a target and its actuals.
- [`PieChart`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/pieChart): parts of a whole, as a pie or a donut.
- [`Sparkline`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/sparkline): a trend in a tile or a table cell.
- [`RadialGauge`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/radialGauge), [`LinearGauge`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/linearGauge): one value against a range.
- [Building blocks](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/parts): the header, states and screen-reader table, for your own visuals.

Not sure which? [Choosing a chart](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/choosing) starts from the question your reader asks.

## Your first chart

Visits.tsx:

```tsx
import { LineChart } from "@once-ui-system/core/data";

export function Visits() {
  return (
    <LineChart
      title="Visits"
      xKey="month"
      series={[
        { key: "visits", label: "Visits" },
        { key: "signups", label: "Signups" },
      ]}
      data={[
        { month: "Jan", visits: 3200, signups: 410 },
        { month: "Feb", visits: 3550, signups: 460 },
        { month: "Mar", visits: 3400, signups: 520 },
        { month: "Apr", visits: 4100, signups: 610 },
        { month: "May", visits: 4600, signups: 700 },
        { month: "Jun", visits: 5200, signups: 790 },
      ]}
    />
  );
}
```

That is the whole contract: `data` is the rows, one per point on the x axis; `series` names the keys to draw; `xKey` names the one on the x axis. Swap `LineChart` for `BarChart` or `LineBarChart` and the same props draw the same data another way. [Data and series](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/data) covers the details: dates, gaps, ordering, typed rows and reshaping API data.

The chart gives you, without asking: a tooltip on hover, keyboard navigation through the points, a legend whose entries hide and show their series, an entry animation that respects reduced motion, and a summary and data table for screen readers. See [States and interaction](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/interaction).

## Server components

The charts are client components, so you can render them from a server component and pass them the rows you fetched there. They draw on the server, so nothing waits for JavaScript. Two things can't cross from the server to the client: function props (`valueFormat={(v) => …}`, `date.onRangeChange`) and values that are not plain data. Use the string and `Intl` forms of `valueFormat`, or wrap the chart in a client component. Details in [Numbers and dates](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/formatting#from-a-server-component).

## Config

App-wide chart settings live in the `dataStyle` section of `once-ui.config`, next to `style`:

once-ui.config.js:

```ts
const { style, dataStyle } = defineConfig({
  style: { /* … */ },
  dataStyle: {
    variant: "gradient", // flat | gradient | outline
    mode: "categorical", // categorical | divergent | sequential
    height: "24rem", // the default chart height
    axis: {
      stroke: "var(--neutral-alpha-weak)",
    },
    tick: {
      fill: "var(--neutral-on-background-weak)",
      fontSize: 11,
      line: false,
    },
  },
});
```

Providers:

```tsx
<ThemeInit config={style} dataStyle={dataStyle} />

<ThemeProvider {...style}>
  <DataThemeProvider {...dataStyle}>{children}</DataThemeProvider>
</ThemeProvider>
```

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `variant` | `gradient` | `flat` | outline |
| `mode` | `categorical` | `divergent` | sequential |
| `height` | `number \| CSS length` | `24rem` | Every chart's height. A number is on the spacing token scale, so write a string: "24rem". |
| `axis.stroke` | `string` | `var(--neutral-alpha-weak)` | The colour of the axis lines. |
| `tick.fill` | `string` | `var(--neutral-on-background-weak)` | The colour of the axis labels. |
| `tick.fontSize` | `number` | `11` | The size of the axis labels, in px. |
| `tick.line` | `boolean` | `false` | Draw tick marks on the axes. |

Every key is optional; what you leave out keeps its default. `ThemeInit` puts the mode on `<html>` before the first paint, so a divergent app doesn't flash categorical colours. Without `DataThemeProvider`, charts use the defaults above.

To change the settings at runtime, such as a mode switch in a settings page, use `useDataTheme()`; see [Recipes](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/recipes#theme-switch-for-charts).

## Props every chart shares

`LineChart`, `BarChart`, `LineBarChart` and `PieChart` take these, and each page lists the props that are its own. Charts also take every [Flex prop](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/flex) for the card: margin, `background`, `border`, `radius` and the rest.

Charts are generic over the row type, inferred from `data`: your own `interface` works as it is, and a `series` key or `xKey` that is not a key of the row is a type error.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `title` | `React.ReactNode` |  | The heading above the chart. |
| `description` | `React.ReactNode` |  | The line under the title. |
| `series (required)` | `SeriesConfig<DataPoint> \| SeriesConfig<DataPoint>[]` |  | Which keys of each row to draw, with their label, colour and format. See Data and series. |
| `data (required)` | `readonly DataPoint[]` |  | The rows: one object per x value, with a number per series key. |
| `xKey` | `SeriesKey<DataPoint>` |  | The row key on the x axis. Defaults to the first key of the first row that is not a series. Pass it when rows carry an id or other extra keys. |
| `valueFormat` | `ValueFormat` |  | How values are written on the axis, in the tooltip and in the summary: "number", "compact", "percent", Intl.NumberFormatOptions or a function. |
| `locale` | `string` |  | The locale numbers are written in, such as "hu-HU". Defaults to "en-US". |
| `summary` | `string` |  | What a screen reader hears for the plot, after the title, in place of the generated summary. |
| `aria-label` | `string` |  |  |
| `legend` | `LegendConfig` |  | Legend visibility, position and direction. |
| `date` | `DateConfig` |  | Date format, the first date range (which filters the rows) and the range picker. See States and interaction. |
| `emptyState` | `React.ReactNode` |  | What to show when data is empty. |
| `errorState` | `React.ReactNode` |  | What to show when error is set. |
| `error` | `boolean` |  | Draw the error state in place of the plot. |
| `tooltip` | `boolean` |  | Show the hover tooltip and make the plot keyboard-navigable. |
| `grid` | `"x" \| "y" \| "both" \| "none"` |  | Which grid lines to draw. Bar charts default to y, line charts to both. |
| `axis` | `"x" \| "y" \| "both" \| "none"` |  | Which axes to label. |
| `variant` | `ChartVariant` |  | How areas and bars are filled. Defaults to dataStyle.variant. |
| `loading` | `boolean` |  | Draw the loading state in place of the plot. |

`data-viz-style` sets one chart's colour [mode](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/colors#modes), overriding `dataStyle.mode`.

# Choosing a chart

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/choosing

> Which Once UI chart fits your data: a question to start from, a table of shapes, and the charts to avoid for each job.

Start from the question the reader brings, not from the data. "How did revenue move this year?" is a line. "Which team has the most open tickets?" is a bar. "What share of sessions came from search?" is a pie, if there are only a few parts. The same rows can answer all three, and each question wants a different chart.

## By question

- **How did it change over time?** [`LineChart`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/lineChart). A line says the value moved continuously between readings.
- **Which is bigger?** [`BarChart`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/barChart). Lengths from a shared baseline are the easiest thing to compare.
- **Which is bigger, with long names?** `BarChart orientation="horizontal"`. Category names read along the row instead of being cut under the bar.
- **What adds up to the total?** `BarChart stack` or `LineChart stack`. Each part sits on the one before it, so the top is the total.
- **What is each part's share, over time?** `stack="percent"`. Every bar or column runs to 100%, so shares compare across rows.
- **What is each part's share, once?** [`PieChart`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/pieChart). Two to five slices. Past that, use a horizontal bar chart.
- **How do a budget and its spend compare?** [`LineBarChart`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/lineBarChart). A line for the target, bars for the actuals, on one scale.
- **How is it trending, in a tile or a table cell?** [`Sparkline`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/sparkline). The shape only: no axes, legend or card.
- **How close is it to a limit?** [`RadialGauge`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/radialGauge) or [`LinearGauge`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/linearGauge). One value against a range, such as a quota or a score.
- **What is each part's size and direction, with many parts?** [`Treemap`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/treemap). Area for size, colour for up or down.
- **Which way did each item move?** [`DivergingBars`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/divergingBars). Gains right, losses left, from one zero.
- **Where are the busy months, or hours?** [`Heatmap`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/heatmap). A grid of two periods, each cell's size in one hue.

## By data shape

- A date and one or more numbers per row: `LineChart`, or `BarChart` for a handful of periods.
- A category and one number per row: `BarChart`, or `PieChart` for a few parts of a whole.
- A category and several numbers per row: `BarChart` (grouped), or `stack` when the numbers add up.
- A target and an actual per row: `LineBarChart`.
- Readings at uneven intervals: `LineChart xAxisType="number"`.
- A plain array of numbers: `Sparkline`.
- One number: a gauge, or a stat tile with a `Sparkline`.

Every chart but `Sparkline` and the gauges takes the same `data` and `series`, so moving between `LineChart`, `BarChart` and `LineBarChart` is a change of the tag name. See [Data and series](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/data) for the shape.

## Things to avoid

- **A pie with many slices.** Past five, the small slices are slivers nobody can compare. Keep the top four and group the rest as "Other", or use a horizontal bar chart. The recipe is in [Recipes](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/recipes#top-n-and-other).
- **A smooth line through jumps.** The default `curve="natural"` claims the value moved between readings. A price tier or a seat count changed in steps: use `curve="step"`.
- **Two scales on one axis.** `LineBarChart` has one y axis. A rate (4%) next to a count (8,000) sits flat on the baseline. Use two charts.
- **Stacking things that don't add up.** Stack revenue by channel, not revenue and margin. The top of a stack should mean "total".
- **A bar chart for a long time series.** Fifty bars become a comb. Use a line, or `barWidth="fill"` if it has to be bars.
- **Colour that only decorates.** A single series doesn't need a hue per bar. Give it the brand (`color: "brand"`) and let the length do the work.

## One example, three charts

The same rows, asked three questions.
