# Data and series

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/data

> The data contract every Once UI chart shares: what a row looks like, how the x axis and the series are found, dates, gaps, ordering, typed rows and reshaping API data.

`LineChart`, `BarChart`, `LineBarChart` and `PieChart` read the same two props. `data` is the rows: one object per point on the x axis. `series` says which keys of those rows to draw. Everything else is presentation.

Rows and series:

```tsx
<BarChart
  title="Orders per channel"
  xKey="month"
  series={[
    { key: "web", label: "Web shop" },
    { key: "store", label: "In store" },
  ]}
  data={[
    { month: "Jan", web: 124, store: 88 },
    { month: "Feb", web: 131, store: 91 },
    { month: "Mar", web: 158, store: 86 },
    { month: "Apr", web: 172, store: 94 },
  ]}
/>
```

## Rows

A row holds the x value and one number per series. The keys can be anything, and a row may carry extra keys the chart ignores (an id, a note), as long as `series` names what to draw.

```ts
{ month: "Jan", web: 124, store: 88, id: "2026-01" }
//  x value      series     series    ignored
```

- **Values are numbers.** A string such as `"1,240"` is not drawn. Convert with `Number()` before passing the rows.
- **Rows are drawn in the order you give them.** The chart doesn't sort. Sort by date or by value first, whichever the reader should scan in.
- **A missing value is a gap.** Leave the key out, or set it to `undefined` or `null`, and a line breaks there instead of dropping to zero. A bar is simply not drawn. Write `0` only when the value really was zero.

## The x axis

The chart has to know which key is the x axis. In order, it uses:

1. `xKey`, when you pass it.
2. Otherwise the first key of the **first row** that is not a series and is not `label`.
3. Otherwise `label`.

So `{ month: "Jan", web: 124 }` puts `month` on the x axis with nothing else said. Key order is fragile, though. Rows from an API or a database often lead with an `id`, and then the id becomes the axis. **Pass `xKey` whenever the rows have more than one non-series key.**

`label` is special: when a row has a `label`, that text is what the axis and the tooltip print for the row, whatever the x value is. Use it to write a friendlier name than the raw value.

```ts
{ date: "2026-01-01", label: "New year", visits: 320 }
```

## Series

`series` is one object, or an array of them, one per line, bar or slice group.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | `string` | `-` | The row key this series plots. With typed rows, a key that is not on the row type is a type error. |
| `label` | `string` | `key` | The name the legend, the tooltip and the screen-reader summary use. Lets the data keep short keys. |
| `color` | `ColorValue` | `auto` | A palette hue (blue, green…), your theme's brand or accent, a token or any CSS colour. See Colors and styling. |
| `format` | `ValueFormat` | `valueFormat` | How this series' values are written in the tooltip, when it differs from the chart's valueFormat. |

Without `series`, a cartesian chart draws every key of the first row except the x key and `label`. It is handy for a quick look and risky in production, because a new field from the API becomes a new line. Name the series.

The order of `series` is the order of the legend, the tooltip, the colours and, when stacked, the stack from the bottom up. In `LineBarChart` it also decides the shape: the first series is the line, the second the bars.

## Dates

Dates on the x axis can be ISO strings (`"2026-03-01"`) or `Date` objects. Either way, set `date.format` to write them on the axis and in the tooltip, as a [date-fns pattern](https://date-fns.org/docs/format):

```tsx
<LineChart
  date={{ format: "MMM d" }}
  xKey="day"
  series={{ key: "visits" }}
  data={[{ day: "2026-03-01", visits: 320 }]}
/>
```

Without `date.format`, the axis prints the value as it is in the row, so `"2026-03-01"` stays `2026-03-01`, and a `Date` prints its long `toString()` (`Sun Mar 01 2026 00:00:00 GMT…`). With `Date` objects, always set a format. A string that is not ISO (`"Mar 1"`) is never parsed: it is printed as written, which is fine for categories that happen to be dates.

`date.start` and `date.end` **filter the rows**: anything outside the range is not drawn. They don't stretch the axis to the range. Use them with `date.selector` to let the reader pick a range in the header (see [States and interaction](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/interaction#date-range)), and leave them out to draw every row.

Dates are not spaced by time. Each row gets an equal slot, so a missing month doesn't leave a gap on the axis. When the spacing matters, put numbers on the x axis (a timestamp, a day index) and set `xAxisType="number"` on `LineChart`:

```tsx
<LineChart
  xAxisType="number"
  xKey="t"
  series={{ key: "latency" }}
  data={samples.map((s) => ({ t: s.time.getTime(), latency: s.ms }))}
/>
```

## Typed rows

Charts are generic over the row type. Your own `interface` works as it is, with no cast and no index signature, and `readonly` arrays are fine. A typo in a series key or in `xKey` is a type error.

```tsx
interface RevenueRow {
  month: string;
  revenue: number;
  cost: number;
}

const rows: readonly RevenueRow[] = await getRevenue();

<BarChart
  data={rows}
  xKey="month"
  series={[{ key: "revenue" }, { key: "cost" }]}
/>
```

`DataPoint`, `SeriesConfig`, `ValueFormat` and the other types are exported from `@once-ui-system/core/data` for the code around your charts.

## Reshaping API data

Charts want **wide** rows: one row per x value, one key per series. APIs and SQL usually return **long** rows: one row per x value _and_ series. Pivot them before passing:

```ts
// [{ month: "Jan", channel: "web", orders: 124 }, { month: "Jan", channel: "store", orders: 88 }, …]
function pivot<T extends Record<string, unknown>>(
  rows: T[],
  x: keyof T,
  by: keyof T,
  value: keyof T,
) {
  const out = new Map<unknown, Record<string, unknown>>();
  for (const row of rows) {
    const key = row[x];
    if (!out.has(key)) out.set(key, { [x]: key });
    (out.get(key) as Record<string, unknown>)[String(row[by])] = Number(row[value]);
  }
  return [...out.values()];
}

const data = pivot(rows, "month", "channel", "orders");
// [{ month: "Jan", web: 124, store: 88 }, …]
```

A series whose key is missing from some rows shows a gap there, which is usually right: no orders recorded is not the same as zero orders. Fill with `0` in the pivot if it is.

## Pie data

A pie reads a name and a value from each row, `name` and `value` by default. `nameKey` and `dataKey` point at other keys. Give the series the same key as `dataKey`, so its `label` and `format` apply:

```tsx
<PieChart
  nameKey="channel"
  dataKey="sessions"
  series={{ key: "sessions", label: "Sessions" }}
  data={[
    { channel: "Direct", sessions: 4200 },
    { channel: "Search", sessions: 3100 },
  ]}
/>
```

A slice takes its colour from a `color` key on its row, or from the palette in order. `series.color` doesn't colour a pie.

## Empty data

An empty `data` array draws the chart's empty state, not an error: the request ran and found nothing. Set `emptyState` to say what that means for this chart. See [States and interaction](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/interaction).

# Numbers and dates

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/formatting

> How Once UI charts write values and dates: valueFormat, per-series formats, locales, currencies and units, date patterns, and what works from a server component.

A chart writes each number in three places: the value axis, the tooltip and the summary a screen reader hears. `valueFormat` and `locale` set all three at once, so the axis never says `1240000` while the tooltip says `1.24M`.

## valueFormat

- `"number"` writes `1240000` as `1,240,000`, for counts.
- `"compact"` writes `1240000` as `1.2M`, for big numbers on a small chart.
- `"percent"` writes `1240000` as `124,000,000%`, for fractions (`0.42` is `42%`).
- `{ style: "currency", currency: "EUR" }` writes `1240000` as `€1,240,000.00`, for money.
- `{ style: "unit", unit: "kilogram" }` writes `1240000` as `1,240,000 kg`, for measurements.
- `(v) => v + " pts"` writes `1240000` as `1240000 pts`, for anything Intl can't write.

With no `valueFormat`, `locale` or series `format` at all, the axis prints plain digits (`1240000`) and the tooltip groups them (`1,240,000`). Set `valueFormat="number"` to group both.

Anything `Intl.NumberFormat` takes is an option: `maximumFractionDigits`, `notation`, `signDisplay` and the rest.

`"percent"` expects fractions. If your data already holds `42` for 42%, write `{ style: "unit", unit: "percent" }` instead, which prints `42%` without multiplying.

## Locale

`locale` is the language the numbers are written in, as a BCP 47 tag. It defaults to `en-US` on the server and in every browser, so the first HTML and the hydrated chart agree. Pass the reader's locale when you know it:

The value axis widens to fit the longest label, so `1 950 000 Ft` is not cut at the edge.

A locale the runtime doesn't know falls back to `en-US` instead of throwing.

## A format per series

`series[].format` overrides `valueFormat` for one series in the tooltip. Use it when one chart shows two kinds of number, such as orders and their average value. The axis keeps the chart's `valueFormat`, because there is only one axis.

```tsx
<LineBarChart
  valueFormat="number"
  series={[
    { key: "orders", label: "Orders" },
    { key: "aov", label: "Average order", format: { style: "currency", currency: "EUR" } },
  ]}
  data={rows}
/>
```

Mixing units on one axis is usually a sign the chart wants to be two charts: see [Choosing a chart](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/choosing#things-to-avoid).

## Stacks in percent

`stack="percent"` writes the axis from 0% to 100% whatever `valueFormat` says, because the axis is a share. The tooltip keeps the real values in `valueFormat`, so the reader sees both "42%" on the axis and "1,240 orders" on hover.

## Dates

Dates are written with `date.format`, a [date-fns pattern](https://date-fns.org/docs/format):

| Pattern | Writes |
| --- | --- |
| `"yyyy"` | `2026` |
| `"MMM yyyy"` | `Mar 2026` |
| `"MMM d"` | `Mar 1` |
| `"d MMM"` | `1 Mar` |
| `"HH:mm"` | `14:30` |
| `"QQQ yyyy"` | `Q1 2026` |

The pattern is applied to ISO strings and `Date` objects on the axis, in the tooltip and in the summary. Month and day names are in English. For another language, write the text yourself in the row's `label` key, which every place that prints the x value uses as it is:

```ts
const data = rows.map((row) => ({
  ...row,
  label: new Intl.DateTimeFormat("hu-HU", { month: "short" }).format(new Date(row.date)),
}));
```

## From a server component

The charts are client components that render on the server, so you can fetch in a server component and pass the rows straight in. Props cross from the server to the client as data, and a function is not data: `valueFormat={(v) => …}` from a server component fails to render.

From a server component, use the string and `Intl` forms, which cover nearly everything. When you need a function, wrap the chart in a small client component and pass it the rows:

```tsx
"use client";

import { LineChart, type DataPoint } from "@once-ui-system/core/data";

export function ScoreChart({ data }: { data: DataPoint[] }) {
  return (
    <LineChart
      xKey="week"
      series={{ key: "score" }}
      valueFormat={(v) => `${v.toFixed(1)} / 10`}
      data={data}
    />
  );
}
```

The same goes for `date.onRangeChange`.

# Colors and styling

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/colors

> How Once UI charts pick colours: the data palette, series colours, the categorical, divergent and sequential modes, the three variants, and sizing and styling the chart card.

Charts draw from their own palette, the `--data-*` tokens, tuned so neighbouring series stay apart in light and dark. You rarely need to pick colours: leave `color` off and the chart assigns them. When a colour carries meaning (a brand, a status, "this year"), set it per series.

## Automatic colours

Without `color`, series take hues spread around the palette, as far apart as the count allows:

| Series | Colours |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | blue |
| 2 | blue, orange |
| 3 | blue, orange, cyan |
| 4 | blue, orange, green, magenta |
| 5 or more | spaced evenly across the 13 hues |

Pie slices follow the same rule, counted by slice.

## Series colours

`series[].color` takes four kinds of value:

- **A palette hue**, such as `"blue"`, `"emerald"` or `"contrast"`: the palette's colour. It follows the theme and the chart's mode.
- **Your theme**, `"brand"` or `"accent"`: the theme's brand or accent colour, at the same step as the palette hues, so it sits with them in light and dark.
- **A token**, such as `"danger-medium"` or `"--my-colour"`: that token. A tone with a weight is that role's text colour.
- **Any CSS colour**, such as `"#6E56CF"` or `"oklch(70% 0.15 160)"`: exactly that, in light and dark alike.

The palette hues are `blue`, `indigo`, `violet`, `magenta`, `pink`, `red`, `orange`, `yellow`, `moss`, `green`, `emerald`, `aqua`, `cyan`, plus `gray` and `contrast` (white in dark, black in light) for a reference series.

A single-series chart in `"brand"` is the usual way to make a dashboard feel like the product. Write `"brand"`, not `"brand-strong"`: a tone with a weight is that role's text colour, which is white in dark and black in light.

Prefer palette hues and tokens to raw CSS colours. A hex value looks the same in light and dark, and on one of them it usually loses contrast.

## Modes

A mode decides what the palette hues mean. Set it for the app in `dataStyle.mode` (see [Setup](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/setup#config)), or for one chart with the `data-viz-style` prop.

- **`categorical`** (default): distinct hues for things that have no order, such as channels, teams or products.
- **`divergent`**: a run from red through yellow to cyan, for values on either side of a midpoint, such as change against last year or sentiment.
- **`sequential`**: steps of the brand colour, for ordered things where more is more, such as age bands or price tiers.

A mode works by redefining the palette hues inside the chart. In `divergent`, `blue` is a red and `cyan` is the far end of the run. So in divergent and sequential charts, **leave `color` off** and let the series take their places in order; a hue name you set means "this step of the run", not that colour. Tokens and CSS colours ignore the mode.

## Variants

`variant` sets how areas and bars are filled. Set it for the app in `dataStyle.variant`, or per chart.

`outline` draws only the lines and bar edges, which keeps overlapping series readable; `flat` fills without the fade.

## The card

Every chart is a `Column`, a card with a border and a radius, and takes the [Flex props](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/flex): spacing, `background`, `border`, `radius`, `shadow` and so on.

Card:

```tsx
<BarChart
  background="brand-alpha-weak"
  border="brand-alpha-medium"
  radius="xl"
  height="16rem"
  title="Signups"
  axis="x"
  legend={{ display: false }}
  xKey="day"
  series={{ key: "signups", color: "brand" }}
  data={rows}
/>
```

- **No card:** `border="transparent"` (or `border={false}`) and no `background`, to set a chart inside your own `Card` or tile.
- **Height:** charts are `dataStyle.height` tall, `24rem` by default. Set `height` as a string, `height="16rem"`. A number is on the spacing token scale, so `height={16}` is 1rem and flattens the chart to a line. The title and description take their room from that height; the plot gets the rest.
- **Width:** charts fill their container. Put them in a `Grid` or a `Row` to lay several out; they resize with it.

# States and interaction

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/interaction

> Loading, empty and error states, the tooltip and keyboard, legend toggles, the date-range picker, and what screen readers get from every Once UI chart.

## Request states

Charts fetch nothing themselves, so the states of a request are props you set from wherever the data comes from. Handled, a chart becomes a readable panel instead of an empty frame, and it keeps its height, so the page doesn't jump when the data lands.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `loading` | `boolean` | `false` | Draws a loading state in place of the plot. The title and description stay. |
| `error` | `boolean` | `false` | Draws the error state in place of the plot. |
| `errorState` | `ReactNode` | `-` | What the error state says. Say what failed and what to do. |
| `emptyState` | `ReactNode` | `-` | What to show when data is empty, or when the date range leaves no rows. |

Request states:

```tsx
const { data, isLoading, error } = useOrders(range);

<LineChart
  title="Orders"
  loading={isLoading}
  error={Boolean(error)}
  errorState={<Text onBackground="danger-weak">Couldn't load orders. {error?.message}</Text>}
  emptyState={<Text onBackground="neutral-weak">No orders in this range yet.</Text>}
  xKey="day"
  series={{ key: "orders" }}
  data={data ?? []}
/>
```

An empty array is not an error: the query ran and matched nothing. That is why `emptyState` and `errorState` are separate. When both `loading` and `error` are false and `data` is empty, the empty state shows.

## Tooltip and keyboard

Hovering the plot shows a tooltip with every visible series at that x value, written in the chart's [format](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/formatting). A line chart draws a cursor line, a bar chart highlights the band (`hover` on `BarChart` paints the whole band).

The plot is also reachable from the keyboard. Tab to it, and:

| Key | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `→` `↓` | Next point |
| `←` `↑` | Previous point |
| `Home` / `End` | First / last point |
| `Esc` | Hide the tooltip |

A pie moves slice by slice with the arrow keys. `tooltip={false}` turns the tooltip off and takes the plot out of the tab order, for a chart that is only a picture next to its numbers.

## Legend

The legend lists the series with their colours. With two or more series, each entry is a button: pressing it hides or shows that series, and the value axis rescales to what is left. That lets the reader take the big series out to see the small ones.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `legend.display` | `boolean` | `true` | Show the legend. Turn it off for one series, where the title already names it. |
| `legend.position` | `string` | `top-left` | Where the legend sits on the plot: top-left, top-center, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-center or bottom-right. |
| `legend.direction` | `row` | `column` |  |

## Date range

A time series can carry a date-range picker in its header. Give it a `start` and an `end`, which set the first range and filter the rows to it, and turn on `selector`:

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `date.start / date.end` | `Date` | `-` | The first range. Rows outside it are not drawn. The picker needs both. |
| `date.selector` | `boolean` | `false` | Show the range picker in the header. |
| `date.presets` | `PresetsConfig` | `week` | Quick ranges beside the calendar: { display, granularity }. granularity year offers this and last year, month adds the months, week adds the weeks. |
| `date.dual` | `boolean` | `false` | Show two months side by side in the calendar. |
| `date.min / date.max` | `Date` | `-` | The earliest and latest day the reader can pick. |
| `date.onRangeChange` | `(range: DateRange) => void` | `-` | Called with the picked range. Use it to fetch that range from the server. |
| `date.format` | `string` | `-` | How dates are written: a date-fns pattern. |

The chart filters the rows it already has. For a long history, fetch the range instead: keep `start` and `end` in state, refetch in `onRangeChange`, and pass the new rows. `onRangeChange` is a function, so this chart lives in a client component.

```tsx
"use client";

const [range, setRange] = useState({ start: startOfMonth(new Date()), end: new Date() });
const { data, isLoading } = useVisits(range);

<LineChart
  loading={isLoading}
  date={{
    ...range,
    format: "MMM d",
    selector: true,
    onRangeChange: ({ startDate, endDate }) =>
      startDate && endDate && setRange({ start: startDate, end: endDate }),
  }}
  xKey="date"
  series={{ key: "visits" }}
  data={data ?? []}
/>
```

## Animation

Charts draw in on mount: lines sweep from the left, bars grow from the baseline. Readers who ask for reduced motion never see it. `LineChart` takes `animation={false}` and `animationBegin`, `animationDuration` and `animationEasing` to tune it. For live data, either match `animationDuration` to the sample interval so updates glide, or turn it off so they snap: see [LineChart](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/lineChart#live-data).

## Screen readers

Each chart's plot is a figure (`role="figure"`), named by its title and a summary written from the data, in the chart's `valueFormat` and `locale`:

- a line or bar chart: "Revenue and Cost, Jan to Dec. Revenue: highest 12,400 in Aug, lowest 3,100 in Feb."
- a pie: "Share by browser: Chrome 62%, Safari 21%, Firefox 9%."

Inside the card, hidden from sight, the chart also renders its data as a table: the x values as rows, a column per series. A reader who wants the numbers can walk them cell by cell. While a chart loads, fails or is empty, the plot is no figure, and its status is read as it is.

The generated summary states only what is in the data. When the point of the chart is something the numbers don't say on their own, write it:

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `summary` | `string` | `generated` | What a screen reader hears after the title, in place of the generated summary. |
| `aria-label` | `string` | `-` | The plot's whole name, title included, in place of the title and summary. The hidden table stays. |

```tsx
<LineChart
  title="Revenue"
  summary="Revenue tripled over the summer and held through December."
  xKey="month"
  series={{ key: "revenue", label: "Revenue" }}
  data={rows}
/>
```

Colour is never the only cue: each series is named in the legend, the tooltip and the table. Use `label` so those names are words a reader knows, not `rev_q_usd`.

---

# Recipes

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/recipes

> Copy-ready patterns for Once UI charts: a dashboard grid, KPI tiles, fetching in a server component, this period against the last, top N and other, targets, live data and switching chart types.

Each recipe is a pattern you can paste and adapt. They use only `@once-ui-system/core` and `@once-ui-system/core/data`.

## Dashboard grid

Charts fill their container, so a dashboard is a `Grid` of them. Give every chart in a row the same `height` so their plots line up, and let the grid collapse to one column on small screens.

Dashboard:

```tsx
<Grid fillWidth columns="2" s={{ columns: 1 }} gap="16">
  <LineChart
    title="Revenue"
    height="18rem"
    axis="x"
    legend={{ display: false }}
    valueFormat={{ style: "currency", currency: "USD", notation: "compact" }}
    xKey="month"
    series={{ key: "revenue", label: "Revenue", color: "brand" }}
    data={revenue}
  />
  <BarChart
    title="Orders by channel"
    height="18rem"
    axis="x"
    stack
    legend={{ position: "top-right" }}
    xKey="month"
    series={[
      { key: "web", label: "Web" },
      { key: "store", label: "Store" },
    ]}
    data={orders}
  />
</Grid>
```

## KPI tiles

A tile is a number, its change and the shape behind it: a [`Sparkline`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/sparkline), not a full chart. Keep full charts for the questions a reader explores; tiles are for glancing.

Tile:

```tsx
<Column padding="20" gap="8" radius="l" border="neutral-alpha-weak" background="surface">
  <Text textVariant="label-default-s" onBackground="neutral-weak">Revenue</Text>
  <Row vertical="end" gap="8">
    <Text textVariant="heading-strong-l">$48.2K</Text>
    <Text textVariant="label-default-s" onBackground="success-weak">+12%</Text>
  </Row>
  <Sparkline data={[32, 35, 34, 38, 41, 39, 44, 48]} variant="area" color="emerald" height={40} showLast />
</Column>
```

Colour the change by what it means for the business, not by its sign: more refunds is up and bad.

## Fetch in a server component

The charts render on the server, so the page can query and pass the rows straight in. The first HTML holds the drawn chart, with no loading spinner and no client fetch.

```tsx
// app/(dashboard)/revenue/page.tsx
import { LineChart } from "@once-ui-system/core/data";
import { getMonthlyRevenue } from "@/lib/reports";

export default async function RevenuePage() {
  const rows = await getMonthlyRevenue(); // [{ month: "2026-01-01", revenue: 32000 }, …]

  return (
    <LineChart
      title="Revenue"
      xKey="month"
      date={{ format: "MMM yyyy" }}
      valueFormat={{ style: "currency", currency: "EUR", maximumFractionDigits: 0 }}
      series={{ key: "revenue", label: "Revenue" }}
      data={rows}
    />
  );
}
```

Rows cross to the client as JSON, so send what the chart draws, not whole database records. `Date` values arrive as `Date`s; numbers stored as strings (Postgres `numeric`) need a `Number()` first. Keep function props out of server components: see [Numbers and dates](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/formatting#from-a-server-component).

## This period against the last

Draw the comparison as a quiet reference: last period in `gray`, this period in a colour.

Align the two periods by position (day 1, day 2…), not by date, so they share the axis. The current period stops where today is: leave its later values out instead of writing `0`, and the line ends there.

```ts
const data = lastMonth.map((row, i) => ({
  day: String(i + 1),
  previous: row.signups,
  current: thisMonth[i]?.signups, // undefined after today: a gap, not a zero
}));
```

## Top N and other

A pie past five slices stops being readable. Keep the biggest and add up the rest:

```ts
function topN<T extends { name: string; value: number }>(rows: T[], n = 4) {
  const sorted = [...rows].sort((a, b) => b.value - a.value);
  const rest = sorted.slice(n).reduce((sum, row) => sum + row.value, 0);
  return rest > 0
    ? [...sorted.slice(0, n), { name: "Other", value: rest, color: "gray" }]
    : sorted;
}
```

`gray` marks "Other" as the leftovers, not a fifth source to compare.

## Target and actual

[`LineBarChart`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/lineBarChart) draws its first series as a line and its second as bars, on one axis: the target as the line, the actuals as bars.

```tsx
<LineBarChart
  title="Spend against budget"
  xKey="month"
  valueFormat={{ style: "currency", currency: "EUR", notation: "compact" }}
  series={[
    { key: "budget", label: "Budget", color: "gray" },
    { key: "spend", label: "Spend", color: "brand" },
  ]}
  data={rows}
/>
```

## Live data

For a chart that updates every second, keep the x range fixed so the axis doesn't rescale on each sample. [`useStreamingViewport`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useStreamingViewport) buffers the samples and pans the visible window; the live examples on [LineChart](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/lineChart#live-data) show it with the animation tuned to glide, and turned off to snap.

```tsx
<LineChart
  animation={false}
  xAxisType="number"
  xDomain={[now - 60_000, now]}
  xKey="t"
  series={{ key: "rps", label: "Requests/s" }}
  data={samples}
/>
```

## Let the reader switch views

`LineChart` and `BarChart` take the same props, so one set of props can draw either. A `SegmentedControl` picks which.

```tsx
"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import { Column, SegmentedControl } from "@once-ui-system/core";
import { BarChart, LineChart } from "@once-ui-system/core/data";

export function OrdersChart({ data }: { data: { month: string; web: number; store: number }[] }) {
  const [view, setView] = useState("line");
  const props = {
    title: "Orders",
    xKey: "month" as const,
    series: [
      { key: "web" as const, label: "Web" },
      { key: "store" as const, label: "Store" },
    ],
    data,
  };

  return (
    <Column gap="12">
      <SegmentedControl
        buttons={[
          { value: "line", label: "Trend" },
          { value: "bar", label: "Compare" },
        ]}
        value={view}
        onValueChange={setView}
      />
      {view === "line" ? <LineChart {...props} /> : <BarChart {...props} />}
    </Column>
  );
}
```

## Theme switch for charts

`useDataTheme()` reads the chart settings and `setChartOptions` changes them for every chart under the provider. A new `mode` is also remembered in the browser.

```tsx
"use client";

import { SegmentedControl, useDataTheme } from "@once-ui-system/core";

export function ChartModeSwitch() {
  const { mode, setChartOptions } = useDataTheme();
  return (
    <SegmentedControl
      buttons={[
        { value: "categorical", label: "Categorical" },
        { value: "divergent", label: "Divergent" },
        { value: "sequential", label: "Sequential" },
      ]}
      value={mode}
      onValueChange={(value) => setChartOptions({ mode: value as typeof mode })}
    />
  );
}
```

# Building blocks

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/parts

> The pieces Once UI charts are made of, exported for your own visuals: ChartHeader, ChartStatus, ChartSummary, Swatch and useDataTheme.

When none of the charts fits, such as a calendar heatmap, a funnel or a map with values, build the visual yourself and give it the same frame as the charts. These parts are what every chart uses, so a custom visual next to a `LineChart` reads as one system.

```tsx
import { ChartHeader, ChartStatus, ChartSummary, Swatch } from "@once-ui-system/core/data";
import { useDataTheme } from "@once-ui-system/core";
```

## ChartHeader

The title, description and date-range picker on top of every chart. It renders nothing when it has neither a title, a description nor a selector.

ChartHeader:

```tsx
<Column fillWidth radius="l" border="neutral-alpha-weak">
  <ChartHeader title="Opening hours used" description="Bookings per hour, last 4 weeks" />
  <Column fillWidth padding="24" borderTop="neutral-alpha-weak">
    {/* your visual */}
  </Column>
</Column>
```

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `title` | `ReactNode` | `-` | The heading. |
| `description` | `ReactNode` | `-` | The line under it. |
| `date` | `DateConfig` | `-` | The same date config a chart takes; date.selector shows the picker. |
| `dateRange` | `DateRange` | `-` | The range the picker shows as picked. |
| `onDateRangeChange` | `(range: DateRange) => void` | `-` | Called with the range the reader picks. |
| `presets` | `PresetsConfig` | `{ display: true, granularity: "week" }` | Quick ranges beside the calendar. |

It takes the `Column` props too, for padding and borders.

## ChartStatus

The loading spinner, the error message or the empty message, centred in whatever box it sits in. Loading wins over an error, and an error over empty. It renders nothing when none is set.

```tsx
<Column fillWidth height="16rem">
  <ChartStatus loading={isLoading} error={Boolean(error)} empty={rows.length === 0} />
  {!isLoading && !error && rows.length > 0 && <Heatmap rows={rows} />}
</Column>
```

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `loading` | `boolean` | `false` | Show the spinner. |
| `error` | `boolean` | `false` | Show errorState. |
| `empty` | `boolean` | `false` | Show emptyState. |
| `errorState` | `ReactNode` | `"An error occurred while fetching data"` | The error message. |
| `emptyState` | `ReactNode` | `"No data available for the selected period"` | The empty message. |

## ChartSummary

The hidden table every chart carries for screen readers: the x values as rows, a column per series, every value in the chart's format. Give a custom visual the same, from the same rows, so its numbers are reachable without sight.

```tsx
<figure aria-label="Bookings per hour">
  <Heatmap rows={rows} />
  <ChartSummary
    title="Bookings per hour"
    data={rows}
    xKey="hour"
    series={[{ key: "mon", label: "Monday" }, { key: "tue", label: "Tuesday" }]}
    valueFormat="number"
  />
</figure>
```

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `data` |  |  |  |
| `series` |  |  |  |
| `xKey` | `string` | `-` | The row key for the first column. |
| `kind` | `"cartesian" \| "pie"` | `cartesian` | pie adds each row's share of the total. |
| `valueFormat` | `ValueFormat` | `-` | How values are written. |
| `locale` | `string` | `en-US` | The locale they are written in. |
| `date` | `DateConfig` | `-` | Writes date x values with date.format. |
| `title` | `string` | `-` | Used for the caption: "Title: data". |
| `caption` | `ReactNode` | `-` | The table's caption, in place of the one from the title. |

## Swatch

The colour sample in legends and tooltips, in the chart variant's fill.

```tsx
<Row vertical="center" gap="8">
  <Swatch color="var(--data-emerald)" />
  <Text textVariant="label-default-s">Booked</Text>
</Row>
```

`color` is a CSS colour as written: use `var(--data-emerald)` for a palette hue, since a bare `"emerald"` is the CSS named colour here. `size` is `"s"` or `"m"`, and `variant` defaults to the app's chart variant.

## useDataTheme

The chart settings from `DataThemeProvider`, the `dataStyle` section of your config, and a setter:

```tsx
const { variant, mode, height, axis, tick, setChartOptions } = useDataTheme();
```

Read `axis.stroke` and `tick.fill` to draw your own axes in the charts' colours, and `height` to match their size. `setChartOptions({ mode: "divergent" })` changes every chart under the provider; see [Recipes](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/recipes#theme-switch-for-charts).

---

# LineChart

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/lineChart

> Draw change over time: one line per series, filled or outlined, stacked or not, with smooth or stepped curves, a numeric x axis and live data.

`LineChart` draws one line per series across the rows of `data`, with the area under each filled. Use it when the reader asks how something moved over time; for comparing categories use [`BarChart`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/barChart). It takes the [props every chart shares](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/setup#props-every-chart-shares) and the ones on this page.

## Labels and numbers

`xKey` names the column on the x axis; without it, the first key that is not a
series is. A series' `label` is the name the legend and tooltip show, so the
data can keep short keys. `valueFormat` writes the numbers on the axis and in
the tooltip: `"compact"`, `"percent"`, any `Intl.NumberFormatOptions` (a
currency, a unit), or a function. `locale` sets the language they are written
in; it defaults to `en-US`, so the server and every browser agree.

## Stacked

`stack` puts each series on top of the one before it, for parts that add up to
a total. `stack="percent"` shows each as its share of the total instead.

## Thresholds and annotations

`thresholds` draws limits across the value axis: a line at `value`, or a band
from `from` to `to` (leave an end out for "above" or "below"). `annotations`
marks moments on the x axis. Each is labelled in the plot and drawn so it reads
without colour: `danger` is a heavy solid line over a hatched band, `warning` a
dashed line, the other tones a thin dotted one. The summary a screen reader
hears says which series crossed each limit, how often and first when.
`yDomain` zooms the value axis to the range that matters.

## Curve

`curve` is how the line runs between points (d3's curve names), and it is a claim about the data between
your points. `natural` and `monotone` draw a smooth line, which implies the
value moved continuously; `step` holds each value until the next reading, which
is honest for something that changes in jumps — a price tier, a headcount, a
setting. `linear` sits between the two.

## Numeric x axis

By default the x axis is categorical: each data point gets an equal slot,
whatever its value. For readings that are not evenly spaced — samples arriving
at irregular times, a measurement against a continuous quantity — set
`xAxisType="number"` so the spacing reflects the actual values, and pass
`xDomain` to pin the visible range.

Numeric axis:

```tsx
<LineChart
  xAxisType="number"
  xDomain={[0, 100]}
  series={{ key: "Response" }}
  data={samples}
/>
```

A fixed `xDomain` is also what keeps a streaming chart from rescaling on every
sample: see [Live data](#live-data) below.

## Live data

For a chart that takes a new sample every second or so, fix the x range with `xAxisType="number"` and `xDomain`, so the axis doesn't rescale with each sample. Both examples get their samples and their moving window from [`useStreamingViewport`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useStreamingViewport).

With `animation` on and `animationDuration` equal to the sample interval (and `animationEasing="linear"`), each update eases into the next, so the line glides:

With `animation={false}`, each sample snaps into place. Choose this when samples arrive faster than an animation can finish:

## Animation

Animation is on by default. The three `animation*` props set the entry
animation's delay, length and CSS easing (`"ease-out"`, `"linear"` or any
`cubic-bezier()`). It is skipped under `prefers-reduced-motion`.

Turn animation **off** for a chart that updates faster than the animation runs:
each new sample restarts the transition, so a streaming line spends its time
animating rather than showing the data.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `curve` | `CurveType` | `natural` | Interpolation between points: natural, linear, step, stepBefore, stepAfter, monotone, basis, bump and their variants (d3's curve names). |
| `stack` | `boolean \| "percent"` | `false` | Stack the series: true sums them, "percent" shows each as its share of the total. |
| `reverseY` | `boolean` | `false` | Move the y axis to the right. |
| `reverseX` | `boolean` | `false` | Move the x axis to the top. |
| `animation` | `boolean` | `true` | Draw the lines in from the left when the chart mounts. Readers who ask for reduced motion never see it. |
| `animationBegin` | `number` |  | Delay before the animation starts, in milliseconds. |
| `animationDuration` | `number` |  | Animation length, in milliseconds. |
| `animationEasing` | `unknown` |  | A CSS easing: ease, ease-in-out, linear or a cubic-bezier(). |
| `xAxisType` | `"number" \| "category"` |  | Treat x values as numbers rather than equally spaced categories. |
| `xDomain` | `[number, number]` |  | Visible x range. Requires xAxisType="number". |
| `legend` | `LegendConfig` | `{}` | Legend position and visibility. |
| `error` | `boolean` | `false` | Render the error state instead of the chart. |
| `tooltip` | `boolean` | `true` | Show a tooltip on hover. |
| `grid` | `"x" \| "y" \| "both" \| "none"` | `both` | Which grid lines to draw. |
| `axis` | `"x" \| "y" \| "both" \| "none"` | `both` | Which axes to label. |
| `loading` | `boolean` | `false` | Render the loading state instead of the chart. |
| `border` | `Colors \| "surface" \| "transparent" \| boolean` | `neutral-alpha-weak` | Panel border colour. false removes it. |
| `thresholds` |  |  |  |
| `annotations` |  |  |  |
| `yDomain` |  |  |  |
| `...ChartMarksProps, ...ChartProps, ...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

---

# BarChart

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/barChart

> Compare categories with bars: one or many series, grouped or stacked, vertical or horizontal, with band highlighting and adjustable bar width.

`BarChart` draws a bar per series for each row of `data`, side by side, stacked, or laid along the x axis. Use it when the reader asks which is bigger: lengths from a shared baseline are the easiest thing to compare. For change over many periods, a [`LineChart`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/lineChart) reads better. It takes the [props every chart shares](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/setup#props-every-chart-shares) and the ones on this page.

One series is a plain bar chart; give it one colour, ideally the brand (`color: "brand"`), rather than a hue per bar. Several series are grouped in each band, in `series` order.

## Horizontal and stacked

`orientation="horizontal"` lays the bars along the x axis, one row per
category: easier to read when the category names are long. `stack` puts the
series on top of each other; `stack="percent"` makes every bar the same length
and shows each series as its share.

## Bar width

`barWidth` takes a t-shirt token, a pixel number, or `"fill"` to let the bars
consume the whole band with no gap between them. Wider bars read better for a
handful of categories; `"s"` or a number keeps a long series legible.

## Moving an axis

`reverseX` and `reverseY` move an axis to the opposite side of the plot — the x
axis to the top, the y axis to the right. They reposition the labels; they do
not reverse the scale, and the data is untouched.

Reach for `reverseY` when the chart sits at the left edge of a layout and the
labels read better on the inside, or when two charts are placed side by side
and you want their axes on the outer edges.

## Hover

`hover` paints the whole band behind the bar on pointer-over, which makes a
dense chart easier to read across — the row you are pointing at is the one
lighting up, rather than just the bar you happened to hit.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `barWidth` | `BarWidth` | `l` | Bar thickness. "fill" removes the gap between bands. |
| `hover` | `boolean` | `false` | Highlight the whole band on pointer-over. |
| `reverseY` | `boolean` | `false` | Move the y axis to the right. |
| `reverseX` | `boolean` | `false` | Move the x axis to the top. |
| `orientation` | `"vertical" \| "horizontal"` | `vertical` | "horizontal" lays the bars along the x axis, one row per category. |
| `stack` | `boolean \| "percent"` | `false` | Stack the series: true sums them, "percent" shows each as its share of the bar. |
| `legend` | `LegendConfig` | `{}` | Legend position and visibility. |
| `error` | `boolean` | `false` | Render the error state instead of the chart. |
| `tooltip` | `boolean` | `true` | Show a tooltip on hover. |
| `grid` | `"x" \| "y" \| "both" \| "none"` | `y` | Which grid lines to draw. |
| `axis` | `"x" \| "y" \| "both" \| "none"` | `both` | Which axes to label. |
| `loading` | `boolean` | `false` | Render the loading state instead of the chart. |
| `border` | `Colors \| "surface" \| "transparent" \| boolean` | `neutral-alpha-weak` | Panel border colour. false removes it. |
| `...ChartMarksProps, ...ChartProps, ...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

---

# LineBarChart

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/lineBarChart

> A line and bars on one shared axis, for two measures of the same unit such as a budget and its spend, or a target and its actuals.

`LineBarChart` draws its first series as a line and its second as bars, against one y axis. Use it for two measures in the same unit where one is a reference for the other: a budget and its spend, a target and its actuals, a forecast and what happened. It takes the [props every chart shares](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/setup#props-every-chart-shares) and the ones on this page.

## Which series is which

Order decides the shape: **the first series is drawn as the line, the second as
the bars.** There is no prop for it, and only the first two series are drawn —
a third is ignored.

## Both series share one y axis

There is a single y axis, so the two measures are plotted against the same
scale. That makes the chart a comparison of two quantities of **comparable
magnitude** — sessions against conversions, budget against spend — not a way to
overlay a rate on a volume.

Pair a percentage with a count and the percentage collapses onto the baseline:
it is not missing, it is drawn at 4 on an axis that runs to 8000. If that is
the chart you want, normalise the small series into the same units first, or
put the two measures in separate charts.

## API reference

The line's shape comes from `curve` and the bars' thickness from `barWidth` —
the same props as [`LineChart`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/lineChart) and
[`BarChart`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/barChart), which is what makes swapping between the
three cheap.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `barWidth` | `BarWidth` | `l` | Bar thickness. |
| `curve` | `CurveType` | `natural` | Interpolation for the line: natural, linear, step, stepBefore, stepAfter, monotone, basis, bump and their variants (d3's curve names). |
| `reverseY` | `boolean` | `false` | Move the y axis to the right. |
| `reverseX` | `boolean` | `false` | Move the x axis to the top. |
| `legend` | `LegendConfig` | `{}` | Legend position and visibility. |
| `error` | `boolean` | `false` | Render the error state instead of the chart. |
| `tooltip` | `boolean` | `true` | Show a tooltip on hover. |
| `grid` | `"x" \| "y" \| "both" \| "none"` | `y` | Which grid lines to draw. |
| `axis` | `"x" \| "y" \| "both" \| "none"` | `both` | Which axes to label. |
| `loading` | `boolean` | `false` | Render the loading state instead of the chart. |
| `border` | `Colors \| "surface" \| "transparent" \| boolean` | `neutral-alpha-weak` | Panel border colour. false removes it. |
| `series` |  |  |  |
| `...ChartMarksProps, ...ChartProps, ...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# PieChart

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/pieChart

> Show parts of a whole as a pie or a donut: slices from name and value rows, per-slice colours, ring size and position, and a legend beside it.

`PieChart` draws one slice per row of `data`, sized by its value and named by its name. Use it for the share of a few parts in one whole: two to five slices. Past that the small ones become slivers, so keep the biggest and group the rest as "Other" ([recipe](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/recipes#top-n-and-other)), or use a horizontal [`BarChart`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/barChart). It takes the [props every chart shares](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/setup#props-every-chart-shares) except `xKey`, `axis` and `grid`, and the ones on this page.

      
## Slice colours

Slices take the palette in order, spread as far apart as their count allows. To colour a slice yourself, give its row a `color`: a palette hue, a token or any CSS colour. Useful when a slice has a meaning, such as `"gray"` for "Other" or the brand for your own product. `series.color` doesn't colour a pie.

Slice colours:

```tsx
<PieChart
  title="Market share"
  ring={{ inner: 55, outer: 70 }}
  valueFormat="percent"
  series={{ key: "value", label: "Share" }}
  data={[
    { name: "Us", value: 0.38, color: "brand" },
    { name: "Competitor A", value: 0.27, color: "blue" },
    { name: "Competitor B", value: 0.21, color: "orange" },
    { name: "Other", value: 0.14, color: "gray" },
  ]}
/>
```

## Ring

`ring` sets the inner and outer radius as percentages of the available space.
`inner: 0` is a solid pie; anything above it is a donut, and the hole is where a
total or a label goes.

Keep `outer` under 100 — the arc is drawn inside the panel, and a value at 100
leaves no room for the labels around it.

## Naming the slices

A pie reads two fields per row: the number that sizes the slice and the string
that names it. Those default to `value` and `name`, and `dataKey` / `nameKey`
point them at different fields when your data is already shaped some other way.

Custom keys:

```tsx
// Rows from an API, unchanged.
const rows = [
  { channel: "Direct", sessions: 4200 },
  { channel: "Search", sessions: 3100 },
];

<PieChart
  dataKey="sessions"
  nameKey="channel"
  series={{ key: "sessions" }}
  data={rows}
/>
```

## Position

`origo` moves the centre of the pie within the panel, as percentages. Shift it
when the legend sits along one side and the default centring leaves the arc
crowded against it.

## API reference

`PieChart` has no axes or grid, so `axis` and `grid` do not apply.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ring` | `{ inner: number; outer: number }` | `{ inner: 0, outer: 80 }` | Inner and outer radius as percentages. inner: 0 is a solid pie. |
| `dataKey` | `SeriesKey<DataPoint>` | `value` | Field holding the number that sizes each slice. |
| `nameKey` | `SeriesKey<DataPoint>` | `name` | Field holding the slice label. |
| `origo` | `{ x: number; y: number }` | `{ x: 50, y: 50 }` | Centre of the pie within the panel, as percentages. |
| `legend` | `LegendConfig` | `{}` | Legend position and visibility. |
| `border` | `Colors \| "surface" \| "transparent" \| boolean` | `neutral-alpha-weak` | Panel border colour. false removes it. |
| `error` | `boolean` | `false` | Render the error state instead of the chart. |
| `loading` | `boolean` | `false` | Render the loading state instead of the chart. |
| `tooltip` | `boolean` | `true` | Show a tooltip on hover. |
| `...ChartProps, ...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

---

# Sparkline

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/sparkline

> A tiny inline trend line, area or bar strip for stat tiles and table cells: pure SVG, no axes, legend or card, and it renders on the server.

`Sparkline` draws the shape of a series in the space of a line of text. It has no axes, legend, tooltip or card, and no recharts behind it: it is one SVG, so it renders in a server component and costs no JavaScript. The drawing stretches to its box (`preserveAspectRatio="none"`) while the line keeps its width, so it fills a table cell or a tile at any size.

Usage:

```tsx
<Sparkline data={[120, 180, 160, 240, 210, 360, 340]} width={240} />
```

It fills its container's width and is 32px tall unless `width` and `height` say otherwise. A number is px; any CSS length, such as `"100%"` or `"2rem"`, passes through. It also ships from the package root, as it pulls in nothing the root does not already have.

## In a stat tile

The usual home of a sparkline: a number, the change, and the shape behind them. `showLast` puts a dot on the latest value.

Stat tile:

```tsx
<Column padding="20" gap="8" radius="l" border="neutral-alpha-weak" background="surface">
  <Text textVariant="label-default-s" onBackground="neutral-weak">Revenue</Text>
  <Row vertical="end" gap="8">
    <Text textVariant="heading-strong-l">$48.2K</Text>
    <Text textVariant="label-default-s" onBackground="success-weak">+12%</Text>
  </Row>
  <Sparkline
    data={[32, 35, 34, 38, 41, 39, 44, 48]}
    variant="area"
    color="emerald"
    height={40}
    showLast
    valueFormat={{ style: "currency", currency: "USD", notation: "compact" }}
  />
</Column>
```

## In a table cell

Give the column a `cell` that draws the row's values. A fixed `width` keeps every row's line the same length.

Table cell:

```tsx
const pages = [
  { page: "/pricing", visits: "12,480", trend: [8, 9, 11, 10, 12, 13, 12] },
  { page: "/docs", visits: "9,310", trend: [12, 11, 10, 10, 9, 9, 9] },
  { page: "/blog", visits: "4,022", trend: [2, 3, 2, 5, 4, 6, 4] },
];

<Table
  aria-label="Pages by visits"
  getRowId={(row) => row.page}
  columns={[
    { key: "page", header: "Page" },
    { key: "visits", header: "Visits", align: "right" },
    {
      key: "trend",
      header: "Last 7 days",
      cell: (row) => <Sparkline data={row.trend} width={96} height={20} showLast />,
    },
  ]}
  rows={pages}
/>
```

## Bars

`variant="bar"` draws one bar per value, from zero, so negative values hang below the line. With `showLast` the latest bar is in full colour and the rest are dimmed.

Bars:

```tsx
<Sparkline
  data={[4, 6, 3, 8, 7, 9, 5, 10, 12, 9, 11, 14]}
  variant="bar"
  color="violet"
  width={240}
  height={40}
  showLast
/>
```

## Curves and range

`curve` joins the points: `"monotone"` (the default, smooth and never past a point), `"natural"` (the charts' spline), `"linear"` or `"step"`. `min` and `max` fix the values at the bottom and top edges, so sparklines side by side share a scale instead of each filling its own height.

Curves:

```tsx
<Sparkline data={values} curve="monotone" />
<Sparkline data={values} curve="natural" color="cyan" />
<Sparkline data={values} curve="linear" color="magenta" />
<Sparkline data={values} curve="step" color="orange" min={0} max={10} />
```

## Rows of data

Pass your rows as they are and name the key to plot with `valueKey`. Without it, the first key holding a number is used.

```tsx
const week = [
  { day: "Mon", signups: 31 },
  { day: "Tue", signups: 44 },
  { day: "Wed", signups: 38 },
];

<Sparkline data={week} valueKey="signups" />
```

## Accessibility

A sparkline is one image to a screen reader (`role="img"`). Without an `aria-label` it is named by a summary of its values, written in `valueFormat` and `locale`: the first example above reads "Trend from 120 to 340, high 360". Pass `aria-label` when the tile around it does not already say what the line is, such as "Revenue, last 8 weeks".

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `data (required)` | `readonly number[] \| readonly T[]` |  | The values, oldest first: numbers, or rows read by valueKey. |
| `valueKey` | `SeriesKey<T>` |  | The row key to plot when data is objects. Defaults to the first key holding a number. |
| `variant` | `"line" \| "area" \| "bar"` | `line` | A line, a line with a filled area under it, or one bar per value. |
| `color` | `ColorValue` | `blue` | A chart colour (blue, emerald), a token or any CSS colour. |
| `width` | `number \| string` | `100%` | A number is px; any CSS length passes through. |
| `height` | `number \| string` | `32` | A number is px; any CSS length passes through. |
| `curve` | `SparklineCurve` | `monotone` | How the line joins its points. Bars ignore it. |
| `showLast` | `boolean` | `false` | A dot on the last point; on bars, the last bar in full colour. |
| `min` | `number` |  | The value at the bottom edge. Defaults to the lowest value (0 or lower for bars). |
| `max` | `number` |  | The value at the top edge. Defaults to the highest value (0 or higher for bars). |
| `valueFormat` | `ValueFormat` |  | How values are written in the summary a screen reader hears. |
| `locale` | `string` |  | The locale the summary's numbers are written in. |
| `aria-label` | `string` |  |  |

# RadialGauge

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/radialGauge

> A radial, tick-based gauge for visualizing health metrics and real-time values using circular or arc-based layouts.

The `RadialGauge` component renders a tick-based circular or arc-shaped gauge that is ideal for health metrics, KPIs, and other real-time values. It supports full circles, semicircles, and custom arcs with configurable angles, direction, density, and visual health states.

Usage:

```tsx
<RadialGauge
    width={260}
    height={260}
    value={72}
    unit="%"
/>
```

## Hue

Use the `tone` prop to colour the active ticks on a ramp for a state (`success`, `neutral`, `warning`, `danger`), or `hueRange` for a ramp of your own. 2.x took both as `hue`.

Hue:

```tsx
<RadialGauge
    width={260}
    height={260}
    value={82}
    unit="%"
    tone="success"
/>
<RadialGauge
    width={260}
    height={260}
    value={56}
    unit="%"
    tone="neutral"
/>
<RadialGauge
    width={260}
    height={260}
    value={28}
    unit="%"
    tone="danger"
/>
<RadialGauge
    width={260}
    height={260}
    value={90}
    unit="%"
    hueRange={[0, 200]}
/>
```

## Angles

You can create semicircular or arc gauges by combining `angle` and `edgePad`. The angle system is **intuitive**:

- `0`° = left
- `90`° = top
- `180`° = right
- `270`° = bottom

Angles:

```tsx
<RadialGauge
    width={300}
    height={150}
    value={68}
    line={{
      count: 24,
    }}
    angle={{
      start: 0,
      sweep: 180,
    }}
>
    <Row fill vertical="end" horizontal="center" padding="20">
      <Text textVariant="heading-strong-xl">68%</Text>
    </Row>
</RadialGauge>
```

## Ticks

Control how many ticks are rendered and how long they are using `lineCount`, `lineWidth`, and `lineLength`.

Density:

```tsx
<RadialGauge
    width={320}
    height={320}
    value={42}
    unit="ms"
    line={{
      count: 80,
      width: 2,
      length: 32,
    }}
/>
```

## Animation

For interactive demos or dashboards, you can animate the `value` over time on the client. The example below simulates accelerating and braking.

Animated speed meter:

```tsx
"use client";

import React, { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { Column, Text } from "@once-ui-system/core";
import { RadialGauge } from "@once-ui-system/core/data";

export function RadialGaugeSpeedDemo() {
  const [value, setValue] = useState(20);
  const [phase, setPhase] = useState<"idle" | "accelerate" | "brake">("idle");

  useEffect(() => {
    let timeout: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;
    let interval: ReturnType<typeof setInterval> | undefined;

    const startAccelerate = () => {
      setPhase("accelerate");
      interval = setInterval(() => {
        setValue(prev => {
          const next = Math.min(prev + 6, 96);
          if (next >= 96) {
            clearInterval(interval);
            timeout = setTimeout(startBrake, 600);
          }
          return next;
        });
      }, 90);
    };

    const startBrake = () => {
      setPhase("brake");
      interval = setInterval(() => {
        setValue(prev => {
          const next = Math.max(prev - 8, 18);
          if (next <= 18) {
            clearInterval(interval);
            timeout = setTimeout(startAccelerate, 800);
          }
          return next;
        });
      }, 90);
    };

    timeout = setTimeout(startAccelerate, 400);

    return () => {
      if (interval) clearInterval(interval);
      if (timeout) clearTimeout(timeout);
    };
  }, []);

  const label = phase === "accelerate" ? "Accelerating" : phase === "brake" ? "Braking" : "Idle";

  return (
    <Column center gap="8">
      <RadialGauge
        width={260}
        height={260}
        value={value}
        unit="km/h"
        angle={{
          start: -120,
          sweep: 240,
        }}
        edgePad={4}
      />
      <Text textVariant="label-default-m" onBackground="neutral-medium">
        {label}
      </Text>
    </Column>
  );
}
```

## Props

The `RadialGauge` component accepts all layout props from `Column` (except `direction`) plus the following gauge-specific props:

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `width` | `number` | `300` | Overall width, in pixels. |
| `height` | `number` | `300` | Overall height, in pixels. |
| `line` | `{ count?: number; width?: number; length?: number; }` |  | The tick marks around the arc: how many, how thick, how long. |
| `unit` | `React.ReactNode` |  | Rendered after the value — a percent sign, a unit, anything. |
| `value` | `number` | `7` | Where the gauge reads, 0–100. |
| `angle` | `{ start: number; sweep: number; }` | `{ start: 0, sweep: 360, }` | Where the arc starts and how far it sweeps, in degrees. 360 is a full ring. |
| `direction` | `"cw" \| "ccw"` | `cw` | Which way the sweep runs from the start angle. |
| `edgePad` | `number` | `0` | Inset between the arc and the edge of the box, in pixels. |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` |  | Rendered in the middle of the gauge, in place of the value. |
| `tone` | `"success" \| "neutral" \| "warning" \| "danger"` |  | Colour the arc by its value on the ramp for a tone. |
| `hueRange` | `[number, number]` |  | Colour the arc by its value on a [from, to] pair of hue degrees. Wins over tone. |
| `color` | `ColorValue` | `contrast` | A single colour for the arc, when it should not vary with the value. Takes a token or any CSS colour. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

Use `RadialGauge` when you need a compact, highly legible representation of a single metric that can be scanned quickly, such as system health, SLO burn rate, or real-time utilization.

# LinearGauge

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/linearGauge

> A horizontal, tick-based gauge for visualizing progress, metrics, and health with flexible label configurations.

The `LinearGauge` component renders a horizontal tick-based gauge ideal for progress indicators, metrics dashboards, and system health displays. It supports flexible label configurations including none, percentage, or custom values.

Usage:

```tsx
<LinearGauge
    width={400}
    height={60}
    value={65}
/>
```

## Labels

Show percentage labels at key intervals (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%).

Percentage:

```tsx
<LinearGauge
    width={400}
    height={80}
    value={75}
    labels="percentage"
/>
```

Provide an array of custom labels distributed evenly across the gauge.

Custom:

```tsx
<LinearGauge
    width={400}
    height={80}
    value={42}
    labels={["Low", "Med", "High", "Max"]}
/>
```

## Reverse order

Flip the order of labels and gauge by using `direction="column-reverse"`.

Reverse:

<LinearGauge

    height={80}
    value={65}
    labels="percentage"
    direction="column-reverse"
/>

## Hue

Use the `tone` prop to represent a state with a colour ramp (`success`, `neutral`, `warning`, `danger`), or `hueRange` for a ramp of your own. 2.x took both as `hue`.

States:

<Column gap="16">

      value={56}
      tone="neutral"
      labels="percentage"
    />
    <LinearGauge
      width={400}
      height={60}
      value={28}
      tone="danger"
      labels="percentage"

      width={400}

<LinearGauge

      width: 2,

## Props

The `LinearGauge` component accepts all layout props from `Flex` (except `direction`) plus the following gauge-specific props:

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |

| `height` | `number` | `80` | Track thickness, in pixels. |
| `line` | `{ count?: number; width?: number; length?: number; }` |  | The tick marks along the track: how many, how thick, how long. |
| `value` | `number` | `50` | Where the gauge reads, 0–100. |
| `labels` | `"none" \| "percentage" \| string[]` | `none` | "percentage" prints the value, or pass your own strings to label the ticks. "none" hides them. |
| `tone` | `"success" \| "neutral" \| "warning" \| "danger"` |  | Colour the fill by its value on the ramp for a tone. |
| `hueRange` | `[number, number]` |  | Colour the fill by its value on a [from, to] pair of hue degrees. Wins over tone. |
| `color` | `ColorValue` | `contrast` | A single colour for the fill, when it should not vary with the value. Takes a token or any CSS colour. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

Use `LinearGauge` for horizontal metrics displays, progress tracking, or any scenario where a linear representation is more appropriate than a radial one.

# Treemap

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/treemap

> Tiles sized by value and coloured by direction: holdings by value and change, spend by category. HTML, server-rendered, every tile focusable.

`Treemap` draws one tile per row of `data`, its area the row's value. With `toneKey` each tile is also coloured by a signed number, such as a change since purchase: above zero in the gain colour, below zero in the loss colour, stronger the further from zero. Use it when there are too many parts for a [`PieChart`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/pieChart) and their sizes matter more than their order. It takes the card, `title`, `description`, `valueFormat`, `locale`, `tooltip`, `loading`, `error`, `emptyState` and `errorState` the other charts take.

Usage:

```tsx
<Treemap
  title="Holdings"
  data={holdings}
  toneKey="change"
  subKey="share"
  valueFormat={{ style: "currency", currency: "EUR", maximumFractionDigits: 0 }}
  toneFormat="percent"
/>
```

Rows without a positive value are left out, and tiles are laid out largest first so the biggest sit top left. A tile writes its name when it fits and `subKey`'s text when there is room for a second line; its hover card and its accessible name always carry the value, the tone and that text.

## Colour

Without `toneKey` every tile is neutral and area alone carries the data. With it, the strongest tone gets the strongest colour; set `toneMax` to fix that scale instead, so two treemaps compare (`toneMax={0.5}` paints anything at ±50% at full strength). Gains are emerald and losses orange by default, a pair that stays apart for colour-blind readers in light and dark; `gainColor` and `lossColor` take any palette name or CSS colour.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `title` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
| `description` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
| `valueFormat` | `ValueFormat` |  |  |
| `locale` | `string` |  |  |
| `tooltip` | `boolean` | `true` |  |
| `loading` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `error` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `emptyState` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
| `errorState` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
| `aria-label` | `string` |  |  |
| `data (required)` | `readonly DataPoint[]` |  | One row per tile. Rows with no positive value are left out. |
| `dataKey` | `SeriesKey<DataPoint>` | `"value" as SeriesKey<T>` | The row key that sizes each tile. Defaults to "value". |
| `nameKey` | `SeriesKey<DataPoint>` | `"label" as SeriesKey<T>` | The row key that names each tile. Defaults to "label". |
| `toneKey` | `SeriesKey<DataPoint>` |  | The row key of a signed number that colours each tile: gains above zero, losses below. |
| `toneMax` | `number` |  | The tone at full strength. Defaults to the largest tone in the data. |
| `toneFormat` | `ValueFormat` |  | How tones are written in the hover card. Defaults to valueFormat. |
| `subKey` | `SeriesKey<DataPoint>` |  | The row key whose text is the tile's second line when it fits. |
| `gainColor` | `ColorValue` |  | Tiles above zero. Defaults to emerald. |
| `lossColor` | `ColorValue` |  | Tiles below zero. Defaults to orange. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# Heatmap

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/heatmap

> A grid of rows by columns, each cell's size in one hue: dividends by month and year, visits by hour and weekday. HTML, server-rendered, every cell focusable.

`Heatmap` draws one row per row of `data` and one cell per column you name, each cell in one of five steps of a single hue against the largest value in the grid. Use it to find patterns across two periods, like which months pay out in which years. Empty, zero and negative cells stay neutral: a heatmap shows how much, not which way ([`DivergingBars`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/divergingBars) shows direction). It takes the card, `title`, `description`, `valueFormat`, `locale`, `tooltip`, `loading`, `error`, `emptyState` and `errorState` the other charts take.

Usage:

```tsx
<Heatmap
  title="Dividends"
  data={[
    { label: "2025", Jan: 8, Feb: 15, Mar: 46 /* … */ },
    { label: "2026", Jan: 10, Feb: 19, Mar: 55 /* … */ },
  ]}
  columns={["Jan", "Feb", "Mar" /* … */]}
  valueFormat={{ style: "currency", currency: "EUR" }}
/>
```

`columns` lists row keys, left to right, or `{ key, label }` when the heading should read differently from the key. `rowKey` names the key each row's name comes from (`"label"` by default). Each cell's hover card and accessible name say its row, its column and its value, or "No data".

## Colour and scale

The cells are emerald by default; `color` takes any palette name or CSS colour. The scale under the grid reads "Less" to "More": rename its ends with `legend={{ less: "Kevesebb", more: "Több" }}`, or hide it with `legend={{ display: false }}`.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `title` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
| `description` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
| `valueFormat` | `ValueFormat` |  |  |
| `locale` | `string` |  |  |
| `tooltip` | `boolean` | `true` |  |
| `loading` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `error` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `emptyState` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
| `errorState` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
| `aria-label` | `string` |  |  |
| `data (required)` | `readonly DataPoint[]` |  | One row per line of cells: a year, a client, a weekday. |
| `columns (required)` | `readonly (SeriesKey<DataPoint> \| HeatmapColumn<DataPoint>)[]` |  | The columns, left to right, as row keys or { key, label }. |
| `rowKey` | `SeriesKey<DataPoint>` | `"label" as SeriesKey<T>` | The row key that names each row. Defaults to "label". |
| `color` | `ColorValue` |  | The hue the cells are drawn in. Defaults to emerald. |
| `legend` | `{ display?: boolean; less?: string; more?: string }` |  | The scale under the grid: display, and the less and more labels. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# DivergingBars

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/data/divergingBars

> A signed value per item on one shared zero: gains grow right, losses left, each value written beside its bar. HTML, server-rendered, every bar focusable.

`DivergingBars` draws one row per row of `data`: its name, a bar from zero, and its value. Gains grow right in the gain colour and losses left in the loss colour, all on one scale, so lengths compare across the list. Zero sits where the largest loss ends: a list with no losses uses the whole width. Every value is written with its sign (`+12%`), so colour is never the only cue. It takes the card, `title`, `description`, `valueFormat`, `locale`, `tooltip`, `loading`, `error`, `emptyState` and `errorState` the other charts take.

Usage:

```tsx
<DivergingBars
  title="Since bought"
  data={[
    { label: "Fjell", value: 0.18 },
    { label: "Halden", value: -0.06 },
    { label: "Quill", value: -0.21 },
  ]}
  valueFormat="percent"
/>
```

Bars are drawn in the order given, so sort the rows first to rank them. `dataKey` and `nameKey` read other keys than `"value"` and `"label"`. Gains are emerald and losses orange by default; `gainColor` and `lossColor` take any palette name or CSS colour.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `title` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
| `description` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
| `valueFormat` | `ValueFormat` |  |  |
| `locale` | `string` |  |  |
| `tooltip` | `boolean` | `true` |  |
| `loading` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `error` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `emptyState` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
| `errorState` | `React.ReactNode` |  |  |
| `aria-label` | `string` |  |  |
| `data (required)` | `readonly DataPoint[]` |  | One row per bar, drawn in the order given. |
| `dataKey` | `SeriesKey<DataPoint>` | `"value" as SeriesKey<T>` | The row key of each bar's signed value. Defaults to "value". |
| `nameKey` | `SeriesKey<DataPoint>` | `"label" as SeriesKey<T>` | The row key that names each bar. Defaults to "label". |
| `gainColor` | `ColorValue` |  | Bars above zero. Defaults to emerald. |
| `lossColor` | `ColorValue` |  | Bars below zero. Defaults to orange. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# CelebrationFx

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/celebrationFx

> The CelebrationFx component creates animated celebration effects like confetti and fireworks using native Canvas 2D API.

The `CelebrationFx` component creates animated celebration effects using the native Canvas 2D API. Choose between confetti or fireworks animations with multiple trigger modes, customizable colors, and intensity controls. Perfect for success states, achievements, milestones, or interactive celebrations.

Usage:

```tsx
<CelebrationFx
  height="20rem"
  type="confetti"
  duration={4000}
/>
```

## Types

Choose between `confetti` (falling particles) or `fireworks` (explosive bursts).

Types:

```tsx
<CelebrationFx
    type="confetti"
    duration={5000}
/>
<CelebrationFx
    type="fireworks"
    duration={5000}
/>
```

## Trigger

Control when the celebration starts with `mount` (on load), `hover` (while the pointer is over it; a tap on touch screens) or `click` (a burst from the click position). A celebration runs for `duration` (3000 ms by default), then what is in the air settles.

Hover:

```tsx
<CelebrationFx
    height="16rem"
    type="confetti"
    trigger="hover"
    center
>
    <Text textVariant="heading-strong-l">
      Hover me!
    </Text>
</CelebrationFx>
```

Use `trigger="click"` to fire celebrations from exactly where users click. Perfect for interactive celebrations!

Click:

```tsx
<CelebrationFx
    type="fireworks"
    trigger="click"
    center
>
    <Text textVariant="heading-strong-l">
      Click for fireworks!
    </Text>
</CelebrationFx>
<CelebrationFx
    type="confetti"
    trigger="click"
    center
>
    <Text textVariant="heading-strong-l">
      Click for confetti!
    </Text>
</CelebrationFx>
```

## Color

Customize celebration colors using design tokens or any valid CSS color.

Colors:

```tsx
<CelebrationFx
  height="16rem"
  type="fireworks"
  duration={5000}
  colors={["accent-background-strong", "danger-background-strong", "warning-background-strong"]}
/>
```

## Intensity & speed

Control particle density with `intensity` and animation speed with `speed`.

Intensity:

```tsx
<CelebrationFx
    height="16rem"
    type="confetti"
    duration={5000}
    intensity={100}
    speed={2}
/>
<CelebrationFx
    height="16rem"
    type="confetti"
    duration={5000}
    intensity={20}
    speed={0.5}
/>
```

Start it from your own state with `active` and `onActiveChange`, like any other stateful component. `onActiveChange(false)` arrives when `duration` ends, so the button below can fire again.

Manual:

```tsx
"use client";

import React, { useState } from "react";
import { Button, Column } from "@once-ui-system/core";
import { CelebrationFx } from "@once-ui-system/fx";

export function demo() {
    const [active, setActive] = useState(false);

    return (
      <Column gap="16" fillWidth>
        <CelebrationFx
          height="16rem"
          type="fireworks"
          active={active}
          onActiveChange={setActive}
        />
        <Button
          onClick={() => setActive(true)}
        >
          Launch Fireworks
        </Button>
      </Column>
    );
}
```

## Custom content

Use `CelebrationFx` as a wrapper to overlay celebrations behind any content.

Overlay:

```tsx
<CelebrationFx
    height="20rem"
    type="confetti"
    duration={6000}
    center
>
    <Column
      gap="16"
      padding="48"
      center
      background="neutral-weak"
      radius="l"
    >
      <Icon name="trophy" size="xl" onBackground="accent-strong" />
      <Text textVariant="heading-strong-xl">Achievement Unlocked!</Text>
      <Text textVariant="body-default-s" onBackground="neutral-weak">
        You've completed all challenges
      </Text>
    </Column>
</CelebrationFx>
```

## Performance

CelebrationFx draws with time-based motion at your screen's pixel ratio (up to 2x), sleeps when everything has landed or the effect is scrolled off screen, and picks its colours up again when the theme changes.

Under the `prefers-reduced-motion` system setting, and on low-end devices, it shows a still frame instead of animating: scattered confetti or a frozen burst while `active`. Override this with the `reducedMotion` prop.

See [useReducedMotion](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useReducedMotion) for details.

## Props

The `CelebrationFx` component extends all layout props from `Flex` plus the following celebration-specific props:

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | `CelebrationType` | `confetti` | Which celebration to render. |
| `speed` | `Speed` |  | Motion multiplier: 1 is the default. "slow", "medium" and "fast" are 0.5, 1 and 2. |
| `colors` | `string[]` |  | Palette: tokens (brand-solid-medium, accent-weak), custom properties or CSS colours. |
| `intensity` | `number` | `50` | How much of it there is: pieces per cannon, or sparks per shell. 0 to 200. |
| `duration` | `number` | `3000` | How long it runs once started, in milliseconds. 0 or Infinity runs until active turns off. |
| `trigger` | `"mount" \| "hover" \| "click"` | `mount` | What starts it by itself: mount, hover or click. |
| `active` | `boolean` |  | Whether it is celebrating. Controlled; pair with onActiveChange. |
| `defaultActive` | `boolean` |  | The first value of active when uncontrolled. Defaults to trigger === "mount". |
| `onActiveChange` | `(active: boolean) => void` |  | Called when it starts (hover) or ends (duration, pointer leaving). |
| `reducedMotion` | `boolean \| "auto"` | `auto` | "auto" follows the reader's system setting, which is the right default for anything ambient. |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` |  | Content drawn above the celebration. |
| `children` |  |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

Use `CelebrationFx` to add delightful, performant celebration animations to success states, milestones, achievements, or any moment worth celebrating in your application.
