# MatrixFx

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/matrixFx

> The MatrixFx component creates an animated dot matrix reveal effect using native Canvas 2D API.

The `MatrixFx` component creates an animated dot matrix reveal effect using the native Canvas 2D API. It supports instant reveal, progressive reveal on mount, or hover-triggered animations with smooth transitions. Perfect for hero sections, backgrounds, or interactive hover cards.

MatrixFx:

```tsx
<MatrixFx
    height="24rem"
    colors={["brand-solid-strong", "accent-solid-strong"]}
    trigger="mount"
    flicker
/>
```

## Speed

Control the reveal animation speed with the `speed` prop. Higher values make the reveal faster.

Speed:

```tsx
<MatrixFx
    height="24rem"
    trigger="mount"
    speed={2}
    colors={["accent-solid-medium"]}
/>
```

## Colors

Use multiple colors for variety. Supports CSS variables and any valid color format.

Colors:

```tsx
<MatrixFx
    height="24rem"
    colors={[
      "brand-solid-medium",
      "accent-solid-medium",
      "danger-solid-medium"
    ]}
/>
```

## Size & Spacing

Customize the size of dots and spacing between them.

Size & Spacing:

```tsx
<MatrixFx
    fill
    height="24rem"
    size={6}
    spacing={8}
    colors={["brand-solid-strong"]}
/>
```

## Direction

Control where the reveal animation starts from.

Direction:

```tsx
<MatrixFx
    height="24rem"
    revealFrom="top"
    colors={["brand-solid-strong"]}
/>
```

## Content

Place content inside the reveal effect.

Content:

```tsx
<MatrixFx
    height="24rem"
    colors={["neutral-solid-medium"]}
>
    <Column gap="16" fill center>
      <Heading textVariant="display-strong-xl">
        Canvas Reveal
      </Heading>
      <Text textVariant="body-default-l">
        Animated dot matrix effect
      </Text>
    </Column>
</MatrixFx>
```

## Flicker

Add a subtle animated flicker to create a dynamic, alive feeling.

Flicker:

```tsx
<MatrixFx
    height="24rem"
    colors={["danger-solid-strong"]}
    flicker
/>
```

## Bulge

Add dynamic wave effects to create fluid, organic motion. Choose between `ripple` (circular waves from center) or `wave` (S-curve flowing diagonally). Tiles are displaced, scale up at the wave front, and fade at the edges.

Ripple:

```tsx
<MatrixFx
    height="24rem"
    colors={["accent-solid-strong"]}
    bulge={{
      type: "ripple",   // Circular wave from center
      duration: 4000,      // Wave duration in milliseconds
      intensity: 15,    // Displacement strength
      repeat: true      // Continuous cycles
    }}
/>
```

The `wave` type creates an organic, flowing S-curve that travels diagonally from bottom-left to top-right. The curve rotates and morphs as it moves, straightening at the edges for a natural liquid motion.

Wave:

```tsx
<MatrixFx
    height="24rem"
    colors={["success-solid-strong"]}
    bulge={{
      type: "wave",     // S-curve diagonal flow
      duration: 3000,
      intensity: 20,
      repeat: true
    }}
/>
```

Use `repeat: false` for a single wave that plays once. Add `delay` for a pause before starting or between cycles (useful for sequencing multiple effects).

Single Wave:

```tsx
<MatrixFx
    height="24rem"
    colors={["danger-solid-strong"]}
    bulge={{
      duration: 3000,
      intensity: 12,
      repeat: false   // Single wave only
    }}
/>
```

## Trigger

Use `trigger="hover"` for native hover support. Dots progressively appear on hover and smoothly reverse when you move away.

Hover:

```tsx

<Row
    fill
    center
    padding="24"
    border
    radius="l"
    overflow="hidden"
>
    <MatrixFx
      position="absolute"
      top="0"
      left="0"
      trigger="hover"
      size={2}
      spacing={2}
      flicker
      bulge={{
        duration: 3000,
        intensity: 12,
        repeat: false
      }}
    />
    <Background
      fill
      position="absolute"
      left="0"
      top="0"
      gradient={{
        display: true,
        colorStart: "neutral-background-weak",
      }}
      pointerEvents="none"/>
    <Column align="center" horizontal="center" pointerEvents="none">
      <Logo showIn="dark" icon="/trademarks/icon-dark.svg" />
      <Logo showIn="light" icon="/trademarks/icon-light.svg" />
    </Column>
</Row>
<Row
    fill
    center
    padding="24"
    border
    radius="l"
    overflow="hidden"
>
    <MatrixFx
      position="absolute"
      top="0"
      left="0"
      trigger="hover"
      size={2}
      spacing={2}
      flicker
      revealFrom="bottom"
    />
    <Background
      fill
      position="absolute"
      left="0"
      top="0"
      gradient={{
        display: true,
        colorStart: "neutral-background-weak",
      }}
      pointerEvents="none"/>
    <Column align="center" horizontal="center" pointerEvents="none">
      <Logo showIn="dark" icon="/trademarks/icon-dark.svg" />
      <Logo showIn="light" icon="/trademarks/icon-light.svg" />
    </Column>
</Row>
```

Use `trigger="click"` to toggle the effect on click.

Click Trigger:

```tsx
<MatrixFx
    height="16rem"
    trigger="click"
    colors={["brand-solid-medium"]}
/>
```

Use `trigger="manual"` with the `active` prop to control the effect from parent state.

Manual Trigger:

```tsx
"use client";

import React from "react";
import { Row, ToggleButton } from "@once-ui-system/core";
import { MatrixFx } from "@once-ui-system/fx";

export function Demo() {
    const [on, setOn] = React.useState(false);
    return (
      <Row gap="8" fillWidth>
        <ToggleButton onClick={() => setOn((v) => !v)}>
          {on ? "Stop" : "Start"}
        </ToggleButton>
        <MatrixFx height="16rem" trigger="manual" active={on} colors={["brand-solid-medium"]} />
      </Row>
    );
}
```

## Performance

MatrixFx automatically detects low-end devices and the `prefers-reduced-motion` system setting. When either is detected, the animation renders a single static frame (no flicker, no bulge animation). You can override this with the `reducedMotion` prop.

See [useReducedMotion](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useReducedMotion) for details.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `speed` | `Speed` |  | Animation multiplier: 1 is the default. "slow", "medium" and "fast" are 0.5, 1 and 2. |
| `colors` | `string[]` | `["brand-solid-medium"]` | Palette for the dots. |
| `size` | `number` | `3` | Dot size, in pixels. |
| `spacing` | `number` | `3` | Gap between dots, in pixels. |
| `revealFrom` | `"center" \| "top" \| "bottom" \| "left" \| "right"` | `center` | Where the reveal starts before spreading out. |
| `trigger` | `"hover" \| "instant" \| "mount" \| "click" \| "manual"` | `instant` | What starts it. "manual" hands control to active. |
| `active` | `boolean` | `false` | Run it, when trigger is "manual". |
| `flicker` | `boolean` | `false` | Randomise dot brightness, for a noisier look. |
| `bulge` | `BulgeConfig` |  | A ripple or wave distortion: its type, duration, intensity, delay and whether it repeats. |
| `fps` | `number` | `60` | Frame cap. Lower it on a large surface. |
| `reducedMotion` | `boolean \| "auto"` | `auto` | "auto" follows the reader's system setting, which is the right default for anything ambient. |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` |  | Content drawn above the dots. |
| `children` |  |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

```tsx
    type="snow"
    data-solid="contrast"
    colors={["brand-solid-strong", "neutral-solid-weak"]}
    intensity={100}
    speed={0.8}
>
    <Column gap="16" fill center>
      <Heading textVariant="display-strong-l">
        Winter Wonderland
      </Heading>
      <Text textVariant="body-default-l">
        Snowflakes with depth and motion
      </Text>
    </Column>
</WeatherFx>
```

## Leaves Effect

Leaves feature gradient colors, rotation animation, and tumbling motion for an autumn feel.

Leaves Effect:

```tsx
<WeatherFx
    height="24rem"
    type="leaves"
    colors={["warning-solid-strong", "danger-solid-strong", "success-solid-medium"]}
    intensity={50}
    speed={0.6}
    angle={5}
>
    <Column gap="16" fill center>
      <Heading textVariant="display-strong-xl">
        Autumn Breeze
      </Heading>
      <Text textVariant="body-default-l">
        Rotating leaves with gradients
      </Text>
    </Column>
</WeatherFx>
```

## Lightning Effect

Lightning features highly realistic bolt generation with chaotic, organic branching at all angles. Each bolt creates dense networks of branches spreading in multiple directions with up to 4 levels of hierarchy. The effect uses small, erratic segments and high branching probability to create the natural, fractal-like appearance of real lightning. Bolts animate from top to bottom with progressively thinner branches. The `intensity` prop controls both the frequency and number of simultaneous strikes.

Lightning Effect:

```tsx
<WeatherFx
    height="24rem"
    type="lightning"
    data-solid="contrast"
    colors={["warning-solid-strong"]}
    intensity={15}
>
    <Column gap="16" fill center>
      <Heading textVariant="display-strong-l">
        Thunderstorm
      </Heading>
      <Text textVariant="body-default-l">
        Dynamic lightning with branching bolts
      </Text>
    </Column>
</WeatherFx>
```

## Lightning Intensity

For lightning, the `intensity` prop controls strike frequency and bolt patterns. The effect alternates between single and multi-bolt strikes for natural variation. Low intensity (1-15) creates single, rare strikes. Medium intensity (16-30) occasionally spawns double bolts. High intensity (31-60) alternates between single and 2-3 bolt strikes. Very high intensity (61+) creates dramatic storms alternating between single and 2-4 simultaneous bolts.

Lightning Intensity:

```tsx
<WeatherFx
    height="16rem"
    type="lightning"
    intensity={5}
    colors={["brand-solid-strong"]}
/>

<WeatherFx
    height="16rem"
    type="lightning"
    intensity={20}
    colors={["brand-solid-strong"]}
/>

<WeatherFx
    height="16rem"
    type="lightning"
    intensity={50}
    colors={["brand-solid-strong"]}
/>
```

## Duration

Control how long particles are emitted with the `duration` prop, in milliseconds. After the duration, `active` turns off (`onActiveChange(false)`): what is falling finishes and no new particles spawn.

Duration:

```tsx
<WeatherFx
    height="24rem"
    type="snow"
    colors={["brand-solid-medium"]}
    intensity={80}
    duration={3000}
>
    <Column gap="16" fill center>
      <Heading textVariant="display-strong-l">
        3 Second Burst
      </Heading>
    </Column>
</WeatherFx>
```

## Trigger

Use `trigger="hover"` to only emit particles when hovering over the element.

Hover Trigger:

```tsx
<WeatherFx
    height="16rem"
    type="leaves"
    trigger="hover"
    colors={["warning-solid-strong", "danger-solid-strong"]}
    intensity={40}
/>

<WeatherFx
    height="16rem"
    type="rain"
    trigger="hover"
    colors={["brand-solid-medium"]}
    intensity={60}
/>
```

Use `trigger="click"` to toggle emission on click.

Click Trigger:

```tsx
<WeatherFx
    height="16rem"
    type="rain"
    trigger="click"
    colors={["brand-solid-medium"]}
    intensity={60}
/>
```

Drive it from parent state with `active` and `onActiveChange`, whatever the trigger.

Manual Trigger:

```tsx
"use client";

import React from "react";
import { Row, ToggleButton } from "@once-ui-system/core";
import { WeatherFx } from "@once-ui-system/fx";

export function Demo() {
    const [on, setOn] = React.useState(false);

    return (
      <Row gap="8" fillWidth>
        <ToggleButton onClick={() => setOn((v) => !v)}>
          {on ? "Stop" : "Start"}
        </ToggleButton>
        <WeatherFx height="16rem" type="snow" active={on} onActiveChange={setOn} intensity={60} />
      </Row>
    );
}
```

## Performance

WeatherFx draws with time-based motion at your screen's pixel ratio (up to 2x), sleeps once the weather has stopped or is scrolled off screen, and picks its colours up again when the theme changes. Lightning never strikes more than twice a second, whatever the `intensity`, to stay clear of flashing that can trigger seizures.

Under the `prefers-reduced-motion` system setting, and on low-end devices, rain, snow and leaves show a still frame instead of animating; lightning shows nothing. Override this with the `reducedMotion` prop.

See [useReducedMotion](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useReducedMotion) for details.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | `WeatherType` | `rain` | Which weather to render. |
| `speed` | `Speed` |  | Fall multiplier: 1 is the default, 2 twice as fast. "slow", "medium" and "fast" are 0.5, 1 and 2. |
| `colors` | `string[]` |  | Palette for the drops or flakes. |
| `intensity` | `number` | `50` | How much of it there is. |
| `angle` | `number` | `0` | Fall angle, in degrees. |
| `duration` | `number` |  | Stop after this long, in milliseconds. Runs indefinitely if unset. |
| `trigger` | `"mount" \| "hover" \| "click"` | `mount` | What starts it by itself: mount, hover (a tap on touch screens) or click (toggles). |
| `active` | `boolean` |  | Whether the weather runs. Controlled; pair with onActiveChange. |
| `defaultActive` | `boolean` |  | The first value of active when uncontrolled. Defaults to trigger === "mount". |
| `onActiveChange` | `(active: boolean) => void` |  | Called when it starts or stops by hover, click or duration. |
| `reducedMotion` | `boolean \| "auto"` | `auto` | "auto" follows the reader's system setting, which is the right default for anything ambient. |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` |  | Content drawn above the weather. |
| `children` |  |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# CountdownFx

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/countdownFx

> The CountdownFx component creates animated countdown timers with wheel effects, counting down to a target date.

The `CountdownFx` component wraps `CountFx` to create beautiful countdown timers. It automatically calculates and displays the time remaining until a target date with smooth wheel animations and colon separators.

CountdownFx:

```tsx
<CountdownFx
    targetDate={new Date(Date.now() + 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)}
    textVariant="display-strong-l"
    format="HH:MM:SS"
/>
```

## Format Options

Choose between different time formats based on your needs.

Formats:

```tsx
<CountdownFx
    targetDate={new Date(Date.now() + 5 * 60 * 60 * 1000)}
    format="HH:MM:SS"
/>

<CountdownFx
    targetDate={new Date(Date.now() + 10 * 60 * 1000)}
    format="MM:SS"
/>

<CountdownFx
    targetDate={new Date(Date.now() + 3 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)}
    format="DD:HH:MM:SS"
/>
```

## Effects

Use different animation effects from CountFx.

Effects:

```tsx
<CountdownFx
    targetDate={targetDate}
    effect="wheel"
/>

<CountdownFx
    targetDate={targetDate}
    effect="smooth"
/>

<CountdownFx
    targetDate={targetDate}
    effect="simple"
/>
```

## Launch Countdown

Create compelling launch countdowns for product releases, events, or promotions.

Launch Countdown:

```tsx
<Column gap="16" fill center padding="32" data-solid="contrast" radius="l">

      Launching Soon
    </Heading>
```

## On Complete Callback

Execute a function when the countdown reaches zero.

```tsx
<CountdownFx

```

# ShineFx

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/shineFx

> Adds a smooth animated shine effect to text. Perfect for highlighting key features or creating eye-catching headings.

ShineFx creates a smooth, animated shine effect that sweeps across text. The effect uses a gradient that moves horizontally, creating a shimmering appearance ideal for drawing attention to important text.

Basic:

```tsx
<ShineFx textVariant="heading-default-xl">
    Shine bright like a diamond
</ShineFx>
```

## Speed

Set how long one pass takes with `duration`, in milliseconds. Higher values make a slower shine, lower values a faster one.

Speed:

```tsx
<ShineFx duration={1000}>
    Fast shine - default (1s)
</ShineFx>

<ShineFx duration={3000}>
    Medium shine (3s)
</ShineFx>

<ShineFx duration={5000}>
    Slow shine (5s)
</ShineFx>
```

## Inverse

Use the `inverse` prop to invert the shine effect.

Inverse:

```tsx
<ShineFx inverse>
    Inverse shine
</ShineFx>
```

## Base opacity

Control the base text visibility with the `baseOpacity` prop (0-1). Higher values improve readability and accessibility, while lower values create a more subtle effect.

Opacity:

```tsx
<ShineFx baseOpacity={0.1}>
    Subtle (0.1)
</ShineFx>

<ShineFx baseOpacity={0.3}>
    Default (0.3)
</ShineFx>

<ShineFx baseOpacity={0.6}>
    More visible (0.6)
</ShineFx>

<ShineFx baseOpacity={0.9}>
    High visibility (0.9)
</ShineFx>
```

## Disabled

Disable the animation with the `disabled` prop to show static text without the shine effect.

Disabled:

```tsx
<ShineFx>
    Animated
</ShineFx>

<ShineFx disabled>
    Disabled
</ShineFx>
```

## Variants

ShineFx works with all Text component variants and styling props.

Variants:

```tsx
<ShineFx textVariant="display-default-xs">
    Display variant
</ShineFx>

    Heading with color
</ShineFx>

<ShineFx textVariant="body-default-m" onBackground="danger-weak">
    Body with color
</ShineFx>
```

## Performance

ShineFx automatically detects low-end devices and the `prefers-reduced-motion` system setting. When either is detected, the shine animation is disabled (equivalent to `disabled={true}`). You can override this with the `reducedMotion` prop.

See [useReducedMotion](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useReducedMotion) for details.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |

| `disabled` | `boolean` | `false` | Stop the shine. |
| `inverse` | `boolean` | `false` | Run it the other way. |
| `baseOpacity` | `number` | `0.3` | Opacity of the content the shine passes over. |
| `reducedMotion` | `boolean \| "auto"` | `auto` | "auto" follows the reader's system setting, which is the right default for anything ambient. |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` |  | What shines. |

| `children` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...LeafProps, ...TextProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# TypeFx

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/typeFx

> Animates text with a typewriter effect, typing and deleting characters one by one. Perfect for hero sections and dynamic headings.

TypeFx creates a realistic typewriter animation that types out text character-by-character. When multiple words are provided, it automatically types, holds, deletes, and cycles through them. With `mode="fade"` it [fades the letters in](#fade-mode) instead.

TypeFx:

```tsx
<Row gap="8" vertical="center">
  <Text textVariant="heading-default-l">
    Build
  </Text>
  <TypeFx
    words={["amazing products", "stunning websites", "modern apps"]}
    charDuration={80}
    hold={2000}
    trigger="instant"
  />
</Row>
```

## Single word

TypeFx can also display a single word that types out once without looping.

Single word:

```tsx
<TypeFx
  words="Welcome to the future"
  charDuration={100}
  delay={500}
  trigger="instant"
/>
```

## Custom trigger

Use the `custom` trigger to programmatically control when the typing animation starts.

Custom trigger:

```tsx
function TypeFxCustomExample() {
  const triggerFnRef = useRef<(() => void) | null>(null);

  return (
    <>
      <TypeFx
        words={["Click the button", "to start typing", "this animation"]}
        charDuration={60}
        hold={1500}
        trigger="custom"
        onTrigger={(fn) => {
          triggerFnRef.current = fn;
        }}
      />
      <Button onClick={() => triggerFnRef.current?.()}>
        Start typing
      </Button>
    </>
  );
}
```

## Fade mode

With `mode="fade"`, TypeFx shows the whole text at once and fades it in letter by letter, from blur to focus, instead of typing it (2.x's `FadingLettersFx`). `state` plays a phase, `delay` offsets the start and `charDuration` sets the gap between letters; an array of `words` is joined with spaces.

Fade:

```tsx
<TypeFx mode="fade"
    align="center"
    words="Welcome to Once UI"
    state="entering"
    textVariant="display-strong-l" />
```

### States

`state` takes one of three phases, and the parent drives it: `entering` (the default), `visible` and `exiting`.

Animation States:

```tsx
<Column gap="16">
    <TypeFx mode="fade" words="Entering Animation" state="entering" textVariant="heading-strong-m" />
    <TypeFx mode="fade" words="Visible State" state="visible" textVariant="heading-strong-m" />
    <TypeFx mode="fade" words="Exiting Animation" state="exiting" textVariant="heading-strong-m" />
</Column>
```

#### Entering
Letters fade in sequentially with a blur-to-focus effect and scale transformation. Each letter has a calculated delay based on its position in the word and message.

#### Visible
Letters remain static without animation. Use this state when no animation is active.

#### Exiting
Letters fade out with blur and scale effects. Each letter has a random exit delay for an organic dissolution effect.

### Staggering

Stagger several messages with `delay`. 2.x's `messageIdx` added 2500ms per step, so `messageIdx={n}` is `delay={n * 2500}`.

Staggering:

```tsx
<Column gap="12">
    <TypeFx mode="fade" words="First message appears" state="entering" textVariant="body-default-l" />
    <TypeFx mode="fade" words="Second message appears" state="entering" textVariant="body-default-l" delay={2500} />
    <TypeFx mode="fade" words="Third message appears" state="entering" textVariant="body-default-l" delay={5000} />
</Column>
```

### Styling

Fade mode takes every Text prop, as typing does: variants, colors and custom styles.

Custom Styling:

```tsx
<TypeFx mode="fade"
    words="Custom styled text"
    state="entering"
    textVariant="display-strong-s"
    onBackground="brand-weak" />
```

### Timing

Each letter's entry delay adds up from:

- **Start**: `delay`
- **Word**: `wordIdx × 200ms`
- **Letter**: `letterIdx × charDuration` (default 40ms in fade mode)

Exiting, each letter waits a random 0 to 400ms.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `words (required)` | `string \| string[]` |  | One string to type, or several to cycle through. |
| `mode` | `"type" \| "fade"` |  | "fade" fades the whole text in letter by letter instead of typing it. |
| `state` | `FadeState` |  | Fade mode: entering, visible or exiting. The parent drives it. |
| `charDuration` | `number` |  | Milliseconds per character (higher is slower). Was speed until 3.0. In fade mode, the gap between letters. |
| `delay` | `number` |  | Milliseconds before typing starts, or before the first letter fades in. |
| `hold` | `number` |  | Milliseconds a finished word stays before the next one. |
| `trigger` | `"instant" \| "custom"` |  | "custom" waits for the function handed to onTrigger. |
| `onTrigger` | `(triggerFn: () => void) => void` |  | Receives a function that starts it, when trigger is "custom". |
| `loop` | `boolean` |  | Cycle back to the first word instead of stopping. |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` |  | Rendered after the typed text. |
| `opacity` | `Opacity` |  |  |
| `...text` |  |  | Also takes these props |
| `...CommonProps, ...LeafProps, ...TextProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# TiltFx

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/tiltFx

> Applies a subtle 3D tilt effect based on mouse movement. Ideal for interactive cards or media blocks.

TiltFx creates a depth-based tilt animation that follows the user's mouse cursor. The effect is driven by `rotateX`/`rotateY` transforms and resets on mouse leave. It's designed for hoverable visual elements like images or feature blocks.

Basic:

```tsx
<TiltFx aspectRatio={3 / 4} radius="l">

</TiltFx>
```

## Intensity

Control the strength of the tilt effect with the `intensity` prop. Lower values create a subtle effect, while higher values make it more dramatic.

Intensity:

```tsx
<TiltFx intensity={1}>
    <Media src="/images/docs/once-ui/purple-worm.jpg" />
    <Text>Default (1)</Text>
</TiltFx>

<TiltFx intensity={4}>
    <Media src="/images/docs/once-ui/purple-worm.jpg" />
    <Text>Strong (4)</Text>
</TiltFx>
```

## Performance

TiltFx automatically detects low-end devices and the `prefers-reduced-motion` system setting. When either is detected, the tilt effect is disabled. You can override this behavior with the `reducedMotion` prop.

See [useReducedMotion](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useReducedMotion) for details.

## API reference

| `intensity` | `number` | `1` | How far it tilts. |
| `reducedMotion` | `boolean \| "auto"` | `auto` | "auto" follows the reader's system setting, which is the right default for anything ambient. |
| `children` |  |  |  |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# FadingLettersFx

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/fadingLettersFx

> Merged into TypeFx in 3.0.

`FadingLettersFx` folded into [`TypeFx`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/typeFx#fade-mode) in 3.0: use `<TypeFx mode="fade" words="…" state="entering">`. The 3.0 codemod rewrites it (see the migration guide, "Components that merged"): `text` became `words`, `animationState` became `state`, and `messageIdx={n}` became `delay={n * 2500}`.

# BlobFx

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/blobFx

> An animated blob gradient effect with pseudo-random variations for dynamic backgrounds.

The `BlobFx` component creates animated blob gradients with smooth horizontal movement. It uses a seed-based pseudo-random system to generate consistent variations, making it perfect for hero sections, backgrounds, or decorative elements.

BlobFx:

```tsx
<BlobFx height="24rem" />
```

## Seed Variation

Use the `seed` prop to generate different pseudo-random variations. Each seed produces a unique combination of animation durations and movement patterns.

Seed Variation:

```tsx
<BlobFx height="16rem" seed={0} />
<BlobFx height="16rem" seed={42} />
<BlobFx height="16rem" seed={123} />
```

## Usage

Combine with other components to create layered backgrounds. The effect uses `pointerEvents="none"` so it won't interfere with interactive elements.

Background Layer:

```tsx
<Row fillWidth height="24rem" overflow="hidden">
    <BlobFx position="absolute" fill seed={7} translateY="50%" />
    <Column fillWidth center gap="8">
      <Heading textVariant="display-strong-xl">
        Layered Content
      </Heading>
      <Text textVariant="body-default-m">
        Interactive elements work normally
      </Text>
    </Column>
</Row>
```

## How It Works

The component uses three animated gradient blobs with:
- **Pseudo-random durations**: Each seed generates animation durations ranging from 6.4s to 14.4s
- **Varied movement**: Horizontal translation offsets are randomized by ±30%
- **Blend modes**: Uses `screen` and `plus-lighter` for smooth color mixing
- **Blur filter**: 2rem blur creates the soft blob effect

The seed-based randomization ensures consistent results across renders while providing variety between different instances.

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `seed` | `number` | `0` | Changes the shape. Same seed, same blob. |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# CountFx

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/countFx

> CountFx is a wrapper for numbers with different animation effects.

CountFx is a wrapper for numbers with different animation effects.

CountFx:

```tsx
const [value, setValue] = useState<number>(0);

useEffect(() => {
    const targetValue = Math.floor(Math.random() * 9000) + 1000;
    setValue(targetValue);
}, []);

<CountFx
    textVariant="display-strong-m"
    value={value}
    duration={5000}
    effect="wheel"
    easing="ease-out"
/>

<CountFx
    textVariant="display-strong-m"
    value={value}
    duration={5000}
    effect="smooth"
    easing="ease-out"
/>

<CountFx
    textVariant="display-strong-m"
    value={value}
    duration={5000}
    separator=","
    effect="simple"
    easing="ease-out"
/>
```

## Decimals

CountFx supports decimal values with the `decimals` prop.

Decimals:

```tsx
const [value1, setValue1] = useState<number>(0);
const [value2, setValue2] = useState<number>(0);

useEffect(() => {
    const targetValue1 = parseFloat((Math.random() * 200 + 50).toFixed(2));
    const targetValue2 = parseFloat((Math.random() * 150 + 25).toFixed(2));

    setValue1(targetValue1);
    setValue2(targetValue2);
}, []);

<CountFx
    textVariant="display-strong-m"
    value={value1}
    decimals={2}
    duration={2000}
    effect="simple"
    easing="ease-out"
/>

<CountFx
    textVariant="display-strong-m"
    value={value2}
    decimals={2}
    duration={2000}
    separator=","
    effect="simple"
    easing="ease-out"
    children=" USD"
/>
```

## Trigger on scroll

Use the [useInViewport](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useInViewport) hook to trigger the count animation when the element enters the viewport. This example starts counting when the element reaches the center of the screen.

Scroll trigger:

```tsx
import { useRef, useState, useEffect } from "react";
import { useInViewport } from "@once-ui-system/core";
import { CountFx } from "@once-ui-system/fx";

function ScrollCountExample() {
    const ref = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
    const [value, setValue] = useState<number>(0);
    
    // Trigger when element reaches center of viewport
    // rootMargin: "-50% 0px" creates a line at the vertical center
    const isInViewport = useInViewport(ref, { 
        rootMargin: "-50% 0px" 
    });
    
    useEffect(() => {
        if (isInViewport) {
            setValue(9876);
        }
    }, [isInViewport]);
    
    return (
      <CountFx
        textVariant="display-strong-l"
        value={value}
        duration={2000}
        effect="wheel"
        easing="ease-out"
      />
    );
}
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value (required)` | `number` |  | The number to count to. Change it and the count runs again — there is no trigger prop. |
| `duration` | `number` | `1000` | How long the count takes, in milliseconds. Was speed until 3.0. |
| `easing` | `"linear" \| "ease-out" \| "ease-in-out"` | `ease-out` | How the count accelerates and settles. |
| `format` | `(value: number) => string` |  | Turn the number into the string shown, for a currency or a unit. |
| `separator` | `string` |  | Thousands separator. |
| `decimals` | `number` |  | Decimal places to hold. |
| `effect` | `"simple" \| "wheel" \| "smooth"` | `simple` | How the digits change: a plain count, a wheel, or a smooth blur. |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` |  | Rendered after the number. |
| `opacity` | `Opacity` |  |  |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...LeafProps, ...TextProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# Effect

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/effect

> One slot for the interchangeable ambient effects, so a template's aesthetic is a single setting.

`BlobFx`, `MatrixFx`, `WeatherFx`, `ParticleFx` and `CelebrationFx` all do the same
structural job: paint a full-bleed decorative layer behind their content. In
practice they are alternatives to each other, but swapping one for another meant
changing an import and rewriting the positioning at every call site.

`Effect` picks between them **by value**. A template can expose its aesthetic as
one setting, and `type="none"` renders the content with no layer at all.

For heavier, cinematic WebGL scenes (a black hole, aurora, liquid glass), see the
[effects gallery on once-ui.com](https://once-ui.com/effects).

Effect:

```tsx
<Effect type={theme.effect} height="12rem" radius="l" />
```

## Content sits above the layer

Children render on top of the effect, and the wrapper is identical for every
`type` — including `"none"`. That is what makes the swap safe: changing the
effect changes the look and nothing else about the layout.

Layered content:

```tsx
<Effect type="matrix" height="20rem" radius="l" colors={["brand-solid-medium"]}>
    <Column fillWidth center gap="8">
      <Heading textVariant="display-strong-l">One setting</Heading>
      <Text textVariant="body-default-m">
        Swap the aesthetic without touching the page
      </Text>
    </Column>
</Effect>
```

## Shared and per-effect settings

`colors` and `speed` apply across the set: `ParticleFx` takes a single colour, so
it uses the first entry, and `blob` is seeded rather than timed and ignores both.
Anything an individual effect needs goes in its own block, which is only read
when that effect is the one showing — so all of them can be configured up front
and still switched with one prop.

Per-effect settings:

```tsx
<Effect
  type="weather"
  colors={["accent-solid-medium"]}
  weather={{ type: "snow", intensity: 0.6 }}
  matrix={{ flicker: true }}
/>
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | `EffectType` | `none` | Which ambient layer to render. "none" renders the children alone. |
| `colors` | `string[]` |  | Palette for the layer, when it takes one. |
| `speed` | `Speed` |  | Multiplier on the layer's own motion: 1 is each effect's default. "slow", "medium" and "fast" are 0.5, 1 and 2. |
| `reducedMotion` | `boolean \| "auto"` |  | "auto" follows the reader's system setting, which is the right default for anything ambient. |
| `blob` | `Omit<React.ComponentProps<typeof BlobFx>, "children">` |  | Props passed through when type is "blob". |
| `matrix` | `Omit<React.ComponentProps<typeof MatrixFx>, "children">` |  | Props passed through when type is "matrix". |
| `weather` | `Omit<React.ComponentProps<typeof WeatherFx>, "children">` |  | Props passed through when type is "weather". |
| `particle` | `Omit<React.ComponentProps<typeof ParticleFx>, "children">` |  | Props passed through when type is "particle". |
| `celebration` | `Omit<React.ComponentProps<typeof CelebrationFx>, "children">` |  | Props passed through when type is "celebration". |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` |  | Content drawn above the layer. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` |  |  |
| `...CommonProps, ...DisplayProps, ...FlexProps, ...SizeProps, ...SpacingProps, ...StyleProps` |  |  | Also takes these props |

# HoloFx

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/holoFx

> A lighting and texture effect that simulates a holographic sheen. Ideal for decorative images, product cards, or hero visuals.

HoloFx simulates a holographic light sheen by layering interactive visual effects like shine, burn, and texture over any content block. It uses radial masks and mouse tracking to shift light and create movement. Not supported on touch-screens.

HoloFx:

```tsx
<HoloFx
    border="brand-alpha-weak"
    maxWidth="24rem"
    aspectRatio={3 / 4}
    radius="l"
    shine={{
      opacity: 30,
      blending: "color-dodge",
    }}
    burn={{
      opacity: 30,
      blending: "color-dodge",
    }}
    texture={{
      opacity: 10,
      image: "/images/textures/foil.jpg",
      blending: "color-dodge",
    }}
  >
    <Media src="/images/docs/once-ui/proxima-b.jpg" />
    <Fade>
      Proxima B
    </Fade>
</HoloFx>
```

## Performance

HoloFx automatically detects low-end devices and the `prefers-reduced-motion` system setting. When either is detected, the mouse-tracking effect is paused. The effect also pauses when the element is outside the viewport. You can override this with the `reducedMotion` prop.

See [useReducedMotion](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useReducedMotion) for details.

# ParticleFx

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/particleFx

> The ParticleFx component fills its area with drifting particles that can react to the pointer.

The `ParticleFx` component fills its area with drifting particles that can push away from or pull toward the pointer. It was called `Particle` before 2.0; that name still works as a deprecated alias until 3.0.

ParticleFx:

```tsx
<ParticleFx
    fill
    interactive
    speed={10}
    intensity={100}
    height="24rem"
/>
```

## Density

The `density` prop controls the number of particles to display.

Density:

```tsx
<ParticleFx
    fill
    height="24rem"
    density={250}
/>
```

## Color

The `color` prop controls the color of the particles.

Color:

```tsx
<ParticleFx
    fill
    height="24rem"
    color="brand-background-strong"
/>
```

## Size

The `size` prop controls the size of the particles.

Size:

```tsx
<ParticleFx
    fill
    height="24rem"
    size="8"
/>
```

## Speed

The `speed` prop controls the speed of the particles.

Speed:

```tsx
<ParticleFx
    fill
    height="24rem"
    speed={16.67}
/>
```

## Interactive

The `interactive` prop controls whether the particles are interactive. Use the `intensity` prop to control the radius of the interaction area.

Interactive:

```tsx
<ParticleFx
    fill
    height="24rem"
    interactive
/>
```

## Mode

The `mode` prop controls how particles interact with the cursor. Use `repel` to push particles away or `attract` to pull them towards the cursor.

Mode:

```tsx
<ParticleFx
    fill
    interactive
    mode="attract"
    height="24rem"
    intensity={30}
/>
```

## Opacity

The `opacity` prop controls the opacity of the particles.

Opacity:

```tsx
<ParticleFx
    fill
    height="24rem"
    opacity={50}
/>
```

## Performance

ParticleFx automatically detects low-end devices and the `prefers-reduced-motion` system setting. When either is detected, particles are placed statically without animation. The animation also pauses when the element is outside the viewport. You can override this with the `reducedMotion` prop.

See [useReducedMotion](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useReducedMotion) for details.

| `interactive` | `boolean` | `false` | React to the pointer. |
| `mode` | `"repel" \| "attract"` | `repel` | Whether the pointer pushes particles away or pulls them in. |
| `intensity` | `number` | `20` | How strongly the pointer acts, when interactive. |
| `opacity` | `DisplayProps["opacity"]` | `100` | Layer opacity, in steps of 10. |
| `reducedMotion` | `boolean \| "auto"` | `auto` | "auto" follows the reader's system setting, which is the right default for anything ambient. |
| `className` | `string` |  |  |
| `style` | `React.CSSProperties` |  |  |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` |  | Content drawn above the particles. |
| `className` |  |  |  |
| `style` |  |  |  |

# OG route handlers

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/utils/ogRoutes

> Ready-made Next.js routes for OgCard and useOgData: Open Graph fetching and an image proxy, with SSRF protection built in.

`OgCard` and `useOgData` read link previews through two routes in your app: one that fetches a page's Open Graph data, and one that serves its image from your origin. `@once-ui-system/core/next` ships both, ready-made. Each factory returns `{ GET }`, so a route file is two lines.

Both routes fetch URLs that your visitors choose, from your server. That makes them a server-side request forgery target, so the handlers only ever request public addresses: every URL and every redirect is checked, and the connection goes to the exact address that was checked.

## Route files

app/api/og/fetch/route.ts:

```tsx
import { createOgFetchRoute } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";

export const { GET } = createOgFetchRoute();
```

app/api/og/proxy/route.ts:

```tsx
import { createOgProxyRoute } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";

export const { GET } = createOgProxyRoute();
```

These are the paths `OgCard` and `useOgData` call by default, so nothing else changes. To serve them somewhere else, see Custom paths below.

The handlers need the **Node.js runtime**, which is the default for route handlers. If a route file you are replacing sets `export const runtime = "edge"`, remove that line.

## Responses

The fetch route answers `GET /api/og/fetch?url=…` with the page's metadata as JSON. `image` and `faviconUrl` are absolute URLs, resolved against the page.

GET /api/og/fetch?url=https://example.com/post:

```json
{
  "url": "https://example.com/post",
  "title": "Post title",
  "description": "What the post is about",
  "image": "https://example.com/images/og.png",
  "faviconUrl": "https://example.com/favicon.ico"
}
```

The proxy route answers `GET /api/og/proxy?url=…` with the image itself, sent with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and a sandboxing `Content-Security-Policy`.

Failures are JSON, `{ "error": "…" }`, and never cached:

- **400**: missing or malformed `url`, or a URL that is not allowed (a private address, a blocked domain, not HTTPS)
- **403**: a cross-origin caller, when `sameOrigin` is on
- **413**: the image is larger than `maxBytes` (proxy)
- **415**: not an HTML page (fetch), or not an allowed image type (proxy)
- **502**: the upstream failed (an error status, too many redirects, a dropped connection); the proxy forwards an upstream 4xx or 5xx as is
- **504**: the upstream did not finish within `timeout`
- **500**: not running on the Node.js runtime

## Options

Both factories take the same options as [`handleOGFetch`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/utils/handleOGFetch) and [`handleOGProxy`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/utils/handleOGProxy), which they wrap. Options are read once, when the route is created.

app/api/og/fetch/route.ts:

```tsx
import { createOgFetchRoute } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";

export const { GET } = createOgFetchRoute({
  userAgent: "bot",
  timeout: 8000,
  blockedDomains: ["tracker.example"],
});
```

app/api/og/proxy/route.ts:

```tsx
import { createOgProxyRoute, DEFAULT_OG_IMAGE_TYPES } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";

export const { GET } = createOgProxyRoute({
  cacheMaxAge: 86400,
  maxBytes: 8 * 1024 * 1024,
  allowedContentTypes: [...DEFAULT_OG_IMAGE_TYPES, "image/tiff"],
});
```

### Both routes

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `allowedDomains` |  |  |  |
| `blockedDomains` |  |  |  |
| `isAllowed` | `(url: URL) => boolean \| Promise<boolean>` | `-` | Your own check, called for the first URL and every redirect target after the built-in checks pass. Return false to refuse. |
| `allowHttp` | `boolean` | `false` | Also fetch plain http: URLs. HTTPS only by default. |
| `maxRedirects` | `number` | `3` | Redirects followed, each checked like the first URL. |
| `userAgent` | `string` | `OG-Fetcher/1.0, OG-Proxy/1.0` | User-Agent sent upstream. |
| `cacheControl` | `string` | `public, max-age=3600` | Cache-Control on successful responses. |
| `sameOrigin` | `boolean` | `false` | Refuse requests whose Origin, or else Referer, names another host. Requests with neither are allowed. |

### Fetch route

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `timeout` | `number` | `5000` | Milliseconds for the whole exchange: DNS, connection, redirects and body. |
| `maxBytes` | `number` | `1 MiB` | HTML read, after decompression. Open Graph tags live in the head, so a longer page is parsed from what was read. |
| `decodeEntities` | `boolean` | `true` | Decode HTML entities in the title and description. |
| `favicon` | `boolean` | `true` | Include faviconUrl. OgCard renders it as given, so with next/image its host must be in images.remotePatterns; false leaves it out and OgCard uses its own favicon source. |

### Proxy route

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `timeout` | `number` | `10000` | Milliseconds for the whole exchange. |
| `maxBytes` | `number` | `5 MiB` | Largest image, after decompression. A larger one is refused, not truncated. |
| `allowedContentTypes` |  |  |  |
| `cacheMaxAge` | `number` | `3600` | max-age in seconds, when cacheControl is not set. |

`DEFAULT_OG_IMAGE_TYPES` is the raster formats: AVIF, WebP, PNG, APNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP and ICO. SVG is left out because it can carry script; add `"image/svg+xml"` only if you need it.

## Custom paths

Mount the routes anywhere, then tell the client where they are. `OgRoutesProvider` sets the paths for every `OgCard` and `useOgData` below it, and `Meta.generate` takes the same object for its default social image.

resources/og.ts:

```tsx
export const ogRoutes = {
  fetch: "/og/fetch",
  proxy: "/og/proxy",
  generate: "/og/image",
};
```

components/Providers.tsx:

```tsx
"use client";

import { OgRoutesProvider } from "@once-ui-system/core";
import { LayoutProvider } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";
import { ogRoutes } from "@/resources/og";

export function Providers({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <LayoutProvider>
      <OgRoutesProvider routes={ogRoutes}>{children}</OgRoutesProvider>
    </LayoutProvider>
  );
}
```

app/about/page.tsx:

```tsx
import { Meta } from "@once-ui-system/core";
import { ogRoutes } from "@/resources/og";

export async function generateMetadata() {
  return Meta.generate({
    title: "About",
    description: "Who we are",
    baseURL: "https://example.com",
    path: "/about",
    ogRoutes,
  });
}
```

Without a provider, the paths are `/api/og/fetch`, `/api/og/proxy` and `/api/og/generate`. `OgCard`'s `serviceConfig` and `useOgData`'s explicit arguments still take precedence.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `routes (required)` | `Partial<OgRoutes>` |  | Any of fetch, proxy and generate. A path left out keeps its default. |
| `children (required)` | `ReactNode` |  |  |

## What is refused

Before anything is requested, and again for every redirect:

- Schemes other than `https:` (and `http:` with `allowHttp`), and URLs with credentials.
- Internal hostnames: `localhost`, `*.local`, `*.internal`, `*.home.arpa` and single-label names such as `http://intranet/`.
- IP addresses that are not public, written any way the URL parser accepts (`127.0.0.1`, `2130706433`, `0x7f.1`, `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]`): private, loopback, link-local, unique-local, carrier-grade NAT, multicast, unspecified, reserved and documentation ranges, and the cloud metadata endpoints (`169.254.169.254`, `fd00:ec2::254`).
- Hostnames that resolve to any such address. Every record is checked, not only the first.

The hostname is resolved and checked inside the connection itself, and the socket connects to the address that was checked. A DNS answer that changes between a check and the request (DNS rebinding) has nothing to slip through.

## Adding your own checks

Rate limiting, authentication or logging wrap the handler:

app/api/og/fetch/route.ts:

```tsx
import { createOgFetchRoute } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";
import { rateLimit } from "@/lib/rate-limit";

const og = createOgFetchRoute({ sameOrigin: true });

export async function GET(request: Request) {
  if (!(await rateLimit(request))) {
    return Response.json({ error: "Too many requests" }, { status: 429 });
  }
  return og.GET(request);
}
```

## Images in OgCard

`useOgData` rewrites a cross-origin `image` to your proxy route, so `OgCard` renders `/api/og/proxy?url=…` through `next/image`. Since Next.js 16, a local image `src` with a query string is only optimized when `images.localPatterns` allows it:

next.config.mjs:

```js
const nextConfig = {
  images: {
    localPatterns: [
      { pathname: "/api/og/proxy" },
      { pathname: "/**", search: "" },
    ],
  },
};
```

## Notes

- The handlers connect directly; they do not read `HTTP_PROXY` or `HTTPS_PROXY`.
- Outside Next.js, use [`handleOGFetch`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/utils/handleOGFetch) and [`handleOGProxy`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/utils/handleOGProxy) from `@once-ui-system/core/server`: they take a standard `Request` and return a `Response`. Import them through a bundler (Vite, webpack, esbuild or a framework's server build); the package is published for bundlers, and plain Node cannot load it on its own.
- The social image route that `Meta.generate` points at (`/api/og/generate`) is yours to design with `next/og`; it renders text you pass it and fetches no URLs from the request.

# OG images

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/utils/ogImages

> One route draws a link preview for every page in your product's skin: the page's title, set large, and your mascot looking at it.

When someone shares a link, the network shows the page's Open Graph image. `createOgImageRoute` draws that image for every page: 1200 × 630, dark, with the page's title in your heading font, an eyebrow above it, your domain below, and your mascot beside it, looking at the title. You describe your product once, in a skin, and every page gets its own card.

![A card for a journal post on Fjell, a made-up outdoor brand: the eyebrow "Journal", the title "Packing for a winter trail" with "winter" in an italic serif, and a blue mascot in a hard hat.](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/images/docs/og-images/page.jpg)

## Route file

app/api/og/generate/route.tsx:

```tsx
import { createOgImageRoute } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";
import { ogSkin } from "@/resources/og";

export const { GET } = createOgImageRoute({ skin: ogSkin });
```

resources/og.ts:

```tsx
import { defineOgSkin } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";

export const ogSkin = defineOgSkin({
  name: "Fjell",
  domain: "fjell.example",
  brand: "blue",
  accent: "orange",
  mascot: { color: "brand", eyes: "round", mouth: "smile", cheeks: true, surface: "glossy" },
  fonts: [
    { name: "Geist", weight: 700, path: "public/fonts/og/Geist-Bold.ttf" },
    { name: "Geist Mono", weight: 500, path: "public/fonts/og/GeistMono-Medium.ttf" },
    { name: "Instrument Serif", weight: 400, style: "italic", google: "Instrument Serif" },
  ],
  headingFont: "Geist",
  monoFont: "Geist Mono",
  emphasisFont: "Instrument Serif",
});
```

`Meta.generate` already points a page without its own image at `/api/og/generate?title=…`, so once the route exists, every page has a card. The route needs the **Node.js runtime** (the default) when the skin reads fonts from disk.

## What a card says

The route reads the query string:

| Parameter | What it does |
|---|---|
| `title` | The headline. Words in `*asterisks*` are drawn in the brand color, in `emphasisFont` when the skin has one. |
| `eyebrow` | A short label above the title: the section, a date, a place. `section` works too. |
| `description` | One line under the title. |
| `mood` | The mascot's expression: `happy`, `surprised`, `wink` and the other `Mascot` moods. |
| `layout` | `page` (the default), `hero` for a launch or a home page, or `photo`. |
| `image` | A photo for the card, from your own origin or a host in `imageHosts`. A card with an image uses the `photo` layout. |
| `v` | Ignored by the route. Change it to give a card a new URL, since networks cache images by URL. |

Build the URL with `ogImageUrl`:

app/journal/winter-trail/page.tsx:

```tsx
import { ogImageUrl } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";

export async function generateMetadata() {
  return Meta.generate({
    title: "Packing for a winter trail",
    description: "What goes in a 30-litre bag",
    baseURL,
    path: "/journal/winter-trail",
    image: ogImageUrl("/api/og/generate", {
      title: "Packing for a *winter* trail",
      eyebrow: "Journal",
      description: "What goes in a 30-litre bag",
    }),
  });
}
```

![The hero layout: the mascot above a centered title, "Once UI 3.0", for a release.](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/images/docs/og-images/hero.jpg)

![The photo layout: a tilted photo on the right, the mascot peeking from its corner, and the title "Three nights at Gjendebu".](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/images/docs/og-images/photo.jpg)

## Skin

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `name` | The product's name, drawn as the wordmark and, faintly, behind the mascot. |
| `domain` | Shown at the bottom of every card. |
| `brand`, `accent` | A scheme name (`emerald`, `violet`, …) or a CSS color. The brand lights the mascot and colors the eyebrow and emphasis; the accent adds a smaller glow. |
| `background` | The ground. Near-black by default. |
| `mark` | A small symbol before the name: SVG markup, or an image path or URL. |
| `logo` | A full logo in place of the wordmark. |
| `mascot` | A look, with the same options as `Mascot` and an `accessory` as SVG markup or JSX, or `{ svg }` for your own drawing in a 200 × 200 box. `false` leaves it out. |
| `fonts` | TTF, OTF or WOFF files (not WOFF2), each from `data`, a `path` read from disk, or a `google` family fetched once per server. If a font can't be loaded, the card still draws in the fallback face. |
| `headingFont`, `bodyFont`, `monoFont`, `emphasisFont` | Which family from `fonts` each role uses. |
| `mood` | The mascot's expression when a card doesn't ask for one. |
| `imageHosts` | Hosts `image=` may load from, besides your own origin. |

Fonts from disk are the safest choice: a card renders on the first crawl of a page, and a Google Fonts outage would otherwise draw it in the fallback face.

## Caching

Cards are served with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, so a CDN draws each one once. When you change the skin, change `v` in your URLs.

## mascotSvg

The card draws your mascot with `mascotSvg`, which returns the mascot as a standalone SVG string: the same look options as `Mascot`, one still expression, every color written out. Use it anywhere React can't animate, such as emails and favicons.

Example:

```tsx
import { mascotSvg } from "@once-ui-system/core";

const svg = mascotSvg({ color: "#10b981", eyes: "round", mouth: "smile", mood: "happy" });
```

Scheme names such as `brand` need a color through `schemes`, since there is no CSS to read them from. Kawaii moods draw their base mood, with blush where they have it.

# handleOGFetch

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/utils/handleOGFetch

> Server-side utility for fetching and parsing Open Graph metadata from URLs.

The `handleOGFetch` function is a server-side utility that fetches and parses Open Graph metadata from any URL. It takes a standard `Request` and returns a `Response`, so it works in any server that speaks the Fetch API, and extracts title, description, image, and favicon information from web pages.

> In a Next.js app, use createOgFetchRoute from @once-ui-system/core/next: a two-line route file built on this function. See OG route handlers.

## Features

- Fetches HTML pages only, up to a byte limit, within a timeout
- Extracts Open Graph metadata (title, description, image, favicon)
- Falls back to standard HTML meta tags if OG tags aren't available
- Returns `image` and `faviconUrl` as absolute URLs, resolved against the page
- Decodes HTML entities in text content
- Supports custom user agents
- Only requests public addresses: private, loopback, link-local and metadata addresses are refused in every encoding, every redirect is checked again, and the connection goes to the address that was checked
- Domain allowlist and blocklist, plus an `isAllowed` hook for your own checks
- Requires Node.js runtime (resolves and checks hostnames)

## Basic usage

Create an API route that uses the utility:

app/api/og/fetch/route.ts:

```tsx
import { NextRequest } from 'next/server';
import { handleOGFetch } from '@once-ui-system/core/server';

export const runtime = 'nodejs';

export async function GET(request: NextRequest) {
  return handleOGFetch(request);
}
```

Then fetch metadata from your client:

Component.tsx:

```tsx
const response = await fetch(
  `/api/og/fetch?url=${encodeURIComponent('https://example.com')}`
);
const data = await response.json();

console.log(data);
// { url, title, description, image, faviconUrl }
```

## With options

Customize timeout, user agent, and entity decoding:

app/api/og/fetch/route.ts:

```tsx
import { NextRequest } from 'next/server';
import { handleOGFetch } from '@once-ui-system/core/server';

export async function GET(request: NextRequest) {
  return handleOGFetch(request, {
    timeout: 5000,
    userAgent: 'MyBot/1.0',
    decodeEntities: true,
    allowedDomains: ['example.com', 'once-ui.com'],
  });
}
```

## Response format

The function returns a JSON response with the following structure:

OGData interface:

```tsx
interface OGData {
  url: string;          // The requested URL
  title: string;        // Page or OG title
  description: string;  // Page or OG description
  image: string;        // OG image URL
  faviconUrl?: string;  // Favicon URL (optional)
}
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `request` | `Request` | `-` |  |
| `options` | `OGFetchOptions` | `-` |  |
| `options.timeout` | `number` | `5000` |  |
| `options.userAgent` | `string` | `'Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; OG-Fetcher/1.0)'` |  |
| `options.decodeEntities` | `boolean` | `true` |  |
| `options.favicon` | `boolean` | `true` | Include faviconUrl; false leaves it out so OgCard uses its own favicon source. |
| `options.maxBytes` | `number` | `1 MiB` | HTML read, after decompression; a longer page is parsed from what was read. |
| `options.maxRedirects` | `number` | `3` | Redirects followed, each checked like the first URL. |
| `options.allowedDomains` |  |  |  |
| `options.blockedDomains` |  |  |  |
| `options.isAllowed` | `(url: URL) => boolean \| Promise<boolean>` | `—` | Called for every URL and redirect target after the built-in checks; return false to refuse. |
| `options.allowHttp` | `boolean` | `false` | Also fetch plain http: URLs. |
| `options.cacheControl` | `string` | `'public, max-age=3600'` | Cache-Control on successful responses. |
| `options.sameOrigin` | `boolean` | `false` | Refuse requests whose Origin or Referer names another host. |

## Error handling

The function returns appropriate error responses:

- **400**: Missing URL parameter or URL failed validation (blocked domain, private IP, etc.). A hostname that does not resolve is refused the same way, so the route cannot tell a caller which internal names exist.
- **403**: Cross-origin caller, with `sameOrigin`
- **415**: The URL is not an HTML page
- **502**: The upstream failed (error status, too many redirects)
- **504**: The upstream did not answer within `timeout`
- **500**: Not running on the Node.js runtime

Error response:

```json
{
  "error": "Failed to fetch Open Graph data"
}
```

## Use with useOgData hook

Combine with the `useOgData` hook for seamless client-side integration:

Component.tsx:

```tsx
import { useOgData } from '@once-ui-system/core';

function MyComponent() {
  const { ogData, loading } = useOgData('https://example.com');

  if (loading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
  
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>{ogData?.title}</h1>
      <p>{ogData?.description}</p>
      {ogData?.image && <img src={ogData.image} alt={ogData.title} />}
    </div>
  );
}
```

# handleOGProxy

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/utils/handleOGProxy

> Server-side utility for proxying external images to avoid CORS issues.

The `handleOGProxy` function is a server-side utility that proxies external images through your server. This is essential for displaying Open Graph images from external sources without CORS restrictions.

> In a Next.js app, use createOgProxyRoute from @once-ui-system/core/next: a two-line route file built on this function. See OG route handlers.

## Features

- Proxies images from external URLs
- Passes raster image types only by default (SVG is opt-in), with `nosniff` and a sandboxing CSP
- Size limit and timeout; a larger image is refused, not truncated
- Configurable cache control headers
- Custom user agent support
- Only requests public addresses: private, loopback, link-local and metadata addresses are refused in every encoding, every redirect is checked again, and the connection goes to the address that was checked
- Domain allowlist and blocklist, plus an `isAllowed` hook for your own checks
- Requires Node.js runtime (resolves and checks hostnames)
- Handles errors gracefully

## Basic usage

Create an API route that uses the utility:

app/api/og/proxy/route.ts:

```tsx
import { NextRequest } from 'next/server';
import { handleOGProxy } from '@once-ui-system/core/server';

export const runtime = 'nodejs';

export async function GET(request: NextRequest) {
  return handleOGProxy(request);
}
```

Then use the proxy in your client:

Component.tsx:

```tsx
const imageUrl = 'https://external-site.com/image.jpg';
const proxiedUrl = `/api/og/proxy?url=${encodeURIComponent(imageUrl)}`;

<img src={proxiedUrl} alt="External image" />
```

## With options

Customize cache duration and user agent:

app/api/og/proxy/route.ts:

```tsx
import { NextRequest } from 'next/server';
import { handleOGProxy } from '@once-ui-system/core/server';

export async function GET(request: NextRequest) {
  return handleOGProxy(request, {
    userAgent: 'Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; ImageProxy/1.0)',
    cacheMaxAge: 86400,
    allowedDomains: ['example.com', 'once-ui.com'],
  });
}
```

## Why use a proxy?

External images often have CORS restrictions that prevent direct usage in web applications. By proxying images through your server:

- **Bypass CORS**: Your server fetches the image and serves it from your domain
- **Caching**: Reduce external requests with configurable cache headers
- **Privacy**: Hide the original image URL from client-side code
- **Reliability**: Handle external failures gracefully

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `request` | `Request` | `-` |  |
| `options` | `OGProxyOptions` | `-` |  |
| `options.userAgent` | `string` | `'Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; OG-Proxy/1.0)'` | User agent string for the fetch request. |
| `options.cacheMaxAge` | `number` | `3600` | Cache duration in seconds (1 hour). |
| `options.cacheControl` | `string` | `—` | Full Cache-Control for successful responses; overrides cacheMaxAge. |
| `options.timeout` | `number` | `10000` | Milliseconds for the whole exchange: DNS, connection, redirects and body. |
| `options.maxBytes` | `number` | `5 MiB` | Largest image, after decompression. |
| `options.allowedContentTypes` |  |  |  |
| `options.maxRedirects` | `number` | `3` | Redirects followed, each checked like the first URL. |
| `options.allowedDomains` |  |  |  |
| `options.blockedDomains` |  |  |  |
| `options.isAllowed` | `(url: URL) => boolean \| Promise<boolean>` | `—` | Called for every URL and redirect target after the built-in checks; return false to refuse. |
| `options.allowHttp` | `boolean` | `false` | Also fetch plain http: URLs. |
| `options.sameOrigin` | `boolean` | `false` | Refuse requests whose Origin or Referer names another host. |

## Response

The function returns the image binary data with appropriate headers:

Response headers:

```tsx
// Response headers
{
  'Content-Type': 'image/jpeg',  // The upstream type, if allowed
  'Cache-Control': 'public, max-age=3600',
  'X-Content-Type-Options': 'nosniff',
  'Content-Security-Policy': "default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; sandbox"
}
```

## Error handling

The function returns appropriate error responses:

- **400**: Missing URL parameter or URL failed validation (blocked domain, private IP, etc.)
- **413**: The image is larger than `maxBytes`
- **415**: Not an allowed image type
- **502**: The upstream failed (too many redirects, a dropped connection)
- **504**: The upstream did not finish within `timeout`
- **500**: Not running on the Node.js runtime
- **Original status**: If the external server returns an error, that status is forwarded

Error response:

```json
{
  "error": "Failed to fetch image"
}
```

## Use with useOgData hook

The `useOgData` hook automatically uses the proxy for external images:

Component.tsx:

```tsx
import { useOgData } from '@once-ui-system/core';

function MyComponent() {
  const { ogData, loading } = useOgData(
    'https://example.com',
    '/api/og/fetch',
    '/api/og/proxy'  // Custom proxy endpoint
  );

  return (
    <div>
      {ogData?.image && (
        <img src={ogData.image} alt={ogData.title} />
      )}
    </div>
  );
}
```

## Security considerations

Both `handleOGFetch` and `handleOGProxy` validate URLs server-side before fetching:

- Only **HTTPS** URLs are allowed (plain HTTP with `allowHttp`)
- **Non-public addresses** are blocked in every form the URL parser accepts: private, loopback, link-local, unique-local, carrier-grade NAT, multicast, cloud metadata, and IPv4 inside IPv6
- Internal hostnames (`localhost`, `*.local`, `*.internal`, single-label names) are blocked
- Every address a hostname resolves to must be public, and the connection goes to the address that was checked, so a DNS answer that changes in between has nothing to slip through
- Embedded credentials in URLs are rejected
- Redirect chains are followed by hand and every hop is checked again (up to 3 redirects)

Use `allowedDomains` to restrict fetching to trusted hosts in production:

Domain allowlist:

```tsx
return handleOGProxy(request, {
  allowedDomains: ['example.com', 'cdn.example.com'],
});
```

Consider also adding rate limiting at the route level to prevent abuse.

# useDebounce

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useDebounce

> React hook that delays updating a value until after a specified delay period.

The `useDebounce` hook delays updating a value until after a specified delay period has passed without changes. This is useful for optimizing performance in scenarios like search inputs, API calls, or expensive computations.

**Used in components:** [Input](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/input), [Textarea](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/textarea) (for character count updates), [EmojiPicker](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/emojiPicker) (for search filtering)

> Most of the time you don't need to use this hook directly. The Input and Textarea components already use it internally when `maxLength` is set. Use this hook when you need custom debouncing logic in your own components.

## Features

- Delays value updates until user stops typing
- Prevents excessive API calls or computations
- Simple and lightweight implementation
- Works with any value type

## Basic usage

Debounce a search input to avoid excessive API calls:

SearchComponent.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from 'react';
import { useDebounce } from '@once-ui-system/core';

function SearchComponent() {
  const [searchTerm, setSearchTerm] = useState('');
  const debouncedSearch = useDebounce(searchTerm, 500);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (debouncedSearch) {
      // This only runs 500ms after user stops typing
      fetchSearchResults(debouncedSearch);
    }
  }, [debouncedSearch]);

  return (
    <input
      value={searchTerm}
      onChange={(e) => setSearchTerm(e.target.value)}
      placeholder="Search..."
    />
  );
}
```

## With API calls

Optimize API requests by debouncing user input:

UserSearch.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
import { useDebounce } from '@once-ui-system/core';

function UserSearch() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const [results, setResults] = useState([]);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false);
  const debouncedQuery = useDebounce(query, 300);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!debouncedQuery) {
      setResults([]);
      return;
    }

    setLoading(true);
    fetch('/api/users?q=' + debouncedQuery)
      .then(res => res.json())
      .then(data => {
        setResults(data);
        setLoading(false);
      });
  }, [debouncedQuery]);

  return (
    <div>
      <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} />
      {loading && <div>Loading...</div>}
      {results.map(user => <div key={user.id}>{user.name}</div>)}
    </div>
  );
}
```

## With expensive computations

Debounce expensive calculations:

DataProcessor.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState, useMemo } from 'react';
import { useDebounce } from '@once-ui-system/core';

function DataProcessor() {
  const [input, setInput] = useState('');
  const debouncedInput = useDebounce(input, 500);

  const processedData = useMemo(() => {
    // Expensive computation only runs after debounce
    return expensiveProcessing(debouncedInput);
  }, [debouncedInput]);

  return (
    <div>
      <textarea
        value={input}
        onChange={(e) => setInput(e.target.value)}
      />
      <div>{processedData}</div>
    </div>
  );
}
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value` | `any` | `-` |  |
| `delay` | `number` | `-` |  |

## Return value

Returns the debounced value that updates only after the specified delay period has passed without changes.

Return type:

```tsx
const debouncedValue = useDebounce(value, delay);
// Type: same as input value
// Updates: only after 'delay' ms of no changes
```

## Common use cases

### Search inputs

SearchBar.tsx:

```tsx
function SearchBar() {
  const [search, setSearch] = useState('');
  const debouncedSearch = useDebounce(search, 300);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (debouncedSearch) {
      // Search API called only after user stops typing
      searchAPI(debouncedSearch);
    }
  }, [debouncedSearch]);

  return (
    <input
      value={search}
      onChange={(e) => setSearch(e.target.value)}
    />
  );
}
```

### Form validation

EmailInput.tsx:

```tsx
function EmailInput() {
  const [email, setEmail] = useState('');
  const debouncedEmail = useDebounce(email, 500);
  const [isValid, setIsValid] = useState(true);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (debouncedEmail) {
      // Validate only after user stops typing
      setIsValid(validateEmail(debouncedEmail));
    }
  }, [debouncedEmail]);

  return (
    <input
      value={email}
      onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)}
      className={isValid ? 'valid' : 'invalid'}
    />
  );
}
```

### Window resize handling

ResponsiveComponent.tsx:

```tsx
function ResponsiveComponent() {
  const [windowWidth, setWindowWidth] = useState(window.innerWidth);
  const debouncedWidth = useDebounce(windowWidth, 200);

  useEffect(() => {
    const handleResize = () => setWindowWidth(window.innerWidth);
    window.addEventListener('resize', handleResize);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', handleResize);
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    // Expensive layout calculations only after resize stops
    recalculateLayout(debouncedWidth);
  }, [debouncedWidth]);

  return <div>Width: {debouncedWidth}px</div>;
}
```

## Performance tips

- **Choose appropriate delay**: 300-500ms for search, 100-200ms for UI feedback
- **Combine with useMemo**: Debounce input, then memoize expensive computations
- **Cancel pending requests**: Clean up API calls when component unmounts

OptimizedSearch.tsx:

```tsx
function OptimizedSearch() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const debouncedQuery = useDebounce(query, 300);

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();

    if (debouncedQuery) {
      fetch(\`/api/search?q=\${debouncedQuery}\`, {
        signal: controller.signal
      });
    }

    return () => {
      // Cancel pending request on cleanup
      controller.abort();
    };
  }, [debouncedQuery]);

  return <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} />;
}
```

# useOgData

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useOgData

> React hook for fetching and displaying Open Graph metadata from URLs.

The `useOgData` hook fetches Open Graph metadata from URLs, including title, description, image, and favicon. It automatically handles image proxying for external sources and provides loading states.

**Used in components:** [OgCard](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/ogCard)

> Most of the time you don't need to use this hook directly. The OgCard component already uses it internally to fetch and display Open Graph previews. Use this hook when you need custom rendering or additional control over the fetching logic.

## Features

- Fetches OG metadata from any URL
- Automatic image proxying for CORS-free display
- Loading state management
- Custom API endpoint support
- Companion `useOgImage` hook for image-only fetching

## Basic usage

Fetch and display Open Graph data:

LinkPreview.tsx:

```tsx
import { useOgData } from '@once-ui-system/core';

function LinkPreview({ url }: { url: string }) {
  const { ogData, loading } = useOgData(url);

  if (loading) return <div>Loading preview...</div>;
  if (!ogData) return null;

  return (
    <div>
      {ogData.image && <img src={ogData.image} alt={ogData.title} />}
      <h3>{ogData.title}</h3>
      <p>{ogData.description}</p>
      <a href={ogData.url}>Visit site</a>
    </div>
  );
}
```

## With custom endpoints

Use custom API routes for fetching and proxying:

CustomLinkPreview.tsx:

```tsx
import { useOgData } from '@once-ui-system/core';

function CustomLinkPreview({ url }: { url: string }) {
  const { ogData, loading } = useOgData(
    url,
    '/api/custom/fetch',  // Custom fetch endpoint
    '/api/custom/proxy'   // Custom proxy endpoint
  );

  return (
    <div>
      {loading ? (
        <Skeleton />
      ) : (
        <Card>
          <img src={ogData?.image} alt={ogData?.title} />
          <h3>{ogData?.title}</h3>
          <p>{ogData?.description}</p>
        </Card>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}
```

## useOgImage hook

For cases where you only need the image:

LinkThumbnail.tsx:

```tsx
import { useOgImage } from '@once-ui-system/core';

function LinkThumbnail({ url }: { url: string }) {
  const { ogImage, loading } = useOgImage(url);

  if (loading) return <Skeleton shape="block" width="200px" height="200px" />;
  if (!ogImage) return <DefaultThumbnail />;

  return (
    <img
      src={ogImage}
      alt="Link thumbnail"
      width={200}
      height={200}
    />
  );
}
```

## With OgCard component

Combine with the OgCard component for rich previews:

RichLinkPreview.tsx:

```tsx
import { OgCard } from '@once-ui-system/core';

function RichLinkPreview({ url }: { url: string }) {
  return (
    <OgCard
      url={url}
      aspectRatio="16 / 9"
      radius="l"
      border="neutral-medium"
    />
  );
}
```

## API Reference

### useOgData

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `url` | `string` | `null` |  |
| `customFetchUrl` | `string` | `OgRoutesProvider's fetch, or '/api/og/fetch'` |  |
| `customProxyUrl` | `string` | `OgRoutesProvider's proxy, or '/api/og/proxy'` |  |

### Return value

Return type:

```tsx
interface OgData {
  title: string;
  description: string;
  image: string;
  url: string;
  faviconUrl?: string;
}

type UseOgDataResult = {
  ogData: Partial<OgData> | null;
  loading: boolean;
};
```

### useOgImage

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `url` | `string` | `null` |  |
| `customFetchUrl` | `string` | `OgRoutesProvider's fetch, or '/api/og/fetch'` |  |
| `customProxyUrl` | `string` | `OgRoutesProvider's proxy, or '/api/og/proxy'` |  |

### useOgImage return value

Return type:

```tsx
type UseOgImageResult = {
  ogImage: string | null;
  loading: boolean;
};
```

## Required API routes

This hook requires two server routes. In a Next.js app, use the ready-made [OG route handlers](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/utils/ogRoutes):

API routes:

```tsx
// app/api/og/fetch/route.ts
import { createOgFetchRoute } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";

export const { GET } = createOgFetchRoute();

// app/api/og/proxy/route.ts
import { createOgProxyRoute } from "@once-ui-system/core/next";

export const { GET } = createOgProxyRoute();
```

Elsewhere, build them on [`handleOGFetch`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/utils/handleOGFetch) and [`handleOGProxy`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/utils/handleOGProxy) from `@once-ui-system/core/server`.

The hook calls `/api/og/fetch` and `/api/og/proxy` unless told otherwise: by its `customFetchUrl` and `customProxyUrl` arguments, or for every caller below it, by `OgRoutesProvider`:

Custom routes:

```tsx
import { OgRoutesProvider } from "@once-ui-system/core";

<OgRoutesProvider routes={{ fetch: "/og/fetch", proxy: "/og/proxy" }}>
  {children}
</OgRoutesProvider>
```

## Image proxying

The hook automatically proxies external images through your server to avoid CORS issues:

- Images from the same origin are used directly
- External images are routed through the proxy endpoint
- The proxy adds appropriate cache headers

## Error handling

The hook handles errors gracefully:

SafeLinkPreview.tsx:

```tsx
function SafeLinkPreview({ url }: { url: string }) {
  const { ogData, loading } = useOgData(url);

  if (loading) return <Skeleton />;
  
  if (!ogData) {
    return (
      <div>
        <p>Unable to load preview</p>
        <a href={url}>{url}</a>
      </div>
    );
  }

  return <OgCard url={url} />;
}
```

## Performance tips

- **Conditional fetching**: Pass `null` as URL to skip fetching
- **Memoize URLs**: Prevent unnecessary refetches
- **Cache responses**: The proxy endpoint includes cache headers

OptimizedPreview.tsx:

```tsx
import { useMemo } from 'react';
import { useOgData } from '@once-ui-system/core';

function OptimizedPreview({ rawUrl }: { rawUrl: string | undefined }) {
  // Only fetch when URL is valid
  const url = useMemo(() => {
    try {
      return rawUrl ? new URL(rawUrl).href : null;
    } catch {
      return null;
    }
  }, [rawUrl]);

  const { ogData, loading } = useOgData(url);

  if (!url) return <div>Invalid URL</div>;
  if (loading) return <Skeleton />;
  
  return <OgCard url={url} />;
}
```
