# useArrowNavigation

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useArrowNavigation

> React hook for implementing keyboard arrow navigation in lists, grids, and menus.

The `useArrowNavigation` hook provides keyboard navigation for interactive elements using arrow keys. It supports row, column, and grid layouts with customizable behavior.

**Used in components:** [Dropdown](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/dropdown), [EmojiPicker](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/emojiPicker), [Select](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/select), [Dropdown openOn="contextmenu"](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/dropdown#context-menu), [MegaMenu](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/megaMenu)

> Most of the time you don't need to use this hook directly. Components like DropdownWrapper, Select, and MegaMenu already provide built-in keyboard navigation. Use this hook when building custom navigable interfaces that aren't covered by existing components.

## Features

- Arrow key navigation (up, down, left, right)
- Support for row, column, and grid layouts
- Automatic focus management
- Enter/Space key selection
- Optional wrapping at boundaries
- Visual focus highlighting
- ARIA-compliant accessibility

## Basic usage

Add arrow navigation to a list:

NavigableList.tsx:

```tsx
import { useRef } from 'react';
import { useArrowNavigation } from '@once-ui-system/core';

function NavigableList({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  const containerRef = useRef(null);
  
  const { handleKeyDown, focusedIndex } = useArrowNavigation({
    layout: 'column',
    itemCount: items.length,
    containerRef,
    onSelect: (index) => console.log('Selected:', items[index])
  });

  return (
    <Column ref={containerRef} onKeyDown={handleKeyDown}>
      {items.map((item, index) => (
        <Button
          key={index}
          data-focused={focusedIndex === index}
        >
          {item}
        </Button>
      ))}
    </Column>
  );
}
```

## Grid layout

Navigate a grid with arrow keys:

EmojiGrid.tsx:

```tsx
import { useRef } from 'react';
import { useArrowNavigation } from '@once-ui-system/core';

function EmojiGrid({ emojis }: { emojis: string[] }) {
  const containerRef = useRef(null);
  
  const { handleKeyDown, focusedIndex } = useArrowNavigation({
    layout: 'grid',
    itemCount: emojis.length,
    columns: 8,
    containerRef,
    onSelect: (index) => selectEmoji(emojis[index]),
    wrap: true
  });

  return (
    <Grid
      ref={containerRef}
      onKeyDown={handleKeyDown}
      role="grid"
      columns={8}
    >
      {emojis.map((emoji, index) => (
        <Button
          key={index}
          role="gridcell"
          data-focused={focusedIndex === index}
        >
          {emoji}
        </Button>
      ))}
    </Grid>
  );
}
```

## Row layout

Navigate horizontally:

TabNavigation.tsx:

```tsx
function TabNavigation({ tabs }: { tabs: { id: string; label: string }[] }) {
  const containerRef = useRef(null);
  
  const { handleKeyDown, focusedIndex } = useArrowNavigation({
    layout: 'row',
    itemCount: tabs.length,
    containerRef,
    onSelect: (index) => setActiveTab(tabs[index].id),
    wrap: true
  });

  return (
    <Row ref={containerRef} onKeyDown={handleKeyDown} role="tablist">
      {tabs.map((tab, index) => (
        <Button
          key={tab.id}
          role="tab"
          aria-selected={activeTab === tab.id}
        >
          {tab.label}
        </Button>
      ))}
    </Row>
  );
}
```

## When it takes focus

`initialFocusedIndex` says which item is *current*, not that focus should move
there. The hook takes focus on its first pass only when `autoFocus` is set, or
when nothing else holds it — the case right after a keyed remount, where the
element that had focus has just been removed and focusing it again restores
rather than steals. Every later pass follows a keystroke, so it always moves
focus.

When it does take focus on that first pass and `initialFocusedIndex` is left at
`-1`, it goes to the item marked `aria-selected="true"` — a native select opens
on the value it is already showing, and a long list told from the top hides it.
With no selection it starts at the first enabled item; a selected item that is
disabled is skipped.

`aria-selected` is yours to author. Do not drive it from `focusedIndex`: that
is what the hook's own `data-highlighted` and `highlighted` class are for, and
conflating the two makes a screen reader announce whichever item the arrow keys
have reached as the selected one.

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `layout` | `'row'` | `'column'` | 'grid' |
| `itemCount` | `number` | `-` |  |
| `columns` | `number` | `8` |  |
| `containerRef` | `RefObject<HTMLElement>` | `-` |  |
| `onSelect` | `(index: number) => void` | `-` |  |
| `onFocusChange` | `(index: number) => void` | `-` |  |
| `wrap` | `boolean` | `true` |  |
| `initialFocusedIndex` | `number` | `-1` |  |
| `itemSelector` | `string` |  |  |
| `autoFocus` | `boolean` | `false` |  |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | `false` |  |
| `disableHighlighting` | `boolean` | `false` |  |

## Return value

Return type:

```tsx
{
  handleKeyDown: (e: KeyboardEvent) => void;
  focusedIndex: number;
  setFocusedIndex: (index: number) => void;
  resetFocus: () => void;
}
```

## Keyboard controls

- **Arrow Up**: Move focus up (column/grid)
- **Arrow Down**: Move focus down (column/grid)
- **Arrow Left**: Move focus left (row/grid)
- **Arrow Right**: Move focus right (row/grid)
- **Enter/Space**: Select focused item
- **Home**: Focus first item
- **End**: Focus last item

## Styling focused items

Use the `focusedIndex` to style the focused item:

StyledList.tsx:

```tsx
function StyledList() {
  const { handleKeyDown, focusedIndex } = useArrowNavigation({
    layout: 'column',
    itemCount: items.length
  });

  return (
    <div onKeyDown={handleKeyDown}>
      {items.map((item, index) => (
        <button
          key={index}
          className={focusedIndex === index ? 'focused' : ''}
          style={{
            outline: focusedIndex === index ? '2px solid blue' : 'none',
            transform: focusedIndex === index ? 'scale(1.05)' : 'scale(1)'
          }}
        >
          {item}
        </button>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}
```

## Accessibility

The hook automatically manages:

- Focus visibility with visual indicators
- ARIA roles and attributes
- Keyboard event handling
- Focus trap within container

For best accessibility, add appropriate ARIA attributes:

Accessible list:

```tsx
<div
  ref={containerRef}
  onKeyDown={handleKeyDown}
  role="listbox"
  aria-label="Options"
>
  {items.map((item, index) => (
    <div
      key={index}
      role="option"
      aria-selected={item === selectedItem}
      tabIndex={focusedIndex === index ? 0 : -1}
    >
      {item}
    </div>
  ))}
</div>
```

## Used in components

This hook is used internally by:

- EmojiPicker
- Dropdown
- Select
- Dropdown with openOn="contextmenu"
- MegaMenu

# useHeadingLinks

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useHeadingLinks

> React hook for extracting heading elements from the page for table of contents navigation.

The `useHeadingLinks` hook extracts all heading elements (h2-h6) from the current page and returns them as a structured array. This is useful for creating table of contents, navigation menus, or document outlines.

**Used in components:** [HeadingNav](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/modules/headingNav)

> Most of the time you don't need to use this hook directly. The HeadingNav component already uses it internally to generate table of contents navigation. Use this hook when you need custom rendering or additional processing of page headings.

## Features

- Automatically finds all headings on the page
- Extracts heading text, ID, and level
- Filters out headings with `data-exclude-nav` attribute
- Generates IDs for headings without them
- Updates on mount

## Basic usage

Create a table of contents:

TableOfContents.tsx:

```tsx
import { useHeadingLinks } from '@once-ui-system/core';

function TableOfContents() {
  const headings = useHeadingLinks();

  return (
    <nav>
      <h2>On this page</h2>
      <ul>
        {headings.map((heading) => (
          <li
            key={heading.id}
            style={{ marginLeft: (heading.level - 2) * 16 }}
          >
            <a href={'#' + heading.id}>{heading.text}</a>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </nav>
  );
}
```

## With styling

Create a styled navigation menu:

DocumentNav.tsx:

```tsx
import { useHeadingLinks } from '@once-ui-system/core';

function DocumentNav() {
  const headings = useHeadingLinks();

  return (
    <Flex
      direction="column"
      gap="8"
      padding="16"
      border="neutral-medium"
      radius="m"
    >
      <Text textVariant="label-default-s">Contents</Text>
      {headings.map((heading) => (
        <a
          key={heading.id}
          href={'#' + heading.id}
          style={{
            paddingLeft: (heading.level - 2) * 12,
            fontSize: heading.level === 2 ? '14px' : '13px',
            fontWeight: heading.level === 2 ? 600 : 400
          }}
        >
          {heading.text}
        </a>
      ))}
    </Flex>
  );
}
```

## Excluding headings

Exclude specific headings from navigation:

MyPage.tsx:

```tsx
function MyPage() {
  return (
    <article>
      <h2>Introduction</h2>
      <p>This heading will appear in navigation</p>
      
      <h2 data-exclude-nav>Internal Note</h2>
      <p>This heading will NOT appear in navigation</p>
      
      <h2>Main Content</h2>
      <p>This heading will appear in navigation</p>
    </article>
  );
}
```

## Return value

Return type:

```tsx
interface Heading {
  id: string;      // Element ID or generated ID
  text: string;    // Heading text content
  level: number;   // Heading level (2-6)
}

const headings: Heading[] = useHeadingLinks();

// Example output:
// [
//   { id: 'introduction', text: 'Introduction', level: 2 },
//   { id: 'features', text: 'Features', level: 2 },
//   { id: 'api', text: 'API Reference', level: 3 }
// ]
```

## With active section tracking

Combine with scroll tracking to highlight active section:

ActiveTOC.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
import { useHeadingLinks } from '@once-ui-system/core';

function ActiveTOC() {
  const headings = useHeadingLinks();
  const [activeId, setActiveId] = useState('');

  useEffect(() => {
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
      (entries) => {
        entries.forEach((entry) => {
          if (entry.isIntersecting) {
            setActiveId(entry.target.id);
          }
        });
      },
      { rootMargin: '-80px 0px -80% 0px' }
    );

    headings.forEach(({ id }) => {
      const element = document.getElementById(id);
      if (element) observer.observe(element);
    });

    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, [headings]);

  return (
    <nav>
      {headings.map((heading) => (
        <a
          key={heading.id}
          href={'#' + heading.id}
          className={activeId === heading.id ? 'active' : ''}
        >
          {heading.text}
        </a>
      ))}
    </nav>
  );
}
```

## Use cases

- **Documentation sites**: Auto-generate table of contents
- **Blog posts**: Create article outlines
- **Long-form content**: Improve navigation
- **Accessibility**: Provide skip links

## Notes

- Only runs once on mount (not reactive to DOM changes)
- Headings without IDs get auto-generated IDs
- Only includes h2-h6 (h1 is typically the page title)
- Respects `data-exclude-nav` attribute

# useStreamingData

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useStreamingData

> React hook for creating smooth, animated streaming data visualizations.

The `useStreamingData` hook creates smooth, animated data streams for real-time visualizations. It interpolates between data points and maintains a sliding window of values, perfect for live charts and dashboards.

**Used in components:** Not used internally by Once UI components

> This is a utility hook for building custom real-time data visualizations. Use it when you need to create live charts, dashboards, or streaming data displays with smooth animations.

## Features

- Smooth interpolation between data points
- Configurable sliding window size
- Customizable update intervals
- Pause/resume streaming
- Reset to initial state
- RequestAnimationFrame-based updates

## Basic usage

Create a streaming line chart:

StreamingChart.tsx:

```tsx
import { useStreamingData } from '@once-ui-system/core';
import { LineChart } from '@once-ui-system/core/data';

type Point = { time: number; value: number };

function StreamingChart() {
  const { data, running, setRunning } = useStreamingData<Point>({
    initialData: generateInitialData(),
    windowSize: 20,
    intervalMs: 1000,
    xKey: 'time',
    numericKeys: ['value'],
    getNextTarget: ({ lastPoint, nextX }) => ({
      value: Math.random() * 100
    })
  });

  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={() => setRunning(!running)}>
        {running ? 'Pause' : 'Resume'}
      </button>
      <LineChart
        xAxisType="number"
        animation={false}
        series={[{ key: "value" }]}
        data={data}
      />
    </div>
  );
}
```

## Multi-series data

Stream multiple data series:

MultiSeriesChart.tsx:

```tsx
function MultiSeriesChart() {
  const { data, running, setRunning, reset } = useStreamingData({
    initialData: [
      { time: 0, cpu: 20, memory: 30, disk: 15 },
      { time: 1, cpu: 25, memory: 32, disk: 16 }
    ],
    windowSize: 30,
    intervalMs: 2000,
    stepMs: 16,
    xKey: 'time',
    numericKeys: ['cpu', 'memory', 'disk'],
    getNextTarget: ({ lastPoint }) => ({
      cpu: Math.min(100, Math.max(0, lastPoint.cpu + (Math.random() - 0.5) * 20)),
      memory: Math.min(100, Math.max(0, lastPoint.memory + (Math.random() - 0.5) * 15)),
      disk: Math.min(100, Math.max(0, lastPoint.disk + (Math.random() - 0.5) * 10))
    })
  });

  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={() => setRunning(!running)}>
        {running ? 'Pause' : 'Resume'}
      </button>
      <button onClick={reset}>Reset</button>
      <LineChart
        xAxisType="number"
        series={[{ key: "cpu" }, { key: "memory" }, { key: "disk" }]}
        data={data}
      />
    </div>
  );
}
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `initialData` |  |  |  |
| `windowSize` | `number` | `-` |  |
| `intervalMs` | `number` | `-` |  |
| `stepMs` | `number` | `16` |  |
| `xKey` | `keyof T` | `-` |  |
| `numericKeys` | `Array<keyof T>` | `-` |  |
| `getNextTarget` | `({ lastPoint, nextX }) => Partial<T>` | `-` |  |

## Return value

Return type:

```tsx
{
  data: T[];                                    // Current data window
  running: boolean;                             // Whether streaming is active
  setRunning: (running: boolean) => void;       // Control streaming state
  reset: () => void;                            // Reset to initial data
}
```

## How it works

1. **Initialization**: Starts with `initialData` trimmed to `windowSize`
2. **New point creation**: Every `intervalMs`, creates a new data point
3. **Interpolation**: Smoothly animates from current to target values
4. **Sliding window**: Maintains only the last `windowSize` points
5. **Animation**: Updates every `stepMs` using requestAnimationFrame

## Performance tips

- Use `stepMs: 16` for 60fps (smooth)
- Use `stepMs: 33` for 30fps (more efficient)
- Keep `windowSize` reasonable (20-50 points)
- Avoid expensive calculations in `getNextTarget`

## Real-world example

System monitoring dashboard:

SystemMonitor.tsx:

```tsx
function SystemMonitor() {
  const { data, running, setRunning } = useStreamingData({
    initialData: Array.from({ length: 20 }, (_, i) => ({
      time: i,
      cpu: 20 + Math.random() * 10,
      memory: 40 + Math.random() * 10,
      network: 10 + Math.random() * 5
    })),
    windowSize: 30,
    intervalMs: 1000,
    xKey: 'time',
    numericKeys: ['cpu', 'memory', 'network'],
    getNextTarget: ({ lastPoint }) => {
      // Simulate realistic system metrics
      const cpuChange = (Math.random() - 0.5) * 15;
      const memoryChange = (Math.random() - 0.5) * 5;
      const networkChange = (Math.random() - 0.5) * 10;
      
      return {
        cpu: Math.min(100, Math.max(0, lastPoint.cpu + cpuChange)),
        memory: Math.min(100, Math.max(0, lastPoint.memory + memoryChange)),
        network: Math.min(100, Math.max(0, lastPoint.network + networkChange))
      };
    }
  });

  return (
    <Flex direction="column" gap="16">
      <Flex gap="8">
        <Button onClick={() => setRunning(!running)}>
          {running ? 'Pause' : 'Resume'}
        </Button>
        <Text>CPU: {data[data.length - 1]?.cpu.toFixed(1)}%</Text>
        <Text>Memory: {data[data.length - 1]?.memory.toFixed(1)}%</Text>
      </Flex>
      <LineChart
        xAxisType="number"
        animation={false}
        series={[{ key: "cpu" }, { key: "memory" }, { key: "network" }]}
        data={data}
      />
    </Flex>
  );
}
```

## Related hooks

- `useStreamingViewport` - Similar but with dynamic viewport adjustment

# useStreamingViewport

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useStreamingViewport

> React hook for streaming data with dynamic viewport adjustment for charts.

The `useStreamingViewport` hook is similar to `useStreamingData` but includes automatic viewport (x-axis domain) management. It's ideal for charts that need to show a moving window of time-series data.

**Used in components:** Not used internally by Once UI components

> This is a utility hook for building custom real-time data visualizations with dynamic viewport adjustment. Use it when you need charts where the x-axis automatically scrolls with incoming data, such as live monitoring dashboards.

## Features

- Smooth data interpolation
- Automatic viewport adjustment
- Sliding window with dynamic x-domain
- Pause/resume streaming
- Reset functionality
- RequestAnimationFrame-based updates

## Basic usage

Create a streaming chart with auto-adjusting viewport:

StreamingViewportChart.tsx:

```tsx
import { useStreamingViewport } from '@once-ui-system/core';
import { LineChart } from '@once-ui-system/core/data';

type Point = { time: number; value: number };

function StreamingViewportChart() {
  const { data, xDomain, running, setRunning } = useStreamingViewport<Point>({
    initialData: generateInitialData(),
    windowSize: 20,
    intervalMs: 1000,
    xKey: 'time',
    numericKeys: ['value'],
    getNextTarget: ({ lastPoint, nextX }) => ({
      value: Math.random() * 100
    })
  });

  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={() => setRunning(!running)}>
        {running ? 'Pause' : 'Resume'}
      </button>
      <LineChart
        xAxisType="number"
        xDomain={xDomain}
        animation={false}
        series={[{ key: "value" }]}
        data={data}
      />
    </div>
  );
}
```

## Real-time metrics

Monitor live system metrics with moving viewport:

LiveMetrics.tsx:

```tsx
function LiveMetrics() {
  const { data, xDomain, running, setRunning, reset } = useStreamingViewport({
    initialData: Array.from({ length: 30 }, (_, i) => ({
      timestamp: Date.now() - (30 - i) * 1000,
      requests: 100 + Math.random() * 50,
      errors: Math.random() * 5,
      latency: 50 + Math.random() * 100
    })),
    windowSize: 30,
    intervalMs: 1000,
    xKey: 'timestamp',
    numericKeys: ['requests', 'errors', 'latency'],
    getNextTarget: ({ lastPoint }) => ({
      requests: Math.max(0, lastPoint.requests + (Math.random() - 0.5) * 30),
      errors: Math.max(0, lastPoint.errors + (Math.random() - 0.5) * 2),
      latency: Math.max(0, lastPoint.latency + (Math.random() - 0.5) * 40)
    })
  });

  return (
    <Flex direction="column" gap="16">
      <Flex gap="8">
        <Button onClick={() => setRunning(!running)}>
          {running ? 'Pause' : 'Resume'}
        </Button>
        <Button onClick={reset}>Reset</Button>
      </Flex>
      <LineChart
        xAxisType="number"
        xDomain={xDomain}
        animation={false}
        series={[{ key: "requests" }, { key: "errors" }, { key: "latency" }]}
        data={data}
      />
    </Flex>
  );
}
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `initialData` |  |  |  |
| `windowSize` | `number` | `-` |  |
| `intervalMs` | `number` | `-` |  |
| `stepMs` | `number` | `16` |  |
| `xKey` | `keyof T` | `-` |  |
| `numericKeys` | `Array<keyof T>` | `-` |  |
| `getNextTarget` | `({ lastPoint, nextX }) => Partial<T>` | `-` |  |

## Return value

Return type:

```tsx
{
  data: T[];                                    // Current data window
  xDomain: [number, number];                    // X-axis domain [min, max]
  running: boolean;                             // Whether streaming is active
  setRunning: (running: boolean) => void;       // Control streaming state
  reset: () => void;                            // Reset to initial data
}
```

## Difference from useStreamingData

The key difference is the `xDomain` return value:

- **useStreamingData**: Returns only `data`
- **useStreamingViewport**: Returns `data` + `xDomain` for chart axis

Use `useStreamingViewport` when you need the chart viewport to move with the data.

## Example with timestamps

TimestampChart.tsx:

```tsx
function TimestampChart() {
  const { data, xDomain, running, setRunning } = useStreamingViewport({
    initialData: Array.from({ length: 20 }, (_, i) => ({
      timestamp: Date.now() - (20 - i) * 2000,
      temperature: 20 + Math.random() * 5,
      humidity: 60 + Math.random() * 10
    })),
    windowSize: 20,
    intervalMs: 2000,
    xKey: 'timestamp',
    numericKeys: ['temperature', 'humidity'],
    getNextTarget: ({ lastPoint }) => ({
      temperature: lastPoint.temperature + (Math.random() - 0.5) * 2,
      humidity: lastPoint.humidity + (Math.random() - 0.5) * 5
    })
  });

  return (
    <LineChart
      xAxisType="number"
      xDomain={xDomain}
      series={[{ key: "temperature" }, { key: "humidity" }]}
      data={data}
    />
  );
}
```

## Performance considerations

- Uses requestAnimationFrame for smooth animations
- Automatically pauses when `running` is false
- Cleans up on unmount
- Efficient sliding window implementation

## Use cases

- **Real-time dashboards**: System monitoring, analytics
- **Live data feeds**: Stock prices, sensor data
- **Performance monitoring**: Server metrics, application stats
- **IoT dashboards**: Temperature, humidity, sensor readings

- `useStreamingData` - Similar but without viewport management

# useInViewport

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useInViewport

> React hook that detects whether an element is currently visible in the viewport using IntersectionObserver.

The `useInViewport` hook uses the `IntersectionObserver` API to detect whether a referenced element is currently visible within the viewport. This is useful for pausing animations, lazy-loading content, or triggering effects only when elements are on screen.

**Used in components:** [Mask](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/mask), [ParticleFx](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/particleFx), [HoloFx](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/holoFx)

> Most animated components already use this hook internally to pause when off-screen. Use this hook directly when building custom components that need viewport awareness.

## Features

- Lightweight wrapper around `IntersectionObserver`
- Returns a simple boolean — `true` when the element is in view
- Accepts standard `IntersectionObserverInit` options
- Cleans up automatically on unmount

## Basic usage

Pass a ref to the hook and use the returned boolean to conditionally render or animate:

Basic:

```tsx
import { useRef } from "react";
import { useInViewport } from "@once-ui-system/core";

function MyComponent() {
    const ref = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
    const isInViewport = useInViewport(ref);

    return (
        <div ref={ref}>
            {isInViewport ? "Visible!" : "Off screen"}
        </div>
    );
}
```

## Custom threshold

Pass `IntersectionObserverInit` options as the second argument to customize when the element is considered "in viewport":

Options:

```tsx
// Trigger when 50% of the element is visible
const isHalfVisible = useInViewport(ref, { threshold: 0.5 });

// Start detecting 100px before the element enters
const isNearViewport = useInViewport(ref, { rootMargin: "100px" });
```

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | `RefObject<HTMLElement \| null>` |  |  |
| `options` | `IntersectionObserverInit` | `{ threshold: 0 }` |  |

## Return value

Returns a `boolean` — `true` when the element is intersecting the viewport, `false` otherwise.

# useReducedMotion

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useReducedMotion

> React hook that detects reduced motion preferences and low-end device hardware to optimize animation performance.

The `useReducedMotion` hook detects whether animations should be disabled based on the user's `prefers-reduced-motion` system setting and low-end device hardware (CPU cores, device memory). It returns a `shouldAnimate` flag that components use to automatically skip or simplify animations.

**Used in components:** [Mask](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/mask), [ParticleFx](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/particleFx), [TiltFx](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/tiltFx), [HoloFx](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/holoFx), [MatrixFx](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/matrixFx), [WeatherFx](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/weatherFx), [CelebrationFx](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/celebrationFx), [ShineFx](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/effects/shineFx)

> All effect components use this hook internally with a reducedMotion prop defaulting to 'auto'. You only need this hook directly when building custom animated components.

## Features

- Detects `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` media query
- Detects low-end devices (≤2 CPU cores or ≤2GB memory)
- Reactive — updates when the user changes their system setting
- Override support: force animations on or off regardless of detection
- SSR-safe — returns safe defaults on the server

## Basic usage

Use the hook to conditionally run animations:

Basic:

```tsx
import { useReducedMotion } from "@once-ui-system/core";

function MyComponent() {
    const { shouldAnimate } = useReducedMotion();

    useEffect(() => {
        if (!shouldAnimate) return;
        // Start animation loop
    }, [shouldAnimate]);
}
```

## Override

Pass `true` to force reduced motion (disable animations), `false` to force full animations, or `"auto"` (default) to detect automatically.

Override:

```tsx
// Auto-detect (default)
const { shouldAnimate } = useReducedMotion("auto");

// Force animations off
useReducedMotion(true);

// Force animations on
useReducedMotion(false);
```

## Return value

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `prefersReducedMotion` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `isLowEnd` | `boolean` |  |  |
| `shouldAnimate` | `boolean` |  |  |

## API reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `override` | `auto` |  |  |

## Hardware detection

The hook checks two signals to determine low-end devices:

- **`navigator.hardwareConcurrency`** — number of CPU cores (≤2 = low-end)
- **`navigator.deviceMemory`** — device memory in GB (≤2 = low-end, Chrome/Edge only)

These checks run once on mount and do not change during the session.

# useHotkeys

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/hooks/useHotkeys

> Keyboard shortcuts that stay out of the way while the user is typing.

`useHotkeys` calls a function when a key combination is pressed. It skips keys typed
into a text field, textarea, select or editable region by default, so a shortcut on
`c` or `space` does not fire while someone is writing a word with a c in it. It
listens on the window, or on one element, and stops when the component unmounts.

useHotkeys:

```tsx
import { useHotkeys } from "@once-ui-system/core";

useHotkeys("c", () => setCount((value) => value + 1));
useHotkeys(["j", "down"], (event, hotkey) => setLast(hotkey));
useHotkeys("g i", () => router.push("/inbox"));
```

The callback receives the `KeyboardEvent` and the hotkey string that matched. It
need not be memoised: the listener is bound once per set of keys and options, and
always calls the latest callback.

## Syntax

The same string drives [`Kbd`'s `keys`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/kbd#shortcuts-with-keys), which draws it as keycaps, so
one constant can register a shortcut and show it.

| Write | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `mod+k` | ⌘K on macOS and iOS, Ctrl+K elsewhere |
| `mod+shift+z` | Modifiers joined with `+`: `mod`, `meta` (or `cmd`), `ctrl`, `alt` (or `option`), `shift` |
| `?` | A character. Characters that need Shift on most layouts match with or without it |
| `escape`, `enter`, `space`, `tab`, `backspace`, `delete` | Named keys. `esc` and `return` work too |
| `up`, `down`, `left`, `right` | Arrow keys (`arrowup` and so on also work) |
| `home`, `end`, `pageup`, `pagedown`, `f1`–`f12` | More named keys. The plus key is `plus` |
| `g i` | A sequence: G, then I within a second |
| `["j", "down"]` | Alternatives: either one |

Modifiers match exactly: `mod+z` does not fire on `mod+shift+z`, and `z` does not fire
on `mod+z`. Letters match by the character typed, and fall back to the physical key
when Option or a non-Latin layout changes the character (⌥K types "˚").

## While typing

Keys pressed in an `input` that takes text, a `textarea`, a `select`, a
`contenteditable` region or an element with the `textbox`, `searchbox` or `combobox`
role are ignored. Checkboxes, radios, sliders and buttons still trigger shortcuts.
Set `allowWhileTyping` for combinations that never type a character, such as
`mod+s` or `escape`:

allowWhileTyping:

```tsx
useHotkeys("mod+s", save, { allowWhileTyping: true });
```

## Scope

By default the hook listens on the window. Pass `target` to listen on one element,
so the keys work only while focus is inside it: a timeline's arrow keys, say, which
should not move the playhead while focus is in the inspector beside it.

target:

```tsx
const timeline = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);

useHotkeys("left", stepBack, { target: timeline });
useHotkeys("right", stepForward, { target: timeline });

<Column ref={timeline} tabIndex={0}>…</Column>
```

Turn a set of shortcuts off with `enabled: false`, while a dialog that uses the same
keys is open, for instance.

## Options

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `boolean` | `true` | Listen at all. |
| `allowWhileTyping` | `boolean` | `false` | Fire while focus is in a text field, textarea, select or editable region. |
| `target` | `RefObject<HTMLElement>` | `window` | Listen on this element instead of the window. |
| `preventDefault` | `boolean` | `true` | Cancel the browser's own action for a matched key, such as saving the page on mod+s. |
| `sequenceTimeout` | `number` | `1000` | How long, in milliseconds, a sequence such as g i waits for its next key. |

The hook binds nothing until the component mounts, so it is safe in a component that
renders on the server. Keys pressed while an input method is composing text are
ignored, and so is a modifier pressed on its own.

---

# React Native (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/overview

> The basic Once UI components for React Native apps, with the same props and the same design tokens as the web package.

`@once-ui-system/native` brings Once UI's basic components to iOS and Android apps built with React Native. They take the same props as the web components and read the same design tokens, so a screen written with Once UI looks and reads the same on a phone.

It is a preview. Most apps should keep shipping Once UI on phones as the web build wrapped in a native shell (the Stack mobile target); use this package when the app itself has to be native.

**Props follow core 3.0.** The components take the 3.0 props of `@once-ui-system/core`, not the 2.x ones: state is `checked` / `defaultChecked` / `onCheckedChange`, `value` / `defaultValue` / `onValueChange` and `open` / `defaultOpen` / `onOpenChange`; accessible names are `aria-label`; colour is `tone` and look is `variant`; Text and Heading take `textVariant`; Badge and Chip are `Tag`; and a number on a spacing or size prop is points (the web reads it on the token scale, which is the same at the default root size). The renames are listed under "Coming from the 2.x props" below.

## Install

Needs React 19, React Native 0.79 or later (Expo SDK 53 and up) and `react-native-svg` 15, which Expo includes. Preview versions are published to the `next` tag. The [quick start](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/quick-start) covers Expo and bare React Native apps, safe areas and fonts.

App.tsx:

```tsx
import { Button, Column, Heading, Text, ThemeProvider } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export default function App() {
  return (
    <ThemeProvider brand="orange" neutral="sand" solid="color">
      <Column padding="20" gap="12" background="page" fill>
        <Heading>Morning Coffee</Heading>
        <Text onBackground="neutral-weak">Three more coffees and the next one is on us.</Text>
        <Button label="Add stamp" onPress={() => {}} />
      </Column>
    </ThemeProvider>
  );
}
```

# Quick start (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/quick-start

> Install @once-ui-system/native in an Expo or React Native app, wrap it in ThemeProvider and build a first screen.

This page sets up `@once-ui-system/native` in a new or existing app. For the web package, see the [web quick start](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/quick-start).

## Requirements

| Package | Version | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `react` | `>=19` | |
| `react-native` | `>=0.79` | Expo SDK 53 and up |
| `react-native-svg` | `>=15` | Draws the icons. Included in Expo. |
| `react-native-safe-area-context` | any | Optional. Reads the safe areas for `ThemeProvider`'s `insets`. Included in Expo. |

The package is a preview. Versions are published to the `next` tag.

## Install with Expo

Install the package, then let Expo pick the versions of the native modules that match your SDK:

Expo:

```bash
npm install @once-ui-system/native@next
npx expo install react-native-svg react-native-safe-area-context
```

React Native:

```bash
npm install @once-ui-system/native@next react-native-svg react-native-safe-area-context
cd ios && pod install
```

App.tsx:

```tsx
import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { ThemeProvider, ToastProvider } from "@once-ui-system/native";
import { SafeAreaProvider, useSafeAreaInsets } from "react-native-safe-area-context";
import { HomeScreen } from "./HomeScreen";

function Themed({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const insets = useSafeAreaInsets();
  return (
    <ThemeProvider theme="system" brand="orange" accent="indigo" neutral="sand" insets={insets}>
      <ToastProvider>{children}</ToastProvider>
    </ThemeProvider>
  );
}

export default function App() {
  return (
    <SafeAreaProvider>
      <Themed>
        <HomeScreen />
      </Themed>
    </SafeAreaProvider>
  );
}
```

App.tsx:

```tsx
import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { useFonts } from "expo-font";
import { Inter_400Regular, Inter_600SemiBold } from "@expo-google-fonts/inter";
import { ThemeProvider } from "@once-ui-system/native";
import { SafeAreaProvider, useSafeAreaInsets } from "react-native-safe-area-context";
import { HomeScreen } from "./HomeScreen";

function Themed({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const insets = useSafeAreaInsets();
  return (
    <ThemeProvider
      insets={insets}
      fonts={{
        heading: "Inter_600SemiBold",
        body: "Inter_400Regular",
        label: "Inter_400Regular",
      }}
    >
      {children}
    </ThemeProvider>
  );
}

export default function App() {
  const [loaded] = useFonts({ Inter_400Regular, Inter_600SemiBold });
  if (!loaded) return null;

  return (
    <SafeAreaProvider>
      <Themed>
        <HomeScreen />
      </Themed>
    </SafeAreaProvider>
  );
}
```

# Configuration (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/config

> Set the theme, colours, borders, scaling, fonts and safe areas of a native app with ThemeProvider, and read the resolved tokens with useTheme.

A native app is configured through one provider, `ThemeProvider`. It takes the style options of the web `ThemeProvider`, with the same names and the same defaults, and resolves them against the same design tokens. A native screen and a web page with the same options get the same colours, spacing, radii and type. For the web setup, see the [web configuration](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/config) and the web [ThemeProvider](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/contexts/themeProvider).

## ThemeProvider

Wrap the app once, at the root:

Providers.tsx:

```tsx
import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { ThemeProvider } from "@once-ui-system/native";
import { SafeAreaProvider, useSafeAreaInsets } from "react-native-safe-area-context";

function Themed({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <ThemeProvider
      theme="system"
      brand="blue"
      accent="indigo"
      neutral="gray"
      solid="contrast"
      solidStyle="flat"
      border="playful"
      surface="filled"
      scaling="100"
      insets={useSafeAreaInsets()}
    >
      {children}
    </ThemeProvider>
  );
}

export function Providers({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <SafeAreaProvider>
      <Themed>{children}</Themed>
    </SafeAreaProvider>
  );
}
```

Custom brand:

```tsx
import { ThemeProvider } from "@once-ui-system/native";

// The same steps as the web app's custom.css.
const copper = {
  100: "#140b06", 200: "#26150c", 300: "#4a2816", 400: "#6b3a1f",
  500: "#8f4f2a", 600: "#b87333", 700: "#cf8c4f", 800: "#e0a874",
  900: "#ebc29d", 1000: "#f4dbc3", 1100: "#f9ece0", 1200: "#fdf7f1",
};

export function App({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return <ThemeProvider brandScale={copper}>{children}</ThemeProvider>;
}

// Or generate the scale from one colour, as core's brandSeed.
export function Seeded({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return <ThemeProvider brandSeed="#b87333">{children}</ThemeProvider>;
}
```

```tsx
type Mode = "system" | "light" | "dark";

export default function App() {

  return (
    <ThemeProvider theme={mode}>

          value={mode}

            { value: "system", label: "System" },
            { value: "light", label: "Light" },
            { value: "dark", label: "Dark" },
          ]}

      </Column>
    </ThemeProvider>
  );
}
```

Stamp.tsx:

```tsx
import { Text, View } from "react-native";
import { useTheme } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Stamp({ count }: { count: number }) {
  const theme = useTheme();

  return (
    <View
      style={{
        padding: theme.space("12"),
        borderRadius: theme.radius("full"),
        backgroundColor: theme.color("brand-solid-strong"),
        ...theme.shadow("m"),
      }}
    >
      <Text style={[theme.text("label-strong-m"), { color: theme.onSolid("brand-strong") }]}>
        {count}
      </Text>
    </View>
  );
}
```

theme.ts:

```tsx
import { createTheme, defaultSettings } from "@once-ui-system/native";

const theme = createTheme({ ...defaultSettings, brand: "orange", theme: "light" }, 390);

export const brandColor = theme.color("brand-solid-strong");
export const cardRadius = theme.radius("l");
```

```tsx
  interface IconLibraryOverrides {
    coffee: true;

  return <Ionicons name="cafe-outline" size={size} color={color} />;
```

# Responsive (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/basics/responsive

> Change layout by screen width with the xl, l, m, s and xs props, show views by theme with dark and light, and keep clear of the notch with safeArea.

`Flex`, `Row`, `Column` and `Card` take the same breakpoint props as on the web: `xl`, `l`, `m`, `s` and `xs`. Each one is an object of props that applies on screens up to its width. For the web version, see [Breakpoints](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/basics/responsive).

## Breakpoint values

| Breakpoint | Applies at | Typical device |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `xs` | 480 points and narrower | Phones in portrait |
| `s` | 768 points and narrower | Small tablets in portrait |
| `m` | 1024 points and narrower | Phones in landscape, tablets in portrait |
| `l` | 1440 points and narrower | Tablets in landscape |
| `xl` | Every width | The base, under the others |

The width is the window's, in points, read by `ThemeProvider` with `useWindowDimensions`. It updates when the device rotates, and when an iPad app runs in Split View or Slide Over. `useTheme().width` and `useTheme().breakpoints` give the same values to your own components.

## Cascade order

The objects apply from the largest to the smallest: the base props, then `xl`, `l`, `m`, `s` and `xs`. Each one the width falls within is merged over the ones before it, so a smaller breakpoint wins. This is the order the media queries apply in the browser.

Panel.tsx:

```tsx
import { Column, Text } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Panel() {
  return (
    <Column
      padding="32"
      gap="16"
      background="surface"
      radius="l"
      m={{ padding: "24" }}
      s={{ padding: "16", gap: "8" }}
    >
      <Text>Padding is 32 on wide screens, 24 on tablets and 16 on phones.</Text>
    </Column>
  );
}
```

Plans.tsx:

```tsx
import { Card, Heading, Row, Text } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Plans() {
  return (
    <Row fillWidth gap="16" s={{ direction: "column" }}>
      <Card flex={1} padding="20" gap="8" s={{ flex: 0 }}>
        <Heading textVariant="heading-strong-m">Free</Heading>
        <Text onBackground="neutral-weak">One loyalty card.</Text>
      </Card>
      <Card flex={1} padding="20" gap="8" s={{ flex: 0 }}>
        <Heading textVariant="heading-strong-m">Pro</Heading>
        <Text onBackground="neutral-weak">Cards for every location.</Text>
      </Card>
    </Row>
  );
}
```

Header.tsx:

```tsx
import { Column, Row, Text } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Header() {
  return (
    <Column gap="8">
      <Row s={{ hide: true }}>
        <Text>Shown on tablets, hidden on phones</Text>
      </Row>
      <Row hide s={{ hide: false }}>
        <Text>Shown on phones only</Text>
      </Row>
    </Column>
  );
}
```

Logo.tsx:

```tsx

    <Column>
      <Column dark>

```

App.tsx:

```tsx
import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { Column, Heading, Text, ThemeProvider } from "@once-ui-system/native";
import { SafeAreaProvider, useSafeAreaInsets } from "react-native-safe-area-context";

function Themed({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return <ThemeProvider insets={useSafeAreaInsets()}>{children}</ThemeProvider>;
}

export default function App() {
  return (
    <SafeAreaProvider>
      <Themed>
        <Column fill background="page" padding="20" gap="8" safeArea={["top", "bottom"]}>
          <Heading>Morning Coffee</Heading>
          <Text onBackground="neutral-weak">The padding grows by the notch and the home indicator.</Text>
        </Column>
      </Themed>
    </SafeAreaProvider>
  );
}
```

# Input (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/input

> A bordered text field with a floating label, error and description lines, for React Native.

`Input` is a bordered text field built on React Native's `TextInput`. Its label sits where the value goes and floats above it once the field is focused or filled. It takes every `TextInput` prop as well, such as `keyboardType`, `autoComplete` and `secureTextEntry`. See the [web Input](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/input) for the same component in the browser.

## Controlled

Read the text with `onChangeText`, which gets the new string. `onChange` is React Native's event, not the web's.

EmailField.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { Input } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function EmailField() {
  const [email, setEmail] = useState("");
  return (
    <Input
      label="Email"
      value={email}
      onChangeText={setEmail}
      keyboardType="email-address"
      autoCapitalize="none"
      autoComplete="email"
    />
  );
}
```

NameField.tsx:

```tsx
import { Input } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function NameField() {
  return <Input label="Display name" defaultValue="Lorant" />;
}
```

PasswordField.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { Input } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function PasswordField() {
  const [password, setPassword] = useState("");
  const tooShort = password.length > 0 && password.length < 8;
  return (
    <Input
      label="Password"
      value={password}
      onChangeText={setPassword}
      secureTextEntry
      error={tooShort}
      errorMessage="Use at least 8 characters."
      description="Letters, numbers and symbols all count."
    />
  );
}
```

Fields.tsx:

```tsx
import { Column, Icon, Input } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Fields() {
  return (
    <Column gap="16">
      <Input label="Search" prefix={<Icon name="search" size="s" onBackground="neutral-weak" />} />
      <Input label="Username" loading />
      <Input label="Bio" maxLength={80} characterCount />
      <Input placeholder="Quick note" variant="ghost" size="s" />
    </Column>
  );
}
```

# Textarea (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/textarea

> An Input that takes several lines of text, for React Native.

`Textarea` is an [Input](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/input) that takes several lines. It takes every Input prop, with `multiline` set and the text aligned to the top. By default it grows with its text; a number in `lines` fixes its height to that many lines, and the text scrolls past them, as on the web. See the [web Textarea](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/textarea) for the same component in the browser.

## Controlled

Feedback.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { Textarea } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Feedback() {
  const [text, setText] = useState("");
  return (
    <Textarea
      label="What could be better?"
      value={text}
      onChangeText={setText}
      lines={5}
      description="We read every message."
    />
  );
}
```

Notes.tsx:

```tsx
import { Textarea } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Notes() {
  return <Textarea label="Notes" defaultValue="Leave at the door." />;
}
```

Review.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { Textarea } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Review() {
  const [review, setReview] = useState("");
  return (
    <Textarea
      label="Review"
      value={review}
      onChangeText={setReview}
      maxLength={280}
      characterCount
      error={review.length > 0 && review.length < 20}
      errorMessage="Write at least 20 characters."
    />
  );
}
```

# Select (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/select

> An Input-styled field that opens its options in a bottom sheet, with search and multiple selection, for React Native.

`Select` looks like an [Input](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/input) and opens its options in a bottom sheet, a [Dialog](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/components/dialog) titled with the field's label. Each option is drawn with [Option](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/components/option). The field shows the chosen option's label. See the [web Select](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/select) for the same component in the browser.

## Basic usage

`Select` is controlled: keep the value in state and set it in `onValueChange`. Picking an option closes the sheet.

CountrySelect.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { Select } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function CountrySelect() {
  const [country, setCountry] = useState("");
  return (
    <Select
      label="Country"
      placeholder="Choose a country"
      value={country}
      onValueChange={(value) => setCountry(value as string)}
      options={[
        { value: "de", label: "Germany" },
        { value: "hu", label: "Hungary" },
        { value: "jp", label: "Japan", description: "Ships in 2 weeks" },
      ]}
    />
  );
}
```

CitySelect.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { Select } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function CitySelect() {
  const [city, setCity] = useState("");
  return (
    <Select
      label="City"
      searchable
      labels={{ search: "Find a city" }}
      emptyState="No city by that name"
      value={city}
      onValueChange={(value) => setCity(value as string)}
      options={[
        { value: "berlin", label: "Berlin" },
        { value: "budapest", label: "Budapest" },
        { value: "tokyo", label: "Tokyo" },
      ]}
    />
  );
}
```

ToppingsSelect.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { Select } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function ToppingsSelect() {
  const [toppings, setToppings] = useState<string[]>([]);
  return (
    <Select
      label="Toppings"
      multiple
      value={toppings}
      onValueChange={(value) => setToppings(value as string[])}
      description="Pick as many as you like."
      options={[
        { value: "cheese", label: "Cheese" },
        { value: "olives", label: "Olives" },
        { value: "basil", label: "Basil" },
      ]}
    />
  );
}
```

# Checkbox (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/checkbox

> A box that is checked, unchecked or indeterminate, with a label and description, for React Native.

`Checkbox` is a 20pt box, filled with the brand colour and a check when checked, or a dash when indeterminate. A tap anywhere on the row, label included, toggles it. See the [web Checkbox](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/checkbox) for the same component in the browser.

## Controlled

Pass `checked` and update it in `onCheckedChange`, which gets the next state.

Terms.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { Checkbox } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Terms() {
  const [accepted, setAccepted] = useState(false);
  return (
    <Checkbox
      label="I accept the terms"
      description="You can read them in Settings."
      checked={accepted}
      onCheckedChange={setAccepted}
    />
  );
}
```

Newsletter.tsx:

```tsx
import { Checkbox } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Newsletter() {
  return <Checkbox label="Send me the newsletter" defaultChecked />;
}
```

SelectAll.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { Checkbox, Column } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function SelectAll() {
  const [items, setItems] = useState([true, false]);
  const all = items.every(Boolean);
  const some = items.some(Boolean);
  return (
    <Column gap="12">
      <Checkbox
        label="All items"
        checked={all}
        indeterminate={some && !all}
        onCheckedChange={() => setItems(items.map(() => !all))}
      />
      {items.map((on, i) => (
        <Checkbox
          key={i}
          label={"Item " + (i + 1)}
          checked={on}
          onCheckedChange={(next) => setItems(items.map((v, j) => (j === i ? next : v)))}
        />
      ))}
    </Column>
  );
}
```

Locked.tsx:

```tsx
import { Checkbox } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Locked() {
  return <Checkbox label="Required for your plan" checked disabled />;
}
```

# Switch (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/switch

> A toggle with a sliding knob, a label and an optional loading state, for React Native.

`Switch` is a 40 by 24 track with a knob that slides to the end when on. A tap anywhere on the row, label included, toggles it. See the [web Switch](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/switch) for the same component in the browser.

## Controlled

Pass `checked` and update it in `onCheckedChange`, which gets the next state.

Notifications.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { Switch } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Notifications() {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(true);
  return (
    <Switch
      label="Notifications"
      description="Order updates and offers"
      checked={on}
      onCheckedChange={setOn}
    />
  );
}
```

DarkMode.tsx:

```tsx
import { Switch } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function DarkMode() {
  return <Switch label="Dark mode" defaultChecked={false} />;
}
```

Sync.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { Switch } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Sync() {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(false);
  const [saving, setSaving] = useState(false);
  return (
    <Switch
      label="Sync contacts"
      reverse
      checked={on}
      loading={saving}
      onCheckedChange={(next) => {
        setSaving(true);
        setTimeout(() => {
          setOn(next);
          setSaving(false);
        }, 800);
      }}
    />
  );
}
```

# RadioButton (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/radioButton

> A circle that turns on to pick one option, with a label and description, for React Native.

`RadioButton` is a 20pt circle, filled with the brand colour and a dot when checked. A tap only turns it on: turning the others off is up to the group. Inside a [RadioGroup](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/radioGroup), a button with a `value` is checked by the group, as on the web. See the [web RadioButton](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/radioButton) for the same component in the browser.

## Controlled

Keep the chosen value in state and check the button that matches it.

Delivery.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";

    <Column gap="16">
      <RadioButton
        label="Standard"
        description="3 to 5 days"
        checked={method === "standard"}
        onCheckedChange={() => setMethod("standard")}
      />
      <RadioButton
        label="Express"
        description="Next day"
        checked={method === "express"}
        onCheckedChange={() => setMethod("express")}
      />
    </Column>
  );
}
```

Options.tsx:

```tsx
import { Column, RadioButton } from "@once-ui-system/native";

  return (
    <Column gap="16">

    </Column>
  );
}
```

```tsx
      ]}
    />
  );
}
```

# Chip (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/chip

> Chip is Tag in Once UI 3.0, on React Native as on the web: a Tag with selected, onClick or onRemove.

`Chip` folded into [Tag](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/components/tag) in Once UI 3.0, as it did on the [web](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/chip), and `@once-ui-system/native` no longer exports it. A Tag given `selected`, `onClick` (or `onPress`) or `onRemove` is the same toggle, with a remove button when it has `onRemove`. `selected` now defaults to false.

Filters.tsx:

```tsx
import { Row, Tag } from "@once-ui-system/native";
import { useState } from "react";

export function Filters() {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(true);
  return (
    <Row gap="8">
      <Tag label="Design" selected={on} onPress={() => setOn(!on)} />
      <Tag label="Removable" onRemove={() => {}} />
    </Row>
  );
}
```

# Slider (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/slider

> A thumb on a track for picking a number in a range, dragged with a finger, for React Native.

`Slider` picks one number between `min` and `max`. Drag anywhere on the track and the thumb follows your finger, landing on a multiple of `step`. Screen readers announce it as an adjustable control and change it by `step` with a swipe up or down. For a range with two thumbs, use [RangeSlider](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/rangeSlider). See the [web Slider](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/slider) for the browser version.

## Basic usage

Without `value` the slider keeps its own state, starting at `defaultValue` (or `min`). `showValue` prints the value beside the label.

Volume.tsx:

```tsx
import { Slider } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Volume() {
  return <Slider label="Volume" defaultValue={40} showValue />;
}
```

Strength.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { Slider } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Strength() {
  const [shots, setShots] = useState(2);
  return (
    <Slider
      label="Espresso shots"
      min={1}
      max={4}
      value={shots}
      onValueChange={setShots}
      showValue
    />
  );
}
```

Steps:

```tsx
import { Slider } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Grind() {
  return <Slider aria-label="Grind size" min={0} max={2} step={0.25} defaultValue={1} />;
}
```

# RangeSlider (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/rangeSlider

> Two thumbs on one track for picking a start and an end, such as a price filter, for React Native.

`RangeSlider` selects a `[start, end]` range. A press on the track brings the nearer thumb to your finger and drags it. The two thumbs never cross, and `minDistance` keeps them apart. Each thumb is its own adjustable element for screen readers, bounded by the other one. See the [web RangeSlider](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/rangeSlider) for the browser version.

## Basic usage

Without `value` the range starts at `defaultValue`, or the whole track.

PriceFilter.tsx:

```tsx
import { RangeSlider } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function PriceFilter() {
  return (
    <RangeSlider
      label="Price"
      min={0}
      max={50}
      defaultValue={[5, 20]}
      showValue
      formatValue={(v) => "€" + v}
    />
  );
}
```

Hours.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { RangeSlider } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Hours() {
  const [hours, setHours] = useState<[number, number]>([8, 17]);
  return (
    <RangeSlider
      label="Opening hours"
      min={0}
      max={24}
      minDistance={2}
      value={hours}
      onValueChange={setHours}
      showValue
      formatValue={(h) => h + ":00"}
      thumbLabels={["Opens", "Closes"]}
    />
  );
}
```

# NumberInput (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/numberInput

> An Input for a number, with minus and plus buttons that step it within a range, for React Native.

`NumberInput` is an [Input](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/input) for a number. The − and + buttons step the value by `step` and stop at `min` and `max`. Typing works too, and `onValueChange` gets a number whenever the text reads as one. The keyboard is a number pad, with a minus key when `min` allows negative numbers. See the [web NumberInput](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/numberInput) for the browser version.

## Basic usage

Without `value` the field keeps its own text, starting from `defaultValue`.

Guests.tsx:

```tsx
import { NumberInput } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Guests() {
  return <NumberInput label="Guests" defaultValue={2} min={1} max={8} />;
}
```

Quantity.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { NumberInput } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Quantity() {
  const [quantity, setQuantity] = useState(1);
  return (
    <NumberInput
      label="Quantity"
      value={quantity}
      onValueChange={setQuantity}
      min={0}
      description="Up to 12 per order."
      max={12}
    />
  );
}
```

Decimals:

```tsx
import { NumberInput } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Settings() {
  return (
    <>
      <NumberInput label="Ratio" defaultValue={1.5} step={0.1} min={0} />
      <NumberInput label="Minute" defaultValue={5} padStart={2} min={0} max={59} />
    </>
  );
}
```

# PasswordInput (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/passwordInput

> An Input that hides what is typed, with an eye button to show it, for React Native.

`PasswordInput` is an [Input](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/input) with `secureTextEntry` on. The eye button after the value shows and hides the password. It also turns off autocorrect and capitals, and offers saved passwords from the platform's password manager. See the [web PasswordInput](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/passwordInput) for the browser version.

## Basic usage

It takes the same props as `Input`, apart from `suffix`.

SignIn.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { PasswordInput } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function SignIn() {
  const [password, setPassword] = useState("");
  return <PasswordInput label="Password" value={password} onChangeText={setPassword} />;
}
```

SignUp.tsx:

```tsx
import { PasswordInput } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function SignUp() {
  return (
    <PasswordInput
      label="New password"
      textContentType="newPassword"
      autoComplete="new-password"
      description="At least 12 characters."
    />
  );
}
```

# SearchInput (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/searchInput

> A search field with a search icon, a clear button and the keyboard's Search key, for React Native.

`SearchInput` is an [Input](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/input) for searching a list or a catalog. It shows a search icon before the value and a clear button once there is text, and the keyboard's return key reads Search. It has no floating label: the placeholder names it, and screen readers read it as a search field.

## Basic usage

Filter as people type with `onChangeText`, or run the search when they press the keyboard's Search key with `onSubmitEditing`.

Venues.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { SearchInput } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Venues() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  return (
    <SearchInput
      placeholder="Search venues"
      value={query}
      onChangeText={setQuery}
      onSubmitEditing={() => search(query)}
    />
  );
}
```

# OTPInput (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/otpInput

> One field per digit of a one-time code, with SMS autofill, for React Native.

`OTPInput` draws one field per digit of a one-time code. Each digit moves focus to the next field, and backspace in an empty field goes back to the one before. A code pasted into a field, or filled in from a text message, spreads across the fields from that one. `onComplete` gets the code once every field has a digit. See the [web OTPInput](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/otpInput) for the browser version.

## Basic usage

Verify.tsx:

```tsx
import { OTPInput } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Verify({ onCode }: { onCode: (code: string) => void }) {
  return <OTPInput length={6} autoFocus onComplete={onCode} />;
}
```

Error:

```tsx
import { OTPInput } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function WrongCode() {
  return <OTPInput length={6} error errorMessage="That code has expired. We sent a new one." />;
}
```

# Form (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/form

> Spacing, columns, grouping and submit state for a set of fields, for React Native.

`Form` takes the same props as on the web (`density`, `columns`, `size`, `as`, `onSubmit`, `pending`). It lays its fields out in rows and columns, gives them all one size, and tells a [`SubmitButton`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/submitButton) when a submit is running. With `density="stacked"` the fields fuse onto shared borders and only the group's outer corners stay round. See the [web Form](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/form) for the same component in the browser.

## Submitting

React Native has no form element, so the `SubmitButton` inside a `Form` with `onSubmit` calls it; `as="form"` is accepted and changes nothing more. Return a promise and the form stays pending until it settles: the button shows its spinner, swaps to `pendingLabel` and ignores taps, so a double tap sends one request.

SignIn.tsx:

```tsx
import { Form, Input, SubmitButton } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function SignIn() {
  return (
    <Form as="form" onSubmit={() => fetch("/api/sign-in", { method: "POST" })}>
      <Input label="Email" autoComplete="email" />
      <Input label="Password" secureTextEntry />
      <SubmitButton label="Sign in" pendingLabel="Signing in…" fillWidth />
    </Form>
  );
}
```

Contact.tsx:

```tsx
<Form density="stacked">
  <Input label="Name" />
  <Input label="Phone" />
  <Input label="Email" />
</Form>
```

Visit.tsx:

```tsx
<Form columns={2}>
  <Input label="Party" />
  <Input label="Time" />
  <Field span={2}>
    <Textarea label="Notes" />
  </Field>
</Form>
```

# Field (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/field

> A label, a hint and an error around one control, wired together, for React Native.

`Field` takes the same props as on the web (`label`, `hint`, `error`, `required`, `span`). It puts a label above one control and the error and hint under it, and hands the control what a screen reader needs: the label as its name, the error and hint as its hint, `aria-required`, and `error` so the control draws itself invalid. See the [web Field](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/field) for the same component in the browser.

Email.tsx:

```tsx
import { Field, Input } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Email({ error }: { error?: string }) {
  return (
    <Field label="Email" hint="We send the receipt here." error={error} required>
      <Input autoComplete="email" keyboardType="email-address" />
    </Field>
  );
}
```

Rating.tsx:

```tsx
<Field label="Rating" error={error}>
  {(control) => <MyStars {...control} />}
</Field>
```

# Fieldset (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/fieldset

> A titled section of a form, laid out like a Form, that can disable its fields at once, for React Native.

`Fieldset` takes the same props as on the web (`legend`, `description`, `disabled`, plus `Form`'s `density`, `columns` and `size`). The legend is a heading a screen reader can jump to, the fields inside are laid out by a [`Form`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/form), and `disabled` disables every field inside. See the [web Fieldset](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/fieldset) for the same component in the browser.

Checkout.tsx:

```tsx
import { Fieldset, Form, Input, SubmitButton } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Checkout({ paid }: { paid: boolean }) {
  return (
    <Form as="form" density="spacious" onSubmit={pay}>
      <Fieldset legend="Delivery" density="stacked">
        <Input label="Street" />
        <Input label="City" />
      </Fieldset>
      <Fieldset legend="Payment" description="Charged when the order ships." disabled={paid}>
        <Input label="Card number" keyboardType="number-pad" />
      </Fieldset>
      <SubmitButton label="Pay" fillWidth />
    </Form>
  );
}
```

# SubmitButton (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/submitButton

> A Button that submits its Form and shows a spinner while the submit runs, for React Native.

`SubmitButton` takes every [`Button`](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/components/button) prop plus `pendingLabel` and `pending`, as on the web. Inside a `Form` with `as="form"` it calls the form's `onSubmit`; while the returned promise runs it shows a spinner, swaps to `pendingLabel` and ignores taps. See the [web SubmitButton](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/submitButton) for the same component in the browser.

Profile.tsx:

```tsx
<Form as="form" onSubmit={save}>
  <Input label="Display name" />
  <SubmitButton label="Save" pendingLabel="Saving…" />
</Form>
```

# FormErrorSummary (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/formErrorSummary

> Every error in a form in one alert after a failed submit, for React Native.

`FormErrorSummary` takes the same props as on the web (`errors`, `title`, `autoFocus`). It renders nothing while there are no errors, so it can sit at the top of a form permanently; after a failed submit it lists every error in a danger alert and moves the screen reader to it. `errors` is a list of `{ id, message }` or a map from field to message, the shape most validation libraries return. See the [web FormErrorSummary](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/formErrorSummary) for the same component in the browser.

Signup.tsx:

```tsx
const [errors, setErrors] = useState<Record<string, string>>({});

<Form as="form" onSubmit={async () => setErrors(await validate())}>
  <FormErrorSummary errors={errors} />
  <Field label="Email" error={errors.email}>
    <Input />
  </Field>
  <SubmitButton label="Continue" />
</Form>
```

# DatePicker (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/form-controls/datePicker

> A month of days to pick a date from, with ranges and localized names, for React Native.

`DatePicker` takes the same main props as on the web (`value`, `defaultDate`, `onValueChange`, `minDate`, `maxDate`, `size`, `range`, `locale`, `labels`). It shows a month of days between previous and next buttons, marks today, and keeps days outside `minDate`…`maxDate` from being picked. With `locale`, the month and weekday names and the week's first day follow that locale, as on the web. See the [web DatePicker](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/form-controls/datePicker) for the same component in the browser.

## Basic usage

Day.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { Card, DatePicker } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Day() {
  const [date, setDate] = useState(new Date());
  return (
    <Card padding="16">
      <DatePicker value={date} onValueChange={setDate} minDate={new Date()} fillWidth />
    </Card>
  );
}
```

Stay.tsx:

```tsx
<DatePicker
  locale="hu"
  range={{ startDate: new Date(2026, 9, 12), endDate: new Date(2026, 9, 16) }}
/>
```

# DateInput (React Native)

`DateInput` takes the same main props as on the web (`label`, `value`, `defaultValue`, `onValueChange`, `minDate`, `maxDate`, `locale`). # Flex (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/components/flex

> The layout view the other native components are built on, with Row and Column presets and the same spacing, size and surface props as the web.

`Flex` renders a React Native `View` and takes Once UI's layout, spacing, size and surface props, so a screen is built by nesting it instead of writing style objects. `Row` and `Column` are `Flex` with `direction` preset. `Flex` is a row by default, as on the web, even though a plain `View` is a column. See the [web Flex page](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/flex) for the full reference.

## Direction and alignment

`horizontal` and `vertical` name the axis you see, so they mean the same thing in a row and in a column. `center` centers on both.

Alignment.tsx:

```tsx
import { Column, Flex, Row, Text } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Alignment() {
  return (
    <Column gap="16" fillWidth>
      <Row gap="8" horizontal="between" vertical="center">
        <Text>Left</Text>
        <Text>Right</Text>
      </Row>
      <Flex center height="64" radius="m" border="neutral-alpha-medium">
        <Text>Centered</Text>
      </Flex>
    </Column>
  );
}
```

Spacing.tsx:

```tsx
import { Column, Row, Text } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Spacing() {
  return (
    <Column padding="20" gap="12" fillWidth>
      <Row paddingX="16" paddingY="8" fit background="neutral-alpha-weak" radius="full">
        <Text>Fits its content</Text>
      </Row>
      <Row width="12rem" height="40" background="brand-alpha-weak" radius="m" />
      <Row width="50%" height="40" background="accent-alpha-weak" radius="m" />
    </Column>
  );
}
```

Surface.tsx:

```tsx
import { Column, Heading, Text } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Surface() {
  return (
    <Column
      padding="20"
      gap="8"
      background="surface"
      border="neutral-alpha-medium"
      radius="l"
      shadow="m"
    >
      <Heading textVariant="heading-strong-s">Order shipped</Heading>
      <Text onBackground="neutral-weak">Arrives on Thursday.</Text>
    </Column>
  );
}
```

Screen.tsx:

```tsx
import { Column, Flex, Text } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Screen() {
  return (
    <Column fill background="page" padding="20" safeArea>
      <Flex gap="16" direction="row" s={{ direction: "column", gap: "8" }}>
        <Text>First</Text>
        <Text>Second</Text>
      </Flex>
    </Column>
  );
}
```

# Button (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/components/button

> A pressable button for React Native with the web's ten variants, five sizes, icons and a loading state.

`Button` renders a React Native `Pressable` with a label, optional icons and the same variants and sizes as the web. Handle taps with `onPress`. See the [web Button page](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/button) for how each variant is meant to be used.

## Variants

`primary` is the default. `secondary`, `tertiary`, `subtle`, `ghost` and `link` are quieter. `tone` sets the colour, as in core 3.0: `tone="danger"`, `"success"` or `"warning"` on a `primary` button is solid in that colour.

Variants.tsx:

```tsx
import { Button, Column } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Variants() {
  return (
    <Column gap="8">
      <Button label="Primary" onPress={() => {}} />
      <Button variant="secondary" label="Secondary" onPress={() => {}} />
      <Button variant="tertiary" label="Tertiary" onPress={() => {}} />
      <Button tone="danger" label="Delete account" onPress={() => {}} />
      <Button variant="link" label="Learn more" onPress={() => {}} />
    </Column>
  );
}
```

Sizes.tsx:

```tsx
import { Button, Column } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Sizes() {
  return (
    <Column gap="8" fillWidth>
      <Button size="s" label="Small" onPress={() => {}} />
      <Button size="l" label="Large" onPress={() => {}} />
      <Button size="l" fillWidth label="Continue" onPress={() => {}} />
      <Button
        variant="secondary"
        fillWidth
        horizontal="between"
        label="Payment method"
        suffixIcon="chevronRight"
        onPress={() => {}}
      />
    </Column>
  );
}
```

Long.tsx:

```tsx
import { Button } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Long() {
  return <Button wrap fillWidth label="Book a table for the whole party tonight" onPress={() => {}} />;
}
```

WithIcons.tsx:

```tsx
import { Button, Row } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function WithIcons() {
  return (
    <Row gap="8">
      <Button prefixIcon="plus" label="Add stamp" onPress={() => {}} />
      <Button variant="secondary" suffixIcon="arrowRight" label="Next" onPress={() => {}} />
    </Row>
  );
}
```

Save.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { Button, Row } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Save() {
  const [saving, setSaving] = useState(false);
  return (
    <Row gap="8">
      <Button label="Save" loading={saving} onPress={() => setSaving(true)} />
      <Button label="Unavailable" disabled />
      <Button label="Rounded" rounded variant="secondary" onPress={() => {}} />
    </Row>
  );
}
```

# Card (React Native)

Source: https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/components/card

> A bordered surface for grouping content on React Native screens, pressable when you give it a handler.

`Card` is a [Column](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/native/components/flex) with a `surface` background, a `neutral-medium` border and an `l` radius. Give it `onPress` and it becomes a button that dims slightly while pressed. It takes every Flex prop, so padding, gap, size and the defaults themselves can all be changed. See the [web Card page](https://next.docs.once-ui.com/components/card).

## Basic card

Summary.tsx:

```tsx
import { Card, Heading, Text } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Summary() {
  return (
    <Card padding="20" gap="8" fillWidth>
      <Heading textVariant="heading-strong-s">Morning Coffee</Heading>
      <Text onBackground="neutral-weak">7 of 10 stamps collected.</Text>
    </Card>
  );
}
```

Shortcut.tsx:

```tsx
import { Card, Icon, Row, Text } from "@once-ui-system/native";

export function Shortcut() {
  return (
    <Card direction="row" vertical="center" gap="12" padding="16" fillWidth onPress={() => {}}>
      <Icon name="gift" onBackground="brand-medium" />
      <Text>Redeem a reward</Text>
      <Row flex={1} />
      <Icon name="chevronRight" size="s" onBackground="neutral-weak" />
    </Card>
  );
}
```

Plans.tsx:

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { Card, Column, Text } from "@once-ui-system/native";

const plans = ["Monthly", "Yearly"];

export function Plans() {
  const [plan, setPlan] = useState("Monthly");
  return (
    <Column gap="8" fillWidth>
      {plans.map((name) => (
        <Card key={name} padding="16" selected={plan === name} onPress={() => setPlan(name)}>
          <Text textVariant="label-strong-m">{name}</Text>
        </Card>
      ))}
    </Column>
  );
}
```
